*Tena kho pana samayena* means at the time when they held the Second Council. *Taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ na sampāpuṇiṃsu* means they did not arrive in time to settle that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) raised by the Vajjiputtaka monks. *No ahuvattha* is a connection (*sambandha*). *Yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā parinibbutā* should be connected as 'having remained for the full span of life, they attained Parinibbāna'. When asked, "What did the elders do before attaining Parinibbāna?", it is said, "Having held the Second Council," and so on. *Aniccatāvasanti* means falling under the power of impermanence. *Jamminti* means low or vile. *Durabhisambhavaṃ* should be connected as 'having thus known impermanence which is insurmountable and cannot be overcome'.

## The method of the explanation of the Second Council is finished.

## Explanation of the Third Council

*Satta vassāni* is the accusative case showing a long duration of time. *Aticchathā* means 'desire beyond'; it means 'go to another house from this one and seek alms'. *Bhattavissaggakaraṇatthāya* means for the purpose of the business of consuming food, for the sake of eating. Because there is the indication (*uddesa*) of 'sixteen years', he is called *soḷasavassuddesiko*, meaning sixteen years of age.

In the words beginning with *tīsu vedesu*, it means in the three Vedas called the *Iruveda*, *Yajuveda*, and *Sāmaveda*. The righteous sages (*isīs*) such as Aṭṭhaka created only the three Vedas for the purpose of showing the path to heaven to the people of the world. Therefore, those sages taught those Vedas. The *Āthabbaṇaveda*, however, was created later by unrighteous brahmins for the purpose of killing living beings and so forth. It should be known that even in the original three Vedas, those same unrighteous brahmins removed the righteous branches and inserted unrighteous branches that show sacrifice, killing, and so forth. *Nighaṇḍū* is a text (dictionary) that shows synonyms of trees and so forth, in accordance with synonymous names. That text in the world...
27: "Nighaṇḍu" is so called. "Keṭubha" is so called because it makes known the analysis of actions and so forth; it is a treatise on poetic embellishment (alankāra) that serves as an aid to poets, involving various methods of planning verbal actions. Here, "kiriyākappavikappo" means that by which verbal actions characterized by speech and so forth are specifically planned; thus it is called "kiriyākappa." This treatise, which is the cause for planning such actions, has many variations due to the analysis of letters (vaṇṇa), words (pada), and the meaning of stanzas (gāthā-pada); hence it is called "kiriyākappavikappo." This statement is made with reference to the original Kiriyākappa treatise. "Sanighaṇḍukeṭubha" refers to the three Vedas together with the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha treatises. "Akkharapabheda" means the analysis of letters through the analysis of the places of articulation (ṭhāna), instruments (karaṇa), and etymology (nirutti); it refers to the Sikkhā and Nirutti treatises. "Sākkharapabheda" refers to those Vedas together with the Sikkhā and Nirutti treatises which analyze the letters. Making the Atharva Veda the fourth, the Itihāsa (history), described as ancient stories connected with the words "Thus it has been, thus it has been," is the fifth; thus they are called "Itihāsapañcama" (the three Vedas with history as the fifth). The two questions beginning with "Yassa cittaṃ" are taught with reference to the moment of arising (uppāda-kkhaṇa) of the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) of Arahants. Among those two questions, in the first question, "uppajjati" (arises) means it is arising because it is endowed with the moment of arising. "Na nirujjhati" (does not cease) means it is not ceasing because it has not yet reached the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-kkhaṇa). "Tassa cittaṃ" (his mind) is the question: "Will that person's mind cease, and will it not arise in the future?" Since this question should be answered by analytical explanation (vibhajja-byākaraṇīya), the answer should be understood thus: At the moment of arising of the final consciousness (parinibbāna-citta) of an Arahant, the mind is arising for that person but is not ceasing; it will certainly cease upon reaching the moment of dissolution, and thereafter, because there is no more rebirth, another mind will not arise. Setting aside the Arahant endowed with the final consciousness, for other persons, the mind endowed with the moment of arising is "arising" because it is at the moment of arising, and "not ceasing" because it has not yet reached the moment of dissolution; however, it will certainly cease upon reaching the moment of dissolution, and another mind will arise and cease either in that same existence or in another existence. In the second question beginning with "Yassa vā pana," "nirujjhisati nuppajjhisati" (will cease and will not arise) refers to an Arahant whose mind, being at the moment of arising, will cease upon reaching the moment of dissolution and will not arise because there is no more rebirth; the question is: "Is that mind of that Arahant arising and not ceasing?" Since this problem should be answered categorically (ekaṃsa-byākaraṇīya), the answer should be understood as "Āmantā" (Yes). "Uddhaṃ vā adho vā harituṃ အသက္ကောန္တော" means being unable to bring the lower term to the upper term or the upper term to the lower term in terms of meaning, or unable to connect them, or unable to determine the meaning by coordinating the preceding and following parts.
28: Because Stream-enterers (Sotāpannas) are fulfillers of the precepts, there is no falling away from the precepts they have undertaken; with this intended meaning, it is said: "Now he is incapable of turning back from the Dispensation." "Vaḍḍhetvā" means having developed the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for the sake of the higher paths. Teeth are cleaned with this tooth-stick; therefore, it is called "dantapona," which is indeed the tooth-stick (dantakaṭṭha). It is proper to accept manual labor and provide support only after well-investigating for two or three days the modest nature of newly arrived guest monks and their endowment with virtues such as patience and loving-kindness. To inform the novice (sāmaṇera) and other monks who might follow the example, the Elder, although knowing the novice's suitability through direct knowledge (abhiññā), performed tasks such as sweeping again. Some also say, "for the sake of disciplining that novice's mind." "Buddhavacanaṃ paṭṭhapesi" means he endeavored to teach the Buddha's word. Since the entirety of the Vinaya practice is prescribed only for the ordained (upasampanna), and learning that Vinaya is also appropriate only for them, he said, "excluding the Vinaya Piṭaka." To show that the Buddha's word, already established in the Elder's mind, was handed over for the sake of preservation, it is said, "placing it in his hands." "Ekarajjābhiseka" refers to the consecration performed by virtue of sole sovereignty over the entire island of Jambudīpa. "Rājiddhi" refers to the powers and majesty that follow the king's influence. "Yato" means from the sixteen pots. It is connected as: "Only the deities bring them every day." "Devasikaṃ" means every day. "Agadamalaka" is the medicinal myrobalan (āmalaka) which is a medicine capable of purifying the body with even a small amount and removing all ailments. "Chaddantadahato" means they bring it from the celestial mansion near Lake Chaddanta or from a wish-fulfilling tree (kappa-rukkha); there are such special wish-fulfilling trees in that place, and they bring it from there. "Asuttamayika" refers to a jasmine cloth made only of celestial jasmine flowers, not woven with thread. "Uṭṭhitassa sālino" refers to self-grown rice; here, the singular form is used with reference to the collective, meaning "of the rice grains." In the phrase "nava vāhasahassāni," the measurements are: 4 handfuls (muṭṭhi) equal 1 kuḍuva, 4 kuḍuvas equal 1 pattha, 4 patthas equal 1 āḷhaka, 4 āḷhakas equal 1 doṇa, 4 doṇas equal 1 mānikā, 4 mānikās equal 1 khārī, and 20 khārīs equal 1 vāha. That 1 vāha is called "one cartload" (sakaṭa) in the Suttanipāta Commentary and other texts. "Nitthusakaṇe karonti" means they make it free from husk and broken rice. It is connected as: "Looking at the Buddha-image created by that King of Nāgas." The use of the term "puññappabhāvanibbatta" (produced by the power of merit) is because the marks created by the Nāga King were similar to the marks produced by the power of merit. In the term "vimalaketumālā," ketumālā is said to be the mass of rays emerging from the head and appearing as a cluster on the top of the crown.
29:
## 
'Bāhirakapāsaṇḍa' refers to the false doctrines taught by heretics outside the Dispensation. 'Pariggaṇhi' means he investigated and accepted. 'Bhaddapīṭhakesu' means on chairs (stools) made of cane. 'Sāro' is the essence of virtue. 'Sīhapañjare' means near the large window (lion's window). He is disciplined because his mind is free from the agitation caused by defilements. He is secure because of the constant presence of the guard of mindfulness. 'Khuraggeyeva' means at the conclusion of the hair-cutting. It should be connected as "he was exceedingly beautiful." 'Vāṇijako ahosi' means he was a honey merchant.

'Pubbe va sannivāsena' means due to having lived together in a past life. 'Paccuppannahitena vā' means due to performing beneficial deeds in the present life. In this way, through these two causes, that affection known as 'sineha' (love) arises. How? It is said, "Like a lotus in water." In the term 'uppalaṃ vā', the word 'vā' is a shortened form and has the sense of including other lotuses like the 'paduma' which are not explicitly mentioned. The word 'yathā' is used in the sense of a simile. The meaning is: Just as the 'uppala' lotus and other lotuses like the 'paduma' arise in water depending on two causes—water and mud—likewise, affection also arises.

'Dhuvabhattāni' means regular alms-food. 'Vajjāvajja' means minor and major faults. "Entrusting the responsibility to Elder Moggaliputtatissa" means that the Saṅgha gave this responsibility to the Elder to make the King aware of the Elder's great power and his leadership as the head of the Saṅgha in the affairs of the Sasana at that time; it was not because others were ignorant. "Heir to the Sasana" (sāsanassa dāyādo) means whether one is an internal relative of the Sasana or not. Those who give up their sons and daughters to be ordained in the Sasana are called blood relatives in the Buddha's Sasana. This is because they have given up their own biological children who are capable of upholding the entire Sasana, and are not merely givers of requisites. With this meaning in mind, the Elder said, "Great King, by this much alone, one is not yet an heir to the Sasana." In the term 'kathañcarahi', the particle 'carahi' indicates dissatisfaction (impatience). 'Tissakumārassa' refers to the King's younger brother born of the same mother. 'Sakkhasī' is a question: "Will you be able?" "They established him in the training" means that in the six training rules, starting from abstaining from taking life and ending with abstaining from eating at the wrong time, they established him in the training after giving the training-agreement (sikkhā-sammuti) by way of undertaking the vows, such as "I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life, not transgressing it for two years." Because six years had passed since the King's consecration, it is called 'chavassābhisēka'.
30:
Theravāda refers to all the Pali texts compiled in the two councils. It is called 'Theravāda' to distinguish it from the divergent views of the Mahāsaṅghikas and others. This Vibhajjavāda is called 'Theravāda' because it was preserved and brought down without confusion by the elders such as Mahākassapa Thera. It is also written as 'Satheravāda'. In the term 'Satheravāda', it should be understood as the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) included in the Tipiṭaka along with the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) and the Theravāda found in those commentaries. 'Entering the fire element' means entering the meditative absorption (jhāna) that takes the fire-kasina (tejo-kasiṇa) as its object.

'In the assembly' (sabhāyaṃ) means in the judgment hall in the center of the city. 'Wrong views' (diṭṭhigatāni) refers to the false views themselves. He thought, 'This matter cannot be settled while living among them,' because one living among them becomes part of their group and his words would not be accepted; therefore, he thought thus. 'Ahogaṅga Mountain' is a mountain of that name. It is also written as 'Adhogaṅgā Mountain', but that spelling is not good. 'Practicing austerities with five kinds of heat' means lighting fires in four directions and standing in the middle, looking up at the sun, thus practicing austerities with the heat of the sun. 'Following the sun' means looking at the sun from sunrise until sunset, turning to face the sun. They strove, saying, 'We will destroy it.'

'Vissaṭṭha' means free from the anxiety of death, fearless. 'Going out for hunting' (migavaṃ) means going out for the purpose of killing deer, a sport of wandering in the forest. The term 'Hatthināga' (noble elephant) is used to distinguish it from snakes (ahināga) and others. In the phrase 'even while he was looking', the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (anādara). In the phrase 'flying into the sky', this kind of flying is not the psychic power of transformation (vikubbaniddhi). He showed this psychic power of determination (adhiṭṭhānaniddhi) even to laypeople, because the power of determination is not prohibited. Only the changing of one's natural form to appear as a dragon (nāga) or similar is called the psychic power of transformation. 'Festive attire' refers to the dress for a festival. 'Padhānaghara' is a secluded dwelling suitable for the exertion of energy through the practice of meditation. 'He also' refers to the King's nephew.

'One with good intentions' means one with a pleasing disposition. 'Dveḷhakajāta' means having fallen into doubt. In the phrase 'accompanied by a thousand monks each', although it was said in the form of a command, 'Bring them here,' the elder monks went for the benefit of the Sasana. This is a proper (kappiya) message, not a worldly matter related to the affairs of laypeople. The elder did not come. Although it was said the King summoned him, and even if it were proper to come for a legal act of the Dhamma, he did not come, considering that being requested twice was inappropriate. The elder was of great power, a practitioner according to the instructions, and a reliable authority. He did not come using an inappropriate speech as a pretext, intending to ensure the success of future Sasana affairs by causing the King and both parties to have great respect and devotion toward him. A raft made by joining two boats together is called a boat-raft (nāvāsaṃghāṭa). Because the enemies of the Sasana were numerous, it was said, 'having arranged for protection.' 'Yaṃ' means 'because'. 'Abbaāhiṃsu' means 'they pulled out'. 'From outside' means from outside the park. It was said, 'shaking a portion of the earth is difficult,' intending to make it appear as an extremely difficult feat to the onlookers. In the act of determination (adhiṭṭhāna), however, shaking a portion of the earth is not particularly difficult.
31:
“The King summons,” even though it was said, it is proper to come for the sake of a legal act of the Dhamma. However, even though he was sent for twice, he did not come, saying, “The request is inappropriate.” He did not come using an inappropriate speech as a pretext, intending to ensure the success of future Sasana affairs by causing the King and both parties to have great respect and devotion toward him, thinking, “The Great Elder is of great power, a practitioner according to the instructions, and a reliable authority.” A boat joined together as one is called a “nāvāsaṃghāṭa” (boat-raft). Because the enemies of the Sasana were numerous, he said, “having arranged for protection.” “Yaṃ” means “because.” “Abbaāhiṃsu” means “they have pulled out.” “Bāhirato” means “from outside the park.” It was said, “shaking a portion of the earth is difficult,” intending to make it appear as an extremely difficult feat to the onlookers. In truth, in the act of determination (adhiṭṭhāna), shaking a portion of the earth is not particularly difficult.

“Dīpakatittira” refers to a “decoy partridge” that bird hunters raise and train to be placed at the site of a snare to catch others of the same species. In the verse “Action does not touch [the one who does not intend],” it means that if your mind is not corrupted by the commission of evil, the evil deed committed by the hunter depending on you does not reach you. For you, being a virtuous person who is unconcerned and detached from the commission of evil, that evil does not smear you; it does not cling to your mind.

“What speech does he habitually utter?” is the meaning of “Kiṃvādī.” Or else, “What kind of doctrine does he have?” is the meaning of “Kiṃvādī.” Those who hold the view that the self and the world are “eternal” are called “Sassatavādī” (Eternalists). The view that arises as “some are eternal” regarding beings or formations is called “Ekaccasassata” (Partial-eternalism), and those associated with that view are called “Ekaccasassatika.” The four views that arise concerning the finite and the infinite as “finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, neither finite nor infinite” are called “Antānanta,” and those associated with them are called “Antānantika.” Because it does not die and is not cut off, it is called “Amarā” (undying). Because there is a rejection (vikkhepa) of views and speech that arise as “I do not hold this view, nor do I hold that view,” etc., they are called “Amarāvikkhepika” (Eel-wrigglers). Or else, there is a species of fish called “Amarā” which is difficult to catch; those who have views that are difficult to catch (rejective) like that fish are called “Amarāvikkhepika.” Those associated with the view that the self and the world have arisen fortuitously without depending on any cause are called “Adhiccasamuppannika” (Fortuitous-originationists). Those who hold the view “the self is percipient” are called “Saññīvāda.” Likewise, it should be understood in the cases of “Asaññīvāda” and “Nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda.” (Those who hold the view) “After the breaking up of the body, the being is annihilated” (are called Ucchedavāda).
32:
Because they say that the being is annihilated, they are called Annihilationists (Ucchedavādā). Because they say that Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering, is achieved by enjoying the five types of sensual pleasures as one desires in this very present self, they are called Proclaimers of Nibbāna in the Present Life (Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā). The Buddha is called an Analyst (Vibhajjavādī) because He has a doctrine that is taught through analysis. This means He does not speak of all things in a uniform manner but analyzes them according to their nature, making them free from entanglement and confusion, so that when taught, doubts regarding views and so forth are dispelled, and conventional realities (sammuti) and ultimate realities (paramattha) appear clearly without being mixed. It means He has the nature of always teaching through analysis. Subduing the doctrines of others means He subdues all external doctrines that arose at that time or would arise in the future, starting with the explanation of the matrix (mātikā) of the Kathāvatthu.

## The Explanation of the Method of the Third Council is finished.

## Explanation of the Lineage of Teachers

To answer the question 'Who brought it?', the commentator first shows the lineage of teachers in Jambudīpa up to the Third Council, and now, to show the lineage of teachers in the island of Sri Lanka, he begins with the words "Tatiya saṅgahato pana uddhaṃ" (But after the Third Council). 'This island' refers to the island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka). It is called 'this island' because the teacher composed the commentary while residing on that island. 'For a long time' uses the second case ending in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga), meaning for a certain period of time. 'Ancient ones' refers to the teachers who composed the Sinhalese Commentaries in the island of Sri Lanka. One named Bhadda refers to the Elder Bhaddasāla. They are called Nāgas (noble ones) because they do not perform evil. It should be connected as 'they taught the Vinaya Piṭaka'. The word 'Tambapaṇṇiyā' is in the locative case (indicating place). In the phrase 'five Nikāyas', since the Vinaya and Abhidhamma are taken separately, the five Nikāyas remaining from them should be taken. 'In the text' means they taught in the Abhidhamma texts. Although it should be said 'Tepiṭako' meaning one who possesses the three Piṭakas that have come well to that Elder, it is said as 'Tipeṭako' to preserve the meter. 'King of stars' refers to the Moon. In this place, 'one named Puppha' refers to the Elder Mahāpaduma and the Elder Sumana; therefore, 'Pupphanāmo' is said twice.

Vanavāsī refers to the Vanavāsī country. 'Hailstorm' refers to rain that falls like snow or rain that is like a torrent of water. 'Having it carried away' means having it removed by a flood of water. 'One who wears cut and ruined clothes' refers to one who wears clothes cut with a small knife and ruined by dye. 'Bhaṇḍū' means a shaven-headed person. 'Being unable to endure the denigration' means, relying on the power of the Elder, being unable to endure the anger characterized by denigrating the virtues of others that arose in himself. 'Thunderbolts break' means they fall with a roaring sound. My terrifying...
33:
Being unable to endure the denigration (makkha) characterized by erasing the virtues of others that arose in himself, and the anger that arose in that manner of denigration. "Thunderbolts break" means they fall with a roaring sound. It is construed as: "May there not be one capable of producing my terror." 'Aññadatthu' means certainly. 'Kasmīragandhāra' refers to the inhabitants of the Kasmīra and Gandhāra regions. 'Isivātapatiivāta' refers to the wind generated by the movement of the monks' robes and bodies, acting as if fanning from all around. 'Dhammacakkhu' refers to the knowledge in the three lower paths. 'Anamataggiya' refers to the Anamataggasaṃyutta. 'Samadhikāni' means having an excess. 'Pañca raṭṭhāni' refers to the five Cina regions. 'Vegasā' means with speed. 'Placed protection all around' means placing protection through the power of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna) so that those rakkhas could not enter. 'Aḍḍhuḍḍhāni sahasāni' means three thousand five hundred (3,500). 'Diyaḍḍhasahassa' means one thousand five hundred (1,500). 'Niddhametvāna' means having expelled or having made them flee.

'Rājagahanagaraparivattakena' means by the path of going around the city of Rājagaha, performing a circumambulation (padakkhiṇa) outside that city, or by the act of going. 'Āropesi' means made to reach or made to move. 'Paḷinā' means they flew into the sky. 'Naguttame' refers to Cetiyagiri mountain. 'Purato' means in the eastern direction. 'Puraseṭṭhassa' means of the noble city of Anurādha. 'Silakūṭamhi' means on the mountain peak of that name. In this place, 'son of Sīhakumāra', they say, "Prince Sīhakumāra was born of a lion in the womb of the Princess of Kaliṅga." Because either the Jeṭṭha constellation or the Mūla constellation occurs on the full moon day of the month of Jeṭṭha, it is said, "It is called the Jeṭṭhamūla constellation." It is called 'Migavaṃ' because of the harming or killing of animals; it is the sport of deer hunting. 'Rohitamigarūpa' refers to the form of a red deer (Gokaṇṇa). 'Rathayaṭṭhippamāṇā' means having the size of a chariot pole. A bamboo stalk named 'Latāyaṭṭhi' is so named because it is made of silver and adorned with golden creepers. It should be understood that in the 'Pupphayaṭṭhi', flowers such as blue ones appear, and in the 'Sakuṇayaṭṭhi', various animals and birds appear as if they were painted. 'Rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni' refers to the noble regalia suitable for kings. 'Saṅkha' refers to the right-spiraled conch used for consecration. 'Vaḍḍhamāna' is the decorative powder; some teachers say "bathing powder." 'Vaṭaṃsaka' refers to the ear-flower ornament. 'Nandiyāvaṭṭa' is a flower made of gold for the sake of auspiciousness in the shape of a Tagara flower. 'Kanyaṃ' refers to the princess. 'Hatthapuñchana' is a costly yellow hand-towel. 'Aruṇavaṇṇamattika' refers to the Aruṇavatī clay produced in the Naga realm. 'Vatthakoṭika' refers only to a pair of cloths. 'Nāgamāha' means the Nagas brought it.
34:
It means 'brought by the Nagas.' Amatosadha is the name of a type of medicinal pill. It is called so because its function is similar to the taste of the deathless (amata). It means 'in the form of a floor covering.' It means 'those who can read omens.' He said, 'Enough, let's go,' rejecting it because 'it is not suitable as it is too close to the city.' It means 'to eight thousand five hundred beings.' The Appamāda Sutta refers to the Mahā-appamāda Sutta or the Rājovāda Sutta found in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

It means 'mostly' or 'greatly.' It means he approached appearing extremely exhausted. The connection should be 'to make you know.' In this context of 'fifty-five,' it should be said as 'fifty-four.' Only then will it agree with the statement 'sixty-two Arahants' mentioned later, as stated in the Sāratthadīpanī. It means crowded with the ten brothers, such as Devānampiyatissa and others, who were the sons of King Muṭasiva. The phrase 'the Buddha seen after a long time' refers to the relics (dhātu). It means all musical instruments or the musicians associated with those instruments. It means having them assemble for the purpose of making offerings. It means in the afternoon (when shadows grow). A lotus-leaf rain (pokkharavassa) is rain that falls without wetting those who do not wish to be wet, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf. The term 'Mahāvīra' refers to the relics themselves, using the name of the Teacher (the Buddha). In this context, 'retreating while facing West' means going towards the West by moving backwards while still facing East. They say 'Mahejavatthu' is the name of such a shrine (devaṭṭhāna).

It means by the Pajjaraka disease caused by non-human beings (amanussa). Deva refers to a rain cloud. Anuppaveccchi means released or rained down. In this context of 'vivādo hoti,' it should be noted that the present tense (vattamanā) is used without regard to the time of the action. This applies to all such similar instances. The word 'tadetaṃ' should be connected with 'ṭhānaṃ tiṭṭhati.' One should supplement the reading with 'and the rays associated with the six colors.' Some also say the connection here is 'and the streams of water of the six colors.' To show that such a miracle occurred through the power of the Blessed One even after His Parinibbāna, the verse beginning with 'Evaṃ acintiyā' was spoken. It means making a protection (paritta) so that the Yakkhas, who were driven away by his own means, would not enter again. Āvijjī means revolved or circled around.
35:
The 'king's brother' (rañño bhātā) refers to the king's younger brother. The one named Anulādevī is the wife of the king's elder brother. 'Sarasaraṃsijālavi-ssajjanakena' means 'by the (Lord) who emits a net of rays that are flavorful and nutritious due to their smoothness.' The phrase 'ekadivasena agamāsi' should be connected as 'went in a single day.' 'Appesi' means he sent and established a message (letter). 'Udikkhati' means expects or longs for. 'Bhāriyaṃ' means heavy or unavoidable. 'Maṃ paṭimāneti' means 'expects me.' 'Kammāravaṇṇaṃ' means the appearance of the king's own natural goldsmith. 'Tihatthavikkhambhaṃ' means three cubits in width.

In the phrase 'sakalajambudīparajjena,' it means he honors with the revenue, authority, and so on arising from the whole of Jambudīpa, which is called the king's 'kingship.' It does not mean honoring with physical objects such as the entire land or palaces. This is because it is improper to give such things as palaces by making a time limit, such as 'I give this for seven days.' If one gives in this way, it is called a temporary gift, whereas the characteristic of a gift (dāna) is the relinquishing of the object, and it is improper to take back land and other objects after relinquishing them. However, when revenue and such are relinquished for a fixed time, they are truly relinquished. Therefore, it is proper to take them back after that fixed time (since there was no further relinquishment). Thus, according to the method stated, here and hereafter, the 'offering of the kingdom' (rajjadāna) should be understood only as the offering of revenue and such.

'Pupphuḷakā hutvā' means water bubbles formed like the sprouts of the screwpine (ketakī) roots. The term 'gavakkhajālasadisaṃ' is an adverbial neuter. It means like a wooden lattice placed in windows in the form of a net. Or, it means like a window (bull's eye) and a net made of thread and such.

In the term 'devadundubhiyo,' 'deva' means a rain cloud. The uncaused thundering of such a cloud, which appears like the sky because of its clear dryness, is called 'devadundubhi' (celestial drum). They also call it 'ākāsadundubhi' (sky drum). 'Phaliṃsu' means they thundered. 'Pabbatānaṃ naccehi' means by the dancing of mountains that revolve here and there due to an earthquake. The Yakkhas, filled with wonder, uttered the sound 'Hi'; therefore, it says 'by the Hi-sounds of the Yakkhas.' 'Sakasakapaṭibhānehi' means by their own respective skills and talents. 'Abhisekaṃ datvā' means having performed the consecration (abhiseka) with water from Lake Anotatta.

'Devatākulāni' should be connected as '(seeing) the groups of deities such as Nagas and Yakkhas who stood surrounding the Great Bodhi tree.' The royal attendants who are guards likewise call them 'animals' (taracchā). In the phrase 'iminā parivārena,' the instrumental case is in the sense of 'saha' (together with). It means 'together with this retinue.' 'Tāmalitti' is a port city of this name on the shore of the ocean. The statement 'this is its third' refers to the offering of the kingdom to the Bodhi branch established in the golden vase. Before that, however, the offering of the kingdom was made once to the Great Bodhi tree itself, with the branch not yet detached.
36:
The King offered his kingship to the Great Bodhi tree four times. It is said that on the days he offered his kingship, he took the revenue collected from the entire island and made offerings only to the Great Bodhi tree.

"Paṭhamapāṭipadadivase" refers to the first day of the waxing fortnight. This term is used as the "first day" in relation to the first day of the waning fortnight. This is stated according to the usage in the island of Tambapaṇṇi. In this Jambudīpa, however, the period from one full moon day to the next full moon day is called one month. Therefore, according to this usage, since the first day of the waning fortnight is the first day here, it should be called "dutiyapāṭipadadivase" (the second first-day).

In the phrase "gacchati vatare", the word "are" is used in the sense of weariness (kheda). "Samantāyojanaṃ" is in the accusative case of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga), meaning in all places within the extent of one league (yojana). "Supaṇṇarūpena" refers to intimidating the Naga kings, who wished to take the Great Bodhi tree by force to the Naga realm, by manifesting the form of a Garuda (supaṇṇa) through psychic power. "Taṃ vibhūtiṃ passitvā" means seeing the greatness of the offerings made by deities and others, and the greatness of the power of the Great Bodhi tree; the sentence should be connected as: wishing to make such offerings himself, he requested the Theri.

"Samuddasālavatthusmiṃ" refers to the site where the Samuddasālā hall was built to mark the place where the King stood and watched the Bodhi tree arriving across the ocean through the power of the Elder, and where the ocean could be seen later. "Therassa" refers to the Elder Mahā Mahinda. "Puppha-agghiyāni" are flower shrines resembling gabled houses. In the phrase "āgato vatare", the word "are" is used in the sense of joy (pamoda). "Aṭṭhahi amaccakulehi aṭṭhahi brāhmaṇakulehi ca" refers to the sixteen families of noble birth.

"Rajjaṃ vicāresi" means relinquishing the kingship to be administered. "Rājavatthudvārakoṭṭhakaṭṭhāne" refers to the place where the gatehouse of the royal garden was situated. "Anupubbavipassanaṃ" refers to successive insight, such as the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa). Although it should be stated in the instrumental case as "saha bodhipatiṭṭhānena", it is expressed in the ablative case as "saha bodhipatiṭṭhānā" through case transformation (vibhattipariṇāma). This is because when used with the word "saha", only the instrumental case should normally occur.

"Dassiṃsu" means they became manifest. "Mahāāsanaṭṭhāne" refers to the place where the Great Stone Seat (Mahāsilāsana) was located nearby. "Pūjetvā vandī" means he paid homage to the future Mahācetiya. It should be understood that since he only made offerings at the site of the Mahāvihāra initially, it indicates that in the future, as it would be a new construction for the Saṅgha, it would not yet be an object of worship. However, the future Buddhas such as Metteyya and the Paccekabuddhas should indeed be worshipped, as they are noble persons by nature, with reference to the moment of their Enlightenment.
37:
Mahā Ariṭṭha refers to the one who was ordained at Cetiyagiri along with fifty-five brothers. "Meghavaṇṇābhaya-amaccassa pariveṇaṭṭhāne" means at the site of the pariveṇa built by the minister of King Meghavaṇṇābhaya. The pleasant sound that arose in the sky as an auspicious sign was like a roar of the sky, thus it is said, "The sky roared a great roar." In reality, the sky is not a phenomenon (dhamma) that can produce sound; that sound should be understood as arising from a particular condition of the elements (utu-visesa) in the sky. "On the first Kattika Pavāraṇā day... he expounded the Vinaya Piṭaka"—this refers to the day he began teaching the Vinaya. "Anusiṭṭhikaraānaṃ" means to those who follow the instructions and advice. The possessive case "rājino" is used in the sense of the accusative (upayogattha), meaning King Devānampiyatissa. "Aññepi" refers to other Elders besides the sixty-eight Great Elders such as Mahinda. To show their identity, it is said, "Tesaṃ therānaṃ", etc. In that context, "the pupils of those Elders" should be understood as combining the pupils of the sixty-eight Great Elders like Mahinda, such as Ariṭṭha, and the pupils of Elder Mahā Ariṭṭha, such as Tissadatta, Kāḷa, and Sumana. "The pupils of the pupils" refers to the lineage of pupils of both types of pupils mentioned. "Of the nature previously mentioned" refers to the lineage of teachers (ācariyaparamparā) shown by the verses beginning with "Mahindo Iṭṭhiyo Uttiyo".

"Na paggharati" means it does not leak, implying it is not forgotten. In the phrase "among those possessed of sati, gati, and dhiti", Sati is the mindfulness in learning and retaining. Gati is the wisdom to discern and grasp the words and meanings. Dhiti is the energy (vīriya) exerted in learning and retaining. "Kukkuccakesu" means among those who have remorse or scruples, investigating "is it allowable or not?". After saying "one who stands in the place of a parent", to support that meaning, it is said, "depending on that Vinaya", etc. Depending on the learning of the Vinaya scriptures (vinaya-pariyatti), one's own aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is well-guarded. Because a conscientious (lajjī) bearer of the Vinaya does not fall into an offense through the six causes such as shamelessness and ignorance, his own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected, free from flaws like breakage. For those oppressed and overwhelmed by remorse arising from what is allowable and what is not, he becomes a refuge by dispelling that remorse in accordance with the Vinaya and establishing them in purity. He is called "visārada" (confident) because he is free from fear (vigata-sārada). Because he speaks only after knowing "speaking thus is an offense, speaking thus is not an offense", he can give decisions in the midst of the Saṅgha without fear.
38:
(voharati) He decides in the midst of the Saṅgha. (paccatthike) refers to one's own enemies as well as enemies of the Dispensation (Sāsana) such as the Vajjiputtakas and others. (sahadhammena) means showing the training rule (sikkhāpada) with reasoned speech and subduing them well so that they cannot establish false doctrine (asaddhamma). (saddhammaṭṭhitiyā) means for the stability and propagation of the threefold True Dhamma, namely: learning (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha).

In the passages beginning with "Vinayo saṃvaratthāya," the learning of the Vinaya or the Vinaya regulation is for the purpose of restraint of the doors of body and speech. (avippaṭisāra) is the absence of remorse or mental distress regarding what has been done or not done. (pāmojja) is tender rapture (pīti). (pīti) refers to strong rapture. (passaddhi) is the tranquility of body and mind. (yathābhūtañāṇadassana) is the discernment of mind and matter (nāmarūpa) along with their causes. (nibbidā) is insight (vipassanā). (virāga) is the Noble Path (ariyamagga). (vimutti) is the supreme fruit, Arahatship (arahattaphala). (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). (anupādā) means by letting go without clinging to any phenomenon (dhamma). (parinibbānatthāya): since Parinibbāna cannot occur in the interval before reviewing knowledge arises, that reviewing knowledge is stated as the cause for Parinibbāna by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) and so forth. (etadatthā kathā) means this Vinaya discourse is for the purpose of this Parinibbāna without clinging. (mantanā) is the consultation regarding Vinaya itself; it is the consultation of monks concerning Vinaya, such as "We shall do this, we shall not do this." (upanisā) means cause (kāraṇa), because the result depends on and resides in this cause. The sequence of causes beginning with "Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint" is also for the purpose of this Parinibbāna. (sotāvadhāna) is listening to understand oneself through this discourse on the sequence of causes; that listening is also for the purpose of this Parinibbāna. (yadidaṃ) is an indeclinable (nipāta). Liberation (vimokkha), which is called the Path of Arahatship or the Fruit of Arahatship, attained by the mind without clinging through the four types of grasping (upādāna), is also for the purpose of this Parinibbāna without clinging. Alternatively, it is also appropriate to apply it by way of close connection, stating that this Vinaya discourse is for the purpose of the mind's liberation, peace, and Parinibbāna without clinging to any phenomenon, because the liberation of the Path and Fruit was mentioned previously. (āyoga) is repeated exertion by way of learning and so forth.

## The method of explanation for the lineage of teachers (ācariyaparamparākathā) is finished.
## Thus, in the Vimativinodanī, the commentary on the Samantapāsādikā Vinaya Commentary,
## the method of explanation for the external prologue (bāhiranidānakathā) is finished.
39:
## Explanation of the Verañja Section (Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā)
"seyyathidaṃ" means "What is that explanation?" or "How shall that explanation be made?" "aniyamaniiddesavacana": Defining one's meaning specifically is called "niyamaniddesa"; that which is not so defined is "aniyamaniiddesa." Because it is a statement that does not define specifically, it is called "aniyamaniiddesavacana." "tassa" refers to the word "tena." "parivitakka" is the thought that arose as: "In which of those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, did the holy life not last long?" and so forth. "In the past or in the future" means in the text taught below the word "tena" or in the text to be taught above it. "Accomplished by meaning" means accomplished by capability (sāmatthiya). "Herein, this is a mere indication" means in explaining the aforementioned logic, this is a mere means (upāya) of indication. This is because the three terms mukha, dvāra, and upāya are identical in meaning.

The word "samaya" is evident; this is the connection of words. "Of that samaya-word" means the meaning of the word samaya is the combination (samavāya) of causes; this is the connection. In the phrase "depending on time (kāla) and occasion (samaya)," kāla is the suitable time for approaching, and samaya is the combination of causes such as physical strength and so forth. It means depending on or because of that time and occasion. "khaṇa" is opportunity (okāsa). This is because the arising of a Buddha and so forth are opportunities for the noble holy life of the Path. That very moment is called samaya. Therefore, it is said to be "khaṇa." "mahāsamaya" is a great assembly of devas. "pavana" means in the forest grove. In the phrase "Bhaddāli, you have the occasion (samaya)," samaya is the cause for not transgressing the training rule. What is that cause? It is the Blessed One's knowledge of one's own misconduct. It means that Bhaddāli did not realize that cause known as samaya. The words beginning with "bhagavā" show the manner of that lack of realization. "uggahamāna" is so called because of the ability to learn bit by bit; this is the name of the wanderer Sumana. Because views (samaya) are proclaimed here, it is the park of Queen Mallikā called "samayappavādaka." Because that park is surrounded by a row of Tinduka trees known as tindukācīra, it is called "Tindukācīra"; and because there is only one hall for staying there, it is called "Ekasalaka." "atthābhisamaya" is due to the attainment of the aforementioned welfare of this life and the next. "mānābhisamaya" is due to the abandoning of conceit (māna). "pīḷanaṭṭha" means the act of oppressing, which is harming the one possessed of suffering and making them non-expansive; oppression itself is the meaning.
40:
The meaning of oppression (pīḷanaṭṭha) refers to tormenting (santāpana) by way of the suffering of suffering (dukkha-dukkhatā) and so forth. Change (vipariṇāma) refers to the state of being subject to change in two ways: through aging (jarā) and death (maraṇa). It is called realization (abhisamaya) because it is to be fully understood and penetrated; that very meaning of being penetrated is the meaning of realization (abhisamayaṭṭha), which encompasses the meanings of oppression and so forth.

In this context, since prefixes (upasagga) merely illuminate the meaning, when extracting the meaning of the word 'samaya', the word 'abhisamaya' together with its prefix is extracted. Among those meanings, it is called 'samaya' (concordance/samavāya) because it is the simultaneous occurrence of causes meeting to produce an effect. It is called 'samaya' (opportunity/khaṇa) because beings arise when the conditions for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) meet. It is called 'samaya' (time/kāla) because it is where conditioned phenomena arise, or because it itself comes and goes. It is called 'samaya' (collection/samūha) because parts come together in it, or because it exists within those parts. It is called 'samaya' (cause/hetu) because an effect arises from it upon meeting other causes. It is called 'samaya' (view/diṭṭhi) because one enters and clings to phenomena pervertedly by the power of perception (saññā). Approaching or reaching is called 'samaya' (attainment/paṭilābha). The departure of well-associated words is called 'samaya' (abandoning/pahāna). The thorough penetration and knowing of the Truths is called 'samaya' (penetration/paṭivedha). Thus, the occurrence of the word 'samaya' in various meanings should be understood.

Here, the word 'samaya' is said to have many meanings in general. A word used in one specific sense does not apply to other senses. Therefore, just as the meanings differ, the words 'samaya' that express those various meanings should also be regarded as distinct. This applies to all extractions of meaning.

In those Suttas and Abhidhamma, the word 'samaya' is used with the accusative and locative cases. In the Vinaya, however, it is used differently with the instrumental case. 'Accantam-eva' means continuously. 'Bhāva' refers to an action (kiriya). Marking one action by another action is called 'bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa' (the characteristic of an action by an action), such as saying, 'The prince was born when the moon rose.' In the Abhidhamma, the word 'samaya' occurs in five meanings: time (kāla), collection (samūha), moment (khaṇa), concordance (samavāya), and cause (hetu). It does not occur only in the sense of time as in the Vinaya. Among those five, the two meanings of time and collection are suitable to be indicated as the basis (adhikaraṇa) for the phenomena such as contact (phassa) mentioned in that Abhidhamma. The three meanings of moment, concordance, and cause are suitable to be indicated as the characteristic markers (upalakkhaṇa) for the occurrence of contact and so forth by their own occurrence.
41:
The statement that they are suitable to be indicated as characteristic markers (upalakkhaṇa) is made to complete the aforementioned meaning through the method of clarification. In that Abhidhamma, when wholesome states arise at a certain time or in a certain 'samaya' which is a collection of phenomena acting as the basis (adhikaraṇa), then contact and other states also occur at that same time or in that same collection; thus the connection through the sense of basis (adhikaraṇa) should be understood. Furthermore, when wholesome states arise while a certain moment, concordance, or cause—which is a 'samaya'—is present, then contact and other states also occur while that moment and so forth are present; thus the connection through the sense of 'bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa' should also be understood. 'Hoti cettha' means that there is a summary verse (saṅgaha-gāthā) regarding this aforementioned meaning. 'Aññatra' refers to the Suttas and Abhidhamma. 'Abhilāpa-matta-bhedo' means the difference is merely in the phrasing due to the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa), not a difference in meaning.

'Avisesena' means generally or by way of similarity. In terms such as 'iriyāpatha' (posture), standing and so forth are called 'iriyāpatha' because they are the places where actions occurring through all doors arise, and because there is no action apart from these postures. That very 'iriyāpatha' is called 'vihāra' (dwelling). Loving-kindness (mettā) and so forth, which proceed by way of a mind intent on the welfare of others and possess a noble nature, are called 'brahmavihāra' (divine abidings). All other lofty (mahaggata) states, which are characterized by illumination and so forth achieved through the removal of all hindrances, are called 'dibbavihāra' (celestial abidings). Because they are taken separately as 'brahmavihāra', loving-kindness and so forth are not included here. Fruition attainments (phala-samāpatti) are called 'ariyavihāra' (noble abidings) because they are the dwellings of only the Noble Ones (ariyas).

Since the word 'mūla' (root) is commonly and traditionally used for the roots of trees and such, to show that specific meaning, it is distinguished by another word 'mūla' and stated as 'mūla-mūla' (the root of roots), just as 'dukkha-dukkha' is stated. Because greed and so forth are not common to (not shared with) hate-rooted consciousness and so forth, it is stated as 'asādhāraṇa-hetumhi' (in the uncommon cause).

'Tattha siyā' means that in those words such as 'Verañjāyaṃ', there might be an objection by someone. What is the purpose of describing the origin (nidāna) in two ways? To answer this, the words 'gocara-gāma-nidassanatthaṃ' and so forth are said. In that phrase, 'assa' refers to the Blessed One. 'Kilamatha' is simply weariness. The weariness of one's own body is 'attakilamatha'. The repeated application or occurrence of that weariness is 'attakilamathānuyoga' (devotion to self-mortification). It is 'kāmasukhallika' because it is a craving for sensual pleasure (kāma-taṇhā) that is attached to and joined with the pleasure having the objects of sensual strings as its basis, or because it is the pleasure of the cords of sensual desire which is the object where that craving is attached and proceeds. The repeated devotion to that craving which is attached to sensual pleasure is 'kāmasukhallikānuyoga'. 'Loke saṃvaḍḍhabhāvaṃ' refers to the state of growing through the enjoyment of material things (āmisa). When it arises, it should be connected as arising only for the welfare and benefit of the many. To clarify the meaning that it is called 'Saṅgha' because it is united by equality in view and virtue, the words 'diṭṭhīti-ādi' and so forth are said. Here, it is said, 'Whatever view is noble and leads out of suffering, which leads one who acts according to it to the complete destruction of suffering; one dwells having reached equality in view with such a view,' and 'Whatever virtues are unbroken... and lead to concentration; one dwells having reached equality in virtue in such virtues...'
42:
Sensual craving (kāmatanhā) is called 'craving for sensual pleasure' (kāmasukhallikā tanhā) because it arises attached to the pleasure of sensual cords, which is its object and co-arising factor. The repeated engagement with that craving attached to sensual pleasure is called 'devotion to sensual pleasure' (kāmasukhallikānuyoga). 'Prosperity in the world' refers to the state of being nourished by material enjoyments. It should be understood that when [the Buddha] arises, he arises solely for the welfare and benefit of many people.

## To clarify the meaning that it is called 'Saṅgha' because it is united by equality of view and virtue, he spoke the words beginning with 'diṭṭhi'.

In this context, 'That view which is noble and leading out, leading one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering; one dwells having attained equality of view with such a view'—by such a view; and 'Those virtues which are unbroken... leading to concentration; one dwells having attained equality of virtue in such virtues'—by the collection called equality of such virtues, the group of recluses is united, thus it is the Saṅgha; this is the meaning. Or, the reading should be 'diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghātasaṅghātena'. The meaning of that reading is: the group of recluses united by the collection which is the equality of view and virtue. With such a reading, the meaning is more grammatically appropriate. 'Assa' means 'of the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus'.

In the phrase 'brahmaṃ aṇati', the word 'brahma' refers to the Veda. That Veda is threefold by way of manta-veda, brahma-veda, and kappa-veda. Among those three, the three Vedas such as the Iruveda are the manta-vedas. These manta-vedas are primary. The other Vedas depend on them. Therefore, only the primary manta-veda should be taken. 'mante sajjhāyati' means he recites the manta scriptures such as the Iruveda. The Iruveda and others are called 'manta' because they are to be spoken secretly. To clarify the two meanings: 'He is a Brāhmaṇa because he has warded off evil; he is a Samaṇa because he has stilled evil' through two examples, he said 'vuttaṃ hetaṃ', etc. Taking the statement 'Because of the stilling of evils, one is called a Samaṇa', he said 'one is called a Samaṇa because he has stilled evil'. The phrase 'bāhitapāpo' (one who has warded off evil) is a statement mentioned in another verse composition. 'yathābhuccaguṇādhigataṃ' means the state of having attained qualities according to reality. 'sakiñcano' means one with faults or one with the defilement of impurities.

In the word 'gottavasena', it is called 'gotta' because it protects knowledge. Here, by the word 'go', both name and knowledge are meant. 'kenaci pārijuññena' means by some loss such as the loss of relatives...
43:
'Pārijuññena' means by loss or decline. 'tato paraṃ' refers to the words beginning with 'Verañjāyaṃ'. 'ittham-bhūtākhyānatthe upayoga-vacanaṃ' means the use of the accusative case in the sense of describing a state that has been reached. Reaching this particular state is called 'ittham-bhūta', and the description of such a state is 'ittham-bhūtākhyāna'. That very sense is 'ittham-bhūtākhyānattha'. Alternatively, the sense of saying 'thus, such a state has arisen' is 'ittham-bhūtākhyānattha', and it means the use of the accusative case in that sense. Here, the word 'abhi' in 'abbhuggato' indicates the manner of rising by overcoming, thus it shows reaching such a state. Because of the connection with that word 'abhi', this accusative case 'taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ', although it is in the sense of possession (sāmi), is said to be 'ittham-bhūtākhyānatthe' because it shows reaching such a state. Therefore, he said it means 'of that Blessed Gotama'.

This is what is meant: Just as in the sentence 'sādhu Devadatto mātaram-abhi' (Devadatta is good towards his mother), the accusative case is used in the sense of describing a state due to the connection with the word 'abhi', so too here, in 'taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ abhi', the accusative case is used in the sense of describing a state—that 'thus a good sound of fame has arisen'—due to the connection with the word 'abhi'. In the sentence 'sādhu Devadatto mātaram-abhi', although there is an occasion to use the locative case (adhikaraṇa) or the genitive case (sāmi) in the sense that Devadatta is good in the sphere of his mother or in relation to his mother, the accusative case is used when connected with the word 'abhi' which indicates the description of a state. Just as in that sentence it is understood that Devadatta has reached the aforementioned state in relation to his mother, so too here it should be understood that the sound of fame related to the Blessed Gotama has reached the state of rising by overcoming. In this context, the taking of 'kitti-sadda' is like the taking of 'Devadatta' there; the phrase 'taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ' is like the word 'mātaraṃ' there; and the word 'uggata' should be understood like the word 'sādhu' there. 'kitti-saddo' means the sound which is fame; to show that it is not just any sound, he specified it by saying 'kitti eva' (fame itself). Then, to show that 'kitti' is praise and the sound expressing that praise is 'kitti-sadda', he said 'thuti-ghoso vā' (or the sound of praise). In the phrase 'so Bhagavā', 'so' is in the sense of renown. That Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, having destroyed all defilements, and shaking the ten-thousandfold world system...
44:
Because He has penetrated and realized the peerless Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), that Blessed One is very famous in the world; thus it is said, "He is the Blessed One" (So Bhagavā). This word "Bhagavā" is an utterance of the Teacher's name, not an utterance of His qualities. However, later on, "Bhagavā" is indeed an utterance of His qualities. By the phrase "For this reason and for that reason," it shows how the terms such as Arahaṃ and others arise based on various groups of qualities respectively.

By the two words "suvidūravidūre," it shows that He is exceedingly far away. Only being exceedingly far is called "far." By the words "Because He has destroyed the defilements along with the habitual tendencies (vāsanā)," it shows that the Blessed One's state of being an Arahat is distinct and not shared with Solitary Buddhas (Paccekabuddhas) and others. This is because those Solitary Buddhas have not yet abandoned the habitual tendencies. What is called "habitual tendency" (vāsanā) is a certain disposition deposited by defilements, which causes defects in the usage of the three doors of body, speech, and mind—such as the inability to know all knowable things—even in one who is free from defilements. It is like the manner of walking with a limp caused by being shackled, which persists even after those who have been shackled for a long time are released from their chains. It is because of such habitual tendencies that defects in usage occur in elders such as the Venerable Pilindavaccha, such as addressing others as "Hey, outcaste (vasala)!" This disposition should be understood as vāsanā. In the word "ārakā," by making the letter 'ā' short and changing the letter 'ka' to 'ha' according to the method of etymology (nirutti), one should understand how the word "Arahaṃ" is formed. In this same way, one should understand the formation of words according to the method of etymology hereafter as appropriate.

"That which is this wheel of Saṃsāra" is the connection. In the word "puññādi," by the word "ādi," it includes non-meritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). Because the taints (āsavas) themselves are the root cause of ignorance (avijjā) and so forth, they are called the origin (samudaya); with this intention, it is said "by way of the origin of taints" (āsavasamudayamayena). Is it not taught that "With the arising of taints, there is the arising of ignorance"? The three planes of existence (tibhava), consisting of the variety of results (vipāka) and kamma-born matter (kaṭattārūpa), are themselves the chariot; in that chariot of the three planes of existence. The wheel of Saṃsāra is the collection of the aforementioned defilements (kilesa), kamma, and results (vipāka).

"The succession of aggregates, and of elements and bases, proceeding uninterruptedly, is called 'Saṃsāra'."

Saṃsāra, thus described, is called a "wheel" (cakka) because it revolves like a wheel. It is connected as "all the spokes (ara) of that wheel have been destroyed." "By Him" (anena) refers to the Blessed One. "Bodhi" refers to knowledge (ñāṇa).
45:
In this context, because that knowledge arises with clarity, it is called the Bodhimaṇḍa (the seat of enlightenment). The "weapon (axe) of knowledge that brings about the end of kamma" refers to the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga-ñāṇa). It should be understood that it is described with the qualifier "bringing about the end of kamma" to show that this Path knowledge cuts through and terminates the kamma known as volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) which ought to be cut.

Thus, having shown the wheel of Saṃsāra through some factors, the chariot of the three planes of existence through the remaining resultant mental and material phenomena (nāmarūpa) which are the results, and the manner of destroying the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra joined to that chariot of existence; now, in order to show the wheel of Saṃsāra alone, devoid of the chariot, through all twelve factors of Dependent Origination (paṭicca-samuppāda), and the different ways of destroying the spokes of that wheel, the phrase "Or else" (atha vā) and so forth is stated. In that passage, "anamatagga" means having a beginning that is repeatedly unknown. It means having an end (beginning) that is not known even by knowledges that follow along in every way. The statement "Because it has ignorance as its root and aging-and-death as its end" is said by grouping the ten factors starting with formations (saṅkhāra) together as spokes. In reality, those formations and so forth do not individually have ignorance as their root and aging-and-death as their end. Why? Because it is not so taught in the Pali text of Dependent Origination. Alternatively, it should be understood that this is said with reference to the fact that those formations and so forth also have ignorance as their root in terms of meaning as appropriate, and have aging-and-death as their end by virtue of the momentary aging-and-death (khaṇika-jarāmaraṇa) which is their respective characteristic. Thus, the status of those phenomena as individual spokes is established.

Having thus shown the wheel of Saṃsāra in all its aspects, now, the knowledge by which the destruction of the spokes of this wheel of Saṃsāra was accomplished by the Blessed One—concerning that Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma (Dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa), since the matrix (mātikā) is stated as "Wisdom in grasping conditions is the Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma," [the text] shows the manner of its occurrence by way of grasping the relationship of condition and conditionally-arisen in ignorance and so forth, which are parts of the wheel of existence. Then, by the passage including the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali such as "Thus, this ignorance is the cause," which is stated by way of concluding that meaning, it shows the Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma in its specific form. After showing the analysis of the occurrence of that Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma in those very factors of ignorance and so forth by way of the four summaries (saṅkhepa) and so forth, then by the passage "Thus is the Blessed One" (iti Bhagavā) and so forth, it shows the fact that the Blessed One has penetrated Dependent Origination in all its aspects through that Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma. Again, by the phrase "By this Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma" and so forth, in order to show the fact that the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra were destroyed by the Blessed One through that knowledge, it is said: "Among those (four truths), ignorance of suffering and so forth is called ignorance (avijjā)." In that context, "of the three bases" means of the three: the eye, ear, and mind bases. This same method applies to the phrases "of the three contacts" and so forth. Only the six groups of craving (taṇhā-kāya) by way of craving for forms and so forth should be understood.
46:
'Saggasampatti' means the attainment of the sensual happy realms. 'Tatheva' means it occurs only because of the cause of sensual clinging (kāmūpādāna). 'Brahmalokasampatti' means the attainment of the fine-material Brahma realm. Since all passion (rāga) that has the three planes (tebhūmaka) as its object is sensual defilement (kilesakāma), existence-passion (bhavarāga) is also just sensual clinging (kāmūpādāna); with this intention, it is said, 'one develops loving-kindness only because of the cause of sensual clinging.' In the remaining applications (yojanā) rooted in clinging, the same method should be understood for those rooted in clinging to views (diṭṭhūpādāna), clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbatūpādāna), and clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādūpādāna). In this regard, the method of application is as follows: Here, someone holds the view, 'There is no other world, the self is annihilated.' That person, because of the cause of clinging to views, commits bodily misconduct, and so on. Another person, holding the view, 'The self is annihilated in such and such an existence,' performs various wholesome deeds for the sake of rebirth in the sensual, fine-material, or immaterial realms; thus, the application rooted in clinging to views should be understood. By this same method, the application rooted in clinging to the doctrine of self should also be understood. Another person, wrongly grasping the path of impurity as the 'path of purity,' thinking 'purity comes through virtue, purity comes through vows,' commits bodily misconduct because of clinging to rites and rituals; thus, the application rooted in clinging to rites and rituals in all realms should be understood.

Now, to show the mode of grasping the causes such as ignorance (avijjā) of the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa), which is capable of destroying the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra, the cause-and-effect (paccaya-paccayuppanna) relationship of ignorance and so on is shown by saying, 'In the sensual realm, ignorance is the cause for formations (saṅkhāra) in the sensual realm,' and so on. Intending to show that same knowledge as a conclusion by bringing the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali along with the mode of occurrence in ignorance and so on, he said 'evamayaṃ' and so forth. However, in the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā, it is stated: 'Now, showing the wheel of Saṃsāra, the causal status of ignorance and the resultant status of formations are shown by saying "In the sensual realm, ignorance is the cause for formations in the sensual realm," and so on. Intending to show that same cause-and-effect relationship as a conclusion by bringing the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, he said "evamayaṃ" and so forth.' This same text is also written in the Sāratthadīpanī Vinaya-ṭīkā. In that commentary, the cause-and-effect relationship of ignorance and so on by saying 'In the sensual realm, ignorance' was not actually stated by the teacher who showed the wheel of Saṃsāra. This is because that cause-and-effect relationship was already shown earlier by saying 'Ignorance is the hub (nābhi) because it is the root,' and because there is no application (upasaṃhāra) by way of bringing it close in the form of a wheel above. Furthermore, although it is said, 'Alternatively, showing that same cause-and-effect relationship as a conclusion,' the cause-and-effect relationship is not shown here as the primary conclusion, but rather as the mode of grasping the causes...
47:
...only the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) is shown as a conclusion of the manner of comprehending the causes as mentioned. For this reason, it is stated: "Thus, this ignorance is the cause, formations are conditionally arisen, both these states are conditionally arisen—wisdom in comprehending the causes is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena. In the past time... in the future time... ignorance is the cause... is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga); thus, dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa alone is shown primarily. As for the statement "Ignorance is the cause, formations are conditionally arisen," and so on, it is spoken of as the object (visaya) for the purpose of illustrating the manner of comprehending the causes of that dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa, which will be called "wisdom in comprehending the causes is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena"; it is not spoken of primarily.

The meaning here is: "Evaṃ" (thus) means by the method mentioned immediately before, this ignorance is the cause of formations, and formations are arisen from that cause. "Ubhopēte" (both these) means: because this ignorance is not causeless, nor permanent and eternal like the "Prakṛti" (Primal Nature) or "Īśvara" (Creator Lord) imagined by others, but rather, according to the word "With the arising of taints (āsavas), there is the arising of ignorance," it is itself a state that has a cause, is conditioned (saṅkhata), and is indeed impermanent (anicca). Therefore, both these—ignorance and formations—are indeed conditionally arisen. "Iti" (thus) means: the wisdom that exists in comprehending the causes in the manner mentioned above is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) because it occurs according to reality regarding the cause, which is known as the stability of phenomena.

In this text, the causality and so on of ignorance and the like are mentioned only by way of clarifying the object of the knowledge; they are not mentioned primarily. Here, only the knowledge is mentioned primarily. Therefore, only for the purpose of showing the manner of comprehending the causes of this knowledge, the causality of ignorance and so on was mentioned below and in the sense-sphere existence by saying "avijjā," and so forth. Here too, it is summarized as a conclusion; it is not summarized for the purpose of showing the wheel of existence (bhavacakka)—this is one's own opinion here.

In that text, if the conditionally arisen phenomena (paccayuppanna-dhamma), which are the effects, are not seen, the causality of the causes cannot be seen either. Therefore, it should be understood that in the description of the knowledge of comprehending the causes, saying "formations are conditionally arisen," the inclusion of conditionally arisen phenomena is also made. "Etēna nayēna" (by this method) means that all terms ending with birth (jāti) should be expanded by the method mentioned regarding ignorance, such as "formations are the cause, consciousness is conditionally arisen," and so on.

Thus, having shown the manner of occurrence of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena regarding ignorance and so on in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, now, the manner of that knowledge occurring through other modes regarding those causes...
48:
The words beginning with "Tattha" are stated to show the manner of occurrence. "Tattha" means in those factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). In this context, because ignorance (avijjā) and so forth are grouped together by commonality of cause or commonality of result, it is called saṅkhepa (summary); it means a collection (saṅgaha), a portion (koṭṭhāsa), or a heap (rāsī). Although that summary is of two types by nature (jāti), it becomes fourfold by the power of the distinction of time (kāla). The phrase "the present period" (paccuppanno addhā) follows. Craving (taṇhā), clinging (upādāna), and becoming (bhava) are included because they are common to defilement and kamma, and because they do not occur apart from craving, etc. The round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) such as ignorance is also just the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa) here because of its similarity in the nature of producing results; thus it is said, "these five things," and so forth. In the Pali passages such as "resultant states" (vipākā dhammā), although only the mental aggregates born of kamma deserve to be called by the word "result" (vipāka), in terms such as mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), the group of five results mixed with matter is called the "round of results" (vipākavaṭṭa) because mentality is predominant and because mentality is abundant. It means the round where results are predominant, or the round where results are abundant. Alternatively, the word vipāka here should be understood as a synonym for kamma-born (kammaja). By referring to them by the names birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa), it means that there is no such thing as birth, aging, and death apart from ultimate realities (paramattha); therefore, it means by referring to those births, etc., by speaking thus, and by making that the starting point. Because they are clearly shown, they are called "modes" (ākāra); they refer to the actual nature of ignorance, etc., meaning from that "mode of conditions" (paccayākāra). The first link (sandhi) should be understood as the cause-effect link (hetu-phala-sandhi) which is the cause for the uninterrupted occurrence; the second link is the effect-cause link (phala-hetu-sandhi); the third link is the cause-effect link (hetu-phala-sandhi).

After showing the manner of occurrence of the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) in ignorance and so forth in many ways, now, in order to show the Buddha's penetration of dependent origination through all modes—both those stated and those not yet stated—and to show how that knowledge is the reason for the occurrence of the term "knowledge of the stability of Dhamma" according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, the words "Thus the Blessed One" (iti Bhagavā) and so forth are stated as a summary. In that Pali, "iti" refers to the modes already stated; therefore, he said "the four summaries" (catusaṅkhepa) and so forth. "By all modes" means he penetrates through all modes—those stated here such as "in the sensual realm of existence, ignorance is the condition for volitional formations in the sensual realm of existence," and those not yet stated that appear in the Vibhaṅga of Dependent Origination and so forth. "Taṃ" refers to that knowledge by which the Blessed One knows thus. "By the sense of being known" (ñātaṭṭhena) means because of the sense of knowing; "by the sense of fully understanding" (pajānanaṭṭhena) means because of the sense of penetrating.

Now, in order to show the usefulness of this knowledge of the stability of Dhamma, which has been shown in detail along with the various modes of grasping conditions, in destroying the spokes of the wheel of existence, the words "by this knowledge of the stability of Dhamma" and so forth are stated. In that statement, it is connected as "he destroys the spokes with the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma." How does he destroy them? He says, "those things," and so forth. Those things such as ignorance...
49:
Knowing things as they truly are with that knowledge of the stability of Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa), which is like the great diamond-weapon; becoming weary with that knowledge, which is like the powerful weapon of insight (vipassanā); and becoming dispassionate and liberated with that knowledge, which is like the weapon of the Noble Path (ariyamagga), one destroys the spokes [of the wheel of saṃsāra]—thus is the connection. The knowledge of the Noble Path is also called 'knowledge of the stability of Dhamma' because it knows the truth of origin (samudayasacca) and so forth by way of its function.

'I shall honor each aggregate of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) with a monastery'—the offering of building a monastery, which arises with the aggregate of Dhamma as its object, is indeed an offering to the Blessed One because it arises solely out of love and devotion toward the Blessed One, and because it is adorned with stūpas containing relics and so forth. Thus it is said, 'referring to the Blessed One,' and so on. In the phrase 'kilesārīna so muni,' there is an elision of the niggahīta; it means he is a 'Muni' (Sage) because he has slain the enemies of defilements. In the phrase 'paccayādīnañcāraho' as well, the elision of the niggahīta should be noted.

In the term 'Sammāsambuddha,' the word 'saṃ' occurs in the sense of 'sayaṃ' (by oneself); thus it is said 'sāmaṃ' (personally). It means one who knows by oneself without being led (taught) by others. The phrase 'sabbadhammānaṃ' (of all dhammas) is established by taking everything without selecting any particular object. When there is no taking of a part, it is understood that the meaning to be taken is the absolute whole; for example, when it is said 'The monk does not give' [it implies he gives nothing at all]. In this way, without regarding a specific meaning, the derivation of the word 'Buddha' should be understood in the agent sense (kattar) only, as there is no intention to express the object (kamma). In this context, only this much is obtained linguistically: 'He is the Sammāsambuddha because he has rightly and personally awakened.' However, the phrase 'sabbadhammānaṃ' is stated by taking what is obtained through the meaning, for the act of awakening cannot occur without an object.

'Abhiññeyya' (to be known through direct knowledge) refers to the Four Noble Truths which are to be known by the distinguished mundane and supramundane knowledge by way of their characteristics and by way of impermanence and so forth. By the term 'pariññeyya' (to be fully understood), he speaks of the Noble Truth of Suffering (dukkha-ariyasacca), which is to be known by defining it through impermanence and so forth. By the term 'pahātabba' (to be abandoned), he speaks of the Truth of Origin (samudayasacca). By the term 'sacchikātabba' (to be realized), he speaks of the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca). The use of the plural here is made in consideration of the distinctions established by way of figurative language, such as [Nirvāṇa] with residue and so forth.

In the verse beginning with 'Abhiññeyya,' by taking the causal dhammas—the Truth of Origin which is to be abandoned and the Truth of the Path (maggasacca) which is to be developed—their results, the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Cessation, are also established. Therefore, it should be noted that this meaning—'that which is to be fully understood has been fully understood, and that which is to be realized has been realized'—is also included here. Thus he says, 'Therefore, I am the Buddha.' Because the four truths have been awakened to by me, therefore I am the Buddha [who knows] all that is to be known; the meaning is 'I have known through direct knowledge.'

Because it arises in the manner of craving for various objects, craving is the primary cause of the variety of sufferings; thus he says, 'by being the root cause.' 'Of the two' refers to the eye and its origin (samudaya). 'Non-arising' refers to the cause (nimitta) of non-arising, not merely to simple non-existence. [Why?] Because that simple non-existence has no ultimate substance and because it is included in many distinctions such as the three truths and so forth. 'Knowing cessation by defining it' means penetrating and knowing cessation by the power of knowing through realization. 'Also by extracting each group' means it is known by distinguishing and extracting each group such as the eye, the origin of the eye, and so forth; the meaning is that it is not known only in a general way like the Truth of Suffering and so forth. Since craving is also included in the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), it is a dhamma to be fully understood, and in order to show its nature as the Truth of Suffering...
50:
(Nirodha is not merely non-existence) because it is not a non-entity and because it is included in many ways, such as being with causes, etc. *Nirodhappajananā* means the penetration of the Truth of Cessation by way of the realization (abhisamaya) which is knowing through direct experience. "Even by extracting each term" (*ekekapaduddhārenāpi*) means it should be known by extracting each group such as the eye, the origin of the eye, etc., and not only by the general nature of the Truth of Suffering, etc. To show that craving (taṇhā) is also the Truth of Suffering, as it is included in the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha) and is thus a thing to be fully understood (pariññeyya), it is said "six groups of craving" (*cha taṇhākāyā*). In whichever individual existence (attabhāva) that craving arises, the craving established in the previous life, which acts as the root cause for that existence, should be taken as the Truth of the Origin.

"*Kasiṇāni*" refers to the jhanas having kasina objects. "*Dvattiṃsākārā*" refers to the thirty-two parts of the body, such as hair, etc., and the jhanas that take those parts as objects. "*Nava bhavā*" refers to the nine types of existence: the three such as the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), the three such as the existence with perception (saññībhava), and the three such as the one-constituent existence (ekavokārabhava). "*Cattāri jhānāni*" refers to the four jhanas in general, without considering the specific differences of the objects. It should be noted that resultant (vipāka) and functional (kiriyā) states are also included in all appropriate places. Here, it should be understood that craving, which is the decisive support (upanissaya) for wholesome states (kusala-dhamma), is the originator; however, for functional states (kiriyā-dhamma), craving is the cause of that individual existence. In the context of "in forward order" (*anulomato*), ignorance (avijjā) is the Truth of Suffering, and the craving and taints (āsava) from the previous life that originate that ignorance should be joined as the Truth of the Origin. In the case of formations (saṅkhāra), etc., ignorance, etc., themselves should be joined as the Truth of the Origin. "*Tena*" means "therefore."

It is called "*Vijjā*" (knowledge) because it makes its own object known. "*Sampannattā*" means because of being endowed with or because of fulfillment. "*Tatra*" refers to the Ambaṭṭha Sutta.
