Regarding "*manomayiddhiyā*", because it is said, "Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk creates another body from this body," the power that proceeds by way of producing another body through the jhanic mind within the body is called mind-made power (*manomayiddhi*); in essence, it is simply wisdom (paññā) associated with jhana. The seven good qualities (*saddhamma*) are faith (saddhā), shame (hirī), fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), great learning (bāhusacca), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), and wisdom (paññā). "*Gacchati amataṃ disaṃ*" means it goes to the direction of the Deathless, which is Nibbāna, because it should be seen by those who desire to escape from suffering; by this, it shows that the *caraṇa* (conduct) dhammas, being the Noble Path included in the three trainings, are certainly to be desired by those who seek Nibbāna. Now, to show that this endowment of knowledge and conduct (*vijjā-caraṇa-sampadā*) is not shared (asādhāraṇa) with disciples (sāvaka), etc., the phrase "*Tattha vijjāsampadā*", etc., is stated. Therein, by the power of the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-vijjā), omniscience (sabbaññutā) is accomplished; among the *caraṇa* dhammas...
51:
By the power of the attainment of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) included within the jhanas, the state of being the Great Compassionate One is accomplished; with this intention, it is said: "*Vijjā... pe... mahākāruṇikataṃ*." In the phrase "*yathā taṃ*", "*taṃ*" is merely a particle. It means that just as another Buddha endowed with knowledge and conduct (vijjā-caraṇa-sampanna) directs (beings toward their benefit), so too does this Buddha. "*Tena*" means by avoiding what is harmful and directing toward what is beneficial. In the word "*attantapādayo*", by the word "*ādi*", one should include those who torment others (*parantapa*) and those who torment both (*ubhayantapa*). One who does not return, not being attached to existences, means one who does not approach (existence) again because the abandoned defilements do not arise again.

The locative case "*tatra*" is used in the sense of accomplishing appropriate speech. "*Abhūtaṃ*" means speech that is untrue. "*Atacchaṃ*" is a synonym for that same "*abhūtaṃ*." "*Anatthasaṃhitaṃ*" means speech associated with faults such as backbiting, etc. "*Sammāgadatttā*" means because of speaking good words. "*Gadanaṃ*" is called "*gado*", meaning speaking (*kathanaṃ*). Because of having good speech (*sundaro gado*), it should be said as "*sugado*", but according to the rules of linguistics (nirutti), the letter 'da' is changed to 'ta', and thus it is called "*sugato*."

"*Sabhāvato*" means by way of the nature of suffering. "*Lokaṃ*" refers to the world of the aggregates (khandha), etc. Desiring to show the aforementioned meaning through a sutta, the phrase beginning with "*yattha*" is stated. Therein, "*yattha*" means in that Nibbāna which is called the end of the world. "*Taṃ*" means the end of the world. The connection is: "I do not say that the end of the world is to be known or reached by physical travel in the world of space (okāsa-loka)." This sutta was taught because the deva Rohitassa asked about reaching the end of the world by physical travel. The phrase "without reaching the end of the world" (*appatvā lokassantaṃ*) is said with reference to the world of the aggregates, etc.

Showing the intention, "What is the use of wandering through the world of space with your feet? I will show the end of the world to those who go with knowledge within this limited body itself," the phrase beginning with "*api ca*" is stated. Therein, "*byāmamatte kaဠေဝရေ*" means in the fathom-long body. By that term, the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is shown. In the term "*sasaññimhi*", starting with perception (saññā), the three mental aggregates such as feeling (vedanā), etc., are shown. By the term "*samanake*", the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) is shown. "*Lokaṃ*" refers to the world of the aggregates, etc., meaning suffering. "*Lokanirodhaṃ*" means the cessation of the world through Nibbāna, or Nibbāna itself. Indeed, although Nibbāna is not a physical place, because it is the cessation of those aggregates, it is as if it depends on them by way of metaphor (upacāra); thus it is said, "In this fathom-long body, I also make known the cessation of the world." It is just as in the passages: "The eye is of a lovely and pleasant nature in the world; here this craving, when ceasing, ceases," etc. "*Kudācanaṃ*" means even at any time. "*Appatvā*" means without knowing or reaching by the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). Therefore, because it cannot be reached by traveling (to the end of the world of space), it is said "*tasmā*." "*Have*" is merely a particle, used in the sense of "certainly."
52:
Alternatively, Lokavidū means one who knows the aggregates and so forth by their nature. He is called 'Samitāvī' because he has fully realized the Four Noble Truths. Or, he is called 'Samitāvī' because he has calmed the defilements. Since there is no further rebirth, he neither yearns nor desires.

Having thus shown the world in brief, he now speaks of 'api ca tayo lokā' etc., to show the world in detail. In that text, the world which is the collection and continuity of the aggregates associated with the sense faculties is called Sattaloka (World of Beings). Indeed, that collection of aggregates is called 'Satta' (being) because of being strongly attached to forms and so forth, and it is called 'Loka' (world) because kamma-defilements and their results are seen therein. The matter which is the collection and continuity of the temperature-produced matter not associated with the sense faculties is called Okāsaloka (World of Locations). Indeed, that collection of temperature-produced matter is called 'Okāsa' (location/space) because it is the support for beings and formations, and it is called 'Loka' because the support and the supported are seen therein. All aggregates of clinging, whether associated with the sense faculties or not, are called 'Saṅkhāraloka' (World of Formations) in the sense of being conditioned by causes and in the sense of repeatedly breaking down.

It is called 'Āhāra' (nutriment) because it brings its own fruit; it refers to a cause. All conditioned things that tend to persist due to that cause, and tend to persist from their arising until their dissolution, are called 'āhāraṭṭhitikā' (sustained by nutriment). By the phrase 'Sabbe sattā' (all beings), only formations are taken, as the teaching is given through the method of personal discourse (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) according to the inclination of those to be led.

'Yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharanti' means in as much space as the moon and sun revolve and occur. 'Virocanā' means because of the brilliance or illumination of those moon and sun; here the ablative case is used in the sense of cause. 'Disā bhanti' means all directions appear clearly, free from the mass of darkness. Alternatively, the word 'disā' is in the accusative plural. Therefore, it means the brilliant moon and sun illuminate as many directions as they shine upon. 'Tāva sahassadhā loko' means the Okāsaloka of a thousandfold variety by that measure, meaning a thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷas). 'Ettha' means in those thousand world-systems. 'Vaso' means the power known as psychic power (iddhi) prevails.

'Tampi' means the world of three kinds. 'Assa' is connected as: by this Blessed One, the world of formations was also known in every way. 'Eko loko' (One world) means, by the method mentioned below, the world of formations is of one kind through the common characteristic of occurring in dependence on causes for all conditioned things. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. In all these terms, only mundane states are intended as 'world', because supramundane states are not things to be fully understood (pariññeyya). The aggregates which are the objects of clinging are the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhas). Satta...
53:
Viññāṇaṭṭhiti (Stations of Consciousness) refers only to beings who have arisen in such and such ways. Beings diverse in body and diverse in perception; beings diverse in body and uniform in perception; beings uniform in body and diverse in perception; beings uniform in body and uniform in perception; and the three lower formless states—in these seven kinds of beings, consciousness establishes itself, hence they are called Viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Among those stations of consciousness, they are called 'Nānatta-kāya' because those beings have diverse bodies. They are called 'Nānatta-saññī' because those beings have diverse perceptions. In this term 'Nānatta-saññī', rebirth-linking consciousness is taken by way of perception as the head; this method applies to the remaining terms as well.

Among those seven, all humans and the six lower sense-sphere deva realms are called 'Nānatta-kāya Nānatta-saññī'. Their bodies are diverse because they are dissimilar to one another, and their rebirth-linking perceptions are diverse because they are of nine kinds. The Brahmakāyika devas in the three first-jhāna realms and the beings in the four woeful states are called 'Nānatta-kāya Ekatta-saññī'. Among them, the bodies of the three kinds of Brahmas, such as Brahmapārisajja, are dissimilar to one another, but their rebirth-linking perception is of only one kind by the power of the first-jhāna resultant. Similarly, all those in the woeful states have only the unwholesome-resultant rootless rebirth-linking perception. The Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara Brahmas born in the second-jhāna realms are called 'Ekatta-kāya Nānatta-saññī'. The bodily size of all those Brahmas is uniform, but their rebirth-linking perception is diverse by the power of the second-jhāna resultant and third-jhāna resultant. In the third-jhāna realms, the three realms such as Parittasubha; in the fourth-jhāna realms, the Vehapphala (excluding the perceptionless beings) and the five Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes)—the beings in these nine realms are called 'Ekatta-kāya Ekatta-saññī'. In all realms, diversity of body is not taken by diversity of radiance, but only by diversity of shape.

Perceptionless beings (Asaññasatta) do not enter into the count of stations of consciousness because they lack consciousness. The realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) is also not taken among the stations of consciousness where the function of consciousness is distinct, because its consciousness is subtle just as its perception is subtle, being neither consciousness nor non-consciousness. Therefore, only the remaining three, such as the sphere of infinite space (Ākāsānañcāyatana), are taken; together with those three, these seven should be understood as the stations of consciousness.

The eight worldly conditions (Lokadhamma) are: gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, happiness and pain. These are called worldly conditions because they are the nature of the world. In this context, it should be understood that only compliance (anurodha) and resistance (virodha) arising due to causes such as gain and loss are spoken of by the words 'gain' and so forth. The nine abodes of beings (Sattāvāsa) are the seven mentioned below...
54:
The seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti) together with the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) and the fourth formless realm are called the 'nine abodes of beings' (nava sattāvāsā). They are called 'abodes of beings' because beings dwell in these realms; it means the dwelling place of beings. In terms of meaning, the collection of beings in this context should be understood as being taken as the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). The ten bases (dasāyatanāni) refer to the ten bases excluding the mind-base (manāyatana) and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana).

In explaining this world of formations, within the three realms of existence, the three feelings (vedanā) alone are spoken of as the world by way of showing gratification. Likewise, the four nutriments (āhāra) are spoken of by way of showing the cause; the six internal bases (ajjhattikāyatanāni) by way of showing the basis for the grasping of a self; the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti) by way of showing existence with coarse perception; the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma) by way of showing compliance and opposition; and the ten bases (āyatanāni) by way of showing the coarse bases are spoken of as the world. By taking these feelings and so forth, all mental and material phenomena (nāmarūpa-dhamma) occurring in the three realms, which depend on them, are connected to them, or take them as objects, are implicitly included. However, by the other groups such as the single-fold group, those mental and material phenomena should be understood as being taken by their own nature.

In the phrases beginning with 'He knows the inclination' (āsayaṃ jānāti), it is called 'inclination' (āsaya) because the mind reaches and dwells in this state. Even when occurring in other objects, the mind enters and remains in a certain state according to its own nature; that dwelling place is of two kinds: the inclination towards the round of rebirth (vaṭṭāsaya) and the inclination towards the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭāsaya). Among those two, the inclination towards the round is also of two kinds by way of the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) and the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). The inclination towards the cessation of the round is of two kinds: conformity-patience (anulomika-khanti), which is called insight (vipassanā), and the knowledge of things as they are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa), which is called the path (magga). Thus it is said: 'The view of eternalism, the view of annihilationism, conformity-patience, and the knowledge of things as they are; these four are called inclinations' (as stated in the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā). The Blessed One knows these two kinds of inclinations of beings in all their aspects, even at times when they are not actively occurring. 'Underlying tendencies' (anusaya) refers to the seven kinds of underlying tendencies by way of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and so forth. 'Conduct' (carita) is spoken of in the description (niddesa) as 'good conduct and bad conduct'. Alternatively, 'conduct' means temperament; those temperaments are the six root temperaments such as lust (rāga) and so forth; they are of many varieties by way of mixing and combining. 'Resolution' (adhimutti) means the element of disposition (ajjhāsayadhātu); it is the state of being inclined by way of the mind's excessive desire for various objects. That resolution is of two kinds: low resolution (hīnādhimutti), which is an inclination towards low things, and superior resolution (paṇītādhimutti), which is an inclination towards superior things. By which resolution, those of no virtue and so forth...
55:
...associate with persons of low disposition; that inclination is called low resolution (hīnādhimutti). The resolution by which they associate with persons of superior disposition is called superior resolution (paṇītādhimutti). The Blessed One knows these two kinds of resolution in all their aspects. Those with little dust (apparajakkha) are those in whom the dust (defilement) of lust and so forth is slight; they are persons in whom the faults of lust and so forth are not thick. Those in whom the faults of lust and so forth are thick are called those with much dust (mahārajakkha). Those endowed with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya) such as faith and so forth, which serve as a strong support, are called those with sharp faculties, while those endowed with weak faculties are called those with dull faculties (mudindriya). Those endowed with good inclinations (āsaya) and so forth as mentioned below should be known as those of good disposition (svākāra), and those endowed with bad inclinations and so forth should be known as those of bad disposition (dvākāra). Persons who are easy to make understand the fixed course of rightness (sammattaniyāma) are called those easy to teach (suviññāpaya), and those who are the opposite (difficult to make understand) are called those difficult to teach (duviññāpaya). Those endowed with the support for realizing the Path and Fruit are called capable (bhabba), and those who are the opposite are called incapable (abhabba). In this way, it should be understood that by knowing the specific qualities of the phenomena within the mental continuities of beings, the world of beings (sattaloka) is also known, because there is no such thing as a 'being' apart from phenomena.

In the phrase "Ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ...pe... paññāsañca yojanāni," the remaining verb "hoti" (is) should be added and read. It refers to the measurement by way of circumference. The entire circumference of a world-system (cakkavāḷa) is three million, six hundred and ten thousand, three hundred and fifty (yojanas); this should be so connected. In that world-system, this earth (vasundharā) is reckoned to have a thickness of two hundred and forty thousand yojanas. In that context, the word "ettakaṃ" should be understood as an adverb. The water that supports the earth stands with such a measurement. In that world-system, [mountains] have the properties of being submerged and rising up. The great Himavā mountain is five hundred yojanas high. It has a trunk circumference of fifteen yojanas. There is a Jambū (rose-apple) tree, which is the name of a tree. That rose-apple tree is one hundred yojanas wide in all parts, in both length and breadth. It stands by the power of that rose-apple tree's greatness, its lasting for the duration of an aeon, and so forth. The Cakkavāḷa mountain stands encircling all that was mentioned below; this is called one world-element (lokadhātu). The letter "ma" in "lokadhātumayaṃ" is stated by way of euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). Otherwise, it should be connected as: this Cakkavāḷa mountain stands encircling that entire world-element.
56:
In this context, 'Tattha' means in that world-element (loka-dhātu). 'Tāvatiṃsabhavana' refers to the celestial city of Tāvatiṃsa. 'Asurabhavana' refers to the realm of the Asuras. The Avīci Great Hell likewise measures ten thousand yojanas. Although this great hell has a length and breadth of one hundred yojanas within its four iron walls, it should be understood as measuring ten thousand yojanas together with the sixteen surrounding Ussada hells. 'Tadanantaresu' means in the intervals between those world-systems (cakkavāḷas). They are called 'Lokantarika' because they exist in the open spaces between the world-systems. In the spaces between every three world-systems—similar to the space between three cartwheels or three alms bowls placed close together—there is a Lokantarika hell measuring eight thousand yojanas, which arises as a cold hell due to the unwholesome results of sentient beings. 'Anantāni' means that in the eight horizontal directions, the world-systems are infinite like space. However, they are finite above and below. In the phrase 'anantena buddhañāṇena' (by infinite Buddha-knowledge), the knowledge should be understood as 'infinite' because of its power to penetrate infinite things that can be known (ñeyya-dhamma).

The word 'attano' is a possessive case used in the sense of the ablative, meaning 'than oneself'. It should be connected as 'more distinguished than oneself in virtues' (guṇehi attano visiṭṭhatarassa). Here, the use of the suffix '-tara' is made by way of explaining the meaning of the word 'anuttaro' (unsurpassed), and not because there exists anyone who is superior. Indeed, in the world including the devas, there is no one even conceivable as an equal to the Tathāgata; how then could there be an equal? Therefore, He said, 'unequalled (asama) even in the virtue of morality,' and so on. In those virtues, He is called 'Asamasama' because He is equal to the Samma-sambuddhas who are themselves unequalled. He is called 'Appaṭima' because there is no counterpart (image) for this Venerable One. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. Therein, a mere resemblance is called 'paṭimā', while a close resemblance is called 'paṭibhāga'. One who stands as a rival or counterpart is to be understood as 'paṭipuggala'. 'Attanā' means 'than oneself'. In the terms such as 'purisadamma', they are called 'damma' because they are to be tamed. Although it could be said as 'dammapurisa', it is stated as 'purisadamma' by placing the qualifier at the end. The inclusion of 'men' (purisa) here is by way of the most prominent, as women are also to be tamed. They are made 'poisonless' (nibbisa) by the removal of the poison of hatred (dosa). 'Atthapada' means a word or sentence that expresses meaning. By being a single term, the Buddha's quality as the 'Charioteer of tamable men' (purisadammasārathi), which is not shared with others, is shown. Therefore, He said, 'Bhagavā hi,' and so on. 'Eight directions' refers to the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti). 'Unattached' (asajjamānā) means moving without attachment due to the attainment of mastery (vasībhāva). The present state of existence is called 'diṭṭhadhamma'. Because it is connected to that present life, it is called 'diṭṭhadhammika', meaning the benefit of the present world. Because it is to be reached by the power of kamma and defilements...
57:
...it is 'samparāya', the future world. Because it is connected to that future world, it is called 'samparāyika', meaning the benefit of the future world. The most excellent benefit is 'paramattha', which is Nibbāna. It is called 'sattha' (caravan) because it proceeds with necessary goods; it refers to a group of people (a caravan of traders) traveling to another region with capital for the purpose of trade. That caravan belongs to him; therefore, by the method of linguistics (nirutti), he is called 'Satthā' or 'Satthavāha' (caravan leader). Because the Blessed One is like that caravan leader, it is said, "The Blessed One is the Teacher (Satthā) also, the caravan leader (Satthavāha) also." Now, to show that meaning by the method of the Niddesa Pali, it is said, "Just as a caravan leader..." and so on. In that context, 'satthe' refers to the people in the caravan. It is called 'kantāra' (wilderness) because water is crossed (tārenti) there (kaṃ); it is a waterless forest region. Forest regions dominated by thieves and so on are also called 'kantāra' because they are similar in being difficult to traverse. Therefore, after speaking generally that "He crosses the wilderness," He said "wilderness of thieves" and so on to elaborate on that statement.

The word 'Bhagavato' is in the genitive case but stands in the ablative (nissakka) sense; it means 'by hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One'. It is like saying, "He learns from the teacher." Or it means 'in the presence of the Blessed One'. 'He took the sign in the sound' means that due to the habit of hearing the True Dhamma during the time of previous Buddhas, he recognized the nature of the sound, thinking, "This is called Dhamma." Indeed, it is only because of past efforts (pubbābhiyoga) that devotion (pasāda) arises in such animals during the hearing of the Dhamma, as in the case of the five hundred bats. Otherwise, there would be the implication that such devotion could arise in all animals. If it could arise, since the Blessed One is able to make all beings in infinite world-systems hear the Dhamma together with miracles in a single moment, there would be the implication that all beings would have been liberated even before this time. However, those such as devas, humans, nāgas, and garuḍas who are naturally endowed with knowledge of kamma-ownership and so on—only they, even if they lacked prior support (upanissaya), are able to first produce devotion which is a support for the ending of the cycle (vivaṭṭူpanissaya) by hearing the True Dhamma of the Blessed One, and not others; this should be understood. In the phrase "Oh... I indeed...", the meaning "having reflected on where I came from to this life and knowing I was a frog" is accomplished by the very words of wonder, "Oh... I indeed...", and thus it should be understood that it was not stated separately. 'Jalaṃ' means shining or radiant. In the verse "I am a frog," the mention of "in the water" shows the place of birth; by that, the state of being a land frog is excluded. Since water-born creatures like turtles also roam on land, to exclude that roaming on land, it is said "water-dweller (vārigocaro)", meaning one who moves and dwells only in water.

In the term 'vimokkhantikañāṇavasena', 'vimokkha' refers to the total liberation from defilements, which is the Path of Arahantship (aggamagga). Its end (anta) is the Fruit of Arahantship (aggaphala). The knowledge existing therein is 'vimokkhantika', which is the entire Buddha-knowledge together with Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Now, from the word 'Sammāsambuddha'...
58:
The phrase beginning with 'Yasmā' is stated to show the distinction of the term 'Buddha'. By the term 'Sammāsambuddha', the power of the Teacher's penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) is intended; however, by this term 'Buddha', the power of the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) is also intended. Therefore, it is stated: 'He also causes other beings to awaken,' and so forth.

The word 'Bhagavā' is a title of respect used out of reverence for the Teacher, who is supreme among all beings because He is endowed with all virtues such as morality (sīla). 'Seṭṭha' (Foremost) is a word denoting excellence because it is associated with noble qualities. Alternatively, it is called 'vacana' (word) because it is 'spoken' (vuccati), and since that meaning is noble, it is called 'Seṭṭha'. The same method should be understood for the term 'Uttama' (Supreme). In the term 'Garugāravayutta', the state of being respected is 'gārava' (reverence). Alternatively, 'gārava' refers to the act of showing respect because of being associated with weighty qualities. He is called 'Garugāravayutta' because He is endowed with a great quality of reverence that is unique to Him and not shared with disciples and others. Alternatively, it should be interpreted as a combination: He is a Teacher (garu) because He instructs all the world, and He is also endowed with reverence (gārava) for that very reason.

A name known by a particular occasion or situation is called 'Āvatthika'. Similarly, one known by physical appearance or characteristics is 'Liṅgika'. A name that arises due to a certain cause or quality is 'Nemittika'. A name that arises spontaneously without regard to the original etymological meaning is called 'Adhiccasamuppanna'. Therefore, it is said: 'without regard to the meaning of the word'. A name that arises from calling as one pleases is 'Yādicchaka'. In this context, external objects such as a staff are 'liṅga' (signs), while internal qualities such as the three knowledges (vijjā) are 'nimitta' (causes). Alternatively, that which is visible to the general public is 'liṅga', and that which is otherwise not apparent is 'nimitta'. 'Sacchikāpaññatti' is a designation based on the personal realization of all phenomena. Alternatively, it is a designation established by direct perception. Whatever qualities that name is based upon, those qualities are directly perceived by the Teacher. Therefore, like those qualities, that name itself is said to be 'realized' for the Teacher; for others, it is merely a conventional expression. 'Yaṃguṇanemittika' means that the name has arisen as a qualitative name because those qualities are the cause. The use of the plural 'vadanti' (they say) is either out of respect for the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, or it refers to the subsequent words of the Reciters (saṅgītikāra).

He is 'Bhagī' because He possesses the sixfold glory (bhaga) such as lordship (issariya). He is 'Bhajī' because He habitually resorts to and associates with noble qualities such as the paths and fruits, and secluded places such as forests. He is 'Bhāgī' (partaker) because He partakes in requisites such as robes and the essence of meaning (attharasa), as well as virtues such as morality; or it means He is an heir (dāyāda). He is 'Vibhattavā' because He has divided and analyzed the Jewel of the Dhamma through various methods such as brief instructions (uddesa) and detailed explanations (niddesa). He is called 'Bhagavā' because He has destroyed (bhagga) evil states such as lust (rāga); this connection should be applied in every instance. Since a teacher is also called 'Bhagavā' in the world, it is said 'Garu' (Teacher). Because He is the Teacher, He is also called 'Bhagavā'.
59:
He is called 'Bhagavā' because He possesses merit (bhaga) known as the sum of perfections (pāramitā). The phrase 'by many methods' (bahūhi ñāyehi) refers to being developed through numerous sequences of meditation, such as the development of the body (kāyabhāvanā). The term 'subhāvitattano' is a word with a genitive ending in the sense of the nominative, meaning 'one whose nature is well-developed'. He is called 'Bhavantago' because He has gone to Nibbāna, which is the end of existences. In all these instances, the derivation of the word 'Bhagavā' should be understood only through the method of linguistics (nirutti).

Now, in order to show the meaning presented by the nine terms in the descriptive verse beginning with 'Bhagī Bhajī', by condensing them into six terms in the verse beginning with 'Bhagavā', along with the methods of word-derivation and syntactic connection, it is stated: 'This, however, is another method' (ayaṃ pana aparo nayo), and so forth. In that text, in the term 'vaṇṇavipariyayo', the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so forth'. By that word 'iti', the three characteristics—transposition of letters, elision of letters, and connection with the meaning of the root—are included. 'Saddanayena' means by the method of grammatical characteristics. Since words such as 'pisodara' belong to the 'ākati' group (an open-ended class), it is said: 'taking the characteristic of inclusion in the pisodara group'. Inclusion itself is the characteristic. Indeed, making a word fall within that 'pisodara' group is called 'inclusion' (pakkhipana). 'Bhagya' means merit (kusala).

The four faults such as greed (lobha) are taken as single items. Those such as shamelessness (ahirika) are taken as pairs. Anger that envelops the mind through repeated provocation, such as 'he abused me', is called 'upanāha' (enmity). 'Makkha' (smearing) is the erasing of the gratitude for favors previously done by others. 'Palāsa' (domineering) is making oneself equal to others, such as the learned, in a competitive manner. 'Māyā' (deceit) is the concealing of one's existing faults. 'Sāṭheyya' (hypocrisy) is the displaying of virtues that one does not possess. 'Thambha' (stubbornness) is stiffness or lack of humility even toward those worthy of respect. 'Sārambha' (impetuosity) is the quality of trying to outdo others. 'Māna' (conceit) is the quality of haughtiness based on birth and so forth. 'Atimāna' (arrogance) is the quality of excessive haughtiness. 'Mada' (intoxication) is conceit itself that has reached the state of intoxication based on birth and so forth. That 'mada' is of twenty-seven types. 'Pamāda' (negligence) is the letting loose of the mind among the strands of sensual pleasure. Bodily misconduct and so forth are the three types of misconduct (duccarita). There are three types of corruption (saṅkilesa) by way of craving, views, and misconduct. Lust, hatred, and delusion are the stains (mala). These stains along with bodily misconduct and so forth are the three disharmonies (visama). Sensual perception, perception of ill-will, and perception of cruelty are the three types of perception (saññā). These perceptions themselves are the three types of thought (vitakka). Craving, views, and conceit are the proliferations (papañca). Seeking through perversion as beautiful, pleasant, permanent, and self are the four perversions (vipariyesa). Favoritism and so forth are the four wrong paths (agati). Cravings for requisites such as robes are the four arisings of craving (taṇhuppāda). Doubt regarding the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, and the training, and anger toward fellow practitioners...
60:
Doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, and anger towards fellow practitioners—these five are called the five 'mental spikes' (cetokhila). Lack of detachment from sensual pleasures, from the body, and from forms; indulgence in the pleasure of eating as much as one wants and the pleasure of sleep, etc.; and practicing the holy life aspiring for a certain group of devas or Brahmas—these five are called the five 'mental bondages' (cetovinibandha). Great delight in forms and so forth are called the five 'delights' (abhinandana). Anger, disparaging, envy, deceit, evil desire, and clinging to one's own views wrongly—these six are called the six 'roots of contention' (vivādamūla). Craving for forms and so forth are called the six 'classes of craving' (taṇhākāya). The opposites of the eight factors of the Noble Path, such as wrong view and so forth, are called the eight 'wrongnesses' (micchatta).

Dependent on craving, there is seeking; dependent on seeking, there is gain; dependent on gain, there is decision-making (analysis); dependent on decision-making, there is desire and lust; dependent on desire and lust, there is passionate attachment; dependent on passionate attachment, there is possession; dependent on possession, there is stinginess; dependent on stinginess, there is safeguarding; and because of safeguarding, many unwholesome states such as the taking up of sticks and weapons arise. Thus, there are nine 'things rooted in craving' (taṇhāmūlaka dhammā). The ten 'unwholesome courses of action' (akusalakammapatha) are the ten things such as killing living beings and so forth. The sixty-two 'views' (diṭṭhigata) consist of: four types of eternalism (sassatavāda), four types of partial-eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda), four types of extensionism (antānantikavāda), four types of eel-wriggling (amarāvikkhepavāda), two types of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppannavāda), sixteen doctrines of percipient survival (saññīvāda), eight doctrines of non-percipient survival (asaññīvāda), eight doctrines of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient survival (nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda), seven types of annihilationism (ucchedavāda), and five doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda).

The six classes of craving, such as craving for forms, each become eighteen through the power of sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). These eighteen become thirty-six through their occurrence in internal and external forms and so forth. Again, through the power of the three periods of time, the modes of craving become one hundred and eight. The word 'pabheda' (division) should be connected to each, such as 'lobhappabheda' (divisions of greed) and so forth. 'Sabbadarathapariḷāhakilesasatasahassāni' refers to the many hundreds of thousands of defilements that cause the distress known as 'daratha' (feverish anxiety) in beings. These divisions of defilements should be understood through the analysis of objects and so forth, and the analysis of the modes of occurrence. It is stated that He has conquered the five Maras. 'Parissaya' refers to dangers and calamities.

Having thus analyzed the meanings of the two terms 'bhajjavā' and 'bhaggavā', the text now states 'bhagavantatāya cassa' and so forth to show the meaning encompassed by those two terms. In that passage, 'satapuñjalakkhaṇadharassa' means: of the Blessed One, who possesses the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) produced by many hundreds of merits. Mastery (issariya) over one's own mind means the attainment of mastery over one's mind, both through the ability to perceive the non-repulsive in the repulsive and so forth, and through the power of mental concentration (cetosamādhi). In the phrase 'aṇimā laghimā' and so forth, the word 'ādi' includes these six: mahimā, patti, pākammaṃ, īsitā, vasitā, and yatthakāmāvasāyitā. Among these eight, making the body minute is called 'aṇimā'. Being light enough to perform actions such as walking in the air is called 'laghimā'. Making the body large is called 'mahimā'. Reaching any desired place is called 'patti'. Accomplishing desired results through the power of resolve and so forth is called 'pākammaṃ'. Sovereignty that makes things follow one's will is called 'īsitā'. Mastery in the various psychic powers (iddhividha) is called 'vasitā'.
61:
The state of being light, such as the ability to travel by foot as one wishes, is called Laghimā. Making the body large is called Mahimā. Reaching a desired place is called Patti. Accomplishing a desired goal through the power of resolution and so forth is called Pākamma. The state of mastery or lordship over oneself is called Īsitā. Proficiency in the various psychic powers is called Vasitā. Reaching the completion of any task, whether traveling through the sky or performing any other action, is called Yatthakāmāvasāyitā. Some also say, 'Displaying forms such as that of a youth is Yatthakāmāvasāyitā.' 'Sabbanga-paccanga-sirī' means the beauty of all major and minor limbs. The word 'atthi' (exists) follows. A desired goal that is accomplished quickly is called Lahu-sādhana. A desired goal that is accomplished slowly over a long period, such as the aspiration for Buddhahood, is called Garu-sādhana. The word 'Bhagavā' is formed according to the rules of grammar with the meaning 'The Blessed One possesses these glories.' All other meanings should be understood as being established through the method of nirutti (etymological interpretation).

In the words such as 'pīḷana-sankhata-santāpa-vipariṇāmaṭṭhena,' the word 'attha' (meaning/aspect) should be applied to each, such as 'pīḷanaṭṭha' (aspect of oppression) and 'sankhataṭṭha' (aspect of being conditioned). In that text, suffering (dukkha-sacca) has the characteristic of oppression by its own nature. The meaning of that suffering, defined as 'oppression itself is the meaning,' is called 'pīḷanaṭṭha.' This meaning is its inherent nature (sabhāva). Because that suffering is conditioned by the origin (samudaya-sacca), its aspect of being conditioned (sankhataṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of the origin. Furthermore, because the Path (magga) is extremely cool as it removes the heat of defilements, the aspect of burning (santāpaṭṭha) of suffering becomes manifest through the vision of the Path, as it is the opposite of it. Through the vision of Cessation (nirodha-sacca), which is of an unchanging nature, the aspect of change (vipariṇāmaṭṭha) becomes manifest. Four aspects are stated for a single natural phenomenon because they can be conceived through its own nature and through the exclusion of the other three truths. Regarding the Origin (samudaya-sacca), the aspect of accumulation (āyūhanaṭṭha) is its inherent nature because it brings things together. Its aspect of being a source (nidānaṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of suffering. Its aspect of bondage (samyogaṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of Cessation, which is disconnected from defilements. Its aspect of impediment (palibodhaṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of the Path, which is the means of escape.

Regarding Cessation (nirodha-sacca), the aspect of escape (nissaraṇaṭṭha) is its inherent nature. Its aspect of seclusion (vivekaṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of the Origin. Its aspect of being unconditioned (asankhataṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of the conditioned Path. Or, its aspect of being deathless (amataṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of suffering, which is of the nature of death. Regarding the Path (magga-sacca), the aspect of leading out (niyyānaṭṭha) is its inherent nature. Its aspect of being a cause (hetwaṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of the Origin, in the sense that 'this origin is the cause of suffering only, but this Path is the cause of attaining Nibbāna.' Its aspect of vision (dassanaṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of the extremely subtle Cessation, in the sense that 'this Path alone is the means of seeing.' Its aspect of dominance (adhipateyyaṭṭha) becomes manifest through the vision of excessive suffering. These sixteen aspects, starting with oppression (pīḷana), are called the sixteen modes.
62:
The state of having a body secluded from sensual pleasures is called physical seclusion (kāya-viveka). The eight attainments secluded from the hindrances and so forth are called mental seclusion (citta-viveka). Because they cause their respective fruits to be established in this [existence], they are called acquisitions (upadhi). These are the four acquisitions: the acquisition of sensual pleasure (kāmupadhi), the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhupadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesupadhi), and the acquisition of volitional formations (abhisankhārupadhi). Nibbāna, which is secluded from these four acquisitions, is called seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka). The Noble Path attained through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), or through the contemplations of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) and impermanence (aniccānupassanā), receives the names Void Liberation (suññata-vimokkha), Desireless Liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha), and Signless Liberation (animitta-vimokkha) respectively, according to the way of its arrival. This is called liberation (vimokkha) because it is liberated from defilements. Just as in the world, the word 'mekhalā' (girdle) is formed by taking one syllable from each of several words, so it is here as well. 'Mehanassa' refers to the private parts. 'Khassa' refers to the open space (opportunity).

In the words such as 'saha devehi' (together with devas), it is called 'sadevaka loka' (the world with devas) because it exists together with devas. The construction of 'that world with devas' and so forth should be understood in this way. By the word 'sadevaka,' the word 'deva' standing as an attribute in the term 'sadevaka' is intended. Since that word 'deva' is included within the term 'sadevaka,' it is a usage where the whole is used to represent a part. Otherwise, if only the world distinguished by devas were taken by that word 'sadevaka,' the five heavens of the sense sphere would not be included; the same applies to the higher realms. In the word 'samāraka' (with Māra), by the word 'Māra,' all the Vasavatti devas who accompany that Māra are included; thus it is said, 'the inclusion of the sixth sense-sphere heaven.' 'Brahmakāyika' refers to the Brahmas of the first jhāna realm. The inclusion of those Brahmas starting from the first jhāna Brahmas up to the formless Brahmas is called 'the inclusion of Brahmas starting with the Brahmakāyika.' Since the word 'loka' (world) is also common to the world of space (okāsa-loka) and so forth, the word 'pajā' (beings) is used to specifically denote the world of beings (satta-loka); thus it is said, 'the inclusion of the world of beings by the word pajā.' Since the devas by rebirth (upapatti-deva) are included by the word 'sadevaka' and the devas by purity (visuddhi-deva) are included by the word 'sassamaṇa' (with recluses), it is said, 'the inclusion of devas by convention and the remaining humans by the word sadevamanussa.' Therein, devas by convention (sammuti-deva) are kings; the remaining humans are those left over from devas by convention, recluses, and brahmins. Since the word 'pajā,' which specifically refers to the world of beings, is taken separately, the use of the word 'loka' in 'sadevakaṃ lokaṃ' is restricted to the world of space (okāsa-loka); thus it is said, 'the world of space by the three words.' This is stated according to the primary meaning expressed by the three terms such as 'sadevaka.' However, in reality, the world of beings such as devas and Māras, which is an attribute of the world of space, is also included here.
63:
Just as in the phrase "saputto āgato" (he arrived with his son), the son and others are understood, so too in this context, the meaning should be understood through its inherent capacity. In this method, by bringing in the conjunction "ca" (and), it should be connected as: the okāsaloka (world of space) together with the devas, together with the Māras, and together with the Brahmās; and the sattaloka (world of beings, pajā) together with the ascetics and brahmins, and together with the devas and humans. Here, by taking the okāsaloka and the sattaloka, it should be noted that the saṅkhāraloka (world of formations), which is the basis for the designation of those two, is also included because it is inseparable from them.

Other teachers, however, say that by the five terms beginning with "sadevaka," only the sattaloka is taken, being qualified by its own constituent parts such as the devas; and by taking that sattaloka, its support, the okāsaloka, and the saṅkhāraloka, which is the domain of the designation of both, are already included. In the view of those teachers as well, the word "pajā" should be made an adjective of the word "loka" and connected as: "the world of beings (pajā) together with the devas... the world of beings together with the ascetics and brahmins."

The arūpāvacara-loka (formless realm) is taken by the method of remainder (pārisesanaya), because the other realms have already been taken by other terms. By taking Māra, the upapatti-devas (devas by rebirth) who are headed by him and similar to him are included; thus it is said, "the six heavens of the sense sphere (chakkāmāvacaradevaloka)." Among the eight assemblies—the assembly of nobles (khattiya), the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā—the four assemblies beginning with the Four Great Kings are already included by the terms such as "sadevaka." Therefore, it is said "by way of the four assemblies," meaning that here, by the term "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ," the assembly of ascetics and the assembly of brahmins are taken, and by the term "sadevamanussaṃ," the assembly of nobles and the assembly of householders are taken. This connects with the statement that the human world is taken. In that context, "human world" means the collective of humans; therefore, it is said, "or the rest of the entire world of beings."

To show another alternative (vikappa), it is said, "the human world together with the conventional gods (sammuti-deva)." By the word "deva," conventional gods (kings) are taken, and by the words "samaṇa, brāhmaṇa, manussa," the rest of the humans are taken. Thus, in both alternatives, the word "pajā" is qualified by the word "manussa" and is called "manussapajā" (human beings). Again, because that collective of humans exists together with the kings, they are called "sadevā." Because they are both with kings and are humans, they are called "sadevamanussā"; that sadevamanussa-pajā is taken. Again, what kind of human beings? It is said, "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ" (human beings together with ascetics and brahmins). In this way, the grammatical derivation (vigraha) should be made so that only humans are taken by the word "pajā." Otherwise, since all humans are taken as qualifiers, there would be no human who is the meaning of another term, and thus taking only humans would not be complete. Now, by the word "pajaṃ"...
64:
By this term [pajaṃ], wishing to show the inclusion of the remaining beings such as Nāgas, he said, "or the rest of the entire world of beings." Here too, it should be connected as: the rest of the entire world of beings by way of the four assemblies, or the rest of the entire world of beings together with the conventional gods and humans.

Having shown the connection by taking the world in parts through this sequence of words, he now says "api cettha" etc., to show the fruitfulness of each qualifier even in the case of taking all worlds without division by each individual term. "Ukkaṭṭhapariocchedato" means that by way of defining and knowing the noble beings included in the divine destination (deva-gati), the sound of fame (kitti-sadda) spreads upwards, making itself heard to those who listen through the word "sadevaka" which is its own constituent part; this is how it should be connected. "Anusandhikkama" means the sequence of connection of meanings and words, the sequence of understanding.

Since the term "abhiññā" is a designation made by dropping the letter "ya," he said "abhiññāyā." "Samantabhadrakattā" means being excellent in all parts. "Sāsanadhamma" is the pariyattidhamma (scriptural Dhamma) that reveals the paṭipattisāsana (dispensation of practice) and paṭivedhasāsana (dispensation of realization). This triad beginning with "buddhasubodhitatāya" is stated by way of the cause (hetu), the nature (sarūpa), and the result (phala) of the Dhamma. Similarly, the triad beginning with "nāthapabhava" is the same. The two triads in the middle should be understood as being stated only by way of the result. "Kiccasuddhiyā" means by the purification of the task, which is called the good practice of those who, having heard the Dhamma, practice according to what they have heard.

Now, the Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma that is good in the beginning (ādikalyāṇa) and so forth, reveals to the listeners the sāsanabrahmacariya (holy life of the dispensation) and the maggabrahmacariya (holy life of the path). The terms such as "sātthaṃ" are stated as qualifiers of the word "brahmacariya" which reveals that holy life; they are not stated as qualifiers of the word "dhamma." Wishing to explain the meaning in various ways, he said the words beginning with "sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ." In that context, the three trainings (sikkhā) and the entire sacred text (tantidhamma) are called sāsanabrahmacariya. Indeed, when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, just as he reveals the trainings such as virtue (sīla), he also reveals the sacred text that expresses those trainings, because the pariyattidhamma is a collection of sounds and meanings. "Yathānurūpaṃ" means as is appropriate. Indeed, the sāsanabrahmacariya and maggabrahmacariya included in the three trainings are "sāttha" (with meaning) because they are endowed with the excellence of meaning, and because they exist with the purpose and meaning of the excellence of attainment to be reached higher and higher; but they are not "sabyañjana" (with phrasing). The sāsanabrahmacariya known as the sacred text (tantidhamma) is both "sāttha" and "sabyañjana" because it exists with the aforementioned meaning and purpose. Although the tribal languages of the Kirāta and Milakkha also have meaning and phrasing, intending the connection with distinguished meaning and phrasing...
65:
Just as it is said, 'Devadatta with hands, Devadatta with wealth,' so it is said, 'with meaning and with phrasing' (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*). In this context, it means 'with meaning' (*sāttha*) due to the perfection of meaning (*atthasampatti*), and 'with phrasing' (*sabyañjana*) due to the perfection of phrasing (*byañjanasampatti*). In that Pali text, the perfection of meaning (*atthasampatti*) refers to that quality of the Dhamma whereby those who hear the meaning and practice accordingly reach the end of all suffering; it means the state of having a perfect meaning. Perfection of phrasing (*byañjanasampatti*) refers to the ability to make even deep meanings clear through the natural expression (*sabhāvanirutti*) of the Magadhan language (*Māgadhī*), which is complete with lax (*sithila*) and aspirated (*dhanita*) sounds; it means the state of having perfect phrasing.

Now, to show the meaning according to the method of the *Nettippakaraṇa*, terms such as 'explanation' (*saṅkāsanā*) are mentioned. Among those six terms, *saṅkāsanā* means that which is shown or illuminated briefly; this meaning should be understood through the sense of the object (*kammasādhana*), and the same applies to the remaining terms. The initial showing is *pakāsanā*. Both of these are the detailed exposition of what is called the brief statement (*uddesa*). Repeating what has been said once constitutes *vivaraṇa* (opening) and *vibhajana* (analysis). Both of these are the exposition of the detailed statement (*niddesa*). Describing more extensively what has been opened and making known in various ways what has been analyzed are *uttānīkaraṇa* (making clear) and *paññatti* (designation). Both of these are the detailed exposition of what is called the further detailed statement (*paṭiniddesa*). The phrase 'by the combination of meaningful words' (*atthapadasamāyogato*) means that the aforementioned six terms are called 'meaningful words' (*atthapada*) because they analyze the meaning of the scriptures (*pariyatti*); it means the state of being endowed with portions of meaning because of being associated with those meaningful words. In a word that is not yet complete, the syllable at the beginning or middle is called *akkhara*; or a word consisting of a single syllable is called *akkhara*. A word ending in a case-suffix is called *pada*. Because it manifests the meaning expressed by a word, it is called *byañjana*, which refers to a sentence (*vākya*). Analyzing the very meaning that has been stated in various ways is called *ākāra*. The etymological definition of the meaning expressed by the *ākāra* is called *nirutti*. The detailed expansion of the etymological meaning is called *niddesa*.

Alternatively, because it is taught: 'He explains briefly by syllables (*akkhara*), he shows initially by words (*pada*), he opens by phrasing (*byañjana*), he analyzes by modes (*ākāra*), he makes clear by linguistic definitions (*nirutti*), and he designates by detailed expositions (*niddesa*)'; the words expressing the brief statement (*uddesa*) known as *saṅkāsanā* and *pakāsanā* are called *akkhara* and *pada*. The words expressing the detailed statement (*niddesa*) known as *vivaraṇa* and *vibhajana* are called *byañjana* and *ākāra*. The words expressing the further detailed statement (*paṭiniddesa*) known as *uttānīkaraṇa* and *paññatti* are called *nirutti* and *niddesa*. It is called 'with phrasing' (*sabyañjana*) due to being endowed with those words.

In the terms such as 'profundity of meaning' (*atthagambhīratā*), 'meaning' (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the Pali text or the result of a cause. 'Dhamma' refers to the Pali text or the cause. 'Teaching' (*desanā*) refers to the preaching of the Dhamma according to its nature. 'Penetration' (*paṭivedha*) refers to the non-perverted understanding of the aforementioned meaning and so forth. These four, beginning with meaning, are called 'profound' (*gambhīra*) because they are difficult for those of dull wisdom to descend into and find a footing, just as the great ocean is for creatures like hares. Among those four, penetration (*paṭivedha*) is also...
66:
Because it relies on the meaning and is of the same nature as the meaning, it is said: 'It is with meaning (*sāttha*) due to the profundity of meaning (*atthagambhīratā*) and the profundity of penetration (*paṭivedhagambhīratā*).' Although the teachings (*desanā*) rely on the meaning, because they themselves take the form of phrasing, it is said: 'It is with phrasing (*sabyañjana*) due to the profundity of the Dhamma (*dhammagambhīratā*) and the profundity of the teaching (*desanāgambhီratā*).' The various types of knowledge regarding the aforementioned meaning and so forth are the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), such as the analytical insight into meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*). Among those analytical insights, *nirutti* means the explanation of the Pali terms by extracting and defining them; it means etymological definition (*nibbacana*). The knowledge regarding the other three analytical insights is the analytical insight into ready wit (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). Since worldly people gain confidence in meanings only through the words of a person worthy of trust, and not through the meaning itself, it is said 'due to being trustworthy' (*saddheyyato*), etc. The word *kevala* is a synonym for 'entirety'; thus it is said 'by way of being entirely complete' (*sakalaparipuṇṇabhāvena*). Here, the word *brahmacariya* (holy life) indicates the entire Dispensation (*sāsana*) which encompasses the Threefold Training (*sikkhattaya*); thus it is said 'due to being encompassed by the Threefold Training,' etc.

To show the same meaning in another way, 'moreover' (*api ca*), etc., is said. In that context, 'with origin' (*sanidāna*) means being together with the introductory words (*nidāna*) that show the place, time, and so forth. 'With circumstances of arising' (*sauppattika*) means being endowed with logical reasons such as the occasion for the discourse (*atthuppatti*). The sequence of linking the Pali text here is as follows: 'The Brahmin Verañja heard: "Friends, the ascetic Gotama... is staying..."; and "A good report of the reputation of that Master Gotama has spread thus: 'Indeed, that Blessed One... proclaims...'"; and "He teaches the Dhamma... good in the end; and while teaching, he proclaims the holy life (*brahmacariya*) endowed with qualities such as being with meaning and with phrasing..."; and "Indeed, the sight of such Arahants is good." Having heard this, the Brahmin Verañja approached the Blessed One.'

In the Commentary, however, it is stated that the Brahmin approached after forming the intention: 'Even the mere sight is good.' Since the passage beginning with 'Indeed, it is good' (*sādhu kho pana*) is stated as the Brahmin's reflection, it might seem that the word 'heard' (*assosi*) should be linked immediately after the words 'proclaims the holy life' (*brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti*). Nevertheless, because it is stated as delimited by the word *iti*, which has the sense of the aforementioned illustration in 'Indeed, the sight of such Arahants is good,' and because the word *iti* is not seen elsewhere, and because the Pali proceeds in another way by showing a further action with 'Then the Brahmin Verañja' (*atha kho verañjo*), it is appropriate to link the word 'heard' (*assosi*) only immediately after the statement 'Indeed, the sight of such Arahants is good' according to the aforementioned sequence. For the Teacher of the Commentary also [intended] the Brahmin's desire according to what he himself had heard...
67:
It should be understood that the phrase 'Even just seeing [him] is excellent' is said with the intention of showing the reason for approaching. 

The phrase 'With hot water like cold water' is said by way of a slip of the tongue in recitation. Since the Brahmin has an unpeaceful nature, it is appropriate for him to be like hot water. Therefore, the meaning should be taken as 'just as hot water becomes one with cold water.' Alternatively, because the Blessed One is endowed with the radiance of wisdom, he is like hot water; and the Brahmin, being devoid of that wisdom, is like cold water. Thus it should be understood. 'Ekībhāvaṃ' means the state of having a single nature through the act of rejoicing. In the passages beginning with 'yāya,' it should be construed as: 'the talk by which the Brahmin rejoiced is called sammodanīya-kathā (courteous talk).'

In that context, 'khamanīyaṃ' (endurable) is an inquiry whether this body, which is full of suffering, can be endured. 'Yāpanīyaṃ' (supportable) is an inquiry whether one can sustain oneself through the maintenance known as long-term continuity. Being free from disease, it is called 'appābādha' (free from illness). Being free from a difficult livelihood, it is called 'appātaṅka' (free from affliction). Because of the ability to rise quickly and without difficulty to perform various duties, it is called 'lahuṭṭhāna' (lightness in rising). 'Balaṃ' (strength) is an inquiry whether there is physical strength capable of enduring all tasks. 'Phāsuvihāra' means living in comfort. The word 'saraṇīya' itself is lengthened to 'sāraṇīya.' Therefore, it is said, 'It is called sāraṇīya because it is of a nature to be remembered.' 'Pariyāyehi' means by various reasons.

'Bhāva' refers to action. The neuter word occurring in that action is called 'bhāva-napuṃsaka-niddesa,' meaning it is an adverbial word. 'Ekamante' means at one side, in a suitable place. 'Khaṇḍiccādi-bhāvaṃ' refers to the state of having broken teeth, grey hair, and so forth. 'Rājaparivaṭṭe' means the succession of kings. It means being aged due to being born in an ancient noble lineage, not just by age; thus it is said, 'in a lineage that has existed for a long time.' Because he takes on the greatness of wealth, he is called 'mahallaka'; thus it is said, 'endowed with greatness of wealth.' In the sense of 'vibhāvane,' it means in the sense of clearly manifesting the natural state. 'Does not pay homage' means not recognizing that [the Buddha] is worthy of homage; it means one who has such a nature of non-recognition. In the phrase 'rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā' (is form permanent or impermanent?), it also means 'is it of a permanent nature or an impermanent nature?' In the phrase 'aniccaṃ vā,' the word 'vā' (or) has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa).

'Sampatijāta' means born at that moment, immediately after birth. In the passage 'Having walked seven steps... he looked,' it should be understood that the looking performed before walking is spoken of as if it were performed after, similar to phrases like 'having closed the door, he leaves.'
68:
It should be understood as being spoken of as if it were already done. 'He looked' means that when the miracle of the opening of the worlds (lokavivaraṇa) occurred, he looked with his physical eye (maṃsacakkhu). 'Seṭṭho' means more excellent or praised. 'Patimānesi' means he honored or worshipped. 'Āsabbiṃ' means supreme or noble.

'That word' refers to the words beginning with 'Brahmin, I am not that person.' 'Should be established through knowledge' means he should be established in the fruit of Arahantship. 'By way of birth' means by way of births such as Kshatriya and so forth. 'By way of rebirth' means by way of rebirth among the devas. 'Āviñchantī' means they pull or draw. The Brahmin, thinking that the essence of harmony (sāmaggirasa) consisting of acts like paying homage does not exist in the Blessed One, said 'arasarūpo' (one who is tasteless). To show that the Blessed One is 'arasarūpo' because of the absence of the essence of harmony in things like craving for forms, which is the opposite of what the Brahmin thought, [the Buddha] said 'vatthārammaṇādi' and so forth, showing how the term 'sāmaggirasa' applies to forms, tastes, and so on.

'Made like a palm-tree stump' (tālāvatthukatā) means that the basis of those forms, tastes, etc., in the mental continuum is made like the site of uprooted palm trees. In this sense, the middle word is elided (majjhepada-lopa) and the letter 'la' is lengthened. Thus it is said, 'like a palm-tree site.' It should be understood that the word 'tālāvatthukatā' is a qualifier placed at the end, meaning 'those whose basis is made like a palm-tree site.' A palm tree with its head cut off is called 'avatthu' (without basis) because it is no longer a cause for leaves, fruits, and so on. Similarly, the mental continuum, which is the basis of those forms, tastes, etc., is made to be 'without basis' like that palm-tree stump. Thus those cravings for forms and so on are called 'tālāvatthukatā.' Taking the meaning by way of another word's meaning (Bahuvrīhi compound) in this way is easy to understand according to the method mentioned before. Therefore, to show the distinction, it is said, 'They are made like a palm tree with its head cut off.' In this way, even though the cravings for forms, tastes, etc., which are like the head [of the tree], are cut off, the mental continuum, which is the basis of those cravings and is like the palm-tree stump, continues to exist until the time of Parinibbāna.

If the meaning is taken by way of a descriptive compound (Kammadhāraya) according to the text of the Commentary, then forms, tastes, and so on would themselves become like palm-tree stumps. The statement in the Sāratthadīpanī to avoid this fault—that forms, tastes, etc., are wholesome or unwholesome—does not agree with the Pali text 'those things are abandoned by the Tathāgata' nor with the Commentary 'craving for forms known as the enjoyment of sensual pleasure.' It should be understood that even for Arahants (khīṇāsava), since the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions occur until Parinibbāna, it is not appropriate to say those wholesome and unwholesome things are like a palm tree with its head cut off. Alternatively, without considering whether the palm tree with its head cut off stands or not, it is said 'made like a palm-tree stump' merely by comparing it to the nature of not arising again.
69:
There is no fault in taking the meaning by way of an adjectival compound (visesana-samāsa). Since the word 'anu' occurs in the sense of 'after', it is said: 'there is no occurrence afterwards (pacchābhāva)', and so forth. 'Anu abhāvaṃ gatā' means having reached non-existence by way of the nature of not arising afterwards. 'Anacchariyā' means performing successive wonders. 'Yañca kho tvaṃ vadesi' means: that cause which you stated as the absence of the essence of harmony (sāmaggīrasa) such as paying homage, in the sense of being without essence—that cause does not exist.

'Sandhāya bhāsitamatthaṃ' refers to the meaning intended when the Brahmin said, 'The Venerable Gotama is without enjoyment (nibbhoga),' and so forth, and the meaning intended when the Blessed One admitted to being 'without enjoyment' in himself; it refers to the meaning spoken with such intention.

'Kulasamudācārakammaṃ' means the conduct and actions of a clan. Misconduct arising from the body-door is called bodily misconduct (kāyaduccarita). 'Anekavihitā' means having many varieties.

'Pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa' refers to the meaning of sensual lust (kāmarāga) associated with the five cords of sensual pleasure, such as visible forms, by way of extreme attachment. By this term 'pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa', it is shown that the sensual lust that arises in Non-returners (anāgāmīs) by way of attachment and delight in clothing, ornaments, etc., is not true sensual lust. This is because the lust occurring in those Non-returners is included within lust for fine-material existence (rūparāga), and so forth. In the term 'avasesānaṃ', it is stated that identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and doubt (vicikicchā) are abandoned by the first path (the Path of Stream-entry), while the remaining defilements are abandoned by all four paths. Therefore, it is said: 'accordingly' (yathānurūpaṃ).

'Jigucchati maññe' means 'as if he loathes', or it is understood as 'he loathes'. 'Akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena' means by reason of being produced from ignorance (aññāṇa).

8-10. 'Tatra' means among the two varieties of meanings mentioned above. In this context, since the word 'gabbha' is also a synonym for rebirth (paṭisandhi), it is said: 'for the sake of obtaining rebirth in the deva world'. 'Apunabbhavabhūtā' refers to the arising of phenomena (dhammas) that occur moment by moment.

11. 'Dhammadhātu' refers to Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa). Because that knowledge bears or upholds the Dhamma according to reality, it is called 'Dhammadhātu'. 'Desanāvilāsappatto' means 'desanāvilāsa' is the ability to teach by varying the method according to one's wish; 'patto' means having reached that. 'Karuṇāvipphāraṃ' is the pervasion of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) toward all beings. Desiring to clarify the characteristic of such a quality (tādi-guṇa) through a simile, it is said: 'having a mind like the earth'.
70:
Precisely because of that nature of a mind like the earth, since there is a nature of not being angry, he is called 'one of unshakeable nature' (akuppadhammatā). 'Jātiyā anugataṃ' means birth (rebirth) is continuously bound. 'Jarāya anusaṭaṃ' means enveloped by old age (jarā). 'Vaṭṭakhāṇubhūtaṃ' means being like a stump fixed immovably in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) because of the inability to be pulled out from it. Because there is constant danger from death for beings who have been born, he said: 'even if one were to die today', and so forth. 'Appaṭisamaṃ purejātabhāvaṃ' means the state of being born first through the peerless Noble Birth, meaning the state of being the eldest of all.

By saying 'pi' instead of 'api', he shows that the word 'pi' is a separate particle (nipāta). 'Sammā adhisayitāni' means well-rested upon without causing injury by the feet and so forth. Although the root 'saya' (to lie/rest) is intransitive (akammaka), it should be understood as becoming transitive (sakammaka) when preceded by the prefix 'adhi'. 'Nakhasikhā' refers to the tips of the claws. Since the wings of birds stand in the place of hands and feet, he said: 'having curled hands and feet'. 'Ettha' means in a place of light. 'Nikkhamantānaṃ' means among the young chicks that are coming out (hatching); here the genitive case (sāmivacana) is used in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa). 'Aṇḍakosa' means the egg-shell.

The world itself is called the 'abode of the world' (lokasannivāsa). Because he realized [the truth] at this tree, the tree is called 'Bodhi'. Because he himself knows, or because one knows by means of that knowledge, both the Path-knowledge and Omniscient Knowledge are called 'Bodhi'. Because it is to be known, Nibbāna is also called 'Bodhi'. The second example, 'antarā ca bodhi', is stated to show that the word 'Bodhi' denotes a tree even without the word 'rukkha' (tree). 'Varabhūrimedhaso' means one of vast wisdom like the great earth. 'The three knowledges' (tisso vijjā) are so called because the Path of Arahatship produces the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa), also known as Right View occurring together with itself, as well as the other two lofty (mahaggata) knowledges, by way of destroying the defilements that obstruct them. In the case of 'the six direct knowledges' (cha abhiññā), the method is the same. 'Sāvakapāramīñāṇa' refers to all mundane and supramundane knowledge to be attained by the Chief Disciples. In the case of 'Paccekabodhiñāṇa', the method is the same.

'Opammasampaṭipādanaṃ' means making the meaning of the simile consistent with the thing being compared (upameyya). 'Atthena' means by the meaning of the thing being compared. By the words 'sharpness, clarity, and courage', he shows the state of Insight (vipassanā) reaching equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā). By the words 'time of maturity', he shows the attainment of the state of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī). At that time, because that insight is as if it were carrying the embryo of Path-knowledge, he said: 'the time of taking the embryo'. 'Anupubbādhigatena' means attained in the sequence of the first path, etc. 'Caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ' means 'certainly, let the skin, sinews, and bones...'
71:
Indeed, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up. This is the effort (viriya) endowed with four factors.

In the passage beginning with "Chando kāmo," weak greed (lobha) occurring in the mode of wishing is called chanda (desire) because of the sense of wanting. Greed that is stronger than that and has the sense of being infatuated is called rāga (lust). Greed that is even stronger than that is called chanda-rāga. Greed occurring by the power of thinking about signs and features is called saṅkappa (thought). Greed occurring only by the power of thinking that is stronger than that is called rāga. Greed even stronger than that is called saṅkappa-rāga. This distinction is stated according to the different modes of occurrence and the different stages of the same single greed.

## Explanation of the First Jhāna

"Seyyathidaṃ" means "How is that?" "Etaṃ" is either an emphasis (avadhāraṇa) on the preceding word or refers to this collection of meanings. "Tannissaraṇato" means because it is the escape from those sense pleasures. "Esā" is the word "eva." The kāmadhātu is the realm of sense pleasures, and nekkhamma is the first jhāna. "Esā" is a restriction (niyama). Tadaṅga-viveka, vikkhambhana-viveka, samuccheda-viveka, paṭippassaddhi-viveka, and nissaraṇa-viveka are called tadaṅga-viveka, etc. Kāya-viveka, citta-viveka, and upadhi-viveka are called kāya-viveka, etc. In this discussion of jhāna, since samuccheda-viveka, etc., are not possible, only the three kinds of seclusion (kāya, citta, upadhi) should be taken here. "Niddese" refers to the Mahāniddesa. "Tattheva" refers to the Mahāniddesa itself. "Vibhaṅge" refers to the Jhānavibhaṅga. "Evañhi sati" means when both kinds of sense pleasures are included.

"Purimena" means by the first, which is kāya-viveka. "Ettha" means in this pair of kāya-viveka and citta-viveka. "Dutiyena" means by the second, which is citta-viveka. "Etesaṃ" refers to the meaning of these words "vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi," which express the two kinds of seclusion from objective sense pleasures (vatthukāma) and defilement sense pleasures (kilesakāma) according to the method already mentioned; this genitive case is in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa). "It is the abandonment of the cause of foolishness" follows as a continuation (anuvattana). For unwholesome states are the cause of foolishness. "Āsayaposana" means the purification and development of the inclination (āsaya). It is connected that "only the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are mentioned in the Vibhaṅga." The reason for mentioning only the hindrances is stated as: "Because of wanting to show the state of being an opponent that abandons the defilements which are contrary to the jhāna factors to be mentioned above." In that statement, "above" refers to the jhāna factors to be mentioned starting with "savitakkaṃ," and it means because of wanting to show the state of being an opponent that suppresses their own enemies (the hindrances). There is also a variant reading: "Because of wanting to show the state of being an opponent that suppresses the enemies of the jhāna factors to be mentioned above." In that reading, the meaning is: "Because of wanting to show the state of being an opponent that suppresses the hindrances as direct enemies of the jhāna factors to be mentioned above, only those hindrances are mentioned in the Vibhaṅga."
72:
The wise say: Peṭaka is a treatise that follows the methods of the Nettippakaraṇa composed by the Elder Mahākaccāyana. Because that treatise is an explanation of the Piṭakas, it is called "Peṭaka." It means "in that Peṭaka treatise." Thinking about the object is called vitakka, therefore it is called "ūhana" (pondering). The occurrence in the object, like the occurrence in the object of one who strikes it repeatedly saying "matter, matter," etc., should be understood as "āhanana" (striking) and "pariyāhanana" (striking all around). Bringing the mind to the object means making it face the object. "Anusañcaraṇa" means wandering around; and that is just the arising of vicāra in that mode at different moments. In reality, in the ultimate sense, there is no wandering of a single state. It is the same in other such instances. "Anumajjana" means repeated stroking. "Tattha" means in that object. It makes the co-nascent (sahajāta) states associate by performing its own function. "In a certain place" means in all minds accompanied by vicāra except for the second jhāna. Although vitakka arises together with vicāra, it is called "the first falling upon" (paṭhamābhinipāta) with reference to its mode of placing [the mind] on the object. Vitakka has an impetus because its nature is not calmed; for that very reason, it becomes a factor to be abandoned in the second jhāna. The phrase "in the first and second jhānas" is said with reference to the fivefold method (pañcakanaya). To show that there is no jhāna devoid of factors, he said "like a tree," etc.

If the word viveka is taken as a state (bhāvasādhana), it is said "because of that seclusion (viveka)"; if taken otherwise, it is said "in that seclusion." Pīti (rapture) pleases or increases. "Pharaṇarasa" means having the function of pervading the body with refined material qualities. "Sātalakkhaṇa" means having a desirable nature, meaning sweetness. "Anuggaha" (favoring) means repeatedly supporting or benefiting the associated states without oppressing or neglecting them. "Vananta" is just the forest. "Udakanta" is just the water. By the phrase "because of being evident at such and such a time," he shows that when a desirable object is obtained, although sukha (happiness) exists, it is not evident, and only pīti is evident; but at the time of experiencing the taste obtained, sukha is more evident than the existing pīti. Here, experiencing the taste obtained should be understood only by way of mental happiness (cetasika-sukha), not by way of bodily happiness (kāyika-sukha), because bodily happiness is not associated with pīti and is not intended here. The passage beginning with "This rapture also" shows an aññapadattha-samāsa (exocentric compound), or it shows a taddhita suffix in the sense of "possessing that." By the second alternative, by the power of the aññapadattha-samāsa itself, he shows that "vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ" is a single term and that the case ending is not dropped.
73:
The term "gaṇanānupubbatā" (numerical sequence) is spoken with reference to the sequence of the teaching. This statement "paṭhamaṃ samāpajjati" (attains the first) is spoken in terms of a beginner (ādikammika); however, for yogis who have mastered the attainments (vasī), jhana arises even out of sequence. "Jhāpeti" means it burns. Regarding how the close contemplation of insight (vipassanā), which has characteristics such as impermanence as its object, belongs to the Path (magga), which has Nibbāna as its object, it is said: "vipassanāya," etc. In that text, "accomplished by the Path" means that the close contemplation of characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna) is accomplished for oneself without confusion, by means of one's own Path which abandons perversions (vipallāsa) such as permanence. Alternatively, "by the Path" means by the function of the Path, which is the abandoning of perversions.

"Añño" means a being. "Avuttattā" means because it is not stated as "one-pointedness of one's own mind" (sacittēkaggatā) in the Vibhaṅga Pali. "Vuttattā" means because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga of that Jhana Pali.

## Commentary on the Second Jhana

"Ajjhattaṃ" (internal) is stated as an attribute of jhana, meaning "in this context, internal relating to oneself is intended." In reality, jhana is not strictly internal (ajjhatta), as only the six sense bases possess that nature. Small waves are called vīci. Large waves are called taraṅga. The words "santā honti samitā" (they are peaceful, they are calmed), etc., are synonyms for each other; the meaning is that they are transcended by the power of jhana. "Appitā" means they are brought to destruction. "Pariyāyo" (metaphor) means that because the term "jhana" is used for the requisites of jhana, it is a figurative expression, not in the ultimate sense (paramattha).

## Commentary on the Third Jhana

"Tadadhigamāya" means for the attainment of the third Path. "Upapattito ikkhati" means one sees through reasoning, such that the state of formations being equitably borne occurs through association with wisdom and through practice. "Vipulāya" means having reached the state of being great (mahaggata).
