"Thāmagatāya" means having reached a state of firmness due to the absence of initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), and rapture (pīti); for this very reason, it will be said later: "because it is not oppressed by initial application, sustained application, and rapture," etc. To clarify the equanimity intended here after showing the different types of equanimity, it is said: "upekkhā pana," etc. In that text, tatramajjhattatā (specific neutrality) itself is called "six-factored equanimity" (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) because Arahants look on with equanimity without abandoning their pure natural state when the six desirable or undesirable objects come into range; it is called "equanimity as a divine abode" (brahmavihārupekkhā) because it proceeds as a neutral mode towards beings; and it is called "equanimity as a factor of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅgupekkhā) because it is the neutral mode of co-nascent states; and as mere...
74:
...tatramajjhattatā itself is called "equanimity as specific neutrality" (tatramajjhattūpekkhā); it is called "jhanic equanimity" (jhānupekkhā) because it is associated with the third jhana and is impartial even towards that sublime bliss; it is called "equanimity of purity" (pārisuddhupekkhā) because it is associated with the fourth jhana and is pure from all opposing states. Thus, it is described as sixfold according to various stages and conditions.

Energy (vīriya) that proceeds in the mode of equanimity towards co-nascent formations that are neither too strenuous nor too slack is called "equanimity of effort" (vīriyūpekkhā). The eight kinds of wisdom (paññā) that arise through concentration (samādhi), which proceed in a neutral mode by reaching a state of non-activity even in the abandoning of hindrances (nīvaraṇa), initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), etc., because they are directed towards abandoning them even in the preliminary stage of attaining the eight fine-material and immaterial jhanas; the four kinds of wisdom that arise through insight (vipassanā) for the attainment of each of the four Paths in the preliminary stage, which proceed in the mode of equanimity towards formations that are the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha); the four kinds of wisdom that proceed by the power of the "unconditioned liberation" (appaṇihitavimokkha) for the attainment of each of the four fruitions in the preliminary stage; and the two kinds of wisdom that proceed by the power of "emptiness liberation" (suññatavimokkha) and "signless liberation" (animittavimokkha)—these eighteen kinds of wisdom together are called "equanimity towards formations" (saṅkhārūpekkhā). Only the aforementioned insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) is called "insight-equanimity" (vipassanūpekkhā) because it is neutral even when investigating characteristics. Feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant is called "equanimity as feeling" (vedanūpekkhā).

To show that the classification of these ten types of equanimity according to the methods found in various Pali texts should be understood as explained in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary (Atthasālinī), it is said: "evamayaṃ dasavidhā" (thus, this is tenfold), etc. In truth, the phrase "tattha tattha āgatanayato" (according to the methods found in various texts) is also stated as a separate heading (mātikā), like the terms "plane" (bhūmi) and "person" (puggala). It does not refer to the source of the classification by way of plane, person, etc., because that source has already been mentioned as the "Atthasālinī," etc. Therefore, the statement in the Sāratthadīpanī: "To show that the classification of these ten types of equanimity by way of plane, person, etc., should be understood according to the methods stated in various places, it is said: 'evamayaṃ dasavidhā,' etc.," should be regarded as a statement made without careful consideration.

"Tattha tattha āgatanayato" means: "In this Dispensation, a monk (an Arahant), having seen a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending"—in this way, six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) is mentioned. "He dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity"—in this way, equanimity as a divine abode (brahmavihārupekkhā) is mentioned. By this method...
75:
By demonstrating the methods found in various Pali texts, these ten types of equanimity (*upekkhā*) should also be understood according to the method stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*; this is how the connection should be viewed.

Regarding planes (*bhūmi*) and so forth: six-factored equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) is of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while divine-abiding equanimity (*brahmavihārupekkhā*) is of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*)—thus it is understood by way of plane. Six-factored equanimity occurs only for Arahants, while divine-abiding equanimity occurs for the three types of persons such as worldlings—thus it is understood by way of person (*puggala*). Six-factored equanimity is associated with consciousness accompanied by joy and equanimity—thus it is understood by way of consciousness (*citta*). Six-factored equanimity has six objects—thus it is understood by way of object (*ārammaṇa*). By way of classification into aggregates (*khandha*), equanimity as feeling (*vedanupekkhā*) is included in the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), while the remaining nine types of equanimity are included in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). By way of simultaneity (*ekakkhaṇa*), since six-factored equanimity, divine-abiding equanimity, equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), equanimity of purification of jhāna (*jhānapārisuddhupekkhā*), and equanimity as specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) are essentially one in nature, when one occurs in a single moment, the others do not; likewise, equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and equanimity in insight (*vipassanārupekkhā*) should be understood. However, equanimity as feeling and equanimity as energy (*vīriyupekkhā*) can occur in a single moment. By way of the Wholesome Triad (*kusalatika*), six-factored equanimity is indeterminate (*abyākata*), divine-abiding equanimity is wholesome or indeterminate, and the rest are similar, while equanimity as feeling can sometimes be unwholesome (*akusala*). In brief, there are only four states: energy (*vīriya*), feeling (*vedanā*), specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*), and knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Thus, these ten types of equanimity should be understood according to the method stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*; this is how the sentence is constructed.

In this context, although these types of equanimity are not explicitly extracted by way of plane, person, etc., in the *Atthasālinī*, their classification by plane, person, etc., can be known through the methods already stated in that *Atthasālinī*. Therefore, by combining what is explicitly stated and what is not in the *Atthasālinī*, they are pointed out through nine ways, such as 'according to the method found in various Pali texts.' For this reason, it is not said 'by the power stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*,' but rather 'only by the method stated.' Indeed, when it is said, 'An Arahant monk, seeing a form with the eye,' etc., the wise can understand that six-factored equanimity, having forms etc. as objects, is only of the sense-sphere by way of plane, occurs only for Arahants by way of person, is associated with consciousness of joy and equanimity by way of consciousness, has six objects by way of object, and is only indeterminate by way of the Wholesome Triad.
76:
In this context, although these types of equanimity are not explicitly extracted by way of plane, person, etc., in the *Atthasālinī*, their classification by plane, person, etc., can be known through the methods already stated in that *Atthasālinī*. Therefore, by combining what is explicitly stated and what is not in the *Atthasālinī*, they are pointed out through nine ways, such as 'according to the method found in various Pali texts.' For this reason, it is not said 'by the power stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*,' but rather 'only by the method stated.' To elaborate, when it is said, 'An Arahant, seeing a form with the eye,' etc., the wise can understand that six-factored equanimity, having forms etc. as objects, is only of the sense-sphere by way of plane. By way of person, it occurs only for Arahants. By way of consciousness, it is associated with consciousness of joy and equanimity. By way of object, it has six objects. By way of the Wholesome Triad, it is only an indeterminate state.

Likewise, when it is said, 'Six-factored equanimity... is essentially one,' etc., it can be known that because six-factored equanimity is included in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), it does not occur simultaneously with divine-abiding equanimity and so forth. Just as the method for extracting the classification of six-factored equanimity by plane etc. is known, the method for extracting the classification of the remaining types of equanimity by plane etc. should be understood according to the method stated in the *Atthasālinī* as appropriate. '*Anābhogarasā*' means having the function of being the opposite of inclining towards that sublime happiness of the third jhāna.

'*Puggalena*' means by way of person-based discourse (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). Guarding states associated with defilements is called '*ārakkhā*'. Reaching the end of a task is called '*tīraṇa*'. Investigation is called '*pavicaya*'. '*Idaṃ*' refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajañña*). The phrase 'the happiness associated with the mental body of one possessed of that jhāna' should be connected with the phrase 'that meaning' and so forth. '*Tassa*' means of the person possessed of jhāna. '*Taṃsamuṭṭhānena*' means by that matter which has as its cause that happiness associated with the aforementioned mental body. '*Assa*' means of the yogi. '*Yassa*' means of the material body (*rūpakāya*). '*Phuṭṭhattā*' means because of being touched by very sublime matter. The meaning intended to be shown here is that even for the person possessed of jhāna who is experiencing the happiness of the mental body which produces the matter that is the cause of physical happiness, it is said, 'he experiences happiness with the body,' by way of metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause. Since the particle '*yaṃ*' is in the sense of cause (*hetu*), it is said, 'because of which jhāna.' '*Sukhapāramippatta*' means reaching the peak or the limit of happiness. In this way, the abandoning of that happiness and so forth should be understood; this is how it should be connected. It should be connected as: 'Why is cessation said to occur only in the jhānas, even though it ceases in the access (*upacāra*) to jhāna?'

## Commentary on the Fourth Jhāna (*Catutthajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā*)
In the sentence '*kattha cuppannaṃ*', the word '*kattha*' is in the locative case (*sattamī*) in the sense of cause (*hetu*), meaning 'when what cause exists?' '*Nānāvajjana*' means in the access (*upacāra*) which has an adverting (*āvajjana*) in previous processes that is different from the adverting of the absorption process (*appanāvīthi*). Fatigue arising from sitting in an uneven position is called '*visamāsanupatāpo*'. The phrase '*upacāre vā*' etc. shows another alternative, meaning 'also in the access having a similar adverting.' By the words '*pītifaraṇena*', he shows the absence of even the mere pervading of sense-sphere rapture in a single process, as in the absorption process. It should be connected as: 'the arising of the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*) for that person is possible.' '*Etaṃ*' should be connected as: 'the faculty of grief arises.' In the term '*vitakkavicārappaccayepi*', the word '*pi*' is misplaced. That word '*pi*' should be placed immediately after the word '*pahīnassa*' mentioned below, resulting in 'also for the faculty of grief which has been abandoned.'
77:
The phrase “pahīnassāpi domanassindriyassa” (for one who has also abandoned the faculty of displeasure) should be connected [here]. In this context of “vitakkavicārabhāve”, the words “the faculty of displeasure arises” should be brought in and connected. This locative case [the -e in bhāve] is used in the sense of cause (nimitta); the meaning is “because of the existence of initial and sustained thought.” In the phrase “vitakkavicārā”, the word “iti” should be understood in the sense of “therefore.” Therefore, because this faculty of displeasure ... does not arise due to the cause of initial and sustained thought; but where it does arise, it arises only when initial and sustained thought are present. Since initial and sustained thought are not yet abandoned in the access concentration (upacāra) of the second jhāna, the arising of that faculty of displeasure might occur there—thus the construction (yojanā) should be understood here.

“Tattha” refers to the access concentration of the second jhāna. “Assa” refers to the faculty of displeasure. The phrase “siyā uppattī” (there might be an arising) is said as a mere possibility (sambhāvana) by showing the mere cause. Indeed, the possibility of the arising of displeasure is appropriate only at the moment of access; however, at the moment of the second jhāna, which is devoid of initial and sustained thought, the possibility of its arising is not appropriate. Otherwise, since the arising of unwholesome displeasure is impossible at the moment of a wholesome consciousness, it should not be said that “there might be the arising of that [displeasure] in that [jhāna].” Alternatively, this locative case is in the sense of proximity (samīpa); the meaning is “in the cognitive processes (vīthi) occurring immediately after the access concentration.” In the phrase “dutiyajjhāne”, the meaning is that it does not arise even in the immediate cognitive processes; the same should be understood for the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) above. It connects as “the arising of the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) [might occur].” The statement “pahīnā” (abandoned) is said because of the statement “due to the destruction of the five lower fetters.” “Dukkhābhāvena” means due to the absence of the state of suffering. The same applies to “evaṃ sukhābhāvena”. “Etena” refers to the statement made by excluding pain and pleasure. “Iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītānubhavanalakkhaṇā” means having the characteristic of experiencing the neutral (majjhatta) object, which is the opposite of the greatly desirable and greatly undesirable objects. For even a neutral object is included only within the desirable and undesirable, as there is no object outside of them.

## The method of the explanation of the fourfold jhāna is finished.

## Explanation of the Recollection of Past Lives

The formless jhānas are also included in the fourth jhāna because of the equality of factors; thus it is said, “which are the basis for certain higher knowledges,” and so on. For this reason, it will be said later (in the Pārājika Commentary), “having produced the eight attainments,” and so on. Among them, only the fourth jhāna is the basis for higher knowledge.
78:
Only the fourth jhāna is the basis for the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), not the others. However, with reference to being a remote cause, the first jhāna and others are also taken together as “the four jhānas”. The phrase “having the benefit of one-pointedness of mind” is said with reference to the pleasant dwelling in this very life for Arahants; thus it is said, “khīṇāsavānaṃ” (for those whose taints are destroyed), and so on. “Accomplishing all tasks” means accomplishing all Buddha-tasks such as the divine dwellings (dibba-vihāra). By the phrase “bestowing all mundane and supramundane qualities”, all that was previously mentioned, such as being the basis for insight (vipassanā), is summarized. Indeed, this jhāna should be understood as being described in this way because it is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) which bestows all the qualities of a Buddha upon the Blessed One. “Yathayidaṃ” means “yathā idaṃ” (as this [mind]). “Abhinīhārakkhamaṃ” means fit (suitable) for directing towards the goal of supernormal powers (iddhividha) and so on.

“Having the acquisition of jhāna as a cause” means those [states] caused by the acquisition of jhāna, or those arising depending on the acquisition of jhāna. “Base” (pāpakānaṃ) means low or inferior. “Moving in the sphere of wishes” (icchāvacarānaṃ) refers to states like conceit (māna) which occur by the power of desire, but have not yet reached the state of being a hindrance (nīvaraṇa) or the same level as a hindrance, and which occur by way of self-exaltation, etc., in such a manner as: “It would be good if the Teacher, having questioned only me, would preach such a Dhamma to the monks.” In some books, the reading “opposed to the acquisition of jhāna” (jhānappaṭilābhapaccanīkānaṃ) is written; that should be taken as a scribal error (pamādapāṭha). This is because it was previously stated under the word “parisuddha” (purified) that it is “purified by being far from the hindrances due to the absence of the hindrances which are opposed to the acquisition of jhāna.” In the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, it is said: “Icchāvacarānaṃ means the various types of anger and dissatisfaction that occur by the power of desire”; this reading should also be taken as inappropriate. For this very reason, this reading is not shown at all in the Visuddhimagga. It should be understood that this reading was rejected because it treats the faults that have reached the state of hindrances as “various types of anger and dissatisfaction”.

In the phrase “of greed (abhijjhā), etc.”, by the word “abhijjhā”, greed and conceit, etc., which are not of the nature of hindrances, should be taken, because the term “having the acquisition of jhāna as a cause” follows. “Both” refers to both the state of being without blemish (anaṅgaṇatta) and the state of being free from defilement (vigatūpakkilesatta); these two should be understood respectively according to the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta and the Vattha Sutta. Although in those Suttas, gross faults that have reached the nature of hindrances are mentioned, here, because it is spoken by the power of the attained fourth jhāna, only subtle faults are taken. The Suttas are cited here only because of the commonality of “blemish” (angaṇa) and “defilement” (upakkilesa). Therefore, it is said “according to the Sutta” (suttānusārena), but not “by the power of the Sutta” (sutta-vasena).
79:
To show the grammatical derivation (vigraha) as "Knowledge in the recollection of past abodes is the knowledge of recollection of past abodes" (pubbenivāsānussatiyam ñāṇam pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇam), the phrase beginning with "pubbenivāsānussatimhi" is stated. Now, to show the distinction between the past abode (pubbenivāsa), the recollection of the past abode (pubbenivāsānussati), and the knowledge therein, the phrase beginning with "tattha" is stated. The word 'pubbe' refers to the past existence; the word 'nivāsa' is used in the sense of the object of action (kammasādhana). Therefore, it is said: "Pubbe atītajātīsu nivuṭṭhakkhandhā" (The aggregates lived in past births). Here, "having lived" (nivuṭṭha) means occurring within one's own continuity (santāna). Thus, "anubhūtā" (experienced) etc., is said. Now, to show the meaning of the word 'nivāsa' by way of its relation to both one's own and others' continuities, it is said "nivuṭṭhadhammā vā nivuṭṭhā" (or the lived phenomena are 'nivuṭṭha'), and to explain that, "gocaranivāsena" etc., is stated. Indeed, even the phenomena that are objects (gocara) are called "lived" (nivuṭṭha) by knowledge. To show that these are of two kinds—as objects of one's own consciousness and others' consciousness—"attano" etc., is stated. Alternatively, it is connected as "lived" because they are known by the consciousness of others. Here too, the word "paricchinnā" (delimited) should be brought in and connected. In the beginningless (anamatagga) Saṃsāra, the aggregates of beings not previously known by oneself are called 'paraviññāṇaviññātā' because they were known only by certain others. Recollecting those aggregates known by others' consciousness is more difficult than the previously mentioned recollection of aggregates known by one's own consciousness. This is because those aggregates became known by others, and they must be known by following the present continuity of those others.

Those aggregates known by others' consciousness are of two types: those who have attained Parinibbāna and those who have not. Among them, recollecting those who have attained Parinibbāna is more difficult because their continuity has been completely cut off in every way. To show that past abode known by others' consciousness which has reached the pinnacle, "chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇādīsu" is stated. There, 'chinnavaṭumaka' refers to Arahants who attained Parinibbāna in the past, as their path through Saṃsāra has been cut. By the word 'ādi', the recollection of aggregates known by others' consciousness of those who have not yet attained Parinibbāna by way of the "lion's leap" (sīhokkantika) method is included. The mindfulness by which one recollects the continuity of aggregates lived in the past is called 'pubbenivāsānussati'.

The word 'vihita' is a synonym for 'vidha', so "anekavidhaṃ" (of many kinds) is said, meaning many kinds by way of existence (bhava), origin (yoni), etc. Or, taking 'vihita' to mean 'payutta' (applied) or 'vaṇṇita' (praised/described), one should say "anekehī pakārehī vihitaṃ," but with the middle word elided, it is stated as "anekehī... saṃvaṇṇitaṃ." "Pakārehi" means by various ways such as name and clan. "Saṃvaṇṇitaṃ" means taught by the Buddhas and others. The prefix 'anu-' indicates immediate sequence, so "abhininnāmitamatte eva" is said; this term shows the state of having undertaken the preliminary work (parikamma). By "pūritapāramīnaṃ" etc., it shows that for those who have fulfilled the perfections, success is possible even without preliminary work.
80:
"Āraddhappakāradassanatthe" means for the purpose of showing the various modes of the aggregates lived in the past that have been undertaken for recollection. Because of the word "jāyati," it is called "jāti," meaning existence (bhava). That existence is a continuity of aggregates rooted in a single kamma, delimited by the taking up and laying down of aggregates; therefore, in this context, "jāti" is intended in this sense, as stated by "ekampi" etc. "Kappo" refers to an incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa). That aeon is, in ultimate reality, a period of time designated based on the phenomena occurring in that manner. The decrease and increase of that aeon should be understood by the power of those temporal phenomena. It is called "saṃvaṭṭo" because it involves dissolution (saṃvaṭṭana); it refers to an incalculable aeon. It is called "saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī" because it persists by nature along with the destruction. The same principle applies to terms like "vivaṭṭo." In that context, "vivaṭṭo" refers to arising or growth. Destruction by fire is called "tejosaṃvaṭṭo." In terms of extent, there is no specific distinction in the limit of destruction, which is why "sadāpi" is stated. To show that it is called the "field of birth" (jātikhetta) because of the extraordinary occurrences at the moment of the Bodhisatta's birth, like those of fellow citizens, "paṭisandhiādīsu kampati" (it quakes at conception, etc.) is said. "Authority (power) pervades" means the desire for the cessation of dangers such as diseases for all beings included within that field of authority (āṇākhetta). The phrase "yaṃ yāvatā vā pana ākaṅkheyya" refers to the "field of range" (visayakhetta), where the Blessed One, acknowledging the ability to make his voice heard everywhere in a single moment and to show his physical form, said "yāvatā vā pana ākaṅkheyya" (as far as he may wish).

The word "etesu" is in the locative case in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa). "Pavattaphalabhojano" means having fallen fruits as food; this is said in reference to the time of being an ascetic. "Idhūpapattiyā" means due to arising in this final existence. "Ekagotto" means having the same clan, specifically the Tusita clan. Others refer to appearance (vaṇṇa), etc. "Titthiyā" refers to those who hold the view of kamma and its results. "Abhinīhāra" refers to the period of accumulating the requisites of merit and knowledge, marked by the initial resolution. "Cutipaṭisandhivasena" means knowing in this way by the power of taking only the rebirth (paṭisandhi) after seeing the death (cuti) of oneself or another in various existences, without considering anything in between; this is the "entering into the desired place," as stated by "tesañhi" etc. "Ubhayathāpi" means both by way of the sequence of aggregates and by way of death and rebirth. "Sīhokkantivasenapi" means also by way of the "lion's descent" method. Energy (viriya) is called "ātāpa" in the sense of burning or consuming the defilements; this is stated by "vīriyātāpena."
81:
## Explanation of the Discourse on the Divine Eye Knowledge

Because it occurs in devas, the sensitive eye (pasādacakkhu) of devas is called 'divine' (dibba); therefore, it is said, "because it is like the divine." In the word 'dūrepi' (even at a distance), by the word 'pi' (even/also), subtle objects should also be included. Because it is accomplished by the power of the exertion of energy, all development (bhāvanā) is called 'development of energy' (vīriyabhāvanā), or specifically because of the development of the bases of power (iddhipāda) associated with the formation of energy; therefore, it is said, "produced by the power of the development of energy."

'Dibbavihāravasena' (by way of divine abiding) means by the power of the four jhānas such as kasiṇa. By this statement, the divine nature of that supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) due to its remote cause is mentioned. By the statement 'dibbavihārasannissitattā' (because of being dependent on the divine abiding), its divine nature is mentioned because it arises from the proximate cause, the foundation jhāna (pādakajhāna). 'Dibbavihārasannissitattā' also means that the divine eye knowledge (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) occurs depending on the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara catutthajjhāna), which is included in the divine abiding, associated with itself, and serves as the dependence-condition.

Intending the connection with the meanings of radiance and movement of the root 'divu', the words beginning with 'ālokaparigghena' (by the grasping of light) are said. Therein, 'ālokaparigghena' means by the power of grasping the light of the kasiṇa. 'Dassanaṭṭhena' (in the sense of seeing) means in the sense of seeing visible forms; by this, its nature as an eye (cakkhu) is shown according to the definition, "it sees visible forms, it makes them clear." 'Cakkhukiccakaranaṇa' (by performing the function of the eye) is the showing of a similar cause by way of metaphor, "an eye like an eye," meaning because it performs the function of the eye, which is characterized by seeing even and uneven things, etc.

'Yathāha' (as it was said) refers to a portion of the Upakkilesa Sutta. In that sutta, among the words beginning with 'vicikicchā' (doubt), while the Blessed One, before his enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree, was seeing various visible forms with the divine eye, doubt arose: "What indeed is this? What indeed is that?" Then, to remove that doubt, when he remained without attending to those forms, sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha) arose. To remove that sloth and torpor, when he again attended to all forms, consternation (chambhitatta) regarding ogres, etc., arose. When he attended with the power of dispelling fear, "Why should I be afraid of this object?", joy based on the household life (gehassitapīti) called elation (uppilla), which destroys concentration, arose due to his skill in attention.

To restrain that joy, when he relaxed the energy of attention, sluggishness (duṭṭhulla) called bodily laziness arose. To restrain that sluggishness, when he again exerted energy, over-strenuous energy (accāraddhavīriya) arose. Again, to restrain that over-strenuous energy, when he relaxed the energy, over-lax energy (atilīnavīriya) arose. Having restrained that energy, when he viewed divine forms, craving called longing (abhijappā) arose. To restrain that craving, when he attended to various low and high forms, perception of diversity (nānattasaññā) called distraction by various objects arose. Again, having abandoned that perception of diversity, when he attended to only a single object, excessive staring (atinijjhāyitatta) at forms arose.
82:
Furthermore, for the Bodhisatta who attends to all visual objects, trembling of the body (fear) regarding ogres, ghosts, and so forth, arises. Again, for the Bodhisatta who attends by dispelling fear, thinking, 'Why should I fear this object?', due to proficiency in attention, there arises 'house-based joy' (gehassitapīti), called 'Uppala', which tends to destroy concentration. When energy (viriya) in attention is relaxed to prevent that joy, a gross state called bodily sluggishness (duṭṭhulla) arises. When energy is exerted again to dispel that gross state, over-exerted energy (accāraddhaviriya) arises. When energy is relaxed to prevent that over-exerted energy, overly sluggish energy (atilinaviriya) arises. For the Bodhisatta who prevents that energy and views celestial visual objects, craving called intense longing (abhijappa) arises. To prevent that craving, for the Bodhisatta who attends to various visual objects such as the low and so forth, the perception of diversity (nānattasaññā), which is distraction among various objects, arises. Again, when abandoning that perception of diversity and attending to only a single object, excessive thinking, which is intense focus on visual objects, arises.

'Obhāsaṃ' refers to the light arising from preliminary practice (parikamma). 'Does not see visual objects' means that because of being occupied with attending to the light of preliminary practice, one does not see visual objects with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu); thus the meaning should be understood according to the sequence of occurrence. 'Mānusakaṃ' refers to the gross visual objects that are the range of the human eye. Because those very gross visual objects are within the range of human vision, it is said, 'manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā' (surpassing the range of human vision). 'Rūpadassanena' means by seeing visual objects that are distant, subtle, and so forth.

Invariably, the divine-eye knowledge (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa), which takes a visual object existing in the present as its object, cannot arise without advertence (āvajjana) and preliminary practice. Furthermore, a visual object that is in the process of arising or ceasing cannot be the object of the divine eye because it is weak. The death-consciousness (cuti-citta) arises only at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa) of karma-born matter, and the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) arises at the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa). Therefore, it is said, 'cutikkhaṇe' (at the moment of death), and so forth. Here, since seeing the visual object is itself seeing the being, it is stated in terms of a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), such as 'cavamāne' (passing away). The phrase 'abhirūpe virūpe' (beautiful or ugly) is stated with reference to the meaning of the word 'vaṇṇa' as denoting shape or form. It is like the words, 'having created the appearance (vaṇṇa) of a great elephant king,' and so forth. They are called 'sugatā' because they have gone to a happy destination (sugati). 'By this word' refers to the word 'yathākammūpage' (faring according to their deeds).

Having seen the bodily appearance of hell-beings, which is torn by flames and the falling of weapons, etc., their experience of suffering is known through the sense-sphere impulsions (kāmāvacara-javana) that occur immediately after that seeing. Because such knowing is also connected to the fruit of seeing, it is said to be 'the function of the divine eye itself.' 'Thus one attends' means that, desiring to know their karma, one enters the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna), emerges, and by the power of preliminary practice, attends as 'Due to what karma?', and so forth. Then, the knowledge associated with the fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna, which arises after the advertence and preliminary practice by taking that karma as its object, is called 'knowledge of faring according to deeds' (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa). The same method applies to seeing deities. 'Separate preliminary practice' means that, unlike knowledges such as recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa), there is no separate preliminary practice apart from the preliminary practice of the divine-eye knowledge. However, some teachers say, 'In this case, there is no need for the preliminary practice of entering the basic jhāna; immediately after attending to the karma, the process of absorption (appanā-vīthi) arises, taking the karma and its associated states as objects. The same applies to the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa). Therefore, there is no separate preliminary practice, and it is accomplished together with the divine eye.' That statement should not be accepted. This is because even for those who have mastered the direct knowledges (abhiññā), the direct knowledge cannot arise without the preliminary practice such as the basic jhāna. Merely the basic jhāna, etc., does not constitute a 'separate preliminary practice.' Therefore, it should be understood that these knowledges are accomplished only through the divine eye. The same method applies to the knowledge of the future.
83:
It should be understood that these knowledges are accomplished through the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) alone. Similarly, for the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa), because of the desire to know the future existence of a being seen with the divine eye, immediately after the base jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) and so forth, in accordance with the power of the knowledge, it takes as its object in a single moment the five aggregates belonging to past existences that are liable to arise in many future aeons, all mundane and supramundane states connected with or based on those aggregates, and also concepts (paññatti). Thus, it should be construed (yojanā) that there is no separate preliminary work (parikamma) for the anāgataṃsañāṇa associated with the fourth jhāna.

Some teachers, however, say that in this anāgataṃsañāṇa, there is indeed the grasping of names, lineages, and so forth, just as in the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). Such grasping does not occur at the moment of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā), but only in the moments of sense-sphere impulsion (kāmāvacara-javana) that immediately follow that supernormal knowledge. This is because when one is thinking of a name, it is impossible to think of other things like lineage, and because there is no limit to the arising of such thoughts. Specifically, when all states and meanings that serve as signs for the preliminary work are seen in a single moment by the supernormal knowledge, the particular conceptualization such as 'he has this name' arises later through sense-sphere consciousness according to one's preference. This is like the conceptualization of 'pillar' or 'pot' regarding many forms seen with the eye. Even if an object is not conceptualized at that time, it is worthy of being conceptualized. Therefore, every object is indeed conceptualized by way of name, lineage, and so forth. They say that just as in this knowledge of the future, it is the same in the knowledge of recollecting past lives; referring to the suitability for conceptualization, it is stated in the Pāḷi together with the designation such as 'he had such a name.' Other teachers say that everything such as name and lineage is perceived in a single moment, but they only express what is desired through speech. These teachers are essentially the same as the former ones. This is because they also essentially accept the seeing of states worthy of conceptualization, since even when expressing what was seen previously, it must be conceptualized. Some teachers say that because of the statement 'having passed away from there, he was reborn in that place,' the knowledge of past and future states occurs only in succession; therefore, grasping together with name, lineage, and so forth is easy. That statement is indeed improper. This is because it would lead to the loss of omniscience (sabbaññutā), as even the Buddhas would be unable to know everything [simultaneously]. In the Pāḷi, the passage beginning with 'Indeed, sirs, these beings' is a demonstration of the mode of occurrence of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa). Here, 'body and speech' refer to bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) and vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti).

The term 'serious' (bhāriyaṃ) is used because it is similar to the heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma). Indeed, if there is no asking for forgiveness, it becomes an ānantariya-kamma itself. 'Of that' (tassa) refers to the insult against a Noble One (ariyūpavāda) which is of a heavy nature. 'Old' (mahallako) means he is old only in age, not in wisdom. It should be understood that he insults by destroying virtues, as it was said in a disparaging sense: 'This person does not know even a little of the world's conventions; he is merely a spoiler of the assembly because he causes us shame.'
84:
With the word "Āvuso" (Friend) and so forth, the Elder, desiring the attainment of the higher paths for that young monk, revealed himself out of compassion. "It became normal" (pākati-kaṃ ahosi) means that there was no longer an obstruction to the Path (maggāvaraṇa). "Older than himself" (attanā vuḍḍhataro) means he himself was also an elder. Here too, it is stated in the Visuddhimagga, "having sat in the squatting position" (ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā). Non-returners (anāgāmi) and Arahants might not forgive for the sake of future restraint, while other Noble Ones might not forgive out of anger; with this intention, it is said, "If he does not forgive" (sace so na khamati).

In the phrase "And those who... cause others to undertake," it should be construed that they are also those who undertake the actions of wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). In the passages beginning with "endowed with virtue" (sīlasampanno), a person standing on the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggaṭṭha) is primarily intended, because for such a person, the attainment of the fruition of Arahantship is certain. Alternatively, it refers to other persons in their last birth (pacchimabhavika) who are established in virtue and so forth, because for them too, the attainment of the 'other' is certain. "The other" (aññaṃ) refers to the fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). "Thus accomplished" (evaṃ sampadaṃ) means having the nature to bring about such a result. Just as that fruition of Arahantship arises without fail, so too this act of insulting a Noble One (ariyūpavāda) brings about rebirth in hell; this is the meaning. To show what is referred to as "this which is thus accomplished," the words beginning with "that speech" (taṃ vācaṃ) are stated. "That speech" refers to the speech insulting a Noble One. "Mind" (cittaṃ) refers to the mind that insults a Noble One. "View" (diṭṭhiṃ) refers to the view that sees no fault in insulting a Noble One. If one remains without abandoning or relinquishing it through asking for forgiveness and confessing the fault with the thought, "I will abandon all this." "Just as if he were carried and laid down, so he is in hell" means just as if he were brought by the wardens of hell and placed in hell, so he is indeed placed in hell. It means that because of the insult to a Noble One, his rebirth in hell is as certain to be accomplished as the fruition is produced by the Path.

Because wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) is the root of all evil, among those faults, wrong view is the greatest and foremost; thus they are called "faults where wrong view is the greatest" (micchā-diṭṭhi-paramāni). The meaning is that among all faults, wrong view itself is the greatest fault. For one who is not free from lust (avītarāga), there is only the taking up of another existence after death; thus it is said, "after death" (paraṃ maraṇā) means at the moment of taking up the aggregates of a new birth immediately following that. Since the body breaks up only through the cessation of that by which it stands, it is said, "with the breakup of the body" (kāyassa bhedā) means through the cessation of the life faculty (jīvitindriya). Happiness comes from this merit, therefore it is called "aya" (merit). "Āyassa" means of the arrival or of the cause. Because it proceeds by way of desirable objects and so forth, it is called "āya," which is gratification (assāda). "Like an Asura" (asurasadisaṃ) means like a Peta-Asura.
85:
## Explanation of the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints

"By penetration of the characteristic of its own nature" (sarasa-lakkhaṇa-paṭivedhena) means by penetrating the characteristic known as nature (sabhāva) without confusion. "Accomplishing" (nibbattikaṃ) means producing (or bringing to completion). "Having reached that state" (yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā) means having reached that Nibbāna which is the cause, acting as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for the Path. "Non-occurrence" (appavattiṃ) refers to the cause of non-occurrence. "By means of defilements" (kilesavasena) means: by means of those defilements or taints (āsavas) whose destruction makes this knowledge the "Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints"; it implies the inclusion of all defilements figuratively (pariyāya). Although the Pali uses the past tense "abbhaññāsiṃ" (I directly knew), it uses the present tense "for one thus knowing, thus seeing" (evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato) to indicate the present state of that knowledge at the moment of realization (abhisamaya). Liberation from the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) should also be understood, as it is inseparable from liberation from sensual taints (kāmāsava) and others.

"Birth is destroyed" (khīṇā jāti) is realized through reviewing the destruction of defilements (kilesakkhaya-paccavekkhaṇā). Knowing "the holy life has been lived" (vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ) and so on occurs through reviewing the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna (maggaphala-nibbāna-paccavekkhaṇā). Therefore, it is said, "its ground (bhūmi) is 'birth is destroyed' and so on." In that phrase, "ground" means the object (visaya). Although it is impossible to make a direct effort toward the destruction of birth in the three periods of time, the phrase "but which..." (yā pana) is said to show the fruitfulness of making an effort toward that destruction and the benefit of the non-arising of future aggregates. By the phrase "but which, because the Path has not been developed..." (yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā), it means that birth of aggregates will occur in the future only because of defilements not yet destroyed by the Path; if those defilements are destroyed by the Path, the aggregates will not arise. Regarding the existence of defilements in the three periods, although they are not destroyed by any other cause in the way mentioned regarding birth, the arising of the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga), which is the opposite of defilements in the mental continuum, is itself the destruction of those defilements. Because of the encounter with the opposing cause (the Path), their non-arising in the future is like the future non-arising of seeds when a heap of fire falls on a collection of seeds. Thus, this meaning is clarified: the non-arising of the aggregates, which are the results of defilements, in the future due to the absence of defilements (known as the arising of the Path-moment) is called the "destruction of birth" (jātikkhaya). Therefore, it is said, "destroyed by attaining the state of non-arising because the Path has been developed." The meaning here is: because the Path, which is the absence of defilements, has been developed (produced), the birth of aggregates, which do not arise due to the absence of conditions, is figuratively called "my birth is destroyed" by reaching the nature of non-arising, which is future non-occurrence. The destruction of conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) is not possible without another cause; if it were possible...
86:
...then there would be the fallacy of that conditioned thing having another cause, etc. The arising of the moment opposite to those [defilements] is itself the production of their destruction. "That" (taṃ) should be connected as "he directly knew that birth is destroyed" (khīṇā-jātiṃ abbhaññāsi). "For this state" (itthattāya): these modes are "thus" (itthaṃ); the state of being thus is "itthattaṃ"; for the sake of that Path-duty. "Showing" (dassento) means showing by way of conclusion.

## The method of explanation for the Threefold Knowledge is finished.

## Explanation of the Declaration of Lay Discipleship

The word "aññāṇaṃ" is used in the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) in the sense of connection (sāmi-attha) due to its association with the word "abhi". "Pādāni" means the feet. "Yasasā" means with a retinue (parivāra). "Kotūhalacchare" means in both excitement and wonder. "Ayaṃ" refers to this word "abhikkanta". The phrase "abhikkantaṃ" is not said twice as a mere repetition (āmeḍita), but is said with two different meanings; to show this, the phrase "or else" (atha vā) and so on was said. The neuter usage "abhikkantaṃ," which is formed with a general meaning without distinction, remains in that same neuter form even when referring to specific meanings like the teaching (desanā) or clarity (pasāda), because it was already formed previously. Therefore, it was said, "abhikkantaṃ... pasāda." "Adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ" means something placed face down by someone. "Heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ" means something that has become face down on its own. "Pariyāyehi" means by various ways, or by reasons for blame such as having an unpleasant nature.

Since the root 'gamu' is not a double-accusative verb, both words in "Gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ" are not in the accusative case. Rather, to show that only the first word "Gotamaṃ" is in the accusative case while the latter "saraṇaṃ" is in the nominative case (paccatta-vacana), it is said, "I go to Gotama as a refuge" (Gotamaṃ saraṇanti gacchāmi). By this, it shows that the word "iti" is elided in the expression. "Aghassa" means from evil (agha). This is because the ablative sense (nissakka) is appropriate in relation to the word "tātā" (protector). By the two words "in the Path attained and the cessation realized" (adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe), only those established in the Fruit (phalaṭṭha) are shown; to show that those on the Path (maggaṭṭha) are not included, it is said, "and for one practicing according to the instruction" (yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne ca). By the word "detailed explanation" (vitthāro), it encompasses the Sutta passage: "Monks, as far as there are things, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is said to be the foremost of them." "Anejaṃ" means free from craving (taṇhā). "Appaṭikūlaṃ" means non-clashing, pure, or sublime, as it illustrates the meaning of non-opposition. It is called "paguṇaṃ" (fluent) because it should be mastered by speech, or because it is endowed with excellent qualities of sound and meaning. "Saṃhato" means joined or combined.
87:
It should be connected. "Yattha" means "in which pairs of men." "Aṭṭha ca puggaladhammadasā te" means those eight persons are seers of the Dhamma because they have seen the Noble Dhamma.

In the words beginning with "saraṇaṃ," the summary of the meaning is as follows: The Triple Gem is called "saraṇa" (refuge) because it has the sense of destroying fear, harm, and so forth. "Saraṇagamana" (taking refuge) is the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that occurs in the manner of making that Triple Gem alone one's protection, shelter, and final resort, by virtue of the Buddha's qualities such as being the Well-Awakened One. One who is endowed with this aforementioned arising of consciousness is said to "go for refuge" (saraṇaṃ gacchati). This taking of refuge is of two kinds: mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). Among these, supramundane refuge is accomplished at the very moment of the Path (magga) by the absolute eradication of the defilements of taking refuge. Mundane refuge occurs in four ways: (1) by self-dedication (attaniyyātana), such as "I dedicate myself to the Buddha"; (2) by making the Triple Gem one's final resort as mentioned; (3) by assuming the status of a disciple; and (4) by prostration (paṇipāta).

In all these cases of mundane refuge, it should be understood that refuge occurs only by way of regarding the Triple Gem as the supreme object of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya), and not because of relatives, fear, teachers, or other such reasons. Thus, for one who pays homage to a sectarian (titthiya) because of relatives and so forth, the refuge is not broken; but for one who pays homage to another sectarian by regarding them as an object of offerings, the refuge is broken. The benefit of mundane refuge, which is the certainty of attaining Nibbāna, is a result similar to supramundane refuge. This is because one who has gone for refuge is certain to attain Nibbāna in the future. The attainment of all mundane prosperity and the transcending of the sufferings of the woeful states (apāya) are its advantageous fruits (āniśaṃsa). Doubt, wrong knowledge, and so forth regarding the Three Objects are the defilements of that refuge. The breaking of refuge is also of two kinds: blameworthy and blameless. Among these, the first (blameworthy) breaking occurs through acts such as paying homage to sectarians preceded by wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). That breaking is blameworthy because it yields undesirable results. The blameless breaking, however, occurs through death. It should be understood that for supramundane refuge, there is no defilement or breaking in any way.

Words beginning with "ko upāsako" are questions asking about the nature, characteristics, and causes of being a lay follower (upāsaka). In those questions, any householder—whether a human, a non-human such as a deva or nāga—who has approached the Three Refuges in the manner described is called an "upāsaka." One is called an "upāsaka" because one attends upon (upāsana) the Triple Gem through acts such as taking refuge. The five abstinences (veramaṇī) are the virtue (sīla) of that upāsaka. Abandoning the five kinds of wrong trade (micchā-vaṇijjā) and other evil livelihoods, and making a living in accordance with the Dhamma and righteousness, is the livelihood (ājīva) of that upāsaka. It should be understood that lack of faith, immorality, and so forth are the failure (vipatti) of the status of an upāsaka, and the absence of those failures is the achievement (sampatti).
88:
"Vihāraggena" means by way of portions of living quarters such as apartments. "Ajjabhāvaṃ" refers to the clarity (pasāda) and so forth that arise on this day. The bodily part which is the cause of bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) is called "kāyanga." The lips, tongue, and so forth, which are the causes of vocal intimation (vacīviññatti), are called "vācanga." "Asopetvā" means without moving.

By these terms—kāyanga, vācanga, and asopetvā—it is shown that the specific mode of the air element (vāyodhātu), which is the cause of the movement of the places and instruments of articulation (ṭhāna-karaṇa) prior to the occurrence of speech, is not a separate bodily intimation. This is because there is no intention to make a separate meaning known by that mode. Since that specific mode assists vocal intimation, it is included only within vocal intimation. Just as in the case of scratching the body with the hand, the specific mode of the earth element (pathavīdhātu) which is the cause of the production of sound is not called vocal intimation because it does not make a separate intention known, so too this specific mode of the air element is not called bodily intimation. Only that which makes an intention known is called "intimation" (viññatti). It is not called intimation merely by being a mode of alteration (vikāra-ākāra) that is a cause for movement or the production of sound in the air or earth elements. Thus, it should be understood that because they are mere alterations, the modes of alteration that are causes for movement and sound in external things like trees are not intimations. 

Although some teachers say that parts of speech such as "Let it be" or "Very well" are "vācanga," that statement does not agree with the word "without moving (asopetvā)." "Khantiṃ cāretvā" means having brought about consent. There is also a variant reading "khantiṃ dhāretvā," which means holding it within without letting it go outside. "Paṭimukho" means facing towards the Blessed One. Therefore, it says "having moved away (apakkamitvā)."

Because the root "yāca" (to beg/request) takes two objects, it is said, "The Blessed One was requested for the rains-residence." To clarify the meaning "even when crops are good," it is said "atisamagghepi" (even at a time of very high prices). This refers to a time when, even if prices are very high (due to scarcity), people give a little and take a lot of grain. "Bhikkhamānā" means begging. "Vuttasassaṃ" means the sown crops.

"Tattha" refers to the city of Verañjā. By the Pali "vuttasassaṃ salākāyeva sampajjati," the definition is shown by placing the attribute at the end: "The sown crops in this city become mere stalks." Or, it can be defined as "All crops in this city arise and succeed only as mere stalks," hence "salākāvutta." Or, to show the definition "one must live by tickets (salākā) in this city," the words beginning with "salākāya" are used. "Dhanyakaraṇaṭṭhāne" means in the place where grain is measured. "Vaṇṇajjhakkhaṃ" refers to an assessor of coins (one who examines kahāpaṇas).

In the phrase "uñchena paggahena," "paggahena" means by means of the bowl, implying "having taken that bowl." Because almsfood is received by this bowl, it is called "paggaha" (the bowl). Therefore, it refers to "almsfood sought by means of the bowl." Alternatively, "paggahena" means by holding, and the meaning is completed as "the bowl is held to seek almsfood."
89:
In the phrase "pagghena yo uñcho" and so forth, "pagghena" means with the bowl, by taking that bowl. Because almsfood is received with this bowl, it is called "paggaha"; it refers to the bowl. Therefore, he said "pagghena yo uñcho" and so forth. Alternatively, "pagghena" means by holding; because the meaning "the bowl is held for the purpose of seeking alms" is established, he said "having taken the bowl."

The region to the north of the Ganges River is called Uttarāpatha. The residence of those merchants is that Uttarāpatha region. Because they come from there, they are called "Uttarāpathaka." Therefore, he said "Uttarāpathavāsikā" and so forth. There is also a reading "Uttarāhakā." By the method of linguistics (nirutti), it has that same meaning. "Mandira" means a horse stable. Although some write "Mandara," it is not good. Because that horse stable is made in a circular shape and in various ways, it is called "assamaṇḍalikā."

The region to the south of the Ganges River is called Dakkhiṇāpatha. People born in that region are called "Dakkhiṇāpathamanussā." Those who are habituated to taking the view "This Buddha is my Buddha alone" are called "Buddhamāmaka." The same method applies to the remaining terms like "Dhammamāmaka," etc. "Evaṃ" means when the meaning is taken by the method stated later. "Paṭivīsa" means a portion (share). "Tadupiya" means what is suitable for that, what is sufficient for that barley. "Laddhā" should be connected as "even if one receives, it does not happen." There is also a reading "laddho." It means they do not even get a place for an attendant. Because he is a relative and is endowed with the most excellent qualities, he is called "ñātiseṭṭha" (noble relative). In such places, only this person is suitable. In times when material gifts (āmisa) are hard to get, it is appropriate only for a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) who is full of affection for relatives, who does not engage in indirect talk (parikathā) or hinting (obhāsa), etc., but stands in purity of livelihood through a very austere way of living, and who arranges material gifts in accordance with the Blessed One's intention.

"Mārāvaṭṭanāya" means the turning of the mind or the delusion of the mind performed by Māra. That person could turn even the Northern Kuru island or the city of the Thirty-three (Tidasa).

"In the dispensation of the Buddha Phussa, I reviled the disciples:
'Eat barley, consume it,
And do not eat choice rice (sāli).'"
This is because the unwholesome deed mentioned in the Apadāna found its opportunity at that time. "Nibaddhadāna" means a gift promised by word, saying "I will give." "Appitavatta" means an object offered by oneself taking the lead. "Visahati" means he is able. "Saṅkhepena" means by bringing. "Byāmappabhā" means the six-colored radiance that is dense in a space of about eighty cubits all around, below, and above. From that radiance, the six-colored rays emerge like channels from a lake and run towards the ten directions.
90:
The rays run towards the directions. Because that radiance appears to be about a fathom (byāma) in extent, it is called "Byāmappabhā" (fathom-wide radiance). Since the minor marks (anubyañjana) on the Buddha's body are each endowed with the perfection of radiance and shine beautifully like the moon and sun in the sky, those minor marks, together with the fathom-wide radiance, are said to be unsurpassable by anyone.

"Anatthasañhite" is in the locative case in the sense of connection regarding the desire for destruction; therefore, it is said, "the destruction of such speech." In this context, the cause for the Dhamma teaching arises, or because the benefit such as the Dhamma teaching arises from this, it is called "Atthuppatti" (the occasion for the discourse), which refers to the present story.

"Ekaṃ gahetvā" means taking the reason for the Dhamma teaching out of the two: the Dhamma teaching and the prescription of training rules. "Ratticcheda" (interruption of the night) refers to going by the power of the seven-day duty (sattāhakaraṇīya) and causing the dawn to rise outside the monastery; it does not refer to the breach of the rains retreat (vassaccheda), because that will be mentioned separately. By this, it should be understood that going for a seven-day duty is permitted even if there is a reason for the breach of the rains retreat. "Na kismiñci" means they do not consider with the power of praise in any quality. The statement "We will undertake the precepts later" is said in reference to the failure of livelihood by displaying existing qualities for the sake of livelihood. "Atimanyiṃsati" means he will despise (avamanyiṃsati).

"Āyasmā" is a term of endearment for both high and low people in general; then, wishing to show it specifically for high-ranking people, it is said, "a name for respect, reverence, and being with a support (sappatissa)." In that context, because of being with a support (nissaya), it is called "Sappatissa," meaning one who has a support. It means a respectful word spoken towards those endowed with heavy (venerable) qualities who have that support. Here, "vacana" (word) itself is "adhivacana" (designation). "Pappaṭakoja" is the earth-essence (pathavī-oja) called Rasātala, which first arose as earth on the water in the beginning of the aeon, resembling a ball of butter, having the nature of floating on water, not dissolving, extremely smooth and sweet, and many thousands of yojanas thick. When the humans of the early aeon took and ate it out of craving for taste, it became hard on the upper part due to the power of their karma, while the lower part remained in its original state. By the power of that earth-essence, this great earth, along with mountains, oceans, and forests, remains steady without sinking into the water below and without breaking apart, like a raft. It refers to the essence-crust of the earth; therefore, it is called "Pathavīmaṇḍa," etc. "Sampannaṃ" means endowed with a sweet taste; therefore, it is said, "sādurasaṃ" (delicious taste).
91:
Upapannaphalo means having many fruits. After saying "nimmakkhika" (fly-free), by saying "nimmakkhikaᅉᄃa," he shows the absence of even fly eggs. Regarding the statement, "I shall move those beings who depend on the earth to that (fertilizer/soil)," if it is questioned whether there is the fault of anāmāsa (touching what should not be touched) when moving human women, female devas, or female animals by hand—it is not a fault. Why? Because it was taught: "Monks, there is no offense for one with psychic power in the sphere of psychic power." Therefore, the Blessed One, without showing the fault of anāmāsa, said, "Beings might also undergo transformation." A small village is called gāma. A large village with a market is called nigama. Padavĩtihārena means by taking steps.

## Commentary on the Request for the Promulgation of the Vinaya

The phrase "vinayapaattiyā mũlato pabhuti" is spoken with reference to the fact that the heavy offenses such as pārājika and other training rules had mostly not yet been promulgated in the order of the Pātimokkha recitation. It is not said because absolutely nothing had been promulgated. Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta requested the Blessed One to promulgate the training rules and recite the Pātimokkha, saying, "May the Blessed One promulgate training rules for the disciples; may he recite the Pātimokkha." In the Khandhaka, before the ordination of Venerable Ānanda and others, when Prince Rāhula was ordained, the training rule was seen to be promulgated: "Monks, a son who is not permitted by his parents should not be ordained; if one ordains him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaᅡa)." In this commentary also, because it is stated, "Food cooked by oneself is not allowable... etc... should not be cooked," and "One should not cause the night to pass or the Rains to pass [without the robe]," it is known that prohibitions against self-cooking and so on existed from the beginning. Thus, although some training rules had been promulgated, it should be understood that it was said, "Sāriputta, the Teacher has not yet promulgated training rules for the disciples," with reference to the pārājikas and others that had not yet been promulgated. One who withdraws from many objects and hides well with the mind in a single object is called paᅡisallĩna (secluded); thus it is said, "one who has reached the state of being alone." It means one who has reached mental seclusion (citta-viveka). The word ciraᅃ is in the accusative case (dutiyā vibhatti) in the sense of continuous duration (accanta-saᅃyoga).

Soᄱasavidhāya paāya refers to the wisdom consisting of sixteen types: the six types of wisdom mentioned in the Anupada Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya—"Monks, Sāriputta is of great wisdom, of wide wisdom, of joyous wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom, of penetrative wisdom"—the nine types of wisdom of the successive attainments (anupubbavihāra-samāpatti), and the one wisdom of the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga). Those disciples of the Buddhas who are manifest in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa),
92:
Only the Buddhas beginning with Vipassĩ are manifest in this world, and therefore they are extracted and shown here; other previous Buddhas are not shown. Therefore, in the Āᅡānāᅡiya Sutta, it should be understood that the devas also took the names of only those Buddhas who were manifest to them, and not others. "Kilāsuno" means living without effort and without concern because there is no purpose or benefit; it is not because of laziness. Therefore, it was said, "They are not those who live without concern due to laziness," and so on. "Niddosatāya" is due to the absence of faults that cause transgressions of body and speech. Because there are training rules of exhortation such as "One should not kill living beings, one should not take what is not given," it is said, "by way of the seven groups of offenses," and so on. Because it is said "once, once" with regard to the day at the end of every six years, the genitive case (sāmivacana) is used here in consideration of that word "once." Connect the meaning as: "In the whole of Jambudĩpa, the entire Saᅃgha of monks performed the Uposatha."

In the verses beginning with "Khantĩ paramaᅃ", patience (khanti) known as endurance (titikkhā) is called the supreme austerity (tapo) because it endures undesirable objects arising from beings and formations, and because it burns away the defilements. The Buddhas say that Nibbāna is supreme among all things because it is the exit from craving known as "vāna." The meaning is: one who harms others (parũpaghātĩ) by killing, cutting, or striking due to the absence of the aforementioned patience, and one who oppresses others through stealing, committing adultery, lying, slandering, or using harsh speech, cannot be called a "renunciant" (pabbajita) because of the absence of abandoned evil, nor can they be called an "ascetic" (samaᅃa) because of the absence of calmed evil. Not committing any evil through the restraint of virtue (sĩla-saᅃvara), fulfilling wholesome states through mundane concentration and insight, and purifying one's mind to a radiant state through all the paths and fruits—these three are the teaching (sāsana) of the Buddhas. "Anupavādo" means not reviling anyone with speech. "Anupaghāto" means not harming anyone with the body. The construction (yojanā) is: restraint in the virtue known as the Pātimokkha which remains after the mentioned non-reviling and non-harming; the practice of virtue regarding purity of livelihood and virtue regarding the use of requisites known as moderation in eating; the restraint of the faculties based on that virtue; dwelling in a secluded monastery known as forest-dwelling (araavāsa); standing in the Great Noble Lineage (mahā-ariyavaᅃsa) known as contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation based on living in the forest; and the exertion to produce mundane and supramundane concentration known as higher mind (adhicitta)—this practice is the instruction (anusiᅡᅡhi) of the Buddhas.
93:
The phrase "until the end of the Dispensation" is spoken because of the absence of the Āṇāpātimokkha. After the Parinibbāna, however, the recitation of the Ovādapātimokkha no longer exists. Indeed, only the Buddhas recite that Ovādapātimokkha; disciples do not recite it. "In the first period of Enlightenment" refers to the period defined as twenty years from the time of attaining Buddhahood at the Bodhi tree. However, the teacher Dhammapāla Thera stated, "Of the forty-five years, the first fifteen years are called the first period of Enlightenment." This statement, "From the time the training rules were prescribed, they recited only the Āṇāpātimokkha," was made with reference to the time the training rules were prescribed, completing it according to the sequence of the Pātimokkha recitation.

"No possibility, no occasion" is a statement of the rejection of cause, by way of rejecting the root cause (hetu) and condition (paccaya) in due order. "Yaṃ" means "for which reason." "In an impure assembly" refers to an assembly that is impure because it is mixed with shameless persons (alajjī). It is not only improper for the Buddhas to recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly; indeed, it is also improper for the disciples. Specifically, the responsibility of purifying through accusation (codanā), reminding (sāraṇā), and so forth, and then performing communion (saṃvāsa) belongs only to the disciples. The Buddhas, however, prescribe the training rules, teach the procedures for performing the Uposatha and so on, and then dismiss the assembly. They do not perform accusations or remindings. For that very reason, the Blessed One sat in silence throughout the night without reciting the Pātimokkha in the impure assembly. The monks, knowing the Blessed One's intention, expelled the impure person. Therefore, it should be understood that for disciples to perform Saṅgha acts such as the Uposatha while knowing the assembly is impure is nothing other than causing an obstacle to the holy life (brahmacariya).

"Disciples present in person" refers to all the very last disciples who were ordained during the time the Buddhas were manifest. To illustrate the great excellence, the word "uḷāra" (noble/grand) is used again in the phrase "by way of a family of noble wealth, etc." By the word "ādi" (etc.), it should be understood that noble, middling, and ignoble, etc., are included. The connection is: "Those last disciples caused it to disappear."

Even if the training rules were not prescribed, if the disciples were of similar birth and status, they would not destroy the Buddha's word, just as they would not destroy the texts handed down through their own lineage. Because the training rules had not yet been prescribed and these monks were not of similar birth and status, they destroyed it; to show this meaning, it is said, "Because they are of the same name... therefore they harass one another," and so forth. In the section on the long endurance of the Dispensation, however, even if the disciples are of various births and lineages, the long endurance of the Dispensation should be understood because of the completeness of the prescription of training rules. If that is so, why do not all Buddhas prescribe training rules?
94:
Because the prescription of training rules is not the only cause for the long endurance of the Dispensation, but also the appearance of persons to be tamed (veneyya) who will learn the Dhamma-Vinaya from the disciples in the future; therefore, the Buddhas prescribe training rules only when such persons exist, and not when they do not. It should be understood that having a complete prescription of the Vinaya is stated as the cause for the long endurance of the Dispensation because it indicates the existence of persons to be tamed.

In the Pāḷi text, in the sentence "Sahassaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ... ovadati" (Exhorts a thousand-fold Saṅgha of monks), the Saṅgha defined by the number of a thousand is called "sahassa." This is similar to the usage in "sahassī lokadhātu" (a thousand-fold world system) (D. ii. 18) and so on. The construction should be: "to that thousand-fold Saṅgha of monks." Although the word "sahassa" ends in the singular, it should be seen that the plural "ovadiyamānānaṃ" is used in reference to the individual members (the monks).

In the sentence "Anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsu" (Without clinging, the minds were liberated from the taints), "āsavehi" is in the instrumental case with the sense of the agent (kattā). "Cittāni" is the nominative plural. "Vimucciṃsu" is a passive formation (kammasādhana). Therefore, the meaning should be taken as: "The minds were liberated by the taints acting as agents, without grasping them by way of making them objects (of clinging)"; this is why it is stated as "tesañhi cittāni," and so on. In the phrase "yehi āsavehi" as well, "āsavehi" is simply the instrumental case in the sense of the agent. "Vimucciṃsu" is a passive formation. "Te" refers to the taints, and "tāni" refers to the minds, which is the accusative plural. If "vimucciṃsu" is taken as an active formation (kattusādhana), it means "they liberated." The meaning is that without grasping those minds by way of an object, the taints became liberated from those minds. Alternatively, "āsavehi" can be taken as the ablative case (nissakka) and "vimucciṃsu" as an active formation. In that case, the meaning should be taken as: "Without clinging to any conditioned phenomenon (saṅkhata dhamma) by way of craving and so on, the minds became liberated."

"Referring to the previous statement" means referring to the earlier statement, "in a certain fearsome forest thicket" (aññatarasmiṃ bhiṃsanake vanasaṇḍe). Because it means there is a reference to that previous statement, it is stated as "yaṃ vuttaṃ," and so on. The act of causing fear is called "bhiṃsanakata." To show the meaning "in that act of making fearsome," it says "bhiṃsanakiriyāyaṃ." Because it causes fear, it is called "bhiṃsana"; that itself is "bhiṃsanaka." Its state is "bhiṃsanakatta"; however, to show the meaning in another way, it is stated as "atha vā," etc., noting that it is said with the deletion of the letter 'ta'. "Or for the majority of beings" is an explanation of the meaning of the word "yebuyyena." By this explanation, in the phrase "yo koci" (whoever), the word "yo"...
95:
"Bhiṃsanakiriyāya" means in the act of causing terror. It is called "bhiṃsana" because it causes fear. That very bhiṃsana is called "bhiṃsanaka." Although the state of being terrifying is expressed as "bhiṃsanakattaṃ" with a double 'ta', it is written as "bhiṃsanakataṃ" by dropping one 'ta' character. Alternatively, to show another meaning, the phrase beginning with "atha vā" is stated. The phrase "bahutarānaṃ vā sattānaṃ" explains the meaning of the word "yebhuyyena." Through that Pali, the meaning of the word "yo ca" is also shown. The phrase "yo pavisati" should be understood with a distributive meaning (vicchā). How so? Because it can be interpreted as "whoever enters, among those many who enter."

A conclusion (nigamana) is the bringing together of the previously stated meanings into a summarized form. This which follows is the sequence of the conclusion (nigamanakkama). Sāriputta, the three Buddhas beginning with Vipassī, because there were no persons to be disciplined through the study of the scriptures (pariyatti) after their own Parinibbāna, were unconcerned (appossukkata) with the detailed prescription of training rules (sikkhāpada) for the benefit of those persons. Having discerned with their own minds the minds of those to be taught (veneyya) who were endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), those Buddhas, having gone even to terrifying forest thickets to admonish them, were diligent only in the teaching of the Dhamma (dhammadesanā) for the sake of producing the paths and fruits (magga-phala). They did not give detailed teachings of the Dhamma and Vinaya (Sutta, Vinaya, Abhidhamma). Sāriputta, this is the cause, this is the reason why the dispensation (brahmacariya) of the three Buddhas beginning with Vipassī did not last long.

"Purisayugavasena" means by the power of the period in which men live (purisayuga), or by the power of men. "Sabbapacchimaka" refers to the last person, such as Subhadda, who was ordained on the day of the Parinibbāna. The phrase "satasahassaṃ saṭṭhimattāni ca vassasahassāni" (one hundred and sixty thousand years) is stated starting from the birth of the Blessed One. If counted from the time of enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, it should be understood as less than that. "Dveyeva" means there are only two generations of men (purisayuga): one while the Blessed One was still alive and one after the Parinibbāna.

20-1. "Asambhuṇantena" means by not reaching. "Ko anusandhī" means what is the connection between the preceding and the following words. "Yaṃ vuttaṃ" means that the request for the prescription of training rules was made. "Yesu" refers to the things that are transgressions. "Nesaṃ" refers to the taints (āsava) occurring in the present life. "Te" refers to those transgressions. "Ñātiparivaṭṭo" is called the circle of relatives because the family itself revolves by way of grandfather, grandmother, son, etc. "Lokāmisabhūtaṃ" is worldly gain (lokāmisa) because it is included in the world and is to be touched by the defilements. "Pabbajjāsaṅkhepeneva" is by means of the summary of ordination, such as giving the ten training rules. "Etaṃ" refers to the non-performance of sexual intercourse and so on. "Thāmaṃ" refers to the power or ability to prescribe training rules. "Sañchaviṃ" refers to the white skin, natural skin, or beautiful skin. "Sesaṃ" indicates the connection of the remaining words. Now, wishing to show the connection of the meaning, the phrase beginning with "ayaṃ vā hetthā" is stated. There, the word "vā" is used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). The word "hi" is used in the sense of renown (pasiddhi). In this sentence, this alone is the meaning. Then, the meaning of the word "satthā" is shown as "tadā satthā." "Ropetvā" means having caused the depressed flesh at the site of the incision to grow evenly.
96:
Having caused the depressed flesh at the site of the incision to grow evenly. "Sake ācariyake" means in one's own status as a teacher or in the work of a teacher. "Vipulabhāvena" means by way of being many. "Ayoniso ummujjamanā" means reflecting in an improper way and thus knowing in a distorted manner. "Rasena rasaṃ saṃsanditvā" means mixing the blameless nature with the blameworthy nature. "Uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ" means acting in a way that exceeds the Dhamma and exceeds the Vinaya, in such a manner that the Dhamma and Vinaya will perish.

In this matter of the Saṅgha (the authority of the Saṅgha), "pabhassaro" means having a radiant nature. "Evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto" means "that venerable one with such a name and such a clan is a stream-enterer"; this person endowed with name and clan should be connected with the distant word "sotāpanno" (stream-enterer). In the phrase "avinipātadhammo," the word "dhamma" refers to nature. That nature, in terms of meaning, refers only to unwholesome states such as wrong view (diṭṭhi) that cast one into the planes of misery; therefore, it is stated as "ye dhammā," etc. Now, to show the meaning by way of nature alone, the phrase beginning with "vinipatanaṃ vā" is stated. "Niyato" refers to one whose final passing away (parinibbāna) of the aggregates is certain within seven lives. The reason for that certainty is stated as "sambodhiparāyaṇo" (destined for enlightenment).

"Anudhammatā" is the nature that follows the supramundane Dhamma. "Pavāraṇāsaṅgahaṃ datvā" means having postponed the Pavāraṇā by giving consent, saying, "We shall perform the Pavāraṇā on the coming full moon day of Tazaungmon." In this way, it is shown that it is proper to postpone the Pavāraṇā for some reason. "Māgasirassa paṭhamadivase" is stated by way of the lunar month and means the first day of the waning moon, immediately following the full moon of Tazaungmon. In the phrase "phussamāsassa paṭhamadivase," the same method applies. This is merely an illustration; because the wisdom of those to be taught (veneyya) was not yet mature, [the Buddha] stayed in that very place for one, two, three, or four months after the month of Pyatho, and then concluded his wandering (cārikā) during the remaining months. "Dasasahassacakkavāḷe" is stated with reference to the devas and Brahmās. As for humans, they can only attain realization of the Dhamma in this universe (cakkavāḷa). However, to arouse the desire in humans of other universes to be born in this universe, [the Buddha] looks at the infinite universes and performs the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya) suitable for them.
97:
In the word "yāmā," the syllable "ā" has the same meaning as the word "āgaccha" (come); therefore, it is said "āgaccha yāmā." It means "Come, let us go." "Suvaṇṇarasapiñjarāhi" means having a golden color like molten gold.
