In the Pali text, regarding the words beginning with "nimantitāmha," the connection should be made as: "Having been invited, we have spent the rains," or "Having been invited, we have already spent the rains."

"Yaṃ" means the collection of all gift-objects (deyyadhamma). "No natthi" means "it is not for us," or the word "no" is an explanation of "natthi" (is not). "Ettha" refers to the household life. "Taṃ" refers to that reason or matter. "Kuto" means "for what reason?" "Yaṃ" means "by which reason or matter." In the second alternative meaning, the phrase "within these three months" is the explanation of "ettha." "Taṃ" refers to that gift-object.

In that merit, having made it intense by bringing it to a sharp and clear state, "vassetvā" means having caused the rain of the jewel of Dhamma, which has the nature of a habitual tendency (vāsanā) for the future. "Yaṃ divasaṃ" means "on which day."

"Pattuṇṇapattapaṭe ca" refers to cloth from the Pattuṇṇa region and cloth from the Cīna (China) region. "Tumbāni" refers to oil-pots made of leather. "Anubandhitvā" means having followed. In this context, the word "abhiranta" is a synonym for "abhiruci" (inclination/desire); therefore, the words beginning with "yathājjhāsayaṃ" (according to one's inclination) are spoken. "Soreyyādīni" refers to Soreyya city and others that are on the route of the great wandering. "Payāgapatiṭṭhānaṃ" is the name of a landing place on the Ganges, and also the name of the village near that landing place. "Samantapāsādikāya" means of that commentary named Samantapāsādikā, because it inspires clarity (pasāda) in every way (samantato).

To show in detail the various ways intended by the term "samantato," the words beginning with "tatridam" are spoken. In that passage "tatridam," the connection is: "In that commentary called Samantapāsādikā, regarding its nature of being Samantapāsādika, this following verse is spoken." It should be understood as showing the varieties of Nidāna (origins) by way of Bāhira-nidāna (external origin), Antara-nidāna (internal origin), and Sikkhāpada-nidāna (precept origin). They also say it is "the proclamation of the Theravāda and the explanation of the varieties of stories (vatthu)." It is also appropriate to say "the explanation of the varieties of present stories of the precepts." Sikkhāpada-nidāna refers to Vesālī and so on...
98:
The specific region which is the cause for the prescription of the training rule should be known.

"Ettha" (Herein) refers to the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

"Sampassataṃ viññūnaṃ" (For the wise who see clearly) is the connection. Therefore, it should be understood that this commentary has arisen specifically as the Samantapāsādikā.

## Thus, in the Vimativinodanī-ṭīkā of the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā,
## the method of explaining the Verañjakaṇḍa is finished.
99:
## 1. Pārājika-kaṇḍa
## 1. First Pārājika
## Sudinna-bhāṇavāra-vaṇṇanā

"Bhaṇḍappayojana" means the selling of goods to be sold and the giving of loans. "Uddhāra" means the effort to take the principal thus lent or sold along with interest. "Sāraṇa" means causing one to remember what was forgotten, such as "It was given on such a day." "Catubbidhāya" means having four types, by way of kings, brahmins, householders, and recluses; or by way of monks and so on.

In the phrase "disvānassa etadahosi," the word "disvāna" (having seen) is in the causal sense. Why? Because it has a different subject from "ahosi." Just as in the passage "Having drunk ghee, strength arises (ghataṃ pivitvā balaṃ hoti)," it is the same in other such instances. The phrase "bhabbakulaputto" (a son of a good family with potential) is said in the sense of having the mere nature of a supporting condition (upanissaya), not because of being a "pacchimabhavika" (one in their last birth). For that reason, due to the remorse (vippaṭisāra) arising from the transgression committed by Sudinna because of his association with bad friends like his mother, an obstacle to the Path (magga) arose. For "pacchimabhavika" persons who have received a prediction (byākaraṇa) in the presence of previous Buddhas, no one can create an obstacle. Therefore, even though Aṅgulimāla Thera and others committed unwholesome acts, they were still endowed with the attainment of the Path. "Carimakacittaṃ" means the death-consciousness (cuti-citta). It is called "saṅkhalikhita" because it is like a conch shell that has been rubbed and polished. Therefore, "dhota" (washed) etc. is said. In the word "ajjhāvasatā," due to the connection with the word "adhi," the word "agāraṃ" (house) is a word with an accusative ending used in a locative sense. Therefore, "agāramajjhe" (in the middle of the house) is said. They are called "kāsāyāni" because they are dyed with an astringent decoction. Therefore, "kasāyarasapītatāya" is said. Indeed, because it is produced from astringent bark, the liquid is also called "kasāya-rasa."

When the word "jānāti" does not have the meaning of knowing (bodhanattha), then in its usage, the masters of grammar desire the genitive case in the instrumental sense (karaṇattha), as in "knowing by means of ghee" or "knowing by means of honey." Therefore, "not experienced with any suffering" is said. It means not experiencing the object with any suffering. In this word "kiñci," the elision of the genitive case in the instrumental sense is made. For that reason, it will be said: "In both alternatives, the elision of the case of the preceding word, which is the same as the following word, should be understood." When the word "jānāti" has only the meaning of remembering (saraṇattha), then as in the passages "remembering the mother" etc., in the accusative sense (upayogattha)...
100:
Grammarians state that the genitive case (sāmivacana) is used in the sense of the accusative; therefore, it is said, "Or else, it means one does not remember (has not experienced) any suffering." It means one does not remember because one has not experienced any suffering. "In both alternatives" refers to both the second and third alternatives mentioned by way of experiencing and remembering. "Of the preceding word" refers to the word 'kiñci'. "By the following word" refers to the word 'dukkhassa'. Since the genitive case is the same, although it should be said as 'kassaci dukkhassa', it should be understood that there is an elision (lopa) resulting in 'kiñci dukkhassa'. In the phrase "maraṇenapi mayaṃ te", to show the meaning of the word 'te' by way of the instrumental case (karaṇa) in the sense of 'with' (sahattha), another meaning is given: "we shall come to separation from you."

Those who are skilled in singing are called gandhabbas. Those who dance are called naṭas. Acrobats and others are called nāṭakas. Since one who serves oneself with the means of happiness is called one who plays or sports, in the second alternative meaning, "laḷā" etc., is mentioned. In the phrase "dānappadānādīni", a regular gift is called dāna, and a special gift is called padāna. By the word 'ādi', virtue (sīla) and so on should be included.

The fourteen types of meals are: Saṅgha-bhatta, uddesa-bhatta, nimantana-bhatta, salāka-bhatta, pakkhika-bhatta, uposathika-bhatta, pāṭipadika-bhatta, āgantuka-bhatta, gamika-bhatta, gilāna-bhatta, gilānupaṭṭhāka-bhatta, vihāra-bhatta, dhura-bhatta, and vāra-bhatta. Here, among the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) based on the three requisites such as lodgings, by taking the primary practices like the forest-dweller's practice (āraññakaṅga), the remaining practices are also understood to be included. "Of the Vajjīs" means of the Vajjian kings. "Among the Vajjīs" is a plural term referring to the country, meaning in the country named Vajjī. Because only the five cords of sensual pleasure are to be used and enjoyed, they are called 'upabhoga-paribhoga'. Since women, clothes, etc., are the accessories of those sensual pleasures, it is said "yehi tesaṃ" and so on. Because one is endowed with the strict alms-food eater's practice (ukkaṭṭha piṇḍapātika dhutaṅga) surrounded by the remaining practices, it is said, "desiring to wander for alms in sequence (sapadānacāraṃ)."

'Dosa' means night. That which is kept overnight is called 'ābhidosika'. Or, that which has reached or passed the time of dawn is called 'ābhidosika'. Therefore, it is said "exceeding one night" and so on.

'Udakakañjiya' refers to drinking water, utility water, and gruel. The word 'tathā' is used in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya). 'Anokappana' means lack of faith, and 'amarisana' means intolerance.
101:
'Taddhitalopa' means the elision of the vowel 'e' which is the cause of the derivative suffix (taddhita) when 'petāmaha' should be said in the sense of 'descended from a grandfather' (pitāmaha). Those whose wealth has been taken are called debtors (iṇāyikā). 'Palibuddha' means one who is oppressed because a prohibition has been made such as 'do not go, do not eat'.

'Attanā' means oneself. This wealth of the owner is called 'sāpateyya' (property). That very property is 'vibhava' (wealth).

'Bhijjanti' refers to being destroyed without having been taken before. The statement 'rebirth-linking is given' means that the rebirth-linking of a being that arises depending on the semen (sukka) given by the father is also said to be given by that father. Or, in this context, semen itself is called 'rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi) because it is the support for rebirth-linking; therefore, it is said, "it is established quickly." For there is no certainty of a being's arising exactly at the moment of the father's union; there is only certainty of the semen being established in that way. When the semen is established, for seven days or about half a month, it is only the field for the formation of the embryo. This is because the mother's flesh and the appearance of blood are always present. Since there were training rules (sikkhāpadas) prescribed previously, the meaning of the phrase 'apanyatte sikkhāpade' is that the first Pārājika training rule had not yet been established. 'Evarūpaṃ' means having such a heavy nature, referring to the subject matter of Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa; therefore, it is said, "He prescribed only the remaining five groups of minor offenses." It should be connected as 'yaṃ ādīnavaṃ'. It means because of the movement produced by bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti).

By the restriction 'teneva', the phrase 'kiṃ pana' etc., is said to show the causes of conceiving an embryo. Among those causes, bodily contact by way of the desire and lust (chandarāga) of both is mentioned. However, the touching of the navel by way of the woman's desire and lust is mentioned separately. For the mother of the wise Suvaṇṇasāma, having a desire to obtain a son, had a mind overwhelmed by sensual lust when she touched her navel; otherwise, the birth of the son would not have been possible. They also say, "Sakka also created the causes for the arising of sensual lust in that Pārikā." Or, it should be understood that this touching of the navel is mentioned separately from bodily contact by way of the story. Due to the wise Mātaṅga touching the navel of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, the youth Maṇḍavya was born. In the navel of King Caṇḍapajjota's mother, a scorpion...
102:
(The scent) spreads; because of that spreading, the birth of King Caṇḍapajjota occurred, thus it is said starting with "Eteneva nayena."

"Ayaṃ" refers to Sudinna's former wife from his time as a layman. "Yaṃ sandhāya" refers to the transgression of conduct. By the phrase "the parents come together," the presence of semen (sukka) is shown. By "the mother is in her season," the presence of blood (soṇita) is shown. "Gandhabba" refers to the being who has come to that state of existence. It means "one who must go" (gantabba) to that existence. Here, the letter 't' is changed to 'dh'. Alternatively, dancers are called "gandhabba." Like those dancers who take various forms in various lives, this being is also called "gandhabba." Because that being arises in that existence within seven days after the moment of the parents' union, it is called "paccupaṭṭhita" (present/arrived).

"Gabbha" refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) together with the kalala form. Here, "gabbha" is intended as the rebirth-linking mind, as in "she conceives a womb (embryo) with him." It relates to Sudinna's transgression. In the Pali, after the sentence "Friends, the community of monks is free from danger and blemish," one should understand the connection by supplying the missing words "in that community of monks" and "Sudinna... produced a blemish."

"Itiha" is a group of particles meaning "thus." "Muhuttena" is a synonym for the word "khaṇena" (in a moment). Even though the sound rises up to the Brahma realm, such a great sound of the devas cannot be an object of human perception, just like their physical forms. Therefore, it should be understood that the monks only knew later when Sudinna told them.

"Maggabrahmacariya" refers to the three trainings (sikkhā) which are the proximate cause of the Path, spoken of by way of metaphor. This is because those three trainings should be practiced for as long as life lasts. "Avipphārika" means not making an effort in recitation and so on. "Vahacchinna" means a severed foot or a severed shoulder. By the word "cintayi," the verbal nature of the word "pajjhāyi" is shown. Therefore, the Pali connection should be made by bringing in the connective "ca" as in "he became thin... and he brooded (pajjhāyi)."

Gathering in a group of people is called "gaṇasaṅgaṇikā." That gathering itself is called "papañca" (delay/proliferation). (It means) by gathering and delaying in that group. "Yassa" should be split into "ye assa." "Kathāphāsukā" means having pleasant talk due to intimacy, meaning comfortable conversation. Since the derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) is embellished and nourished only based on the primary materiality (bhūta-rūpa), the words starting with "pasāda" are spoken. The particle "dāni" here functions in the sense of the word "pana" (but). Since the word "etarahi," which expresses that time, exists separately, it is said "so pana tvaṃ" (but you). The word "no" is also like the word "nu"...
103:
...in the sense of questioning, as in "viya," therefore it is said "kacci nu tvaṃ" (are you...?). "Tam eva" refers to the dissatisfaction (anabhirati) characterized by the longing for the state of a layman. In the word "anabhiratim eva," to show the existence of a dissatisfaction other than that which is excluded by the word "eva," the words starting with "adhikusalānaṃ" are spoken. Tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are called "adhikusala." The words starting with "idaṃ pana" show the distinction to be mentioned above. "Pariyāyavacanamattaṃ" means merely an explanation of the word's meaning.

"Tasmiṃ" means when it occurs in the Dhamma taught for the sake of dispassion (virāga). The word "nāma" is used in the sense of reproach. "Lokuttaranibbānaṃ" is used as a distinction to differentiate it from the Nibbāna that is the destruction of defilements taught with "virāgāya" and so on. Pride arising based on birth/caste is called "mānamada" (intoxication of pride) because it produces intoxication. Pride that arises as "I am a man" is called "purisamada" (intoxication of manhood). Some teachers say, "Pride based on the ability to practice the conduct of the ignoble, or simply lust (rāga), is purisamada." By the word "ādi," intoxications such as the intoxication of strength (balamada) are included. "Tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ" is called the "round" (vaṭṭa) because kamma, defilements, and results revolve in the three planes. "Virajjati" means it fades away. "Yoniyo" refers to the egg-born (aṇḍaja) and so on. Although beings are not mixed with those egg-born origins, they are said to be mixed because they have a common nature of birth; thus they are called "yoniyo."

In the phrase "ñātatīraṇapahānavasena," the discerning of mentality-materiality along with its conditions by way of characteristics etc., is called "full understanding of the known" (ñāta-pariññā). Mundane insight occurring by way of comprehension of groups (kalāpa-sammasana) etc., is called "full understanding by investigation" (tīraṇa-pariññā). The Noble Path is called "full understanding by abandoning" (pahāna-pariññā). However, in this context, since the functions of ñāta-pariññā and tīraṇa-pariññā are also accomplished at the moment of the Path without delusion, all three types of full understanding are mentioned referring only to the Noble Path. Therefore, it is said, "Only the supramundane path is taught." "Kāmesu pātabyatānaṃ" means of the cravings that grasp the aspects such as beauty (subha) which are said to be enjoyed in the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma). Here, the possessors of the objects (visayī) are taken by way of the objects (visaya). "In the three instances" refers to the instances taught as "The Dhamma is taught for the sake of dispassion... not for the sake of grasping."

"Kalisāsanāropanatthāya" means for the purpose of attributing blame. "Kali" is a name for anger (kodha). The instruction of that anger is "kalisāsana," which is reproach spoken by the power of anger. "Ajjhācāra" is indeed transgression (vītikkama). "Samaṇakaraṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ" refers to the qualities such as shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) that make one a recluse. In the Pali, because of the association with the word "kathaṃ," the future tense "na sakkhissasi" is used. Some also say the future tense is used because of the association with the word "nāma." Extremely...
104: Dukkha-vipāka (suffering as a result) means that even an action that is not very blameworthy for laypeople is very blameworthy for monks, because it involves transgressing the Buddha's authority and destroying the three trainings they have undertaken. Something originating in water is called 'odaka'; the task of washing is referred to as 'udakakicca' and so forth. The future tense word 'samāpajjissasi' is used because of its association with the word 'nāma', as stated: 'nāma-saddena yojetabbaṃ'. Lack of restraint (asaṃvara), which is the cause of difficulty in being supported and so on, is referred to here by the term 'dubbharatā' (difficulty in being supported), using the effect to represent the cause, as stated: 'dubbharatādinaṃ vatthubhūtassa asaṃvarassa'. 'Atta' refers to the individual form (attabhāva). 'Dubbharatā' means the state of being difficult to support, whether by oneself or by one's attendants. Association with beings and defilements is meant by 'saṅgaṇikā', thus it is stated as 'gaṇasaṅgaṇikā' and so forth. The fulfillment of the eight grounds for laziness (aṭṭha-kusītavatthu) consists of: (1) being lazy thinking 'work must be done'; (2) similarly, being lazy thinking 'work has been done'; (3) being lazy thinking 'a journey must be taken'; (4) being lazy thinking 'a journey has been taken'; (5) being lazy thinking 'I did not get enough almsfood to be full'; (6) being lazy thinking 'I have eaten almsfood until full'; (7) being lazy thinking 'I am ill'; (8) being lazy thinking 'it has not been long since I recovered from illness'. Here, laziness (kosajja) is expressed by the word 'kusīta'. Even without a suffix indicating the state (bhāva), the meaning of the state can be understood, just as in 'paṭassa sukkaṃ' (the whiteness of the cloth). 'Vivaṭṭa', which is the destruction of all defilements, refers to Nibbāna, the cause for the exhaustion of all defilements such as lust. 'Saṃvarappahānapaṭisaṃyutta' means being endowed with the five kinds of restraint, such as restraint through virtue (sīla-saṃvara), and the five kinds of abandonment, such as abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna). 'Asuttantavinibaddha' means not composed in the form of a Sutta, which is called Pali in the three Pitakas, and not included by the elders of the councils; therefore, it is called 'pāḷivinimutta' (released from the Pali). Such miscellaneous teachings are the original source of the Commentaries. 'Okkantikadhamma-desanā' refers to the Dhamma teaching delivered by introducing it on various occasions and using various methods; therefore, it is stated: 'bhagavā kira' and so forth. 'Paṭikkhipanādhippāya' means having the intention to disregard even a prescribed training rule, thinking 'what is the use of this training rule?'. 'Vuttatthavasena' means by way of the means of attaining a basis. In the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga, in order to show that the abstinences (virati) from sensual misconduct at that time, the intentions (cetanā), and the states such as contact (phassa) are training rules, it is stated: 'ayañca'...
105: ...the meaning should be understood exactly as explained in the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga. Regarding the words 'nāmakāya' and 'padakāya' found in that Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga, the authors say they are mentioned in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. 'Nāmakāya' is simply the designation of names (nāma-paññatti), which is a collection of names; the remaining terms like 'padakāya' are just synonyms for it. 'Sikkhākoṭṭhāsa' (portion of training) refers to the abstinences (virati) and so forth, as well as the words that express those abstinences. 'Atthavasa' refers to specific benefits and specific advantages. Since these advantages are the reasons for the prescription of training rules, it is said 'by way of the cause' (kāraṇavasa). If there is no living in comfort, there can be no living together; therefore, living in comfort itself is called 'sahajīvitā' (living together). 'Dussīla' (immoral persons) refers to those without virtue and those with corrupted virtue. In the context of the Pārājika training rules, it refers to those without virtue; in the context of the remaining training rules, it refers to those with corrupted virtue due to various transgressions, resulting in broken or flawed virtue. It should be understood that in this context, both types of shameless (alajjī) persons are called 'dussīla'. Since all training rules are prescribed based on the ten reasons (atthavasa), the same method applies to the phrase 'depending on an immoral person' mentioned above. For this reason, the meaning is stated in a way that applies to all training rules: 'I shall rebuke those who are shameless (maṅku)...' and so forth. In that passage, 'maṅku' means being without luster and having a downcast face (looking ungraceful). Among the terms such as 'dhammena', 'dhamma' refers to a factual matter. 'Vinaya' refers to accusation (codanā) and reminding (sāraṇā). 'Satthusāsana' (the Teacher's instruction) refers to the completeness of the motion (ñatti-sampadā) and the completeness of the proclamation (anussāvana-sampadā). 'Sandiṭṭhamānā' means being in doubt. 'Ubbāḷhā' means being oppressed. It is shown that because of an immoral person, the Uposatha is not established, the Pavāraṇā is not established, Sangha acts do not proceed, and there is no harmony; thus, it is not proper to perform the Uposatha and all other Sangha acts together with shameless persons, as it would result in the misuse of the Dhamma (dhamma-paribhoga). It should be understood that Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are mentioned separately from other Sangha acts because they have fixed time periods and must be performed without fail. 'Akitti' means blame. 'Ayasa' means loss of followers. The fourteen Khandhaka duties are those mentioned in the Vattakkhandhaka: the duty of a guest (āgantuka-vatta), the duty of a resident (āvāsika-vatta), the duty of one departing (gamika-vatta), the duty of giving thanks (anumodana-vatta), the duty of the refectory (bhattagga-vatta), the duty of an alms-collector (piṇḍacārika-vatta), the duty of a forest-dweller (āraññaka-vatta), the duty of lodgings (senāsana-vatta), the duty of the sauna (jantāghara-vatta), the duty of the toilet (vaccakuṭi-vatta), the duty toward a preceptor (upajjhāya-vatta), the duty toward a co-resident (saddhivihārika-vatta), the duty toward a teacher (ācariya-vatta), and the duty toward a pupil (antevāsika-vatta). These fourteen duties must be practiced by all monks at all times as appropriate. However, the eighty-two major duties are to be practiced only during times such as when one is undergoing an act of rebuke (tajjanīya-kamma), and not at all times. Therefore, they are counted separately. These duties begin with 'I shall prescribe the duty for monks undergoing probation (parivāsa)...' and include 'one should not perform an ordination... one should not sit on the ground...'
106:
The duties ending with the words "A monk walking on a walkway should walk on the walkway" are sixty-six. Beyond that, the duties stated as "Monks, a monk undergoing probation (parivāsa) should not stay in a residence under a single roof with a monk undergoing probation who is senior to him, or with a monk liable to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanā), or with a monk practicing penance (mānatta), or with a monk liable to penance, or with a monk liable to rehabilitation (abbhāna)" (Cūḷavagga 82), etc., are not counted separately because they are not different from the duties to be practiced by regular monks (pakatatta). However, since they are to be practiced towards specific individuals such as senior monks undergoing probation, they are grouped according to those individuals and counted as five. Thus, there are seventy-one duties. In the duties of monks subjected to the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma), there is one duty stated as "He should not accept the salutation, rising to greet... or the massage of the back during a bath from a regular monk" (Cūḷavagga 86), which is the non-acceptance of salutation, etc. And there are ten duties beginning with "He should not accuse a regular monk of a lapse in virtue" (Cūḷavagga 51). Thus, there are eighty-two duties. Among these, since some are duties of the act of censure (tajjaniyakamma), etc., and some are duties of probation (parivāsa), etc., if one counts without repeating what has already been taken, there are exactly eighty-two. However, in other places in the Commentaries, it is mentioned as "eighty Khandhaka duties" (asītikhandhakavatta), considering that a slight decrease or increase does not affect the count. Alternatively, all duties found in the Vinaya that are not included in the previously mentioned fourteen duties should be understood by grouping them to make eighty-two or eighty.

The Discipline of Restraint (saṃvaravinaya) is fivefold: restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara), restraint of mindfulness (satisaṃvara), restraint of knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvara), restraint of patience (khantisaṃvara), and restraint of energy (vီriyasaṃvara). All five are called "restraint" (saṃvara) because they restrain bodily misconduct, etc., which ought to be restrained and removed, and they are called "discipline" (vinaya) because they remove them. The Discipline of Abandoning (pahānavinaya) is fivefold: abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna), abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna), abandoning by eradication (samucchedapahāna), abandoning by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhipahāna), and abandoning by escape (nissaraṇapahāna). It is called "abandoning" (pahāna) in the sense of giving up, and "discipline" (vinaya) in the sense of removing; therefore, it is called "the discipline of abandoning". The Discipline of Settlement (samathavinaya) refers to the seven ways of settling legal processes (adhikaraṇasamatha). The Discipline of Regulation (paññattivinaya) refers to the training rules (sikkhāpada) themselves. Indeed, those training rules are supported only by the Blessed One's regulation of training rules, for they exist only when that regulation exists. The connection is: "what was stated by applying the chain method and by applying the combination ten times." Therein, because each preceding word is combined only with the immediately following word, it is like an iron chain; thus it is called "the chain method" (saṅkhalikanaya). Because each single word among the ten words is combined with each of the remaining nine words, it is called "the method of each single word as the root" (ekekapadamūlikanaya).
107:
Regarding "one hundred meanings, one hundred dhammas" (atthasataṃ dhammasataṃ), in the Parivāra (Pari. 334), the chain method (saṅkhalikanaya) is stated by way of the partial cycle (khaṇḍacakka), starting from "Whatever is for the well-being of the Saṅgha, that is for the comfort of the Saṅgha" and ending with "Whatever is for the endurance of the True Dhamma, that is for the support of the Vinaya." In that root-method, when the fixed cycle (baddhacakka) is formed by also combining the phrase "Whatever is for the support of the Vinaya, that is for the well-being of the Saṅgha" according to the fixed cycle method found in the single-root method, there are twenty words: ten preceding Dhamma-words and ten succeeding Attha-words. However, in the single-root method, only nine Attha-words are obtained in one turn. Thus, in ten turns, there are ninety Attha-words and ninety Dhamma-words. It should be understood that when these ninety words are combined with the ten Attha-words and ten Dhamma-words stated in the chain method, they become the aforementioned one hundred meanings and one hundred dhammas.

In this regard, although the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭီkā states a way of combining one hundred meanings and one hundred dhammas separately in both the chain method and the single-root method, that does not agree with the verse "atthasataṃ dhammasataṃ" (Pari. 334). This is because it would then have to be stated as "two hundred meanings, two hundred dhammas, four hundred linguistic expressions, and eight hundred knowledges." Therefore, it should be understood that "one hundred meanings, one hundred dhammas" is stated only according to the method mentioned here in this Vimativinodanီ. "Two hundred linguistic expressions" (nirutti) means: one hundred linguistic expressions by way of those clarifying the meaning, and one hundred linguistic expressions by way of those that are dhammas; thus two hundred. "Four hundred knowledges" (ñāṇa) means: one hundred knowledges in the hundred meanings, one hundred knowledges in the hundred dhammas, and two hundred knowledges in the two hundred linguistic expressions; thus four hundred. "Atirekānayanattho" means the sense of including what has not been stated.

## The Explanation of the Method of the First Regulation is finished.

## The Explanation of the Sudinna Recitation Section is finished.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Female Monkey

"The present tense used in the sense of frequency" (pacuratthe hi vattamānavacanaṃ) means that because there is a desire to indulge daily without refraining after having indulged once, the present tense "indulges" (paṭisevati) is used to denote continuity and frequency, even at a moment when the act of indulgence is not occurring, just as in the phrase "The Mallas are fighting in this place." "Āhiṇḍantā" means while wandering about.
108:
“Sahodha-gahito” means being caught along with the stolen goods; or rather, this “Sabhaṇḍag-gahito” is the original text of the Commentary. “That training rule remains the same” means that without specifying any particular person such as a human or a non-human, but speaking generally, as it was said, “Whatever monk should indulge in sexual intercourse” (Pārājika 39), it is intended that for a monk who indulges in sexual intercourse in any of the thirty types of passages of women, men, pandakas, or hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanakas) among humans, non-humans, and animals, that training rule results in the cutting of the root (Pārājika) only.

By this, it is shown that this supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) arose through the context of the story (vatthu) for the sake of clarity by expressing the intention of the original regulation (mūlapaññatti), and not by way of showing a specific new meaning. Mere touching is called “āmasana.” Contact firmer than that is called “phusana.” Making it even firmer than that contact and rubbing one’s body against another’s body is called “ghaṭṭana.” “All that” refers to all actions such as looking, etc., that occur through lust.

To show the nature of lokavajja (worldly fault) of sacittaka training rules such as killing living beings and acittaka training rules such as drinking intoxicants with a single defining characteristic, it is said: “For whom the mind is only unwholesome in the sacittaka aspect, that act is called lokavajja.” In that sentence, although the term “sacittaka-pakkhe” (in the sacittaka aspect) should be said referring only to acittaka training rules because only they can have a sacittaka aspect, yet since the worldly expression “he kills a being” can occur even in sacittaka training rules during activities like walking (caṅkama) without the intention to kill, the acittaka aspect is conceived, and “sacittaka-pakkhe” is said in common to both sacittaka and acittaka training rules. Otherwise, the characteristic of the lokavajja nature of sacittaka training rules would not be stated in this sentence.

However, if it is said, “In the sacittaka aspect, the mind is only unwholesome,” it should be understood that this meaning is established by implication: that in sacittaka training rules, the mind is only unwholesome; in acittaka training rules, the unwholesome state is certain only in the sacittaka aspect, but not in the acittaka aspect. In that acittaka aspect, it could be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate (abyākata) as the case may be. In the phrase “sacittaka-pakkhe,” it should be taken only as the mind that knows the transgression of the object (vatthu), not as the mind that knows the regulation (paññatti). If it were taken as the mind knowing the regulation, it would follow that all training rules are lokavajja. The reason is that for one who knows “This is forbidden; it is not proper to do,” even in a paññattivajja (fault by regulation), a mind of resentment (paṭigha) usually arises due to disrespect. Therefore, if taken this way, this sentence would be useless, as it would lead to the conclusion that “all training rules are lokavajja.”
109:
In this sentence, since the restriction “the mind is unwholesome only in the sacittaka aspect” is not made, it is not possible to restrict that in drinking intoxicants, etc., the mind is definitely not unwholesome in the acittaka aspect. Rather, the restriction is established here as: in the sacittaka aspect, the mind is only unwholesome, not wholesome, etc. This being so, for those who drink without knowing it is an intoxicant, the act of drinking is done only with an unwholesome mind; and for bhikkhunīs who apply scents and colors without knowing their nature, the act of applying is done even without an unwholesome mind; in both cases—drinking intoxicants and applying scents and colors—the occurrence of an offense is established.

The statement in the Sāratthadīpanī saying, “From the words ‘the mind is only unwholesome in the sacittaka aspect,’ it should be understood that there is no such restriction that the mind is only unwholesome in the acittaka aspect through not knowing the object of an acittaka training rule,” is inappropriate. For among the thirteen acittaka rules that are lokavajja, only in drinking intoxicants is the unwholesome mind certain even in the acittaka aspect. This is because in the twelve training rules other than drinking intoxicants, an offense is reached even with an unwholesome mind, etc.

The statement made to show this restriction—which is not desired by anyone and is not evident even by the words—as having another meaning, saying, “If the mind of an acittaka rule were only unwholesome even in the acittaka aspect, this qualifier ‘sacittaka-pakkhe’ would be useless,” etc., is itself useless. This is because no one desires such a restriction. Indeed, no teacher learned in grammar desires that restriction which would make the qualifier “sacittaka-pakkhe” useless. Rather, they desire only this: in the sacittaka aspect, the mind is only unwholesome; but in the acittaka aspect, the mind is not fixed—it could be only unwholesome, or it could be any one of the wholesome states, etc.

Therefore, the qualifier “sacittaka-pakkhe” is also meaningful. The lokavajja nature of acittaka training rules is established by the unwholesome restriction in their sacittaka aspects. And among those acittaka training rules, only for drinking intoxicants do the lokavajja nature and the unwholesome mind exist even in the acittaka aspect. But for the twelve acittaka rules other than drinking intoxicants, the view that the lokavajja nature and the unwholesome mind exist only in the sacittaka aspect is not contradictory. Therefore, there is nothing inconsistent in this view.

As for what is said in the Sāratthadīpanī: “For one who drinks without knowing it is an intoxicant... because an offense can occur even without an unwholesome mind... the lokavajja nature of acittaka training rules like drinking intoxicants would not exist,” etc., and the words cited from the Gaṇṭhipadas to establish that meaning, which have been greatly elaborated—these should not be believed as the essence because they contradict the Commentaries. The contradiction is as follows: “In this drinking of intoxicants, the acittaka nature should be known by the ignorance of the object; the lokavajja nature should be known because it must be drunk only with an unwholesome mind.” For this...
110:
The commentary statement (the explanation in the Sāratthadīpanī) which says, "It is a worldly fault (lokavajja) because it is drunk only with an unwholesome mind in the aspect of being with intention (sacittaka)," is not good (not appropriate). This is because it has already been stated generally in this Pārājika Commentary for all worldly faults that "in the aspect of being with intention, the mind is only unwholesome," and in the Commentary on the Surāpāna training rule, it is specifically stated as "because it is drunk only with an unwholesome mind," thus indicating the presence of an unwholesome mind even in the aspect of being without intention (acittaka).

In fact, it cannot be said that "the meaning already stated generally in this Pārājika is merely repeated in the Surāpāna Commentary," because there is no benefit in repeating what has already been said, and it would lead to the consequence that it should also be stated for other worldly faults that are acittaka. Furthermore, one cannot assume that a method stated in one place is automatically stated for others due to having the same characteristics, and thus say "it is stated only in the Surāpāna training rule"; for it should then have been stated in the Uyyutta training rule, which is the very first among the acittaka worldly faults, or if stated in the Surāpāna training rule, it should have been cross-referenced by saying "this method also applies to the remaining acittaka worldly faults."

Alternatively, a teacher who intends only the meaning already stated should have spoken according to the sequence previously stated, saying "because it is drunk only with an unwholesome mind in the aspect of being with intention," since repetition is beneficial for removing doubt and so forth. In the context of training rules, what should be specified is indeed specified; otherwise, the distinctions such as whether there is an offense or not would be difficult to understand. For this very reason, in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Commentary, the worldly fault and the presence of an unwholesome mind are specifically stated only for the sacittaka aspect of the Giraggasamajja training rule and others, saying: "They are called acittaka because they can be committed even without intention; however, when there is intention, they are both worldly faults and involve unwholesome minds because they are committed only with an unwholesome mind." This is not stated in such a way for Surāpāna. In the case of Surāpāna, it is stated as "because it is drunk only with an unwholesome mind" in a way that applies to both aspects, without specifying "in the aspect of being with intention."

Therefore, it is well-established that this statement, "It is a worldly fault because it is drunk only with an unwholesome mind," is made separately specifically to show that this Surāpāna is a worldly fault and involves an unwholesome mind in both the sacittaka and acittaka aspects. By this very explanation, the statement in the Sāratthadīpanī—which, with the notion that it fulfills the meaning of "It is a worldly fault because it is drunk only with an unwholesome mind in the aspect of being with intention," says "By this intention alone, only the presence of an unwholesome mind is stated for other worldly fault acittaka training rules, but not the presence of the three types of minds (ticittaka)"—is also refuted. For this reason, it is stated in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Commentary: "These ten training rules—the Giraggasamajja training rule, the Cittāgāra training rule, Saṅghāṇi, Itthālaṅkāra, Gandhavanṇaka, Vāsitakapiññāka, and the training rules concerning the massaging of bhikkhunīs, etc.—are acittaka and involve an unwholesome mind." The meaning of this phrase 'acittaka unwholesome mind' is: they are called acittaka because they can be committed even without intention; when there is intention..."
111:
In the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Commentary, it is stated: "These ten training rules—the Giraggasamajja training rule, the Cittāgāra training rule, Saṅghāṇi, Itthālaṅkāra, Gandhavanṇaka, Vāsitakapiññāka, and those concerning the massaging and rubbing of bhikkhunīs, etc.—are training rules that are acittaka (can be committed without intention) and involve an unwholesome mind. The meaning here is that they are called acittaka because they can be committed even without intention (unintentionally). If there is intention, they are both worldly faults (lokavajja) and involve an unwholesome mind because they are committed only with an unwholesome mind." This statement has also been refuted by demonstrating the opposite meaning as explained above.

Therefore, it should be understood that this statement is made specifically to show this distinction: that even in the acittaka aspect of Surāpāna (drinking intoxicants), the mind is only unwholesome. The meaning here is that in the phrase "vatthu-ajānanatāya cettha," the syllable "ca" highlights a special meaning and is synonymous with "api ca." Therefore, in other acittaka worldly fault training rules, the characteristics of being a worldly fault and having an unwholesome mind are stated as: being acittaka because they can be committed without intention, and being a worldly fault and having an unwholesome mind because they are committed only with an unwholesome mind if intention is present. That characteristic does not apply to this Surāpāna training rule. It means that there is a distinction in this training rule.

If it is asked, "What is that distinction?" It should be understood that it is acittaka only because it is committed without the mind that knows the substance (alcohol), due to not knowing the substance. In this regard, there is no distinction in being acittaka. However, the distinction here is that even in the acittaka aspect, which is the state of not knowing the substance, the Surā-meraya is swallowed only with an unwholesome mind; thus, the state of being a worldly fault (lokavajjatā) and having an unwholesome mind (akusalacittatā) should be understood in both the sacittaka and acittaka aspects of this training rule. Since it is stated generally as "only with an unwholesome mind" without specifying "if there is intention," it should be understood that being a worldly fault and having an unwholesome mind are established in both aspects.

For this very reason, in the explanation of the training rules in the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary named Paramatthajotikā, it is stated: "The training rule of Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna has two origins (samuṭṭhāna): from the body, and from the body and mind." Because of the absence of the mind that knows it is liquor, the body alone, devoid of the mental factor (of knowing), is called a single origin (ekasamuṭṭhāna) here. Even at that moment of having a single origin, the volition (cetanā) with which one drinks is strictly unwholesome. Therefore, in that same commentary, it is stated: "Among these ten training rules, the first five are abstinences from natural faults (pakativajja) because, like the taking of life and so forth, they have strictly unwholesome minds as their origin. The remaining five are abstinences from faults by enactment (paṇṇattivajja)." In this way, the state of having an unwholesome mind and being a natural fault, which is called a worldly fault, is stated generally for all five. Also, among the factors (aṅga), the factor of knowing (jānananga) is not mentioned. For that reason (it is stated as follows):
112:
The factors of the training rule concerning the state of negligence through surā, meraya, and majja are stated as these four: it must be an intoxicating liquid of the types such as surā; the intention to drink must be present; one makes the effort to drink; and it enters the stomach when drunk. It is not stated as five factors together with the factor of knowing it is surā. If knowing it is surā were also a factor, it should certainly have been stated, but it was not. Just as in this Khuddakapāṭha, so too in other commentaries of the Sutta Piṭaka, etc., the factor of knowledge is not mentioned anywhere. Therefore, regarding the commentary text "It is a worldly fault (lokavajja) because it is to be drunk only with an unwholesome mind," it should be concluded here that even in the case of not knowing (acittaka), the meaning is exactly this: "It is a worldly fault because it is to be drunk only with an unwholesome mind."

Furthermore, there is a point to be discussed: in the Gaṇṭhipada texts, it is said, "Just as for one who intends to kill a certain being but kills another being lying in that same place, it is an act of taking life (pāṇātipāta) because of the commonality of being a living being; so too, for one who intends to drink a certain intoxicant but drinks another intoxicant, it is unwholesome because of the commonality of being an intoxicant. However, just as for one who kills a snake perceiving it to be a piece of wood, it is not an act of taking life; so too, for one who drinks an intoxicant perceiving it to be coconut water, it is not unwholesome." This statement, comparing it to taking life as being identical in all respects, is highly improper. This is because there is no rule that all training rules and unwholesome acts like taking life must be identical to one another. Indeed, taking life is accomplished even by indirect means (pariyāya), but stealing (adinnādāna) is not so. That stealing is accomplished even by command (āṇatti), but not so in sexual misconduct (methuna), etc. Therefore, it is improper to make identical in all respects those things like taking life which are different in their factors of effort (payoga), etc. If someone says, "Just like taking life, stealing, sexual misconduct, etc., are also accomplished by indirect speech, etc.," why is that not accepted? Because there is no such statement in the scriptures. Here too, since there is no scriptural statement saying "drinking intoxicants is similar to taking life," this Gaṇṭhipada statement should also not be accepted. Moreover, a Vinaya expert who wishes to refute a meaning already established by the commentary text should do so only by showing its contradiction with the Suttas, Suttānuloma, and so forth, and not merely by making it identical with another training rule that is entirely different in its factors of effort, etc. Indeed, in the view that "it is unwholesome even for one who drinks without knowing it is an intoxicant," there is no contradiction with the Suttas, etc. Firstly, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, no Sutta or similar text is seen that contradicts this meaning, nor is any seen in the Sutta Piṭaka, etc.

Regarding this, some teachers say: "Because it is said 'Mind is the forerunner of all states' (Dhp. 1, 2), all unwholesome acts occur only for one who previously knows the object of transgression." That statement of those teachers...
113:
...only demonstrates their ignorance of the intended meaning of the Sutta. For the statement 'Mind precedes all mental states' does not illustrate the meaning that unwholesome states arise only for one who first knows the object of transgression. Rather, it illustrates the meaning that when wholesome and unwholesome states arise, they arise only by depending on the co-nascent mind (sahajāta-citta) which is the precursor in the sense of being the condition for their arising; they do not arise without the mind. In this matter [of drinking intoxicants], when it is said, 'It is an unwholesome act even for one who drinks without knowing it is an intoxicant,' it does not lead to the meaning that unwholesome mental factors such as greed (lobha) arise even without the co-nascent mind. Thus, this Sutta should not be cited to refute that [unwholesome] view. There is also no contradiction with the Abhidhamma here, because it is stated that wholesome and unwholesome impulsions (javana) arise in the five-sense-door process (pañcavijñāṇavīthi) even for one who does not know [the object] beforehand by way of name, species, and so forth.

Furthermore, the impulsions that arise at the six doors for foolish worldlings (bālaputhujjana) are mostly unwholesome. Wholesome states arise for them only rarely, by the power of decisive support (upanissaya) such as noble friends (kalyāṇamitta). This is because even for those who remain silent or those who are asleep and dreaming, unwholesome impulsions such as restlessness (uddhacca) mostly occur, and there is no impulsion for those worldlings that is devoid of both wholesome and unwholesome states. Unwholesome states arise according to the object, according to latent tendencies (vāsana), and according to conditions; in such arising, what does it have to do with prior knowing or not knowing? In fact, there are those such as taking life which are accomplished when endowed with factors like knowing, and there are those such as drinking intoxicants and wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) which are accomplished even without knowing. The Fully Enlightened One, having known each of these [paths of action] as they truly are, pointed them out accordingly. In accepting them according to how they were pointed out, how could there be any contradiction with the Abhidhamma? Thus, because there is no contradiction with the Suttas and so forth, and because it is stated in the Commentary, the meaning should be taken only as stated above.

If this is so, why is it stated in the Commentary that 'A novice (sāmaṇera) reaches a breach of virtue (sīlabheda) only if he drinks knowingly, but not if he drinks unknowingly'? This is not a fault. The breach of virtue for novices is dependent on the authority (āṇā) of the Blessed One, similar to the breach of virtue for those who follow a suspended monk (ukkhittānuvattika) and so forth. For them, the breach of virtue does not occur merely by the arising of an unwholesome state; it is prescribed only immediately after the formal act of admonition (samanubhāsana) involving the Saṅgha. Similarly, in this case of drinking intoxicants, [the breach of virtue] is prescribed only for drinking knowingly, not for drinking unknowingly. Indeed, the sphere of training rules (sikkhāpada-visaya) is one thing, and the sphere of unwholesome acts (akusala-visaya) is another. For that very reason, if one of the first five training rules of novices is broken, all the training rules are broken. As for the unwholesome act, it occurs only through the one [rule] that is broken, not through the others. Therefore...
114:
Even if a novice (sāmaṇera) drinks [alcohol] unknowingly, although there is no breach of virtue (sīla-bheda), it should be understood as an unwholesome act (akusala) that reaches the path of action (kammapatha).

In the Sāratthadīpanī, the statement made by some teachers—"For a novice who drinks without knowing it is alcohol (surā), there is no Pārājika (breach of virtue), but it is indeed unwholesome"—is rejected with the claim: "That statement is merely the opinion of those teachers." The reason given there is: "For a monk (bhikkhu), even if he drinks unknowingly, from the moment it is a fermented seed-base, he incurs a Pācittiya offense. For a novice, it is only when he drinks knowingly that he incurs a breach of virtue; if he drinks unknowingly, he does not. Only this much is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā); it is not stated that it is unwholesome." However, this reasoning is not valid. This is because, in the context of discussing the breach of virtue—stating that for novices virtue is breached only when drinking knowingly and not when unknowingly—the absence of the phrase "but it is unwholesome" does not serve as a reason for the absence of unwholesomeness in the case of unknowing. This is because there was no occasion to discuss unwholesomeness in that context, and because in the appropriate place (the Surāpāna-vaṇṇanā), it is stated: "Because it must be drunk only with an unwholesome mind, it is a worldly fault (lokavajja)." Furthermore, those teachers who say "but it is unwholesome" did not speak based solely on this passage from the Khandhaka Commentary which explains the breach of virtue for novices, such that one should say "only this much is stated in the Commentary." Rather, they spoke based on various statements found in the Surāpāna Commentary, the Sutta Piṭaka Commentary, and the traditional instructions (paveṇi-upadesa) of the Mahāvihāravāsī elders. The view that unwholesomeness occurs only for one who drinks knowingly is the view of those with wrong views, such as the Abhayagiri sect. Therefore, the statement made by some teachers—"For a novice who drinks without knowing it is alcohol, there is no Pārājika, but it is indeed unwholesome"—should be regarded as well-spoken.

In the Sāratthadīpanī, the statement of some teachers—"Even if drinking unknowingly, alcohol does not enter the mouth of a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), because it must be drunk only with an unwholesome mind that reaches the path of action"—is rejected as "not good." It is stated there: "Just like the virtue of the Bodhisatta’s mother while the Bodhisatta is in the womb, this virtue of the Noble Disciples (ariyasāvaka) should be understood as accomplished by natural law (dhammatā)." To support this accomplishment by natural law, the following Commentary passage is shown: "Even in another birth, a Noble Disciple does not kill a living being nor drink alcohol even for the sake of life. If one were to mix alcohol and milk and put it into their mouth, only the milk enters, not the alcohol. How so? Just as when water mixed with milk is given to cranes (koñca), only the milk enters and not the water. If it is said that this is accomplished by species-nature (yoni-siddha), then this [case of the Noble Ones] should be understood as accomplished by natural law (dhammatā-siddha)." Showing this Commentary passage is also inappropriate. Because, just like the virtue of the Bodhisatta’s mother, the accomplishment by natural law of the Noble Disciples...
115:
In this context, the "natural law" (dhammatā) of the Bodhisatta’s mother is simply the certainty of the non-arising of unwholesome states due to the power of the Bodhisatta’s and her own perfections (pāramī). Similarly, for Noble Disciples (ariyasāvaka) in another birth, the "natural law" is simply the certainty of the non-arising of unwholesome states that cause the breach of various precepts, due to the power of the Path (magga) which absolutely abandons the ten paths of unwholesome action (kammapatha) such as killing (pāṇātipāta) and other unwholesome states that lead to the lower realms (apāya). Natural law here is not "causelessness" like the natural law of the Sabhāvavādīs (Naturalists). Or rather, just as in this method of natural law, the presence or absence of a result follows the presence or absence of a cause, and it is not an absence of cause and condition; so too here, the absence of those paths of action (kammapatha) like killing is due to the absolute absence of the defilements (kilesa) which are their cause, and the presence of the remaining unwholesome states is due to the presence of their causes—this is natural law, not causelessness. Therefore, the statement of some teachers—"Even if drinking unknowingly, alcohol does not enter the mouth of a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), because it must be drunk only with an unwholesome mind that reaches the path of action"—is indeed well-spoken, because alcohol is not swallowed by Noble Ones even unknowingly due to the absence of greed (rāga) that leads to the lower realms. It is not understood by what reason that statement became "not good," or how that statement was rejected by saying it is "accomplished by natural law."

Furthermore, the statement in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary—"Mixing alcohol and milk... this is accomplished by natural law"—also proves that even in the case of drinking without [conscious] intent (acittaka), it occurs only with an unwholesome mind. Indeed, when it is said, "Even in another birth, a Noble Disciple does not kill a living being, does not take what is not given... does not drink alcohol even for the sake of life," an objection (codanā) might arise: "While it is easy to abstain from the first four paths of action because they involve conscious intent (sacittaka), how can one abstain from the last one, drinking alcohol, since it can occur without conscious intent (acittaka)?" Considering this, the teacher providing the explanation—meaning that although there is no [specific] intent due to not knowing the object, alcohol must be swallowed only with an unwholesome mind that reaches the path of action, and since such an unwholesome occurrence has been destroyed by the Path of the Noble Disciple, alcohol does not enter that Noble One's throat—said, "If one were to [put] alcohol and milk into his [mouth]..." and so on. In that statement, "only the milk enters, not the alcohol" is intended to show that alcohol does not enter the throat in any way; it is not intended to show the ability to separate milk from a mixture of alcohol. The meaning here is: if anything from the milk mixed with alcohol were to enter, only the milk would enter, not the alcohol. If the milk is inseparable from the alcohol, then nothing...
116:
Regarding the term "enters": the fact that water does not enter the mouth [of certain birds] is accomplished by birth (yonisiddha). Here, 'yoni' refers to birth or species. Therefore, because the physical forms known as beaks are not the cause for swallowing water mixed with milk, that non-entering is accomplished for those of the crane species (koñca-jātika). This is the meaning. Similarly, even if liquor mixed with milk enters the milk, it does not enter the other side of the throat [of a Noble One].

Accomplished by the nature of things (dhammatāsiddha) means it is accomplished for noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) by the nature of being devoid of the defilements (kilesa) that are the cause for drinking liquor. Thus, even in the case of being unintentional (acittaka), since liquor is to be drunk only with an unwholesome mind, the non-drinking of noble disciples is established as firm. If one wishes to assert that not drinking liquor is the nature of the Noble Ones even when it would be drunk without an unwholesome mind in a state of ignorance, that statement is not appropriate, as it contradicts other statements in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). The meaning should be taken only in a way that does not contradict other statements.

Furthermore, the non-performance of the five courses of action (kamma-patha), such as killing (pāṇātipāta), even in another life, is the natural virtue (dhammatā-sīla) of the Noble Ones. If those courses of action were the same as drinking liquor in terms of being done unknowingly, then a noble disciple might also commit the other four courses of action unknowingly. If that were so, for the Noble Ones who do not know, bodily and vocal activity (kāya-vacī-pavatti) in killing others or taking what belongs to others would not occur even with wholesome or indeterminate (avyākata) minds. However, it is not that it does not occur; it does occur. This is because the loss of life of beings occurred due to the walking of the Elder Cakkhupāla, and the touching of the path with the path (physical contact) occurred due to the violation of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā. Therefore, it should be understood that it is specifically stated that liquor does not enter the other side of the throat of the Noble Ones because liquor is to be drunk only with an unwholesome mind, even in a state of being unintentional (acittaka).

If it is asked, "Is it not said that all courses of action occur only for one who knows the object (vatthu)?" No, it is not. Because wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) occurs only through distorted grasping. How indeed can a wrong view that grasps a non-omniscient one as omniscient, or the impermanent as permanent, know the object? If it knew, it would not be wrong view. Since that wrong view is counted among the courses of action, where is the rule that a course of action occurs only for one who knows? If it is said, "Even if grasping the non-omniscient as omniscient, because it grasps his identity as 'this being', wrong view also knows the object?" No, because it is the same as grasping the identity in drinking liquor as 'this is not liquor'. If it is said, "Even though 'this' refers to the object, because there is no specific knowing as 'liquor', he does not know," it is the same: even though knowing 'this person' as a person, because there is no specific knowing as 'non-omniscient', wrong view also does not know the object. Thus...
117:
For those people, regarding the Buddha as one who does harm, or regarding those like Pūraṇa Kassapa who do harm as those who do good, or in the arising of resentment or affection, the method is the same. For all unwholesome states are preceded by perversion (vipallāsa).

Furthermore, liquor being drunk has the nature of producing unwholesomeness by necessity, just like liquor already drunk. For a person who drinks liquor perceiving it as milk, etc., the sequence of unwholesome states like lust and hatred toward even mothers or sisters arises due to the very nature of the object (vatthu-sabhāva), which is liquor. Thus, even at the moment of drinking, sharp lust arises. Because of that, when the Elder Sāgata drank without knowing, there was the falling away from the five higher powers (abhiññā) and meditative absorptions (jhāna). Later, the sequence of unwholesome states like disrespect toward the Buddha and others continued until the effects of the liquor faded. Therefore, the Blessed One, by way of showing the occurrence of unwholesome states like disrespect in that Elder, revealed the fault of liquor and laid down the training rule (sikkhāpada).

Indeed, there is no falling away from jhāna without the arising of the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Therefore, for one who does not know, liquor being drunk or already drunk is a producer of unwholesomeness by its own nature. This meaning is established both by the sequence of the Elder Sāgata's falling away from jhāna and by the exclusion (vyatireka) of liquor not entering the mouth of the Noble Ones who are devoid of defilements. This should be the conclusion here. Indeed, taking it this way follows the view of the Proponents of Analysis (Vibhajjavādī).

However, the view that "unwholesomeness occurs only for one who drinks knowingly" is only the view of those with divergent beliefs, such as the dwellers of Abhayagiri (Abhayagirivāsī). Not knowing that it was "another's view," the authors of the Gaṇṭhipada and others wrote it down, harmonizing it with their own opinions. Thus, it entered the circle of the Vibhajjavādīs and continues to corrupt the Dispensation (Sāsana) to this day. Long ago, in this Damila country, a certain Elder named Nāgasena, who held divergent views, wishing to show the method of crushing others' views through the story of Kuṇḍalakesī, had it written in the form of Damila poetry. In having it written, he instructed the poet in many distorted meanings, such as: "In this drinking of liquor, the method is that unwholesomeness occurs only when drinking knowingly; and the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) cannot know the infinite objects of knowledge, which differ by region, time, etc., by way of their individual characteristics, because if they were delimited by knowledge, the infinity of the objects of knowledge would be lost. It can only know them by way of general characteristics like impermanence"; and "In ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma), just as there are distinctions like mind and matter, conventional terms (sammuti) like 'person' are also distinct objects." He caused the poem to be composed by confusing the poet's mindfulness with fallacious reasons. Relying on that poem, this view of those with divergent beliefs is here...
118:
In the Vibhajjavādī view, that erroneous view had existed in a mixed state for a long time. Later, although the Acariya Buddhappiya Mahāthera had cleared the net of views (diṭṭhijāla) that had come from outside to the inside and purified the Sāsana, some individuals with perverted minds raised their heads again. They relied on the decision in the Sāratthadīpanī Vinaya Sub-commentary regarding the drinking of intoxicants, which stated, "The mind is unwholesome only in the aspect of being with intention (sacittaka)." The Mahātheras, having deliberated on that view, designated it as a censurable view and suppressed it. They removed the bhikkhus who held that view and, through the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Sāsana of the Teacher, brought it to peace for a long time. For this reason, in this text, we have rejected it in detail, thinking, "Let not other Vibhajjavādīs destroy this view." Therefore, one should carefully note the reasons mentioned and not yet mentioned in this text and grasp the meaning so that it does not contradict the transmitted Pali texts.

"Sesaṃ" refers to all those training rules where there is no fixed rule that "the mind is only unwholesome" in the aspect of being with intention (sacittaka) through the mind that cognizes the object. "Rundhanti" means preventing the taking of a pretext (lesa) for the absence of an offense, such as "there is no fault in a female animal," etc. "Dvāraṃ pidahanti" means closing the door, which is the cause for taking a pretext, such as "that training rule applies only to human women," etc. "Sotaṃ pacchindamānā" means cutting the stream of transgression that occurs continuously by the power of those two doors of taking pretexts. "Gāḷhataraṃ karonti" means making the offense firm, which was already established in the primary regulation (paṭhama-paññatti) by the aforementioned reasons, and not giving an opportunity for the absence of an offense.

That supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) arises while making the rule lax, even in cases of worldly faults (lokavajja), when there is no transgression or when the transgression is negligible (abbhohārika) because it is not within one's scope. Therefore, desiring to show the manner of such occurrence and the cause of occurrence, he said "Aññatra adhimānā," etc. The reason for this supplementary regulation, "Aññatra adhimānā," is stated as "due to the absence of transgression." The reason for this supplementary regulation, "Aññatra supinantā," is stated as "due to being negligible (abbhohārika)." Therein, "due to the absence of transgression" means the absence of transgression characterized by the intention to deceive, which is the declaration of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) that one does not possess, out of evil desire. For a person with overestimation (adhimānika), because they perceive they have attained what they have not yet attained, the aforementioned transgression does not exist. "Due to being negligible (abbhohārika)" means that according to the teaching, "Bhikkhus, there is intention, but that intention is negligible (abbhohārika)," although there is the intention to release semen and the effort, because one is overcome by sloth and torpor (thīna-middha), one is unable, and thus it is not called a cause for an offense...
119:
Because one is overcome by sloth and torpor and is unable, it is negligible (abbhohārika); the meaning is that there is an absence of the conventional term for the cause of an offense. In this sentence, the word "vā" should be understood as having a conjunctive meaning (samuccaya), or there is also a reading as "abbhohārikattā ca." The intention is that this supplementary regulation, which causes the absence of an offense in two ways, has been stated.

"Akate vītikkame" means when the bhikkhus have not committed a transgression of the training rule even during dangers, as in the cases of "Kukkucca na bhuñjiṃsu" (They did not eat due to remorse), etc.; it means when they have reported their own distress to the bhikkhus without having committed a transgression. "Sithilaṃ karontī" means relaxing the rule by releasing the training rule that was generally bound at first and making it an absence of offense within its own scope. "Dvāraṃ dadamānā" means giving an opening for the absence of an offense. "Aparāparampi anāpattiṃ kurumānā" means showing the state of non-offense repeatedly through that given door. Although the training rule was regulated, because it was regulated in the case where Ven. Udāyī transgressed by taking the pretext that "there is no fault with a prostitute for a moment" and reached the offense of Saṅghādisesa for acting as a go-between, it is said "kate vītikkame" (when a transgression is committed). The intention is that in terms of meaning, it is the primary regulation (mūla-paññatti) itself.

## The explanation of the story of the monkey (Makkaṭīvatthu) is finished.

## Santhatabhāṇavāra (The Recitation Section on Rugs)

## Explanation of the story of the Vajjiputta monks

43-44. In the Pali of the Vajjiputta story, in the phrase "Vesālikā... pe... methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseviṃsu," it should be understood that those Vajjian monks went to their relatives' houses, took the guise of laypeople, and engaged in sexual intercourse with the perception that "we have become laypeople." Therefore, the words "ñātibyasanena pi phuṭṭhā," etc., are said. Since the ruin of relatives occurs due to reasons such as royal punishment, the words "rājadanda," etc., are said. Wealth such as grain, silver, female slaves, male slaves, cattle, and buffaloes, which fulfill one's enjoyment, are called "bhoga" (possessions). Since those possessions also perish due to royal punishment, etc., it is said, "In the second word also, this is the method." Desiring to show their own suitability, those who were dissatisfied with the three objects (Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha) and perceived themselves as unsuitable for the Sāsana said, "We are not [unsuitable]," etc., as should be understood. In the Pali "aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu" (in the thirty-eight objects), it is stated by excluding the light kasina and space kasina which had not yet appeared. If those light and space kasinas are included, there are forty. "Vibhattā kusalā ဓမ္မာ" refers to the mahaggata wholesome states along with access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) shown by way of analysis as "in this object, this wholesome state arises." "Gihi-palibodha" is the anxiety regarding laypeople by power of being companions, etc. "Senāsana-palibodha" is the constant anxiety regarding lodgings by power of doing new work, etc. It should be understood that by the power of these impediments (palibodha) which are difficult to abandon, all impediments are also included. "Yena" means because of a reason, and the word "asaṃvāsa" (non-communion) is said with reference to the meaning that in that state of the person, having become a monk by some means, he is not fit to associate with other monks. Therefore, it is said, "Asaṃvāso ti paññattaṃ samūhaneyya." Because it is only said "he should not be ordained [as a monk] (upasampadā)" and not "he should not be made a novice (sāmaṇera)" if he comes, it should be understood that for a monk who has fallen into a pārājika, the state of a novice is permitted. Therefore, the words "sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ pana ṭhito," etc., are said. Because it is said "yo pana bhikkhu," a person who has given up the training is no longer a monk.
120:
Together with the light-kasiṇa and the space-kasiṇa, there are forty [meditation subjects]. The phrase "Vibhattā kusalā dhammā" refers to the wholesome states of the sublime level (mahaggata) together with access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), which are shown through analysis as "this wholesome state occurs in this object."

Lay-impediment (gihi-palibodha) refers to being preoccupied with laypeople through shared grief and so forth. Dwelling-impediment (āvāsa-palibodha) refers to being constantly preoccupied with lodgings through new construction work and so forth. It should be understood that by means of these two types of impediments, which are difficult to relinquish, all impediments are included.

"Yena" means "by reason of." Regarding the word "asaṃvāsa" (non-communion), it is said with reference to the meaning that a person who has become a monk in that existence through any means is not worthy of communion with other monks. In the phrase "panyattaṃ samūhaneyya" (one might abolish what is prescribed), since it is not said "that person who comes should not be made a novice" but only "he should not be ordained (upasampadā should not be given)," it is understood that the status of a novice (sāmaṇera) is permitted for a monk who has fallen into a Pārājika offense; therefore, it is said "remaining in the stage of a novice," and so forth. Because it is said "whatever monk" (yo pana bhikkhu), a person who has disrobed is no longer a monk and thus does not fall into a Pārājika offense by engaging in sexual intercourse; therefore, if the status of a monk is granted to him when he comes, it does not mean that the Pārājika is abolished. Thus, it is said "by the state of being a monk with uncorrupted virtue." The highest goal (uttamattha) refers to the fruit of Arahantship or Nibbāna itself.

## Catu-vinayādikathā-vaṇṇanā

"Nīharitvā" means having extracted from the Pali text. Just so, from the Pali text beginning with "Upāli, a monk endowed with five factors should not interrogate; what five? He does not know the Sutta, he does not know the Suttānuloma," they extracted the Sutta and the Suttānuloma. From the text beginning with "He says, 'Such is the learning and questioning of our teachers, there is no offense,'" they extracted the Teacher's Tradition (ācariyavāda). From the text beginning with "The Venerable Upāli said this: 'Friends, there is no offense for what is done in a dream,'" they extracted their own opinion (attanomati). That personal opinion of the Elder, being included in the Sutta, becomes the Sutta itself; likewise, it should be understood that other personal opinions are to be accepted only if they are included in the Sutta and so forth, and not otherwise. Alternatively, "nīharitvā" means having analyzed; having placed the entire Vinaya Piṭaka together with its commentary into the four categories such as the Sutta, and having analyzed the Vinaya in four ways...
121:
...they explained [the Vinaya] because there is no Vinaya outside of these four; this is the meaning. "It is said" refers to what was spoken by Elder Nāgasena in the Milindapañha. A word spoken through one's own verbal intimation (vacī-viññatti) produced by the vocal apparatus such as the throat is called an impromptu word (āhaccapada).

"Rasa" means essence (sāra), as in the term "pattarasa" (essence of the bowl) and so forth; it means the essence of the Suttas that prohibit or permit. Alternatively, "rasa" means characteristic (lakkhaṇa), because it is spoken in accordance with the characteristic without extracting a deceptive counterpart. The commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) brought down by the lineage of teachers such as the Recorders of the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka) is called the lineage of teachers (ācariyavaṃsa). Therefore, it is said, "The lineage of teachers is the Teacher's Tradition (ācariyavāda)."

Although "Pali in the Vinaya Piṭaka" is said here with reference to the Vinaya, the four methods such as the Sutta can also be found appropriately in the other Piṭakas. The Great Authorities (mahāpadesa) are those with great scope and great influence. In terms of meaning, they are simply methods of interpretation (attha-naya) taken by individuals in various ways according to the Pali text beginning with "Whatever, O monks..." in conformity with what is unallowable (akappiyānuloma) and in conformity with what is allowable (kappiyānuloma).

Indeed, although those methods of meaning were not spoken by the Blessed One in detail, they are of great scope because they are the causes for abstaining from or performing the remaining actions that conform to what is prohibited or permitted. Therefore, those methods of meaning are called "Great Authorities." The method of calling only the Pali text, which was spoken with its intention beginning with "O monks, this which I have not prohibited...," as a Great Authority is because that Pali text is included in the Sutta. It is said, "The Suttānuloma should also be compared with the Sutta... the Sutta itself is the strongest." This Pali text, which contains the intention, does not need to be compared with the Sutta, nor is it not to be accepted, whereby it would become Suttānuloma. Therefore, this "Whatever, O monks" Pali text is Suttānuloma.

Thus, only the meanings already mentioned, which are taken by individuals relying on the intention of this Pali text, are called Suttānuloma. However, because it explains them, this Pali text itself should also be taken as Suttānuloma. Therefore, the statement beginning with "The Blessed One has thus spoken..." is made. The meaning is that the points such as conformity to the unallowable, which are to be taken by individuals through the Pali methods such as "Whatever, O monks," are called the Great Authorities.

The commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) is both the miscellaneous teaching (pakiṇṇaka-desanā) of the Blessed One and also Suttānuloma. Because it was compiled and spoken by the Elders who held the Councils in the order of explaining the Pali, it is called "Teacher's Tradition" (ācariyavāda). By this, it should be understood that the commentary is included in the Sutta and Suttānuloma in terms of meaning. Just as this [commentary] is authoritative, so too is one's own opinion (attanomati). For even the Chief Disciples (aggasāvaka) and others, without relying on the word of the Blessed One and what conforms to his word, [cannot establish anything] by the power of their own knowledge...
122:
Even the Chief Disciples and others are unable to state any meaning, distinguished by way of conventional truth (sammuti) and ultimate truth (paramattha), in the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya, without relying on the words of the Buddha and the meanings that conform to those words. Therefore, all words are included in the Sutta and in conformity with the Sutta (suttānuloma). Since the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) and so forth are taken separately as the teacher's tradition (ācariyavāda) and personal opinion (attanomati), the remaining words, apart from that teacher's tradition and personal opinion, are taken as Sutta and conformity with the Sutta, and thus the Vinaya is shown in four divisions.
