Although personal opinion arises only by relying on the Suttas and so forth, it is said, "excluding the Sutta, conformity with the Sutta, and the teacher's tradition," because it does not appear directly in its own form in those Suttas and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "by taking the method with a following intellect." In that context, it means by an intellect that follows the Suttas and so forth, and by taking the method obtained from those Suttas and so forth.

Theravāda refers to the views of the great elders such as Mahāsumatthera (identified as Mahākassapa Thera in the Nissaya). Personal opinion (attanomati) can arise in a distorted way even while relying on the Suttas and so forth; therefore, the phrase beginning with "taṃ pana" is stated. "Atthena" means by the meaning taken by oneself through the method. "Pāḷiṃ" refers to the Pali together with the Commentary, which is the basis of one's own view. "Pāḷiyā" means by the Pali together with the Commentary brought by the opponent (paravādī) to refute that proponent's view (sakavāda), and it means by comparing the meaning one has taken with the Pali that is the basis of that meaning. "Ācariyavāde" means in the Commentary extracted either by oneself or by another. "It both enters and agrees" means it enters by way of comparison with the meanings extracted by oneself, and it agrees with the meaning extracted by another. "Entirely weak" is said because of the inability to fully understand the meaning as it truly is, due to the trace of defilement (dosavāsanā) in a person who is not omniscient. Due to the power of a text written through negligence, the teacher's tradition might not compare with the conformity with the Sutta; therefore, it is said, "the other view should not be taken."

By the words "only that which agrees should be taken," it is shown that only such meanings that compare with the Sutta should be extracted by way of the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa). Since only such extracted meanings are in conformity with the Sutta, it is said, "The Sutta is indeed stronger than the conformity with the Sutta." "Appaṭivattiyaṃ" means that which should not be rejected. "Kārakasaṅghasadisaṃ" means it is like the Saṅgha that performed the Recital (sangīti) because it is worthy of being a standard. "Buddhānaṃ ṭhitakālasadisaṃ" means it is like the time when the living Buddhas were present. In the passages such as "the Sakavādī takes the Sutta and speaks," the one who is accustomed to taking and speaking the meaning as it truly is, is called a Sakavādī. "Suttaṃ" refers to the Pali words included in the Three Councils. "Paravādī" refers to anyone, whether a resident of the Mahāvihāra or a member of another sect, who is accustomed to taking and speaking the meaning in a distorted way; only such a person is called a "Paravādī" here. "Suttānuloma" refers to any word, whether included in the Three Councils or not, that is presented either through distortion or deception as "this is a word that came from the Three Councils." Some teachers say, "In another sect..."
123:
...some say "conformity with the Sutta" (suttānuloma), but that is not appropriate. This is because both the Sakavādī and the Paravādī must take only the Suttas and so forth that were included in the Three Councils. For this reason, it will be said later: "That which is known to have come in the Pali included in the Three Councils should be accepted," and so forth. Indeed, the Sakavādī does not accept the Suttas and so forth of another sect as authoritative; if he did, when those Suttas and so forth were shown, he would have to stand by them. For this reason, he does not accept them. It will also be said: "The Paravādī shows many reasons and decisions from the Sutta to prove that it is unallowable (akappiya) for that Sakavādī... having accepted it by saying 'Very well,' he should stand only by what is unallowable." Therefore, even the Paravādī shows what was not included in the Three Councils as indeed not included. The only difference is the fraudulent nature (kūṭatā) of those various Suttas and so forth that did not come in the Three Councils, and the application of a different meaning to those that did come, by way of the shadow of the phrasing (vyañjanacchāyā).

Among those fraudulent ones and those with different applications of meaning, the Sutta that is fraudulent should be rejected. For the Sutta that is applied with a different meaning, a comparison with other Suttas and so forth should be made to show its distorted nature. If a meaning taken by a Paravādī compares well with another Sutta and so forth, the Sakavādī should also abandon his own view and accept it. Therefore, it should be understood that for both the Sakavādī and the Paravādī, only the Suttas and so forth that come from the Three Councils are the standard. For this reason, in the Kathāvatthu text, five hundred Suttas in the Sakavāda and five hundred Suttas in the Paravāda—thus one thousand Suttas—are taken only from those that came from the Three Councils by way of difference in understanding the meaning; nothing from another sect is taken.

"Khepa" means rejection or discarding, as in "What is the use of this view?" "Garaha" means reproach or censure, as in "What does this fool know?" "Sutte otāretabbaṃ" means that which one has made as "conformity with the Sutta" (suttānuloma) by inference; it should be entered (compared) by way of comparing the meaning in that Sutta or in any other suitable Sutta. The meaning is that it should be shown by comparing: "For such and such a reason, it compares with this Sutta." "Ayaṃ" refers to the Sakavādī. "Paro" refers to the Paravādī. "Ācariyavādo sutte otāretabbo" means this teacher's tradition exists by way of the explanation of a certain Sutta; it should be entered (compared) by way of comparing the preceding and following meanings in that Sutta or in another Sutta of such nature. "Gārayhācariyavāda" (reproachable teacher's tradition) refers to a teacher's tradition that exists because it was written through negligence or established by those of wrong views. This method applies everywhere.

To show that any fraudulent Sutta or words from outside the Dispensation (bāhiraka) should not be accepted, the passage beginning with "Sutte suttānulome otāretabbaṃ" is stated. The Guḷhavessantara Jātaka and so forth are the texts of those belonging to schismatic sects such as the Mahāsaṅghika. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), texts such as the Guḷha-ummagga Jātaka are included.
124: Taking (Gahaṇa) means that a proponent of one's own view (Sakavādī) speaks by grasping the Sutta; a proponent of another view (Paravādī) also starts with the Sutta, and since others who rely on different views can be known by the method already mentioned, they are not mentioned here. Having thus shown disputes in general through the Sutta, the conformity to the Sutta (Suttānuloma), and so on, the phrase "Atha panāyaṃ kappiyaṃ" etc., is stated to specifically show the cause of dispute and the Sutta etc., by way of deciding that dispute. In the phrase "Sutte ca Suttānulome ca", the word "ca" has the sense of alternative (vikappa); by that "ca", the views of the teachers (Ācariyavāda) etc., are also included. Therefore, it was said, "It shows the cause and the decision." In that context, "cause" (kāraṇa) refers to the reason extracted by one's own opinion based on the method of the Sutta etc. "Decision" (vinicchaya) refers to the decision of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). "Shadow of a cause" (kāraṇacchāyā) refers to an unclear cause that is difficult to establish, which is the basis for taking something as "allowable" (kappiya) or "unallowable" (akappiya) in the Sutta etc.; it means a semblance of a cause. The explanation of "having reached the Vinaya" is "having reached the consideration of what is allowable and unallowable." "Should be restrained" means the transgression committed with the perception that it is allowable should be restrained; the mind that prevents that transgression should be made very firm. "The stream should be cut" means the occurrence of transgression in that training rule should be cut off. "The state of being heavy" refers to the state of being unallowable. "By the Sutta, decision, and causes" means by the causes obtained through the Sutta and the decision of the Commentary. The word "Evaṃ" etc., is a concluding statement for the meaning already mentioned. "Superior cause" refers to the preceding superior cause in the Sutta etc., or it means many causes. Mastered by speech (vacyuggata) means ascended to the speech; it means remaining continuously in that speech. Since it was said that "the Sutta is the entire Vinaya Piṭaka," the repeated mention of "Suttato" refers to the words of the Sutta and Abhidhamma Pali that express that meaning. The explanation of "Anubyañjanato" is "from questioning (paripucchā) and the Commentary." In that context, "questioning" (paripucchā) means hearing the meaning of the Pali from a teacher. "Commentary" (Aṭṭhakathā) means the decision that is independent of the Pali. Since both of these follow the Pali and express the meaning, they are called "Anubyañjana" (according to the phrasing). "In the Vinaya" (vinaye) means in the practice of Vinaya; therefore, it will be said later, "without abandoning the Vinaya, without deviating," etc. In that context, "standing in the Vinaya" means not committing an offense intentionally etc., so it is said, "stands by way of being conscientious (lajjī)"; this means he is conscientious. If it is asked what the use of this state of being conscientious is when the characteristics of a master of Vinaya (vinayadhara) are being stated, it is said, "For the unconscientious (alajjī)..." etc. In that context, by the phrase "even if he is very learned (bahussuta)," the possession of the first characteristic is shown. If there is no standing in the Vinaya due to prioritizing gain (lābha) etc., the possession of the first characteristic is not effective.
125:
Indeed, it shows that he does not perform his duty and only performs what is harmful. A dispute that is a precursor to a schism in the Saṅgha is called a crack in the Saṅgha (*saṅgharāji*).

"Trembles" (*vitthunati*) means he shakes, or he groans, or he is unable to stand firm in his own view; therefore, the phrase "whatever" (*yaṃ yaṃ*), etc., is said. "Lineage of teachers" (*ācariyaparamparā*) refers to the succession of decisions by the teachers; therefore, it will be said later, "Having abandoned one's own opinion... as the teacher and the teacher's teacher speak regarding the Pāḷi and the questioning, so it is proper to know." For there is no benefit in knowing the lineage merely by the names of the teachers. "By the connection between preceding and following" (*pubbāparānusandhito*) means by knowing the connection of the meaning of the preceding words with the following words. "By way of the meaning" (*atthato*) means by way of the meaning of words, the collective meaning, the intended meaning, etc. "By way of the reason" (*kāraṇato*) means by way of the origin of that meaning. "Factor of the Theravāda" (*theravādaṅgaṃ*) means the sequence of the Theravāda, meaning the sequence of their decisions.

"By these three characteristics"—in this phrase, the first characteristic states the state of having well-learned the Vinaya. The second characteristic states his standing in that Vinaya by way of being scrupulous and by way of being unshakable. The third characteristic states the ability to decide according to the method given by the teachers in accordance with the Pāḷi and Commentaries, even for what has not appeared [directly] in the Pāḷi and Commentaries, by way of what is in accordance with them (*tadanuloma*). "When a case has arisen" (*otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ*) means when a case of transgression has come into the midst of the Saṅgha by way of an accusation (*codanā*). "When what should be said has been said by the accuser and the accused" (*codakena cuditakena ca vutte vattabbe*) means when, based on the case that has thus arisen, the accuser says what should be said, such as "It was seen, it was heard," etc., and the accused says, "It exists, it does not exist," etc. Since the *thullaccaya* (grave offense) and *dubbhāsita* (wrong speech) offenses do not appear in the *mātikā* (matrix), it says "of the five classes of offenses." "A triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses" (*tikadukkaṭaṃ*) refers to the triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses mentioned in such passages as: "If one has the perception of one ordained in an unordained person and complains or grumbles, there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*)," etc. The phrase "or another offense" (*aññataraṃ vā āpattiṃ*) refers to the pairs of *dukkaṭa* offenses (*dukadukkaṭaṃ*) such as: "If one has the perception of the wrong time during the right time, there is an offense of wrongdoing; if one is in doubt during the right time, there is an offense of wrongdoing," etc. "Intermediate offense" (*antarāpatti*) refers to the offenses taught at various intervals from the introduction (*nidāna*) to the conclusion of the settled case (*vinītavatthu*), excluding the transgression of the case mentioned in each specific training rule, but involving the transgression of another case. Here, however, because "observing the case" (*vatthuṃ oloketi*) is taken separately, the offenses remaining from those taught at intervals are taken as "intermediate offenses." The phrase "He throws the firebrand" (*paṭilātaṃ ukkhipati*) appears in the training rule on unpicking stitches (*visibbanasikkhāpada*). In that training rule, a burning firebrand that has fallen outside from a potsherd, etc., and is not yet extinguished...
126:
Paṭiukkhipati means putting back in its original place. For a monk who puts in an extinguished firebrand, it is only a Pācittiya offense. In this context of "Anāpatti" (no offense), there are also instances of no offense taught in between, such as "Monks, there is no offense for one with psychic power in the sphere of psychic power," and these are also included here.

The statement "It should not yet be called a Pārājika offense" refers to cases like theft (adinnādāna) which are difficult to decide even if the person who committed the offense stands in the nature of a conscientious person (lajjī) and reveals it as it truly is. However, in matters that are easy to know, such as sexual intercourse (methuna), it should indeed be called [a Pārājika]. Therefore, it is said, "The transgression of sexual intercourse..." and so on. If a monk, being shameless (alajjī), does not give a confession but makes an evasion, his offense cannot be decided even if it is gross. As long as he does not reveal it as it truly is, and as long as the Saṅgha's doubt about the offense is not cleared, he will remain a destroyed one (nāsitaka).

"Sukhumā" (subtle) means subtle because of the subtlety of the occurrence of the mind. Therefore, it is said "Cittalahukā" (lightness of mind); it means his mind is light. "Te" refers to the transgressions. "Taṃvatthukaṃ" means having theft and so on as the root.

The entire statement "Do as the teacher says" and so on is said only with reference to the remorse (kukkucca) of a conscientious and well-behaved (lajjī-pesala) monk. For a monk who reveals the truth and seeks only purity, it is said that one should not say "You are a Pārājika," because the side of no offense is also to be considered. For that reason, it is called the "shadow of Pārājika."

"Purifying the virtues" means, where there is doubt of a Pārājika in a transgression, taking the side of it not being a Pārājika and purifying the virtues by way of purifying those offenses that lead to rehabilitation (vutthāna) through confession (desanā).

"Dvattiṃsākāra" (the thirty-two parts of the body) is mentioned by way of illustration (upalakkhaṇa) because it is well-known; it is proper to reflect on any preferred meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). "The meditation subject connects" means the mind connects continuously without showing any break in between due to distraction rooted in remorse. "Saṅkhāra" (formations) is said by way of the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna). For a monk with an offense, even a familiar meditation subject does not appear clearly, let alone for one who has reached a Pārājika. For him, the mind is not one-pointed because of its inclination toward remorse. However, for some who have many distractions of thought and so on, even if their virtue is pure, the mind does not become concentrated; that should not be taken here as being rooted in Pārājika. "The meditation subject does not connect" is said here with reference to the lack of concentration of the mind only due to remorse rooted in the evil done. Therefore, it is said, "By the fire of remorse..." and so on. "Attanā" (by oneself) means the person, as the agent, knows by means of the mind as the instrument; or it is the third case (instrumental) used in the sense of the first case (nominative), meaning "he himself knows."

## The explanation of the fourfold Vinaya and so on is finished.
127:
## Commentary on the Word-for-word Analysis

He is seen like whom, therefore he is "yādiso" (such as). Since the word "yathā" occurs in the sense of the word "yaṃ," it is said "yena vā tena vā yutto" (endowed with this or that reason). By the two words "yena tena," the meaning of the word "yaṃ" is shown indefinitely. "Vāsadhurayutto" means one devoted to the burden of insight (vipassanā-dhura). Whatever birth (jāti) that person has, he is called "yaṃjāti"; that same "yaṃjāti" becomes "yaṃjacco" by applying the suffix 'ya' in the reflexive sense (sakattha). By way of lineage (gotta), it should be connected as: "whether he be of this lineage or that lineage, whether he has this lineage or that lineage." "Sīlesu" means in natural states (pakati). This word "atha kho" is in the sense of "kintu" (but/however). What is meant is: in this matter of Pārājika, this person is one endowed with the aforementioned modes.

"Ariyāyā" (for the noble) refers to the kind of request that is stated as: "The noble ones stand for the purpose [of alms]; this is the request of the noble ones," and not the kind of request of the poor who say "Give to me." "Liṅgasampaṭicchanena" (by accepting the mark) means by accepting the mark of the monkhood which is dependent on alms-food, even if there is no mental intention like "I will go for alms." "Kājabhattaṃ" means food brought by carrying poles. "Adhammikāyā" (unrighteous/false) is said because of the absence of monkly qualities such as the training in higher virtue (adhisīla); therefore, it is said "abhūtāyā" (untrue). It means they are monks only by mere profession (paṭiññā) when they say "We are monks," but not in reality (atthato). This is said because the profession "We are monks" is possible. Even if they do not profess "We are monks," they are indeed called those who profess to be monks by taking up the mark (robes/appearance) which is the cause for the designation "monk," and by accepting the portion of requisites given to monks. Thus it is said in the Puggalapaññatti Commentary:

"'One who is not a celibate but professes to be a celibate' means: seeing other celibate monks who are well-dressed, well-covered, carrying beautiful bowls, and wandering for alms in villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals to make a living, he himself behaves in such a manner, and thus it is as if he is giving a profession that 'I am a celibate.' One who enters the Uposatha hall and so on saying 'I am a monk' is certainly one who professes to be a celibate; likewise, one who takes the communal gains of the Saṅgha."

Therefore, communal use and enjoyment (sambhoga) with such monks who have such professions and who only reach the stage of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) is not proper; it is only the enjoyment of the shameless (alajjī). The characteristic of the shameless, such as deliberately committing an offense, is said with reference to monks who are extreme [in their shamelessness].
128:
This is because the term 'alajjī' (shameless) is also shown to apply to novices (sāmaṇeras) and others. Indeed, it is stated (in the Saṅghādisesa Commentary): "One should not even have manual labor performed by shameless novices." Not abiding by the prescribed practice is the common characteristic of all who are shameless. Immoral persons (dussīla), from the moment they take up the monk's mark, are indeed purely shameless because they lack the prescribed practice, similar to those of other sects like the Mahāsaṅghika, or like those who are "thieves of the mark" (liṅgatthenaka), and so on.

As long as their claim to be a monk (bhikkhu-paṭiññā) continues, they are indeed monks. Using requisites with them is merely the usage of the shameless (alajjī-paribhoga). An offering given to them with the perception of them being the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is considered as given to the Saṅgha. For it was said by the Blessed One: "Ānanda, in the future there will be those of the lineage (gotrabhū) who wear the yellow robe around their necks, who are immoral and of evil nature. People will give offerings to the Saṅgha designated for those immoral ones. Even then, Ānanda, I say that an offering made to the Saṅgha is of incalculable and immeasurable merit."

Because it is given designating the Saṅgha of the Blessed One, the offering becomes incalculable and immeasurable. If it is argued that this does not happen because it is given to the immoral, that should not be said. Why? Because in saying it is given designating the Saṅgha among them, they are touched upon as the recipients of the lineage (gotrabhū); otherwise, it would lead to the consequence of having to say "designating the Saṅgha among any laypeople or monastics," and if that were so, the purpose of showing the lowest limit by saying "Even then, Ānanda" would not exist. Therefore, if even the gotrabhū do not exist, there is no offering designating the Saṅgha. As the lowest limit, an offering made to the Saṅgha given even to those gotrabhū is of incalculable merit; it is established that after them, there is no offering made to the Saṅgha. Therefore, it should be understood that they too are indeed monks by their claim.

"Brahmaghosa" means a noble voice, or a voice similar to that of Brahma. In the phrase "Ehi bhikkhu," "bhikkhu" is a form of address. You who see danger in Saṃsāra, come to the Dispensation (Sāsana) which is the Three Refuges, for the sake of completely destroying that danger. Enter and approach with the mind, thinking, "This is the protection, this is the shelter." Having approached, "practice the holy life" (cara brahmacariyaṃ); practice the holy life of the Dispensation and the holy life of the Path. "Bhaṇḍu" means one with a shaven head. "Vāsī" means an adze for cutting tooth-sticks and so on. "Bandhana" means the waistband. One who has effort exerted by way of concentration and wisdom is called "yuttayoga." The remaining words "these eight are his requisites" should be added. The remaining words "he is characterized only by the requisites donned on his body" should be added. Where "tīṇi satāni" should be said, "tīṇi sataṃ" is said for the sake of ease in composing the verse.
129:
With the word "Therefore," the Blessed One refers to the words spoken below. Below, it is said: "Kassapa, I speak 'I know' only when knowing; I speak 'I see' only when seeing." It is a reference to those very words spoken below. Because I speak while knowing, it means "therefore."

"In this" means in this Dispensation (Sāsana). "Intense" means great. "Will be established" means that even before approaching the elders and so forth, one first reflects regarding them: "May my sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) be established."

"Associated with the wholesome" means depending on faultless states. "Making it a matter of importance (aṭṭhiṃ katvā)" means either making oneself purposeful through that Dhamma, or making that Dhamma one's purpose, thinking, "This is my benefit." "Lending an ear" means placing the ear (attending) to the Dhamma.

"Kassapa, you should train thus" means that by lending the ear of wisdom and the ear of faith, you should train in this way: "I will listen to the Dhamma with respect." "My mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by joy" refers to mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by the happiness of the first jhāna, based on foulness (asubha) or mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). The respectful acceptance of this advice itself was the going forth (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā) of the Elder Mahākassapa.

The jhāna that takes the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) of a bloated corpse as its object is called "perception of the bloated" (uddhumātakasaññā). The fine-material sphere jhāna (rūpāvacarajjhāna) that takes a kasina as its object is called "perception of form" (rūpasaññā). These two states of jhāna are referred to by the name "perception" (saññā). When the Blessed One questioned the novice Sopāka, he replied: "They are the same in meaning as fine-material states, but differ only in phrasing (byañjana)." "With a satisfied mind" means having gladdened the mind. The higher ordination (upasampadā) through the acceptance of the heavy rules (garudhamma) and so forth will become clear by itself later (in the Khandhaka).

"By the very last method" means by the very lowest limit. The formal act with a motion as the fourth (ñatticatuttha-kammavācā) is called "ground" (ṭhāna) because it is the cause for the act of higher ordination. An act that is free from defects of the basis (vatthu-dosa) and so forth, because it is suitable and appropriate for that "ground" (the kammavācā), is called "worthy of the ground" (ṭhānāraha). This is because an act accompanied by defects of the basis and so forth is naturally unfit for the formal motion. Alternatively, "ground" (ṭhāna) refers to the Dispensation (Sāsana) comprised of the three trainings, as it is the cause for attaining Nibbāna. An act appropriate for that Dispensation is called "worthy of the ground."

Only one who is ordained through an act endowed with the prescribed characteristics is worthy to undertake and fulfill the entire Dispensation. Therefore, every Sangha activity that concludes with a pure kammavācā is called "worthy of the ground." Thus it is said, "worthy of the Teacher's Dispensation." It means appropriate for fulfilling the entire Dispensation, starting with virtue (sīla). In this sense, since only those ordained by the formal act with a motion as the fourth are taught regarding all training rules, even though pure beings ordained by the "Come, bhikkhu" (ehi bhikkhu) ordination and so forth are incapable of or free from fault in transgressing the prescribed training rules (paṇṇatti-sikkhāpada) according to the letter, yet in meaning, it is possible for such monks to incur an offense through unknowing actions regarding prescribed faults (paṇṇatti-vajja) or minor worldly faults (loka-vajja) such as drinking intoxicants before attaining the path of Arahantship. For this very reason, it is said: "Two types of persons... and the bhikkhunīs as well." However, the statement "one ordained by the formal act with a motion as the fourth" is spoken generally, referring to monks of all times who are capable of transgressing all training rules. "By way of language" (niruttivasena) means by the power of derivation. "By way of expression" (abhilāpavasena) means by the power of designation. "By way of qualities" (guṇavasena) means by the power of the qualities that are the reason for being called a "bhikkhu."
130:
Even if it is apparent by the word "vā" (or), in terms of meaning, for those monks, in the prescribed faults (paṇṇatti-vajja) and in the worldly faults (loka-vajja) such as drinking intoxicants (surāpāna) which are minor training rules, before the arising of the Path of Arahantship, the occurrence of an offense through unintentional action and so forth is indeed established. Because of this, it was stated (in the Parivāra): "Two persons are incapable of committing an offense: the Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas. Two persons are capable of committing an offense: the monks (bhikkhus) and the nuns (bhikkhunīs)." However, the phrase "one ordained by the motion-and-fourfold-proclamation act" (ñatticatuttha-kamma) is spoken generally, referring to all monks of all times who are liable to transgress all training rules. "Niruttivasena" means by way of etymological derivation. "Abhilāpavasena" means by way of designation or usage. "Guṇavasena" means by way of the attributes that are the basis for the designation 'bhikkhu'.

## Sājīvapada-bhājanīya-vaṇṇanā

(The commentary) beginning with "Katamam pana" is undertaken to show that virtue (sīla) and so forth, which are supports for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya), are called by terms such as 'higher virtue' (adhisīla) because they are superior to mundane virtues. In that context, the phrase "fivefold and tenfold virtue" (pañcaṅga-dasaṅga-sīla) is spoken with reference to virtue during a time when a Buddha has not appeared, because such virtue lacks the nature of being a support for liberation. However, the five, eight, or ten precepts observed during the appearance of a Buddha by laymen (upāsakas), laywomen (upāsikās), novices (sāmaṇeras), and probationers (sikkhamānās) who have well-established faith in the Dispensation, having known the qualities of the Triple Gem as they truly are—that virtue is also indeed 'higher virtue' (adhisīla) because it is a cause for the arising of the Path. Indeed, because it is a basis for the arising of the Path of Insight (vipassanā-magga), the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) becomes 'higher virtue' (adhisīla) compared to the virtues of mundane persons, just like 'higher mind' (adhicitta). Apart from being a basis for the Path of Insight, no other distinction of 'higher mind' (adhicitta) from the mundane mind is found. Both that virtue and mind are supports for liberation because they are practiced by one who, having known as they truly are: the fact that the beginningless round of rebirth (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa) is struck by the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) due to being devoid of essence such as 'self'; the fact that it is rooted in the faults of ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā) which proceed in the manner of "I" and "mine"; the cessation of that round of rebirth through Insight (vipassanā) which is capable of destroying those root faults and is supported by the power of virtue and mind; and the fact that the Fully Enlightened One, who points out that liberation, is the teacher of the unerring True Dhamma due to being endowed with infinite groups of qualities such as omniscience. It is for this reason, and no other, that they become supports for liberation. If that nature of being a support for liberation is also common to the five precepts and so forth within the Dispensation, why should these five precepts etc. not be 'higher virtue'? For the Path arises even for laypeople like Anāthapiṇḍika who are established in a mere five precepts. Indeed, the arising of the Path does not occur without higher virtue and higher mind, and although that virtue for some...
131: ...due to the lack of immediate support (nissaya), it does not become a cause for the arising of the Path in that very existence, yet it will certainly become a cause in a future existence. Therefore, it is like the Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla of noble worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) who pass away while practicing higher virtue. Thus it is said: "It occurs only during the appearance of a Buddha," and so forth. The five precepts etc. observed while aspiring for liberation also occur only during the appearance of a Buddha. The statement "That virtue is not a prescription (paṇṇatti)," however, is spoken with reference to the entire Pātimokkha in an excellent sense. It also includes the lay virtue of abstaining from taking life, taking what is not given, etc., which are parts of it. Only the Buddhas, by way of what has come down in the Vinaya, such as the Pārājika and Sutta Vibhaṅga, are able to prescribe (rules) as the proximate cause for the arising of the Path, having cut off the stream of transgression which obstructs the arising of the Path in all doors of body and speech; others cannot. For the status of 'higher virtue' is spoken of with reference to the arising of the Path. Therefore, it is said: "Even beyond the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, only the virtue associated with the Path and Fruit (magga-phala) is 'higher virtue'." For only in that (virtue associated with the Path) is there 'higher virtue' because the Path has its foundation there without any interval. The phrase "not intended here" means that in this context of the first Pārājika, the word "sikkhā" (training) is not intended. "Eight mundane attainments of mind" (lokiya-aṭṭha-samāpatti-cittāni) refers to the eight states of consciousness associated with the fine-material and immaterial jhānas to be attained by mundane people who do not know the nature of the Dispensation. Indeed, in sublime (mahaggata) states, there is no distinction between mundane and supramundane such that the qualification 'mundane' would exclude the supramundane. Therefore, the qualification 'mundane' is made only to exclude the sublime jhānas to be attained by those within the Dispensation. Just as in this case, in the phrase "eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta), the qualification 'mundane' must also be made. Indeed, the arising in a person who does not know the Dispensation is the only distinction of (ordinary) mind from 'higher mind' (adhicitta). In this way, even in the time when a Buddha has not appeared, the virtue and mind of Paccekabuddhas and others who know the nature of the Dispensation are established as 'higher virtue' and 'higher mind'. The statement "It does not occur without the appearance of a Buddha" is spoken because Paccekabuddhas, Bodhisattas, and others lack the teaching ability to be the cause of realization (abhisamaya) for others. However, they do indeed teach virtue and mind as a cause for future habitual tendencies (vāsanā). Although that virtue and mind are 'higher virtue' and 'higher mind' due to being causes for the Path, it should be understood that the restriction "only during the appearance of a Buddha" is made because they are negligible (abbhohārika) due to being few and not being widespread among many people. In the explanation of 'higher mind' here and 'higher wisdom' (adhipaññā) later, by the commentarial statements such as "It is not one who has attained that attainment," only the higher mind and higher wisdom associated with the Path and Fruit are excluded, thus mundane—
132: In this context, higher mind (adhicitta) and higher wisdom (adhipaññā) are intended. It is understood that even for one endowed with both, there is the nature of engaging in sexual intercourse (methunadhamma). However, in the Pali, since it is stated, "This training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā) is the training intended in this sense," it is understood that mundane higher mind and higher wisdom are not intended. Therefore, the intention in the Pali and the Commentary should be understood thus: as soon as the thought "I will engage in sexual intercourse" arises in the mind, mundane higher mind and higher wisdom decline and perish. Higher virtue, however, does not decline merely by the arising of a thought; therefore, only the training in higher virtue is taught in the Pali. In the Commentary, however, for a monk who has attained the supramundane path, the thought "I will engage in sexual intercourse" does not arise at all because he is of an unshakable nature (akuppadhamma) in every way. For worldlings (puthujjana) who have attained meditative absorptions (samāpatti), that thought may arise due to some cause because they are of a shakable nature (kuppadhamma). To show this distinction, it should be understood that only supramundane states are excluded by saying, "One who has reached that absorption does not engage." In the phrase "Atthi dinnaṃ," "dinnaṃ" refers to the intention (cetanā) of giving. It means there is a result of that gift given. This same method applies to the phrase "Atthi yiṭṭhaṃ." By the word "ādi," "huta" etc., are included. In that context, "yiṭṭhaṃ" refers to a great sacrifice (mahāyāga), which is a great gift common to all. "Hutaṃ" refers to the hospitality shown to guests. Whether it be one's own or another's, the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusalakamma-patha) or all unwholesome states are not called "one's own kamma" (sakakamma) because they produce harm. Wholesome states, which are the opposite of those, are called "one's own" (saka). Or, according to the words "I am the owner of my kamma" (kammassakomhi) etc., both wholesome and unwholesome are called the "own" of beings in the sense of conviction as long as the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) continues. Thus, the knowledge that arises regarding one's own property by way of being the owner of kamma is called "knowledge of the ownership of kamma" (kammassakatā-ñāṇa). This is merely an illustration (upalakkhaṇa). In fact, all wholesome wisdom leading to the round of rebirth that is based on the Dispensation (Sāsana) is included in the knowledge of the ownership of kamma. All wisdom leading to the end of the round (nibbāna) based on the Dispensation is called "knowledge in conformity with the truths" (saccānulomika-ñāṇa). That alone is called higher wisdom (adhipaññā). All other remaining knowledge should be understood as knowledge of the ownership of kamma. Therefore, the Blessed One included all knowledge within the group of four knowledges: knowledge of the ownership of kamma, knowledge in conformity with the truths, knowledge of one possessed of the path (maggasamaṅgī-ñāṇa), and knowledge of one possessed of the fruit (phalasamaṅgī-ñāṇa). The knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) which discerns the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) is mentioned specifically because it is the most proximate cause of the path. Other wisdoms, such as the recollection of the Triple Gem (Ratanattaya), should be understood as being equal in being higher wisdom because they are also causes for the path. ## The method of the explanation of the classification of the training rules is finished.
133:
## Commentary on the Analysis of Renunciation (Paccakkhānavibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā)

"Manifesting weakness" (dubbalye āvikate) means making one's weak state clear by saying, "What if I were to renounce the Buddha?" and so on. "Being on the tip of the tongue" (mukhāruḷhatā) means it is according to the common parlance of people in the world, such as saying "seven or eight," and so forth. In the phrase "two nights or three nights" (diraṭṭhatiraṭṭhaṃ) (Pācittiya 52), just as "two nights" is mentioned without an interval to ensure that one takes three nights by way of continuously sleeping with an unordained person until dawn, rather than taking three nights intermittently, so too in this training rule, the phrase "without manifesting weakness" (dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā) is stated to show that there is indeed a purpose for its inclusion; thus it is said, "Since for the renunciation of the training..." and so on.

Now, to show that the phrase "without manifesting weakness" should be taken as having its own distinct meaning rather than just being an explanation of the preceding term, the word "apica" (moreover) is used. In the term "distinction and non-distinction" (visesāvisesaṃ), if a sentence only manifests weakness (dubbalyāvikamma) and does not constitute renunciation of the training (sikkhāpaccakkhāna), then there is a mutual distinction between renouncing the training and manifesting weakness in that sentence. If both occur through a single statement, then there is no distinction, and thus it is also non-distinct; this is called "distinction and non-distinction." Because the root "kaṭha" is listed in the sense of living with difficulty, it is said, "one who has reached a difficult life" (kicchajīvikappatto). In truth, "ukkaṇṭhā" is living with difficulty, and reaching such a state is called "ukkaṇṭhita" (dissatisfied/longing). "Ukkaṇṭhā" also refers to the neck being raised upwards due to lack of delight. A person who, due to dissatisfaction, seeks an exit like a herd of cattle locked in a pen, often has their neck raised; reaching that state of dissatisfaction is also called "ukkaṇṭhita." To show this meaning, it is said, "living with the neck raised upwards." Since that state of dissatisfaction occurs only through distraction, the word "vikkhi tto" (distracted) and so on are stated.

"From the state of a recluse" (samaṇabhāvato) means from higher ordination (upasampadā). "By way of imagining a state" (bhāvavikappākārena) means that after falling away from the state of a monk, one desires to reach a state such as that of a layman, and thus imagines one's own existence by thinking, "I shall be [a layman]." It means by way of the manner of imagining the state of a layman, etc., which is the cause of one's desired existence.

In the Pāḷi, "yadi panāhaṃ" means "If I were to renounce the Buddha, it would indeed be good." In the terms "apāhaṃ" and "handāhaṃ," the meaning should be taken according to the method already stated. He says, "The thought arises in me: I would renounce the Buddha."
134:
By the words "Na ramāmi" (I do not delight), he shows the absence of happiness due to the abundance of suffering in the life of a monk. By the words "Nābhiramāmi" (I do not take delight), he shows his own lack of delight even though there is blameless happiness in the life of a monk.

By the words "Teneva vacībhedena" (By that very breaking of speech), he prohibits making it known by other bodily gestures even after speaking. Even if one does not have proficiency in the language and thus lacks understanding of the meaning of every word in all its aspects, such as "This person wishes to leave the Sasana," if he understands at least this much of the intended meaning—"This person wishes to give up his state as a monk and is making this specific statement"—it shows that the renunciation of the training is effective. Therefore, it was said, "He understands even this much." "Padapacchābhaṭṭha" means the occurrence of a word in another way (padaparāvatti). All languages other than the Māgadhi language should be known as "Milakkha languages." "Khettameva otiṇṇam" means entering the very field which is the place where the renunciation of the training takes effect.

"Dūta" means an oral message (mukhasāsana). "Sāsana" means a written message (paṇṇasāsana), which includes showing letters carved on walls, pillars, and so on. The phrase "associated with the mind" (cittasampayutta) is said with reference to the occurrence of speech while the mind intending to renounce the training is still present; it means "mind-produced" (cittasamuṭṭhāna). To show the distinction in understanding by way of being specified or unspecified, it is said, "If only this person knows," and so on. This analysis should be understood as being obtained by the aforementioned method: in the context of "he speaks, he makes known," the understanding of the very person to whom he speaks is intended. Here, the meaning that he speaks to one person but makes it known to another is not possible. Since it is said, "Even if one of them understands," it should be understood that even if he informs two people with the restriction, "Let only these two know, let not the other one know," if any one of them understands, the renunciation is effective. "Parisaṅkamāno" means fearing that "they will prevent me." "Samayaññū" means knowing the conventions in the Sasana; however, here, one is called a Samayaññū even by knowing just the intention. Therefore, it was said, "Ukkhaṇṭhito" (dissatisfied), and so on. Therefore, even if one fully knows the meaning of the words of the field such as "Buddhaṃ paccakkhāmi" (I renounce the Buddha), if he does not know the intention, "This person is speaking because he wishes to fall away from the state of a monk," the training is still not renounced. But even without knowing the word-meaning, if he knows the intention, "He is speaking because he is dissatisfied," the training is indeed renounced. Since the ear-consciousness process (sotaviññāṇavīthi) only grasps the sound, while the grasping of the meaning occurs through the sequence of the mind-consciousness process (manoviññāṇavīthi), it was said, "At that very moment," and so on.
135:
Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna is a treatise that explains the qualities of the Teacher. "In the Upāli verses" refers to the verses spoken by the lay devotee Upāli in the Upāli Sutta, beginning with "Dhīrassa vigatamohassa" (Of the wise one, free from delusion). "Yathāruta" means exactly as spoken in the Pali text. "Anantabuddhi" and others are names that appear in the Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna. "Dhīra" and others appear in the Upāli verses. Among those names, omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) is called "Bodhi." Because it is the cause of knowing, that Buddha who possesses that mark is called "Bodhipaññāṇa." In "Svākkhātaṃ dhammaṃ" and so on, the word "dhamma" is used to show that it is a synonym for terms like "Svākkhāta." Therefore, renunciation is indeed achieved by using a synonym, as in "Svākkhātaṃ paccakkhāmi." However, if it is spoken together with the word "dhamma," it should be understood as renunciation according to the literal word (yathāruta). The same method applies to "Suppaṭipannaṃ saṅghaṃ" and so on. "Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ" and others are names spoken with reference only to the Dhamma as in "wholesome states, unwholesome states" (kusala dhammā, akusalā dhammā). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that there is no fault in renouncing unwholesome states; therefore, it was said, "In the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates," and so on. By "Paṭhamapārājikaṃ" and so on, it should be understood that only the training rules (sikkhāpada) are taken, not the offenses (āpatti).

"Yassa mūle" means in the presence of whom. Among the synonyms for teacher (ācariya), the phrase "He who ordained me" (Yo maṃ pabbājesi) is said with reference to a teacher who, without being the preceptor (upajjhāya), acted as the teacher and gave ordination. "Tassa mūle" means in the presence of that teacher. "Okallaka" is a designation for laypeople who have emaciated and rough bodies and appearances, being afflicted by the suffering of hunger, thirst, and so on. "Moḷibaddha" is a layperson with hair tied in a bundle. "Kumāraka" is a very young novice (sāmaṇera) in the stage of a boy. "Cellaka" is a novice slightly larger than that. "Ceṭaka" is a middle-sized novice. "Moḷigalla" is a senior novice. "Samaṇuddesa" is a general designation for novices without distinction. "Asucisaṅkassarasamācāra" is one endowed with conduct that is impure and should be suspected by oneself—"Do others know what I have done or not?"—and by others—"Was this done by such and such a person?" "Kasambujāta" means one who has become like rubbish because of the filth of arisen lust and so on. "Koṇṭha" is a designation for the immoral (dussīla). "Tihetukapaṭisandhika" (one with triple-rooted rebirth) is said with reference to those capable of understanding very quickly, as this is not possible for those with double-rooted rebirth (duhetuka). "Sabhāga" (similar) is for a man. "Visabhāga" (dissimilar) is for a woman. "Potthakarūpasadisa" is for one who is like a statue made of clay and so on.
136:
To one who is like a puppet. "Garumedha" means one who has heavy wisdom, a dull-witted person, because of having a slow gait due to the absence of rapid occurrence in sense objects.

Now, in this section on the renunciation of the training (sikkhāpaccakkhānavāra), the decision should be understood by way of combining the methods mentioned in the Pali and the Commentary. In that regard, the limitation of the mind (cittaniyama) is shown by words such as "desiring to fall away from the state of a recluse." The limitation of the field (khettaniyama) is shown by words such as "the Buddha." The limitation of time (kālaniyama) is shown by the words "I renounce, consider me." The limitation of effort (payoganiyama) is shown by the word "he speaks." It is shown that the renunciation of the training occurs even by way of unspecified time (anāmaṭṭhakāla) through words such as "I have no use for the Buddha, what use is he to me, I do not need him, I am well-freed." The limitation of understanding (vijānananiyama) is shown by the word "he makes [someone] understand." The limitation of the person (puggalaniyama) is shown by words such as "a madman renounces the training, in the presence of a madman." It is shown that there is no renunciation due to the absence of the limitation of understanding by words such as "and that person does not understand." It is shown that there is no renunciation due to the absence of the limitation of the mind by words such as "desiring to joke," and due to the absence of the limitation of effort by the words "desiring to make [someone] hear, he does not make [them] hear." By the words "he makes an ignorant person hear, he does not make a wise person hear," it is shown that the renunciation is successful only by the hearing of the specific person intended, and not by another. The statement "if he does not make [anyone] hear at all, the training is not renounced" is said to show that the renunciation of the training occurs only through the limitations of mind and so forth, and not otherwise. Therefore, one should understand the renunciation of the training by way of mind, field, time, effort, person, and understanding, and understand the non-renunciation by their absence.

How? The renunciation of the training occurs only with the mind desiring to fall away from the state of a monk, not for one who speaks in jest or speaks accidentally. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by the power of the mind, and not in its absence. Similarly, for one who intends to say any of the twenty-two terms of the field—namely, the fourteen terms starting with "the Buddha" and ending with "fellow practitioners," and the eight terms starting with "layman" and ending with "non-Sakyaputta"—and speaks any of them by way of any of their synonyms, the renunciation of the training occurs. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by the power of the field, and not in its absence. In that field, there is the present tense statement "I renounce" and "consider me," and there are the four terms such as "I have no use for [the Buddha]" which are spoken in combination with the previous fourteen terms without specifying the time by way of the verb (anāmaṭṭhakāla). By the power of those terms in the present tense or unspecified time, along with their synonyms...
137:
...the renunciation of the training occurs. However, it does not occur for one who speaks words of the past, future, or hypothetical (parikappa), such as "paccakkhāsiṃ" (I renounced), "paccakkhissaṃ" (I will renounce), "māṃ dhāresi" (you considered me - past), "māṃ dhāressasi" (you will consider me), or "yannūna paccakkheyyaṃ" (what if I were to renounce?) and so forth. Thus, the renunciation occurs by way of the present tense and the unspecified time (anāmaṭṭhakāla), and not in their absence.

Effort (payoga) is also of two kinds: bodily effort and vocal effort. Among these, the renunciation of the training occurs only through vocal effort by speaking in any language in the manner of "I renounce the Buddha" and so forth. It is not successful for one who performs bodily effort such as writing letters or showing hand gestures. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs only through vocal effort, and not in its absence.

The person (puggala) is also of two kinds: the one who renounces and the one to whom it is renounced (the hearer). Among these, if the one who renounces is not one of those who are mad, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by pain, and if the one to whom it is renounced is a human being, is not one of those who are mad and so forth, and is present in person, the renunciation of the training is successful. Informing someone who is not present in person, whether by a messenger or by a letter, is not successful. Thus, the renunciation occurs by way of the person as described, and not otherwise.

Understanding (vijānana) is also of two kinds: specified and unspecified. In that regard, when one speaks with the intention of informing this person or these persons, if a human being understands the meaning of the words in any manner—such as "this monk is dissatisfied" or "he wishes to become a layman"—immediately after his speech, just as people in the world normally understand upon hearing and reflecting on words, then the training is indeed renounced. If they understand only after thinking "what did this person say?" later on, or if others [not intended] understand, the training is not renounced. For one who informs without specifying, if any human being understands the meaning of the words in the manner described, the training is renounced. Thus, the renunciation occurs by way of understanding, and not in its absence. It should be understood that the renunciation of the training occurs only by way of the mind and so forth as described, and not otherwise.

## The Method of the Explanation of the Renunciation of the Training is Finished.
138:
## Commentary on the Original Rule

"From this point" means starting from the word *duṭṭhulla*. Just as sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*) is coarse by its own nature, it is also shown to be coarse because it is surrounded by coarse practices such as looking and so forth; thus, the words beginning with "yasmā" are stated. "Avassutānaṃ" means those who are moist (lustful) with sexual desire. "Pariyuṭṭhitānaṃ" means those whose minds are overwhelmed by sexual desire. Since the word *methuna* is a synonym for the word *sadisa* (similar), it is stated as "sadisānaṃ" (of those who are similar); it means those who are similar in terms of lust and so forth. This word "sadisānaṃ" is stated as a general rule, because even if one of the two lacks lust, the performance of sexual intercourse is accomplished by the other. Alternatively, the word *methuna* is a synonym for the word *ubhaya* (both); *methuna*, *yugaḷa*, *yamaka*, and *ubhaya* are identical in meaning. Therefore, it is said, "of the two who are lustful." In the Pāḷi text, is it not also stated as "the union of a pair"? "Nimittena" uses the instrumental case in the sense of the locative; it means one inserts one's own organ into the female organ. *Nimitta* and *aṅgajāta* (organ) are identical in meaning. "Tilaphala" refers to a sesame seed about the size of a mustard seed; it does not mean the fruit together with its pod. Therefore, it is stated, "even as much as a sesame seed." "Allokāsa" (moist area) refers to the moist part of the organ that is naturally closed and not touched by natural air. Even if such a place becomes dry due to some disturbance of wind and so forth, if a monk makes an effort considering it as "anal-lokāsa" (not moist), he still incurs a *Pārājika* offense.

"Vemajjha" (middle) refers to the internal surface of the opened female organ, as if entering without touching the four sides. Regarding the male organ, however, "majjha" (middle) is said with reference to the tip. "Upari" (above) refers to the tip of the organ that is bent at the middle joint and inserted, which is like the back of the middle joint of a bent finger. "Entering from the lower side" means entering while touching the lower part of the female organ; it means entering such that even a sesame-seed-sized portion of one's own organ touches the lower internal surface, which is the moist area of the female organ. In this context, touching itself is called entering; the same principle applies to entering from the other four sides and so forth. "Entering by the middle" means entering while touching the internal surface; it means entering such that it touches the internal surface. If a monk enters without touching anywhere and withdraws the organ while it is only in the open space, he does not incur a *Pārājika*; however, he incurs a *Dukkaṭa* offense, as in the case of the severed head (Pārājika 73). "Entering while touching only with the middle" means entering while touching with the tip. "Bending with the back of the middle joint" means one's own organ...
139: Even if one inserts [the organ] by bending it with the back of the middle knuckle and touching with the upper part, it should be understood as being like a bent finger. Or, it is connected as "like a finger bent with the back of the middle knuckle." Or, it should be construed as "like inserting a bent finger with the back of the middle knuckle." "With the upper part" means with the upper edge of the contracted organ. Now, in order to show the ten-fold division of the male organ by taking the four sides separately based on the sixth location called "above" among the six locations mentioned below the male organ, [the teacher] said "Tattha" and so on. Below, however, six locations are mentioned by way of taking what was not yet taken. For a monk who inserts it like a balance beam, it means for one who inserts it straight without bending. Cammakhīla is a skin-sprout that grows on the organ like those on the necks of goats, etc.; they also call it "wool-boil" (uṇṇigaṇḍa). By saying "destroyed body-sensitivity" instead of "impaired body-sensitivity," it shows that while the state of being "clung-to" (upādinnaka) exists, even if the body-sensitivity is impaired by some cause, it is still a Pārājika, as in the case of a base with impaired faculties. As for the female organ, it should be understood that even if the state of being "clung-to" is destroyed, it does not lose its status as a field for Pārājika, as in a dead body. The phrase "by sexual enjoyment" (methunassādena) means that if there is lust for physical contact, it becomes a Saṅghādisesa. Bījāni means the testicles. Sitting without even covering a laugh that arose through negligence with a fan is said to be disrespectful. Alternatively, "covering" (apidhāya) means having covered; the meaning is that one should not sit laughing while covering the mouth with a fan. "Showing the teeth" (dantavidamsaka) means laughing while showing the teeth. "With boldness" (gabbhitena) means without shrinking back thinking "this is improper talk," having the enthusiasm to speak the entire intended meaning. ## Commentary on the Supplementary Regulation "Those who are the basis for Pārājika" means all those, such as women and men, in whose three paths there is an opening for the entry of the organ even as much as a sesame seed; others are not included. Here, however, in accordance with the Pali word "tiracchānagatāya," it is spoken by way of the feminine gender with the word "sabbā" and so on. Gonasā are a specific type of snake that have large circles on their backs. Although tortoises and frogs are four-footed...
140:
Due to the similarity of being aquatic, four-legged creatures such as turtles and frogs should be included together with legless creatures. 'Mukhasaṇṭhāna' means the shape of the skin of the lips. 'Vaṇasaṅkhepa' means the inclusion of scars. The occurrence of a thullaccaya (grave offense) regarding a wound should also be understood by the power of this sutta: 'If one inserts a non-path into a non-path, there is a thullaccaya offense.' 'Maṅgusa' refers to mongooses. 'Etam eva hi atthaṃ' means that because this Parivāra verse arose in the context of defining terms like Pārājika and so forth, it refers to the meaning: 'Whichever monk transgresses that offense, it causes that monk to be defeated.' 'Bhaṭṭha' means one who has fallen away from the Sasana. 'Niraṅkata' means one who is discarded. 'Etaṃ' refers to the Pārājika which has the nature of an offense. 'Chinna' means one who is interrupted in between.

In the phrase 'pakatattehi bhikkhūhi', those who have not yet committed a Pārājika offense and those who are not suspended (ukkhittaka) are called pakatatta (monks of normal status). Some teachers say, 'Because it is stated in the Commentary that it should be done together with pakatatta monks, there is no fault in performing Sangha acts such as the Uposatha together with alajjī (shameless) monks who are pakatatta.' This statement is not appropriate because that meaning cannot be established by these words. If a Sangha act is to be performed, it should be performed only with pakatatta monks; it should not be performed with those who are not pakatatta. This statement is intended only to forbid communion with those who are not pakatatta. It is not a statement prescribing that Sangha acts must be performed together with all alajjī and so forth.

This is because in the regulation of communion, performing acts together with those who have committed a common offense (sabhāgāpatti) or with alajjī monks is forbidden, even among pakatatta monks. For it is said: 'If the entire Sangha, while having common offenses, performs the Uposatha without following the prescribed method, the entire Sangha incurs an offense,' and so on. In the Commentary, it is forbidden to use things together with alajjī monks, stating: 'Where the use of material things (āmisa-paribhoga) is allowable, the use of the Dhamma (dhamma-paribhoga) is also allowable.' This is because performing acts together is also a form of dhamma-paribhoga.

Therefore, just as in the Pali, when defining the person who incurs a Pārājika offense, the words 'He who is ordained by a motion-and-fourth-proclamation act... this is the one intended as a monk in this context' do not establish that all who are ordained by such an act are necessarily those who incur Pārājika. This is because there can be sekha (noble learners) who do not incur Pārājika. Rather, this definition establishes that among those ordained by the motion-and-fourth-proclamation act, only the alajjī and foolish worldlings are those who can incur a Pārājika offense, but not those ordained by the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' method and so on. Similarly, here too, among pakatatta monks, only the lajjī (shame-fearing), kukkuccaka (scrupulous), and sikkhākāma (desirous of training) monks who are without offense are those suitable to perform acts together.
141:
It is established that such persons are not found among those who are not pakatatta. This is because those who are not pakatatta cannot complete a quorum (gaṇapūraka) and are strictly defined as being in non-communion (asāṃvāsika). As for the alajjī monks, they are not included among the asāṃvāsika because they can complete a quorum and fulfill the act. However, it should be understood that for those monks who perform an act by overriding the rules and acting together with those alajjī monks, the offense and the state of being alajjī do not depart. For it has been said: 'One shameless monk makes even a hundred others shameless.' Therefore, it will be stated later: 'All lajjī monks dwell together in these acts,' and so on. This meaning will become clear in detail later.

By the word 'tathā', the phrase 'sīmāparicchinnehi' and so forth is referred to. Training in the training rules prescribed by the Blessed One through harmonious actions such as worshipping together, eating together, entering the village together, performing major and minor duties, learning, questioning, and reciting together is called 'samasikkhatā' (equal training). To show that those training rules must be learned together only with lajjī monks and not with alajjī monks, it is said: 'But that which is prescribed... is called samasikkhatā.' In that Pali, the training rules that should be learned together with lajjī persons through non-transgression and through learning, questioning, etc., are called 'samasikkhā'. The meaning is that the state of learning those trainings together with lajjī monks in the manner described is called 'samasikkhatā'. In the aforementioned 'single act' (ekakamma) and so on, there is no communion with alajjī monks until they have entered into the state of lajjī (the state of being peaceful). It is intended that they are seen only outside of those 'single acts' and so on, which is why it says 'All lajjī monks...'

The word 'yaṃ taṃ' should be connected with the word 'vuttaṃ'. The statement 'It is not even a basis (vatthu)' is said to remove the doubt of a Pārājika offense regarding the genital organs of female figures made of gold and so on, since the term 'sign' (nimitta) is used for them. Therefore, in the Vinītavatthu, it is stated that a monk who becomes scrupulous regarding objects such as paintings does not incur a Pārājika offense.

## Paṭhamacatukkavaṇṇanā

'Assa' is a verbal form (ākhyāta). Desiring to show its meaning, he says 'hoti'. It means 'it would be'. The intention is 'hoti'. In the second alternative meaning, the word 'hoti' is an ellipsis (vacanasesa).

In the word 'sādiyantasseva', the term 'consenting' (sādiyana) means merely the arising of the thought desiring to indulge. Thus, he says 'paṭisevanacittasamaṅgissa' (one endowed with the thought of indulgence). 'Opposite' (paṭipakkha) means...
142:
It has the meaning of being undesirable and disadvantageous. When it is said, "The enemies of monks are the monks' enemies" (by way of a tappurisa compound), the king's enemies and others to be mentioned later would also be included in this (term 'monks' enemies'). Therefore, to exclude that (interpretation), the meaning is shown as "Only monks are the enemies," in accordance with terms like 'king's enemy'.

"At that moment" means at the moment of insertion. Indeed, the period of the act of insertion from the tip to the base is called the moment of insertion (pavesanakkhana). "When entered" means when the part of the organ that is fit for insertion has entered completely without remainder; it means the moment the act of insertion is completed. "Staying" (ṭhita) refers to the organ remaining inside during the interval before making an effort to withdraw it, or the state of that organ remaining. In the Commentary, however, referring to the time when a woman reaches the discharge of semen and stops all effort in every way, it is said "at the time of the discharge of semen"; both these moments should be understood as "staying."

"Withdrawal" (uddharaṇa) is the period during the act of pulling out until the tip; thus it is said, "at the time of withdrawal, he arouses the mind to indulge."

In this matter, the reason is that since there is bodily movement of the organ, etc., being instigated by others, as soon as the mind to indulge arises, the movement of the organ, etc., produced by the mind-born matter (cittajarūpa) at that moment is indeed caused by this mind to indulge. Alternatively, when the mind to indulge arises, even if not instigated by others, movement in the organ certainly occurs, and that movement is said to be done by that mind. Therefore, he indeed commits a pārājika offense arising from body and mind, like the ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā (offense involving the area above the knees). In that case (ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā), it is stated that an offense occurs merely by consenting: "If he should consent to the touching... or the pressing of the area below the collarbone and above the kneecaps." However, in the case of a monk's bodily contact (kāyasaṃsagga), it is stated "If he should fall into bodily contact," where one's own effort is mentioned as the cause of the offense. Therefore, for a monk being touched by a woman, even if there is lustful consent in the bodily contact or bodily movement caused by the woman, it should be understood that there is no offense (anāpatti) because of the absence of his own effort.

Some teachers say: "In the case of the first saṅghādisesa as well, if a monk who is being forcibly instigated by others with hands, etc., feels consent in the discharge of semen, and if semen is discharged due to that consent, it is a saṅghādisesa; if not discharged, it is only a thullaccaya." "Aṅgārakāsu" means a heap of glowing coals or a pit full of glowing coals. "Non-consent when being instigated by a woman" is not within the scope of all...
143:
"Scope" (visayo) refers to the words beginning with "Imamhi". "By the eleven fires" (ekādasahī aggīhi) means (being burned) by the eleven fires known as lust, hatred, delusion, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. "To him" (assa) refers to the monk who does not consent.

"He set aside the fourfold set" (catukkaṃ nīharitvā ṭhapesi): here, although there is only one 'no-offense' section (anāpattivāra) because it concerns a single individual, it is called a "fourfold set" (catukka) by virtue of the four terms: insertion (pavesana), entered (paviṭṭha), staying (ṭhita), and withdrawal (uddharaṇa). In this "Discussion of the First Fourfold Set" (paṭhamacatukkakathā), although it should be called "Five Fourfold Sets" (pañca catukkā) according to the method of teaching the five sections including the 'no-offense' section, it is called the "First Fourfold Set" by attributing unity to them since they concern a single path (magga). Therefore, it will be said later: "By virtue of the three paths, there are three pure fourfold sets," and so on.

## Explanation of the Discussion of the Two Hundred and Sixty-Ninth Fourfold Set

59-60. "Intoxicated" (mattaṃ) means intoxicated by liquor and so on. "Unconsumed marks" (akkhāyitanimittā) is expressed here by the word "unconsumed" (akkhāyita) by dropping the latter part of the compound; thus it is said "unconsumed mark" (akkhāyitanimittaṃ). Because they are devoid of qualifiers such as "waking" (jāgranti), they are called "pure fourfold sets" (suddhikacatukkāni). "Elder fellow-students" (samānācariyaka-therā) are senior pupils who studied under the same teacher. The other side of the Ganges river is called "Across the Ganges" (aparagaṅgaṃ). "Wata re" is a particle used in the sense of reproach. By these words, "of those who thus respect the Vinaya" (evaṃ vinayagarukānaṃ), the reason for the necessity of respecting the decision to be mentioned later by the Elder Upatissa is stated.

"Having exhausted everything" (sabbaṃ pariyādiyitvā) means taking the entire scope of pārājika without remainder. For if it were prescribed leaving a remainder, the shameless ones (alajjī) would use that as a pretext, and a stream of transgression would flow; therefore it is said, "having cut off the stream" (sotaṃ chinditvā). It is only in the training rules involving prescribed wrongs (paññattivajja), such as the rule on sleeping together (sahaseyya), that a prescription leaving a remainder is possible; it is not possible in training rules involving worldly wrongs (lokavajja). Thus it is said, "For this..." and so on.

In the training rule on sleeping together, although a pācittiya is shown for a dwelling that is mostly roofed or mostly enclosed as the minimum limit, and a dukkaṭa for one that is half-roofed or half-enclosed, yet because the prescription leaves a remainder, the Commentary shows only a pācittiya even for dwellings that are mostly roofed and half-enclosed, etc. But here (in pārājika), because the prescription is without remainder, the Blessed One showed that generally there is no scope for pārājika below the unconsumed mark (flesh); only thullaccaya and so on can be found there.

Desiring to show another supporting reason for the decision stated by the Elder Upatissa, he said "Moreover" (api ca) and so on. If even a slight streak of flesh remains on the mark...

If even a small amount of flesh or skin remains, that organ is simply called 'mostly eaten' (yebuyyakkhāyita). To show that if the entire organ is completely eaten beyond that small remainder, it is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), it is said: 'Beyond that (mostly eaten state), there is no grave offense (thullaccaya).'

In this matter, some teachers divide the excretory path (vaccomagga) and so forth into four parts and say: 'Among those four parts, if it is eaten beyond two parts up to the end of the third part, it is called "mostly eaten" (yebuyyakkhāyita). After those three parts are finished, there is no more grave offense (thullaccaya). If it is eaten up to the end of the fourth part, that organ is also merely a basis for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).' Such a statement is not appropriate. The phrase 'should be known only in a dead body' is stated because of the teaching 'a dead body that is mostly not eaten,' and so forth.

Although the word 'organ' (nimitta) and so forth are stated with reference to a living body, it is because the living body is the primary subject. For that very reason, it is stated in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: 'In the aforementioned tracts of a living body, even if the skin and so forth are completely cut away without remainder,' and so forth. 'Completely eaten' means all the flesh of the organ is cut. 'Form of the organ' (nimittasaṇṭhāna) refers to the shape of the hole penetrating as far as the bladder (vatthikosa) within the cut flesh, which is the internal skin and membrane that constitutes the form of the female organ. Therefore, it is said: 'Insertion occurs.' 'Without leaving the form of the organ' means without leaving the internal flesh and so forth that exists in the shape of a hole suitable for insertion. By this, it is shown that as long as insertion is possible, that place is indeed a tract (magga). This phrase 'a piece of flesh fallen from the organ' is stated with reference to the internal part of the flesh that lacks the form of the organ. However, in the case of a piece of flesh that is cut and removed from all sides without destroying the form of the organ, for a monk who makes an effort, it is a pārājika offense, just as in the case of an organ of a dead body that is mostly not eaten.

Having thus shown the specifics found in a living human body, it is now said, 'In a dead body, however,' and so forth, to show it in a dead body. 'In the vatthikosas' refers to the sheaths of the male organ. According to the words 'The great wound with nine openings' (navadvāro mahāvaṇo) and so forth, the eyes, nose, and so forth of humans are bases (khetta) for grave offenses (thullaccaya) in the sense of being wounds. Therefore, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is also stated for those eyes and nose. This is the same for the dead body of humans. Therefore, it is said, 'In a fresh dead body,' and so forth. There, 'fresh body' (allasarīra) is stated with reference to a body that is not putrefied. 'In the base of pārājika' is stated with reference to a body that is mostly not eaten. 'In the base of thullaccaya' is stated with reference to a body that is half-eaten and so forth. Here, in the thullaccaya bases such as the eyes and nose, even if they are mostly not eaten, it is only a grave offense (thullaccaya); in conditions such as being half-eaten, it should be known as an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 'Of all beings' means other than the aforementioned elephants and so forth...
145: It is stated for the purpose of including animals. Regarding the Dukkaṭa offense in the eyes, ears, and wounds of animals, it should be understood by taking the Commentary as the authority. If a Thullaccaya offense were to occur only in the wounds of humans, then a Thullaccaya offense should not be mentioned in the sense of inclusion regarding wounds in the nostrils and sheaths (vatthikosa) of elephants, horses, etc., or in the mouth-shape of the frog named Paṭaṅgamukha; yet it was indeed mentioned. ## Commentary on the Classification of the Fourfold Spread (Santhata-catukka-bheda-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

61-2. Paṭipannakassa means for a monk who has undertaken insight meditation (vipassanā). Upādinnaka is said with reference to the body-faculty (kāyindriya). "Touches with the upādinnaka" means it is touched by the body which is upādinnaka; the meaning should be understood through the passive sense (kamma-sādhana). Otherwise, the meaning is that a monk doing so does not touch any upādinnaka with an upādinnaka. Lesaṃ oḍḍessanti means they will set forth a pretext (excuse), they will plan. It means distinguishing (specifying) by the distinctions such as santhata (spread) and so on. The term santhata is a designation where the name of the part (ekadesa), the passage (magga), is applied to the whole (samudāya), the woman. It is like saying "the hole of a burnt cloth." In reality, only the burnt part, which is a portion of the cloth, is literally called a hole. Just as that term for the part is figuratively attributed to the whole cloth, and then that whole is referred to as "the hole of the burnt cloth" by virtue of its connection to the hole known as the burnt area; so too in this case, the term for the woman's passage is attributed to the whole woman, and then that woman is made connected to the spread passage (santhata-magga) and it is stated as "by the anus (vaccamagga) of the woman who is spread," and so on. In the Sāratthadīpanī, however, it is said in this matter that "it is the use of the term for the whole for the part." That statement...
147:
Since only the woman, who is the whole, is understood by the name of the organ, which is a part, the statement (in the Sāratthadīpanī) that the part is called by the name of the whole is not appropriate. For if the part were to be made known by the name of the whole, then in the phrase 'santhatāya vaccamaggena' (by the anus of a woman who has been spread out), the feminine gender and the connection with the organ would not be possible. However, by way of a metaphor (metonymy) where the name of the whole is attributed to the part, the part itself is the meaning. This is like saying 'the tree is cut' when only a branch is cut.

The word 'paliveṭhetvā' (having wrapped) is said with reference to wrapping clothes and so on only on the outside, without inserting them into the organ. By way of a metaphor where the part is attributed to the whole, the monk is also called 'santhata' (one who has been spread out) and so on. When penetration occurs even to the extent of a sesame seed, although the eyes, nose, etc., are spread out, it is according to the nature of the object; therefore, it is said 'thullaccayakkhette thullaccayaṃ' (a thullaccaya offense in the case of a thullaccaya), and so on. 'Khāṇuṃ ghaṭṭentassa dukkaṭaṃ' means that if one strikes a stump that is placed inside the female organ and is either level with the outside or extends beyond it, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred because there is no penetration. However, if the tip of a stump that is not produced by kamma (anupādinna) is slightly inserted into the moist area inside and one touches it with the male organ, it is a pārājika offense. 'Tassa talaṃ' refers to the inner surface of a bamboo tube and so on. 'Bahiddhā khāṇuke' is said with reference to the tip of a bamboo joint, etc., that has been inserted inside but protrudes outside. Just as striking a stump in a woman's urinary tract is mentioned, the characteristics should be understood in the same way in all places such as the anus (vaccamagga).

## Explanation of the Miscellaneous Discussion (Pakiṇṇakakathā)

'Pakiṇṇaka' means a mixed or miscellaneous method. 'Samuṭṭhāna' means the cause of arising. The word 'kiriya' (action) and so on is merely an illustration, as it also includes 'akiriya' (non-action) and so on. It should be connected as 'wholesome (kusala) along with feeling (vedanā) should also be known'.

By way of encompassing all training rules (sikkhāpada), there are six origins of offenses (āpattisamuṭṭhāna) stated as: 'body, speech, body and speech, body and mind, speech and mind, body, speech and mind'.
