By the words "What is called nissaggiya... is a pārājika," it is shown that throwing [goods] outside the customs house is a nissaggiya-payoga (effort of abandonment). Since it is said, "If one, with the intention to steal, drops a load held in the hand onto the ground, there is an offense of pārājika," it should be understood that throwing another's property—which was taken with a pure mind—into a hidden place such as a thicket with the intention to steal is also included in this nissaggiya-payoga. It is called atthasādhaka (accomplisher of the purpose) because it accomplishes the result known as the pārājika offense even before the act of theft is completed. Alternatively, it is called atthasādhaka because, although the act of theft is not yet completed at the present moment, it will inevitably accomplish the result of the offense in the future. The phrase "when you are able to steal such-and-such a good" is merely an illustration. This is because the effort of putting shoes, etc., into another person's oil jar is also an atthasādhaka. Indeed, it is stated in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā: 

"What is called atthasādhaka is commanding another, 'When you are able to steal so-and-so's property, steal it then.' In that case, if the other person steals it without any hindrance, the pārājika offense occurs for the commander at the very moment of the command. Or, if one puts shoes, etc., into another's oil jar, making the valuable oil undrinkable, the pārājika offense occurs as soon as they leave the hand."
174:
What is the difference between this atthasādhaka-payoga and āṇattika-payoga? Urging to take [the object] at that very moment is āṇattika-payoga; urging to take it at a later time is atthasādhaka-payoga. This is the difference between them. Therefore, it is said: "When you are able to steal such-and-such a good," and so on. "Laying down the burden" (dhura-nikkhepa) should be understood by the power of the goods deposited; this is merely an illustration. The same method applies to the attempt to seize a monastery (ārāma) and the refusal to return goods given for temporary use. Since the command (āṇatti) occurs before the effort of taking the goods, it is said: "By the power of the command, it should be understood as the preliminary effort (pubba-payoga)." Theft that occurs along with the effort is called sahappayoga; thus it is said: "By the power of moving from its place." This too is merely an illustration, for even in cases like moving a boundary post where there is no actual displacement from its place, it is still sahappayoga. Indeed, it is stated in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā: "Sahappayoga should be understood by the power of seizing fields, etc., by moving boundary posts, etc., through the power of displacement from their place."

"Tulayitvā" means having reflected. "Sāmīcī" means duty. They say there is no offense for a monk who does not give [something back] thinking it is his own property. "Sammadda" means mixing and agitation. "Bhaṭṭhe janakāye" means when the group of people has gone away. The instruction "Make it your own property and give it to this monk" is said to dispel the remorse (kukkucca) of both parties. For the one who took it might feel remorse, thinking, "I have not given it with my own hand; this is a good that must be compensated." And the other [the owner] might feel remorse, thinking, "I first laid down the burden and then took it without it being given [by the other]."

"Samaggha" means of little value. "It accomplishes the purpose of wood" means it fulfills the task to be done with wood. The loss of value mentioned, such as cutting a tooth-stick on a certain day, refers only to what the owner of the goods had purchased. All this should be understood by taking the decision of the Commentator as the authority. "Pāsāṇa-sakkhara" means stones and gravel.

In the term "akkhadassa," it is said that the word "akkha" refers to the hall of judgment (vinicchaya-sālā). Because they sit there and investigate what is an offense and what is not, the judges (dhamma-vinicchayaka) are called "akkhadassa." What is called "killing" (hanana) includes striking with hands, feet, etc., as well as cutting off hands, noses, etc. Thus it is said: "They should kill means they should both strike and cut."

In the Padabhājanīya as well, it is said: "They should kill with the hand, or with the foot, or with a whip, or with a cane, or with a half-staff, or with a sword." There, "with a half-staff" (aḍḍhadaṇḍakena) means...
175:
With a short stick of two cubits' length, or with a piece of split bamboo (this refers to striking). "Sejjāya vā" means by cutting off hands and so forth (as punishment). With this knife, hands, feet, and so forth are cut; therefore, it is called "sejjā," meaning a weapon (knife); it also means "with that weapon." "Nīhareyyuṃ" means they should banish him from the country. In the passage "You are a thief... pe... you are a robber," the word "paribhāseyyuṃ" (they should threaten and revile) should be inserted to understand the meaning; thus it is said, "You are a thief... pe... paribhāseyyuṃ." It is connected as "shows the goods which are shown."

"Yattha yattha ṭhitaṃ" means the goods situated in whatever place, such as on the ground. "Yathā yathā ādānaṃ gacchati" means in whatever manner it reaches the state of being taken.

## Commentary on the Earth-bound Items (Bhūmaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā)

"Vācāya vācāya" means in every word that expresses each individual meaning. "Upaladdho" means known. In the Pāḷi and in the remaining commentaries, only these two—"a hoe or a basket"—are mentioned, and since billhooks and axes are not mentioned, the phrase "saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ" and so forth is stated to show that those billhooks and axes also appear in the Saṅkhepa Commentary and others. Because it is done with the intention to steal, it is said, "Pācittiya offenses together with dukkaṭas."

In the passage beginning with "Aṭṭhavidhaṃ hetaṃ," it is connected as: the noble Elders who were the Recorders of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka) collected this which is called dukkaṭa in this place and showed it to be of eight kinds. Since all dukkaṭa offenses are to be included only within these eight, the dukkaṭa that is distinct from the other seven dukkaṭas should be included only in the Vinaya-dukkaṭa. "Dasavidhaṃ ratanaṃ" refers to the ten kinds of gems mentioned as: "pearl, sapphire, cat's eye, conch, crystal, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and emerald-colored stone (masāragalla)."

It is said:
"Pearl, sapphire, cat's eye, and conch,
Crystal, coral, silver, and gold,
Ruby and emerald-colored stone,
These ten gems the wise should know."

"Sattavidhaṃ dhaññaṃ" refers to these seven kinds of grain: sāli rice, paddy (vīhi), barley (yava), millet (kaṅgu), kudrūsa, varaka, and wheat (godhuma). In the term "āvudhabhaṇḍādi," the word "ādi" includes musical instruments, female figures, and so forth. A dukkaṭa that occurs regarding an object that should not be touched is called an anāmāsa-dukkaṭa. "Durūpaciṇṇadukkaṭa" is so called because it is the performance of an act that has been prohibited as "not to be done."
176:
Because it is a practice that is badly performed, it is called "durūpaciṇṇa"; a dukkaṭa offense occurring in that bad practice is called a "durūpaciṇṇadukkaṭa." The remaining dukkaṭa offenses prescribed in the Vinaya are called "Vinaya-dukkaṭa." The eleven formal admonitions (samanubhāsana) are: five in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, namely the four Saṅghādisesas involving the third admonition and the Ariṭṭha training rule; and six in the Bhikkhuṇī Pātimokkha, namely the one Pārājika involving the third admonition, the four Saṅghādisesas, and the Caṇḍakāḷī training rule.

Regarding the digging of these earth-bound goods, the phrase beginning with "atha dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā" is stated with the intention that the preceding offenses starting from the simultaneous effort (sahappayoga) are subsided. Because it is said "without giving up the effort," it is said that for one who gives up the effort and then digs again, the preceding offenses do not subside. Although it is said, "He is released by confessing the dukkaṭa offense due to the reason of cutting," since the confessability of offenses in the preceding efforts is not mentioned, it should be understood that when the simultaneous effort is reached, the offenses in the preceding efforts subside.

Aparaddha, viraddha, and khalita are all synonyms for the dukkaṭa mentioned in the term "yañca dukkaṭaṃ"; the passage beginning with "yaṃ manusso kare" is an illustration by way of a simile. The term "saṃyogabhāvo" is stated with reference to the doubling (dvitta); it should be understood that by this, the reason for the shortness (rassatta) is also shown. "Ekassa mūle" means in the presence of one monk. In all cases, there is a dukkaṭa for touching and a thullaccaya for making it shake, but this occurs only for one who performs the efforts of touching and shaking separately. However, it is said that for one who takes it with a single effort, there is only a pārājika upon lifting it up, and dukkaṭa and thullaccaya do not occur. Yet, that statement should not be accepted because touching and shaking are present even for one who takes it with a single effort. For it is not possible to take anything without touching and shaking it. In the Kurundī Commentary, it is stated with the understanding that even in similar efforts such as digging the soil, the preceding offenses reach the subsequent offenses and subside, with the phrase "he is released by confessing only one." In other commentaries, however, it should be understood that the offenses incurred in each effort due to the different efforts of digging do not subside upon reaching the subsequent offenses because they are similar to each other; only when they reach the state of shifting (viyūhana) do all those offenses subside because that is a dissimilar effort. By this, the arrangement for the subsidence of offenses is stated. By this, he points out the near side which is close to the thief.

"Tattheva" means only at the rim of the pot. "Bundena" means with the bottom surface of the pot. It should be understood that the moving of a pot situated in one place from its position is to be known by six ways. "Ekaṭṭhāne" also means in one place without being bound by a chain...
177:
It means "in the place where it stands." "Even if he moves a stump by as much as a hair's tip from its place" means moving the stump from its standing place in five ways. "A Pārājika at the moment of cutting" means that if it falls without fail, it is a Pārājika at the very moment of cutting. "Defining" means defining the gravity of the value, such as five māsakas and so on. "Removing" means making a heap by way of removing from its place. "Having done so" means separating the connection between the goods in the pot and the goods in the vessel by using the rim of the vessel's mouth. "In half a pot" means in a pot that is half full. "The nature of Vinaya" means it is the nature of Vinaya judgment when no superior specific reason is found.

To show that in this matter, it is not only about the gravity of the value but also about following the Pāḷi text, he said "api ca" and so on. "When defined by the throat" means when swallowing the ghee that is in the mouth. In this case, only swallowing is called "defining"; blocking the throat is not "defining." "Cikkana" means hard, thick, or dense.

If a monk, with the intention to steal, puts a cloth (dukūla) or a piece of leather into another's pot containing ghee or oil worth a pāda, and if he thinks it will definitely soak it up, it is a Pārājika at the moment it leaves his hand; in this commentary statement, the act of theft (avahāra) should be examined. If the Pārājika occurs with the intention of the ghee or oil entering the cloth, since the oil that has entered the cloth is still connected to the oil in the pot, it does not yet constitute theft, unlike when taking it by pouring it into another vessel. For it was said: "For one who takes by submerging a vessel, as long as it is connected, it is protected," and so on. Alternatively, if the Pārājika occurs due to the destruction of the oil, then as in the case of burning grass, there is no act of theft; there is only the obligation to return the goods along with a dukkaṭa offense. If that were the case, a monk who removes a cloth that has soaked up oil worth a pāda would not incur a Pārājika, because at the moment of taking, the oil that entered the cloth does not exist in the sense of being destroyed. If it does exist, the Pārājika should be declared only upon removal, not at the moment it leaves the hand. However, since all commentaries state that a Pārājika occurs at the moment it leaves the hand when putting in a cloth, etc., that statement cannot be rejected. But this should be taken by regarding the commentary as the authority; as for the logic here, the wise should extract it by comparing the preceding and following contexts.

"Palibujjhisati" means "it will prevent." "Pārājika by the method already mentioned" means it is a Pārājika at the very moment it leaves the hand. The phrase "It is not theft, nor is it because it is one's own vessel" is said because it is one's own vessel. It means that since it only mentions the absence of an offense, it should not be scrutinized further in this way. "It is said to have gone outside" means that from that point on, it is no longer the place of the oil, and because it is facing downwards, it is said to have gone outside. If a hole is made starting from the inside, the place where the oil flows out and reaches is still counted as the pot. Therefore, it is said, "If oil worth a pāda leaks from the outer edge, it is a Pārājika." "For one who has done it in any way" means from the outer edge...
178:
It is said because it is one's own vessel; it only means there is no offense, and it should not be scrutinized in detail in this way. "It is said to have gone outside" means that from that point on, it is no longer the place of the oil, and because it is facing downwards, it is said to have gone outside. If a hole is made starting from the inside, the place where the oil flows out and reaches is still counted as the pot; therefore, it is said, "If it leaks about a quarter (pāda) from the outer edge, it is a Pārājika." "Done in whatever way" refers to a hole made starting from either the outer edge or the inner edge. "A hole made by leaving [a piece] in the middle" refers to a hole made by leaving a small piece of the pot-shard in the middle and later cutting that shard.

Referring to eating food, drinking drinks, or consuming ghee, etc., it is said, "He makes it something that should not be eaten or should not be drunk." Why is it called a dukkaṭa here? It is said, "It is a dukkaṭa because there is no moving from its place." "The first pair" refers to breaking and discarding. "Making the pot decayed" means making a full pot unstable; "making the channel straight" means making a water-filled channel straight. "Having the same characteristic" means that breaking the pot is similar in nature to making the pot decayed, and discarding is similar to making the channel straight. "The last pair" refers to burning and making it unusable. "In this matter, they give this decision" means that some teachers give this decision regarding the meaning stated in this Mahā-aṭṭhakathā.

"It is said with reference to the last pair"—in this context, since the decision for the first two terms can be known by the method already mentioned below, it means "It is a dukkaṭa because there is no moving from its place" with reference to the last two terms, without saying anything about the first two. "With the intention to steal" means with a thieving mind that arises from the desire to act for oneself or for another. "With the desire to destroy" means with the mere desire to destroy, like cutting off hands or feet. "For one who breaks or discards by the method mentioned" refers to one who breaks by striking with a hammer or mallet, or one who causes overflow by pouring in water or sand. "It is not proper" means if you have an objection that saying "Pārājika in the first pair" is improper because the Pāḷi text also states only a dukkaṭa for the first pair. "Not" (na) negates the impropriety and gives the reason: "Because there is a meaning to be taken in another way."

"Thus some teachers say" means showing his own dissatisfaction with the method of interpretation mentioned below, and he himself, by comparing the Pāḷi and the Commentary in another way, the meaning...
179:
Desiring to show his own way of reconciling the Pāḷi and the Commentary by presenting an alternative interpretation of the meaning, he said: "Ayaṃ panettha sāro" (This is the essence here), etc. "Acāវេtukāmova" (Desiring not to move it) means simply desiring not to move it from its place with theftuous intent. In the phrase "Achaḍḍetukāmoyevā" (Desiring not to discard it), the word "thayyacittena" (with theftuous intent) should also be connected. This is because this statement is made with reference to the side of theftuous intent, as the side of the desire to destroy will be mentioned later. Therefore, he said: "Nāsetukāmatāpakkhe pana" (But on the side of the desire to destroy), etc. "Itarathāpi yujjati" (Otherwise it is also applicable) means that even for a monk who desires to move it from its place without theftuous intent, the incurring of a dukkaṭa offense is appropriate.

## The Method of the Būmaṭṭhakathā-vaṇṇanā is finished.

## Ākāsaṭṭhakathā-vaṇṇanā
In the Ākāsaṭṭhakathā, "antovatthumhi" (inside the property) means inside a property that is fenced. "Antogāme" (inside the village) means inside a village that is fenced. However, in a property or a village that is not fenced, the spot where it stands is itself the "place" (ṭhāna). "Aṭavimukhaṃ karoti... rakkhati" (Makes it face the forest... protects) means that because it has reached the creature's desired place through that effort, he protects it. "Gāmato nikkhantassa" (For one who has left the village) refers to leaving a fenced village. The kapiñjara is a species of bird bred by foolish people for the purpose of making them fight each other.

## Vehāsaṭṭhakathā-vaṇṇanā
In the Vehāsaṭṭhakathā, the words "chinnamatte muttamatte" (just cut, just released) are spoken with reference to the cutting and releasing, such that just as what is cut or released does not remain in its original place, it is so.

## Udakaṭṭhakathā-vaṇṇanā
In the Udakaṭṭhakathā, because an object placed in flowing water does not remain, he said: "asandanake udake" (in non-flowing water). The word "anāpatti" (no offense) is spoken with reference to the absence of a dukkaṭa offense in cases of handling with the hands or treading with the feet. "Kaḍḍhati" (pulls) means he sinks it downwards. "Sakalamudakaṃ" (the whole water) means all the water in the space touched by the stick. "Na udakaṃ ṭhānaṃ" (water is not the place) is said because the place he himself made is not a [permanent] station. "Paduminiyaṃ" (in the lotus) means in a lotus plant. "Kalāpabandhaṃ" (a bundle) means a bundle made small and tied by hand. "Bhārabandha" refers to a load tied for the purpose of carrying on the head and so on. "Muḷālaṃ" means the lotus tuber. The phrase "pattṃ vā pupphaṃ vā" (a leaf or a flower) refers to the mud...
180:
...refers to what has entered and stayed inside the mud. "Niddhamanatumba" means the outlet pipe for water in a tank. "Udakavāhaka" means a large canal. By the passage "avahārena so na kāretabbo" (he should not be made to [die] by theft), it is shown that in all cases of depriving a being of life, one is not exempt from the offense. "Mātikaṃ āropetvā" means putting it into a small canal. In the passage "maritvā... tiṭṭhanti" (dying... they stay), because only the dead fish belong to those donors, there is no theft for a monk who takes the non-dead fish.

## Nāvaṭṭhakathā-vaṇṇanā
In the Nāvaṭṭhakathā, regarding the statement "thullaccayampi pārājikampi hoti" (there is both a thullaccaya and a pārājika), it should be understood that if one releases it without first moving it from its place, it is a thullaccaya; but if one releases it after first moving it from its place, it is a pārājika. With reference to the judgment stated as "like a pig caught in a snare," etc., he said: "The logic in that matter is just as stated before."

"Vipannaṭṭhanāvā" (a distressed boat) refers to a boat blown to another place by irregular winds, or a boat that has reached destruction by breaking and is sinking in the water but has not yet reached the ground below, and whose ownership has not yet been abandoned by the owners. By the passage "a strong wind coming," it is shown that this effort is made when there is no wind. The statement "there is no theft for the person" is made by the method of straightening a dry canal.

That statement is appropriate if the boat is tied to a pole or similar object without treading with one's feet or lifting with one's hands. However, for a monk who stands treading with his feet and lifting with his hands, when a strong wind strikes the umbrella, robe, etc., he would have to make a new effort, such as treading or holding more firmly, abandoning the natural state. Otherwise, the umbrella, robe, etc., would fly away, or the thief himself would fall, and the boat would not move at that time. Therefore, if there is such a new effort, it should be considered theft.

The statement that there is no task to be done when water comes because it is straight in a dry canal cannot be an example here. It is our preference that the example here should be like telling a slave who is naturally running, "Go quickly!", thereby causing him to go faster than his natural pace; this should be accepted after careful consideration. Even when the wind comes, if the thief stands in a natural state without making any effort because the boat is very light, it should be understood that this is what is stated in the Commentary.

## Commentary on the Section on Vehicles (Yāna)
In the commentary on vehicles, the phrase 'ubhosu passesu' (on both sides) refers to a type of vehicle called a palanquin (sandamānikā). This is constructed by placing a rectangular wooden frame on top of four pillars, and on the left and right sides of that frame, structures resembling the two wings of a Garuḍa bird are made to dispel dangers such as wind and sun. 'Dukayuttassa' refers to a cart yoked with two oxen. 'Ayuttakaṃ' refers to a cart not yoked with oxen. Regarding the term 'kappakatā', a cart-support that is fitted by placing two ends like ox horns at the junction of two branches is called kappakatā; this support rests on the ground with both ends, therefore it is said to have '6 places' (points of contact). '3 or 4 places' means that with a non-fitted (akappakatā) support and the two wheels, there are 3 places, and by means of a fitted (kappakatā) support, there are 4 places; similarly, it should be connected that there are 3 places for a cart placed on the ground.

'Akkhasīsehi' refers to the two ends of the axle-wood. 'Akkhuddīhi' refers to the two pieces of wood fitted at the lower part to receive the axle-wood, which are called akkhuddhi (axle-pins); the four fitted ends in this context are called 'akkhuddhi', therefore it is said 'with 4 akkhuddhis'. With those four places supported by the axle-pins and one place supported by the yoke (dhura), there are 5 places in total. The axle-pins themselves are called 'uddhikāṇuka'; when there are no axle-pin stumps, to show the resting place of the axle-heads, it says 'making the side-frames even' and so on. In that text, 'samameva' means that without letting the axle-pins hang down, the bottom part of the side-frame is made even, and a hole the size of the axle-head is made in the middle of the two side-frame timbers, and the axle-heads are inserted into those holes; thus, the entire bottom part of the side-frames stands touching the ground, which is why it is said 'it stands touching the whole earth'. 'The rest is similar to what was said regarding the boat'—by this statement, it is indicated that if one cuts off the natural movement of such a moving cart and leads it to another direction, it is a pārājika offense. If it reaches any place by itself and one sells it without moving it from that spot, there is no avahāra (theft), but it is bhaṇḍadeyya (restitution of goods); this is the method shown.

## Commentary on the Section on Burdens (Bhāra)
In the commentary on burdens, the meaning of the matrix term 'bhāraṭṭha' is shown by the words 'bhāro nāma', thus it is said 'bhārayeva bhāraṭṭhaṃ' (the burden itself is the meaning of burden). 'Purimagale' means at the front part of the neck. 'Galavāṭako' is the gullet located above the neck.
182:
'Uraparicchedamajje' means in the middle of the boundary of the chest. Regarding the phrase 'sāmikehi anāṇatto' (not commanded by the owners): if the owners had commanded, 'Take this burden and give it at such a place,' then the goods taken by that monk would be considered 'deposited' (upanikkhitta). In that case, even for a monk who lowers it from his head etc. with the intent to steal, theft (avahāra) would not occur; theft would only occur upon the owners' relinquishing of the responsibility (dhuranikkhepa). Therefore, to distinguish it from the state of being deposited goods, it is said 'not commanded by the owners'. For this very reason, it will be said later, 'Because he was not commanded by them, it is a pārājika.' 'Ghaṃsanto' means carrying by rubbing/dragging without lifting from the head. If he lifts it, a pārājika occurs as soon as it is lifted. Therefore, it was said 'even as much as a hair's tip from the head' and so on. 'Yo cāyaṃ' refers to this particular decision.

## Commentary on the Section on Parks (Ārāma)
In the commentary on parks, regarding the phrase 'ārāmaṃ abhiyuñjati' (lays claim to a park), this act of litigation is also applicable to others' goods situated on land and so forth. However, since immovable property such as parks is mostly capable of being seized through litigation, the act of litigation is mentioned specifically here in the Ārāma section of the Pali; it should be understood that by this method, it can be known for all cases. By the phrase 'adinnādānassa payoga', it refers to joint effort (sahappayoga). Because the effort is made on the object itself, this dukkaṭa offense occurs by way of joint effort. 'Sayampi' means the litigating monk himself conducts himself as if listening, saying 'What shall I do? What shall I do?'; thus he is called a kiṅkārapaṭissāvī (one who responds to 'what should be done'). The state of being such a person is kiṅkārapaṭissāvibhāva, which means being in a state of following another's will. 'Ukkoca' means a bribe (lañja). 'Sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ' means the occurrence of pārājika for all, including the corrupt judge (kūṭavinicchayika). It should be understood that a pārājika occurs at the moment of making the effort that causes both parties to relinquish the responsibility (dhuranikkhepa), such as saying 'This person is the owner'. If, however, doubt (vimati) and relinquishing the responsibility arise in the owner sequentially, a pārājika occurs at the moment of the mind that originates the effort, not a thullaccaya. If only doubt arises, then it should be understood as only a thullaccaya; this method should be applied appropriately in all cases. By the words 'defeat occurs only by relinquishing the responsibility', it shows that if the owner does not relinquish the responsibility, saying 'I will not let go', the monk does not become one who has committed a pārājika even if the case is lost.

## Explanation of the Commentary on Dwellings (Vihāra)
In the Commentary on Dwellings (Vihāra), 'dwelling' (vihāra) refers to the entire monastery complex known as the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā). 'Precinct' (pariveṇa) refers to the specific areas within that monastery demarcated separately by walls and so forth. 'Residence' (āvāsa) refers to just a single building. Regarding property belonging to a group (gaṇa), because there is a designated owner, it is said, 'of a group such as the Dīgha-reciters (Dīghabhāṇaka),' meaning the responsibility (dhura) can be relinquished. In this group, if even one person does not relinquish the responsibility, it is still considered guarded. This same principle applies to property owned by many in all cases.

## Explanation of the Commentary on Fields (Khetta)
In the Commentary on Fields (Khetta), in the phrases beginning with 'or by pressing' (nirumbhitvā vā), the word 'of one who takes' (gaṇhantassa) should be applied to each. In that context, 'taking by pressing' (nirumbhitvā gahaṇa) means grasping the ear of grain with the hand as it stands, without cutting it, and pulling it to take only the seeds. 'Each one' (ekamekaṃ) refers to a single ear of grain. The words beginning with 'in which seed' (yasmiṃ bīje vā) should be applied in order to 'taking by pressing' and so forth. Because it is said, 'at the mere moment of being released from the stalk,' if that seed is released from the stalk, even if it has not been moved from that spot, since there is no other place for it, it is indeed a pārājika offense. If a certain ear of grain is entangled or connected with something else, then if it is released from the stalk, it is a thullaccaya offense; if it is released from the other place, it should be understood as a pārājika offense. Therefore, it says 'the stalk of grain' (vīhināḷaṃ) and so on. 'With husk' (sabusaṃ) means together with the straw. 'By a stake' (khīlena) means by a stump. Here, in the shifting of stakes and so forth, both simultaneous effort (sahappayoga) and the relinquishing of responsibility (dhura-nikkhepa) are possible. Shifting the stake is the simultaneous effort here. Even if that effort is made, if the owners do not relinquish responsibility and still wish to take it back, it does not yet constitute theft. Knowing that 'this monk, a favorite of the king, wishes to take the field by shifting the stake,' and relying on his power and harshness, if the owners relinquish responsibility even before the act of shifting the stake is completed, it is not theft, because the responsibility was relinquished before the completion of the effort. When the relinquishing of responsibility occurs only because of the effort of shifting the stake, only then does it constitute theft. For this reason, it is said, 'only by the owners' relinquishing of responsibility.' Even the owners' acceptance without knowing that the stakes have been shifted should be understood as relinquishing responsibility here. By the phrase 'thus in all cases,' the aforementioned meaning is extended to the shifting of ropes and so forth. 'Staff' (yaṭṭhi) refers to a measuring rod. If one [measure] has not yet been reached, it is a thullaccaya; when that one is reached...
184:
...it is a pārājika. If one intends to take [the land] merely by driving in wooden posts, the pārājika offense occurs at the last post. If one intends to take it by covering the gaps between the bases of those posts with thorn branches and so forth, making it inaccessible to anyone, the pārājika offense occurs at the last branch. Therefore, it is said, 'He is able to make it his own only by the enclosure of branches.' The meaning is that he can make it his own property only by driving in the posts and making an enclosure of branches. To clarify the meaning of 'the boundary of the field,' it is called 'the embankment of the rice-field' (kedāra-pāḷi). This method of taking by shifting stakes and so forth is also applicable to parks (ārāma) and so on.

## Explanation of the Commentary on Sites (Vatthu)
In the Commentary on Sites (Vatthu), 'three types of walls' refers to the three types of walls made of brick, stone, and wood.

In the Commentary on Villages (Gāma), the phrase 'a village is...' is not mentioned in the Pāli text because all the characteristics of a village have been stated previously.

## Explanation of the Commentary on Forests (Arañña)
In the Commentary on Forests (Arañña), 'having pierced through' (vinivijjhitvā) means having pierced through straight. 'Cut with a mark' (lakkhaṇacchinna) refers to having marks such as letters made by those who buy from the forest owners. 'Covered with bark' (challi-pariyonaddha) shows that it has been abandoned for a long time without any concern from the owners; therefore, it is said, 'it is allowable to take it.' If the owners still have concern, it is not allowable. 'Those things are completed and inhabited' means those houses and so forth are finished and inhabited by people. 'Woods' (dārūni) refers to the remaining wood after the houses and so forth have been built. The statement 'it is allowable to take' is said because the owners have no attachment; if the owners see [the person] at the time of taking and, having attachment, forbid it, then it is certainly not allowable to take. Regarding 'if it is said "give it," it must be given,' this means that for one who goes away with the intention 'I will give it' when told 'give it,' if he is not told 'give it' again and goes without giving, there is no offense. If they demand it later, it must be given.

'If he goes without seeing, he must pay for the goods (bhaṇḍadeyya)' means that for one who goes with a pure mind, restitution of goods is appropriate. Even if one passes through a guarded place with a pure mind and then the intention to steal arises, the theft (avahāra)...
185:
Since the protected area (ārakkhaṭṭhāna) has not been crossed, it does not constitute theft (avahāra). Some teachers, however, say: "Even if the timber is taken to an unspecified place, because the timber belongs only to the owner of the forest, if one moves it with a renewed intention to steal, it is indeed a Pārājika." That statement is not appropriate. This is because it is stated that an offense is incurred only upon crossing the protected area, in such phrases as "having reached the protected area... one crosses it unintentionally," and "one crosses that place suddenly," etc. The statement, "This is a Pārājika even for one who, carrying it with the intention to steal, travels by air," is said in reference to crossing the protected area. The reason given that "even if the timber is taken to an unspecified place, it belongs only to the owner of the forest" cannot be a reason for incurring a Pārājika offense outside the protected area, because that factor is only a reason for being liable for compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya). Indeed, it is only because the timber belongs to the forest owners that a monk who has reached the outside becomes liable for compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya); otherwise, he would not even be liable for compensation, as in the case of crossing a customs post. Only the property given by travelers belongs to the customs collectors, not what is ungiven; therefore, a monk who crosses that customs area with a pure mind due to some reason is not even liable for compensation. In this forest, however, because it is the property of the forest owners, one is liable for compensation in all places. For this reason, the protected area in this forest is even more serious than a customs post. If theft (avahāra) were to occur even outside the protected area when there is an intention to steal, then the specification of the place in such phrases as "having reached the protected area" would be useless, as it should simply be said that a Pārājika occurs whenever an intention to steal arises in any place. Therefore, the conclusion should be reached here that theft (avahāra) does not occur for one who travels with an intention to steal outside the protected area. The phrase "for one who carries it with an intention to steal" means for one who travels even by way of crossing through the air that region which, if crossed, is called crossing their forest and their protected area.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Water (Udakakathāvaṇṇanā)
In the discussion of water, a wide-bellied water-jar is called an udakamaṇika. Some also say, "A jar with ridges at the middle is called an udakamaṇika." Therein, in those vessels. In the phrase "together with vegetation (bhūtagāma) also," the word "also (pi)" includes unallowable ground (akappiya-pathavī). "For the sake of protecting the tank" means for the sake of protecting the tank so that "much water may not come and break the embankment of the tank." Regarding the term "drainage water" (nibbahanodaka), it is called "nibbahana" (drainage) because the excess water from one high side of the tank flows out or exits through this [conduit].
186:
A channel that drains excess water is called an adhikajalanikkhamanamātikā. The water flowing in that outlet channel is called drainage water (nibbahanodaka). A drainage pipe (niddhamanatumba) is a water-exit pipe made of bricks etc., for the sake of crops and so on.

In the phrase "making the embankment weak" (mariyādaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā), even if one does not make it weak, if the aforementioned effort is made, it should be decided as theft (avahāra) according to the value of the water that exits after breaking the boundary of the embankment. The phrase "as much crop as is produced because of that" is said in reference to the surplus profit (adhikalābha) obtained after deducting expenses such as seeds and plowing. Indeed, this monk does not need to pay even the labor costs incurred by those farmers.

This statement is appropriate only for a monk who destroys water while young crops are growing. A monk who destroys water before the crops are even planted must pay only the value of the water. He does not need to pay for all the crops that would have been produced because of that water, because he is responsible for compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya) only for the property he actually destroyed. Otherwise, if one steals goods kept by others for trade etc., one would end up having to pay both the value of the goods and the potential profit, which is not appropriate; this is our accepted view.

In the phrase "by the owners' relinquishing of responsibility" (sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepena), if the tank and the field belong to a single person, a Pārājika is incurred by that person's relinquishing of responsibility. If, however, the tank is common property but the fields are individually owned, theft (avahāra) occurs only when each respective person relinquishes responsibility. If the fields are also common property, it should be understood that a Pārājika is incurred only when all owners relinquish responsibility; if they do not relinquish it, there is no Pārājika.

"Not gone out" (aniggata) means not yet exited, staying within the tank itself. "The mouth of others' channel" (paresanaṃ mātikāmukhaṃ) means the mouth of a small channel. "Before reaching" (asampatteva) means while still in the main channel after exiting the tank. "Bound when not exited, well bound" means that because the water is common property, if it has not exited the tank, one is not even liable for compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya); this is the meaning. But if it has exited, it becomes individual property, so it is said: "Bound when exited, liable for compensation."

In this case, because it has not entered the small channel, theft (avahāra) does not occur. The two alternatives mentioned below, "not gone out from the tank" and "not yet reaching the mouth of others' channel," are stated for the purpose of connecting them respectively with these two: "bound when not exited, well bound" and "bound when exited, liable for compensation." In the phrase "there is no theft (avahāra)," some say, "There is no theft, but one is liable for compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya)." That is not appropriate. In the phrase "the object... does not meet," the meaning is that because the water in the tank is common property, it cannot be another's property (parasantakavatthu).

## Explanation of the Story of the Tooth-stick

In the Dantakaṭṭhakathā, when it is said that from that time onwards there is no theft (avahāra), it is because [the tooth-sticks] are placed for the purpose of being taken as much as desired without being specifically allocated, with the thought, "Let the Bhikkhu Saṅgha use them as they wish." Because they are unguarded and belong to all in common, they are not like other Saṅghika property; thus, even for a monk who takes them with the intention to steal, it does not constitute theft. The words of some elders should be connected here: "Let them eat; later, the novices will bring more."

## Explanation of the Story of the Lord of the Forest

In the Vanappatikathā, the phrase "because it is supported" is said regarding a tree that has been cut and is about to fall, but remains standing merely by being supported; it is not said regarding a tree that was previously entwined by black pepper vines and the like. Even if such a tree is cut, there is no theft, just as with the vines entwined in the Arañña-aṭṭhakathā. By the phrase "it stands upright," it shows that the absolute cutting of a tree that is not connected with vines and the like is a release from all surrounding areas such as the sky, as before; thus, in this context, displacement from its place (ṭhānācāvana) is distinct. Some teachers, however, say, "Because it stands slightly inclined due to the weight of the tree, displacement from its place indeed occurs." That statement is not appropriate, because the tree does not exceed the entire space of the sky it touches in five or six ways. "Clearing the face of the wind" means that just as the wind comes and fells a tree, one clears it by cutting and removing branches and thickets that stand blocking the path of the wind. "Maṇḍūka-kaṇṭaka" is said to be a thorn located at the tip of the tails of frogs; some also say it is a "poisonous fish-spine."

## Explanation of the Story of the Taker

In the Haraṇakakathā, "haraṇaka" refers to property being carried by the owner. If that property is worth one pāda, it is indeed a Pārājika. Because it is a part of a cloth that was noted generally as "I will take this cloth" without specifically noting "I will not take the edge," and because one desires to take that part as well, it is called a Pārājika. "Sabhaṇḍahāraka" means "together with the carrier of the goods"; because the substitution of the letter "sa" is optional, the word "saha" remains; it means that property together with the carrier of the goods. "Sāsaṅka" means "If...
188:
...approaching to take the goods, he might strike me with a weapon"—thus, one who has suspicion born of fear. "Ekamantaṃ paṭikkamma" means not approaching because of fear, but moving away from the path oneself. "Santajjetvā" means threatening with harsh speech and with bodily gestures such as brandishing a weapon. "Anajjhāvutthaka" means property that is not taken possession of. Since property that is not inclined towards by attachment is also called "unoccupied" (anajjhāvutthaka), it is said, "If it is requested, it must be given." By this, it is shown that even if attachment was first relinquished, if the perception of "my property" arises later, it becomes the property of those very persons. There is no fault in taking it with the perception of "my property," even by force; theft occurs only for one who does not give it up. If the owner has doubt, thinking, "I relinquished it first; is this property mine now or not?" then it is not proper to take it by force. This is because the state of being fit to be taken back occurs only when the perception of "my property" is strong. According to the statement "It is a Pārājika for one who does not give," it is shown that even if the stealing monk has the perception of "my property," if the owners still have attachment, it is not proper to refuse to give it. "Anyesu" refers to texts such as the Mahāpaccari. Since there is no rejection in those texts either, it is shown that this is the only meaning to be understood.

## Explanation of the Story of Deposits

In the Upanidhikathā, regarding property deposited in one's hands for safekeeping, if no other effort is made such as saying "I will not take it," other than the act of storing it in a secure place, and if during times of civil unrest both parties remain in their respective places and relinquish their responsibility (dhura-nikkhepa), thinking "Now I will not give it to him" and "Now he will not give it to me," it does not constitute theft. Some teachers, however, say, "It is indeed a Pārājika because the act of storing it was performed." That is merely their opinion and should not be accepted as the essence. For at the time of storing, that monk had no intention to steal. At the moment the intention to steal arises, thinking "Now I will not give it to him," there is no bodily or vocal act (payoga) that is the cause for the owner's relinquishment of responsibility. Without such an act, one cannot fall into an offense. In truth, this offense is not one that arises from non-action (akiriya-samuṭṭhāna). Since there is effort to give and he is still guarding it for that long, and because it was not said with the intent to steal, the act of lying by saying "I will not take it" etc., results only in a Pācittiya offense, not a dukkaṭa. This should be understood because there is no coinciding act (sahappayoga) since there is no intention to steal. Even if one says with the mouth, "I will give"... in the context of "it is a Pārājika," by which act does the offense occur? It is not yet an offense by the first act of storing the goods, because at that time there was no intention to steal. Nor by the mouth...
189:
If it is asked: "Since the action of saying 'I will give' is allowable (kappiya), is there no offense even if a mind of theft (theyyacitta) exists at that time?" The answer is stated: Even if the owner repeatedly asks, "Please give," and the person does not give, but through some action makes his unwillingness to give known to the owner, and because of that action the owner, realizing "This person does not want to give and is procrastinating," gives up his claim (drops the burden), then by that very action, an offense is incurred for that monk. In the case of these entrusted goods (upanikkhiṭṭha-bhaṇḍa), there is no escape through prevarication (pariyāya). If the owner is made to give up his claim through evasive words such as "When did I give it to you? Where did I give it to you?" an offense is indeed incurred. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "What are you saying... thus, by the dropping of the burden by both, it is a Pārājika for the bhikkhu." It should be understood that escape through prevarication exists only in causing others to take someone else's property, not in all cases. Regarding the phrase "because it was placed in one's own hand," because the owner placed it in his hand and he stands in the position of a storekeeper, there is no theft (avahāra) even if he moves it from its place; however, it should be known that if he takes it with a mind of theft, he is not exempt from the dukkaṭa offense.

"In this same manner" means that in the act of lifting [the bowl], the thief incurs a Pārājika. Why? Because a mark shared with others has been mentioned. "It is appropriate if he takes another of such a nature" means that if he takes another bowl similar to the thief's bowl in terms of its mark and location, it is appropriate [to charge a Pārājika]. The meaning is that even if someone removes that bowl from the place marked by the thief and places another similar bowl there, and he takes that one, it is still appropriate [to charge a Pārājika]. By this, it is shown that although the bowl marked during the day was moved elsewhere and another similar bowl was placed there, the mind of theft that arises in the thief later at night arises by taking as its object that other similar bowl placed in the location marked during the day. "By footstep" means the offense is incurred by the footsteps of the thief who goes away after taking the bowl brought out and given by the Elder. "It is appropriate if he takes one that is not of such a nature" means that since theft does not occur at the moment the Elder holds a bowl that is not similar, if he later takes the bowl that has come into his hand, perceiving it as "that one" or "another," and goes away thinking "I will take this and go," the theft (avahāra) is appropriately determined by the footsteps.

"There is no Pārājika" means it should be understood that there is no Pārājika even in the footsteps, as in the case of entrusted goods. "Village gate" is mentioned to show the starting point of entering the village because the monastery is situated outside the village; it means "inside the village." In the lifting by both...
190:
The words "Indeed a Pārājika" are spoken because the Elder is not a storekeeper. If that Elder were a storekeeper, all the goods would be considered as deposited; and even if one takes deposited goods with thievish intent, there is no theft (avahāra) yet for the Elder, but theft only for the thief. "Wrongdoing for both" means that for the Elder, because it is his own property, and for the thief, because it was given by the owner, theft (avahāra) does not occur; the meaning is that for both monks, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred because of taking with an impure mind.

"Because of being taken by command" means because of taking by the command given by the Elder, such as "Take the bowl and robe." "He enters the forest, it should be made [an offense] by footstep" means that because the Elder has designated the wandering from the monastery, on the village path, and throughout the entire village, saying "Take the bowl and robe, we shall go to such-and-such a village for alms," the offense is said to be by footstep only for one who goes deviating from the path. From the precinct (upacāra) on the other side of the monastery to the precinct on the other side of that village, the entire area is the precinct for wandering by the Elder's command for the junior monk; but not beyond that. Therefore, it is said: "If he crosses the precinct, it is a Pārājika. If he crosses the village precinct, it is a Pārājika." The same method applies when returning or when being sent for purposes such as washing robes.

In the phrase "without standing or sitting," if he enters the monastery and, without putting the load carried on his head etc. on the ground, stands or sits to rest, and after the thievish intent has subsided, he again arouses thievish intent and goes, it should be determined by the lifting of the foot (pāduddhāra). If he puts it on the ground and then takes it again and goes, it should be determined by lifting [the object] (uddhāra). Why? Because whatever was to be done according to the command of the one who gave the order is completed by that much. If it is said generally, "We shall go into the village," without specifying "such-and-such a village," they say that all the alms-resort villages near the monastery where they have previously entered for alms are the field (khetta). "The rest" refers to all things such as deviating from the path, going towards the monastery, etc. "Just like the previous" is said considering that even if taken without a command, because it was taken after informing the owner, all the monastery precincts etc. mentioned below are the field. By the words "This same method," he refers to the method stated as "having aroused thievish intent midway on the path," etc.

"Or when a hint is made" occurs when a hint is made such as "My robe is soiled; who, I wonder, will dye it for me?" "By the same method as stated" means by the method already stated for a monk who is not commanded but goes taking the bowl and robe together with the Elder. "On one side" means on one side without showing himself because the monastery is large. "Consuming with thievish intent, he causes it to wear out" means when thievish intent arises, he does not move it from its place but uses it by way of wearing it until it is worn out. For a monk who moves it from its place, however, it is indeed a Pārājika. How? It is like moving a load from the head to the shoulder, etc. "It is destroyed in this way or that" means destruction by fire, etc. By the words "or any other," it should be understood that whichever monk is appointed, that monk is also included. "For the other" means for the thief monk. Because he is released from the deposit only by the words "Take another robe" or "Bring the robe," and because even if he takes a robe other than his own, the owner still has concern for his own robe, it is said: "Pārājika in lifting (uddhāra)." If the owner [thinks], "Let this robe which is my property also be" ...
191:
When going taking the bowl and robes together with the Elder, it is in the same manner as already stated. "Ekapasse" (on one side) means staying on one side without showing oneself because the monastery is large. "Theyyacittena paribhuñjanto jīrāpeti" (wearing it out while using it with the intention to steal) means when the intention to steal arises, one uses it and wears it out in the same manner as wearing or covering oneself without moving it from its place. If a monk who moves it from its place has the intention to steal, he incurs a Pārājika, just as in the case of shifting a load from the head to the shoulder, etc. "Yathā vā tathā vā nassati" (it is destroyed in one way or another) means destruction by fire, etc. By the words "añño vā koci" (or anyone else), it should be understood that whoever placed it is also included.

"Itarassa" (to the other) refers to the thief monk. In the phrase "itaraṃ gaṇhato uddhāre pārājikaṃ" (Pārājika upon lifting when taking the other), it is said to be a "Pārājika upon lifting" because he is released from the status of a deposit by the very words "Enter and take your robe," and because the owner still has an attachment to his own robe even while taking the other. If the owner is completely free of attachment, thinking, "Whether my property is this robe or another, what is the use of it? This robe is enough for me," then there is no Pārājika for the thief. "Na jānanti" (they do not know) means they do not know because they do not hear the words spoken by him. In the phrase "eseva nayo" (this is the same method), it should be understood that even if they know but do not accept it in their mind, it is the same. In the phrase "paṭikkhipanti" (they reject), it should be understood that rejection by mind is also included.

"Upacāre vijjamāne" (while the vicinity exists) means there is a place for excrement and urine near the storehouse. In the phrase "mayi ca mate saṅghassa ca senāsane vinaṭṭhe" (when I am dead and the Saṅgha's lodging is destroyed), even if they say "We will kill you," it is proper to open [the door] because he is in the position of a sick person and it is said to be beyond his capacity. For there is no illness or incapacity greater than death. Even if they say "We will cut the door and take the requisites," it is proper to open it. "Sahāyehi bhavitabbaṃ" (there should be companions) means those monks should search by going for alms, etc., and give a little of their own property. This is the duty of those residing in the storehouse.

"Lolamahāthera" refers to an Elder who is dull, deluded, and habitually associates with many people. "Itarehi" (with others) refers to the other monks living in that same room. One engaged in guarding the monastery is called a "vihāravārika," who guards the monastery on his turn according to seniority. "Nivāpa" refers to food rations. "Corānaṃ paṭipathaṃ gatesu" (when they have gone to the path of the thieves) means knowing the thieves are coming and thinking "We will go first and make a sound..."
192:
...knowing the thieves are coming and going towards them thinking "I will act for the best," or following the path of the thieves thinking "I will bring back the goods stolen by the thieves," it is the same method. "Nibaddhaṃ katvā" (having made it permanent) means making a rule such as "The gruel and meal in such-and-such a family is only for the monastery guards." The phrase "even if one receives two or three gruel-tickets, or four or five meal-tickets" is just an example. Whether it is less or more than that, the measure is simply obtaining enough for the sustenance of oneself and one's attendants. "Nissitake jaggenti" means they have the monastery guarded by those pupils. "Asahāyakassa" means for one without a companion. "Attadutiyassa" (one with self as second) refers to that monk of few desires whose own body is his only companion, having no other. The word "yassa" etc., clarifies the meaning of both terms. By all this, it is shown that the turn should not fall to a single monk. "Pākavattatthāya" means for the purpose of the cooking-duty, known as the gruel and meal that must be cooked constantly. "Ṭhapenti" means the donors set it aside. "Taṃ gahetvā" means taking the portion given by the monastery attendants (ārāmika), etc. In the phrase "na gāhāpetabbo" (he should not be made to take), even for a monk who practices the dhutaṅga of living in the open air (abbhokāsika), if he has surplus requisites or attachment to a share of the Saṅgha's robes, etc., he too must be made to take his turn. "Diguṇaṃ" means double what others receive. "Pakkhavārena" means by a turn of half a month (a fortnight).

## Explanation of the Discussion on Customs Houses

In the discussion on customs houses (suṅkaghāta), the place where king's men strike (seize) the property of those who do not pay customs, even by snatching or beating, should be understood as "suṅkaghāta." The word "tañhi" etc., is said to clarify the aforementioned meaning. In the phrase "dutiyaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmeti" (he steps past with the second foot), having placed the first foot outside the boundary, a Pārājika is incurred just by lifting the second foot. Even if the foot is lifted but not yet placed outside, it is said to have reached the outside; thus it should be understood for all steps. The phrase "if one turns and places the inner bundle outside, a Pārājika is incurred" refers to standing outside oneself and first lifting the inner bundle or lifting them together to change their position. For by merely lifting while standing outside, the entire bundle reaches the outside. If that monk, though standing outside, first puts the outer bundle inside and then lifts the inner bundle to place it outside, even then, because the state of being connected is not yet abandoned, theft (avahāra) is not evident. Some teachers say, "A load that falls to the ground and rolls, even if it later enters inside, a Pārājika is indeed incurred..."
193:
Even if the outer bundle enters the inside, he is not exempt from the offense because it has reached the outside. Some say that regarding the bundle that was inside, whether first or later, merely by placing it outside, a pārājika is incurred; however, that statement is not appropriate. An object fallen on the ground has no connection with anything else; therefore, even if it enters the inside, it is appropriate to say it is a pārājika. However, this bundle on the end of the carrying pole is connected [to the pole], so it is not the same as the object fallen on the ground. Therefore, just as there is no connection with what has entered the inner ground, it should be understood that theft (avahāra) is accomplished only when both sides are proven to have gone outside; this should be examined and accepted. As for those teachers who interpret the word 'parivattitvā' as 'having submerged' (nivattitvā), they take the meaning as placing the internal property outside, and thus there is no doubt regarding that act of placing it outside. 'Ekābaddha' refers to being tied with a rope to the end of the carrying pole. If it is merely placed on the end of the carrying pole without being tied, and if the property placed on the end of the carrying pole held outside is worth one pāda, it is indeed a pārājika; the meaning is that this is because there is no connection with the property placed inside.

'In a moving vehicle... etc... he places' means placing it whether having entered the customs station or not. 'Situated outside the customs station' means it is situated outside because it was carried by vehicles and such. Some teachers, considering the reading 'bahi ṭhapitaṃ', interpret it as being placed outside even before reaching the customs station, but that interpretation is not good. This is because even if it is placed on a vehicle after entering the customs station, there is no offense, just as if it had rolled away. If a person, after entering the customs station and knowing 'this is the customs station', turns back along the path he came with the intent to steal, and if they take tax from the hands of those going in that direction, it is indeed a pārājika. 'In this place' refers to the act of taking it out by vehicles and such. 'Therein' refers to that Eḷakalomasikkhāpada.

## Pāṇakathā-vaṇṇanā

In the Pāṇakathā, 'āṭhapita' refers to a child being handed over to creditors by parents who have taken a debt, saying, 'Let this child stay with you as long as the debt is not repaid.' 'There is no theft (avahāra)' means that theft is not established because the parents have not completely relinquished the son, and because the child is not the property of the parents [in a way that constitutes theft by others]. It is said that by the words 'wealth increases in the place where it goes', it is shown that the wealth taken as a pledge, together with the interest, falls upon the neck (as a debt to be repaid) of the monk who takes the pledged son. 'The son of a slave' is said to show the most prominent characteristic. Even if he is the son of a non-slave man born from the womb of a slave woman, in this context...
194:
...he is also counted in this meaning. 'Having taken from another region' (paradesato paharitvā) means being carried away by royal thieves and such who plunder the regions of others. 'Live happily' is said with the intent to make them flee from their masters with a mind of theft. If one says 'Go and live happily' out of compassion without such a thought, there is no theft (avahāra), only the obligation of repayment (gīvā). 'Dutiyapadavāra' means if he is about to lift the second foot without fail, at the very moment the monk says 'Flee and live happily', it is a pārājika. By the passage 'anāpatti pārājikassa', it is shown that even if the speed of fleeing is not increased because of that monk's words, he is not exempt from the dukkaṭa offense. Because it is stated as 'one should take what is not given, known as theft' (adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyeyya), he is exempt from pārājika by the aforementioned method.

## Catuppadakathā-vaṇṇanā

In the Catuppadakathā, 'pāḷiyaṃ āgatāvisesā' refers to animals other than elephants and such mentioned in the Pāḷi text, because the word 'pasu' (beast) is common to all animals. 'Bhiṅkacchāpa' is a young elephant so named because it makes the sound 'bhiṅkā bhiṅkā' (or 'bhu-bhu'). 'Antovatthumhi' means in an enclosed area. The phrase 'situated outside the city' (bahinagare ṭhitassa) is said with reference to a walled city. In an unwalled city, the place where the elephant stands within the city is itself the 'station' (ṭhāna). 'Khaṇḍadvāra' refers to a gate broken by oneself. In the phrase 'eko nipanno' (one lying down), the word 'bandho' (bound) should be brought in and connected; therefore it is said 'two for one lying down'. Regarding the word 'ghāteti' (kills), it is said that for a monk who destroys with the intent to steal, it is only a dukkaṭa because it is a common effort (sahappayoga).

## Ocarakakathā-vaṇṇanā

In the Ocarakakathā, the statement 'he is exempt from taking what is not given by method' is said with reference to the effort of command (āṇattikapayoga). However, in cases such as personal involvement in a lawsuit, there is no exemption even by method.

## Oṇirakkhakakathā-vaṇṇanā

In the Oṇirakkhakakathā, 'oṇi' means 'brought' (āṇīta). Property placed with a custodian (oṇirakkhaka) is not like a deposit (upanidhi) placed in a secure place for protection, but is placed merely to be looked after for a moment in the place where it was originally set; therefore, merely by moving that property from its place (ṭhānācāvana), a pārājika occurs for the custodian.
195:
## Explanation of the Discussion on Theft by Arrangement (Saṃvidāvahārakathāvaṇṇanā)

In the discussion on theft by arrangement, 'saṃvidhāya' means having arranged or consulted. The statement "Therefore, they incur a dukkaṭa offense" is made because a pārājika offense is not possible through the power of the command [in that specific context]. If the commanded monks steal according to the command, the commanders incur a pārājika offense at the very moment of the command.

In the Pali: "When many monks arrange and one steals the goods, all incur a pārājika." Here too, it should be understood that for the commanders, the offense occurs at the moment of command, while for the thief, the offense occurs when the goods are moved. In cases such as "Many monks command one, saying 'Go and bring this property,' and when that person moves it, all incur a pārājika," the meaning should be understood in this same way.

Stealing by one's own hand is not a factor of the commander, nor is the command a factor of the one who steals by his own hand. They cannot be factors of each other because they occur at different times. For a monk stealing with his own hand, the offense occurs at the moment of moving the property from its place; for a monk causing theft by command, the offense occurs at the moment of the command. Thus, the offenses are distinct due to the difference in time.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Acts by Signal (Saṅketakammakathāvaṇṇanā)

In the discussion on acts by signal, "in the same manner as stated in the discussion on scouts (ocarakakathā)" means in the manner stated as "property that must certainly be taken," etc. In the Pali, "before or after that signal" means in the time before or after that agreed signal. In the phrase "before or after that sign," the same method applies.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Acts by Sign (Nimittakammakathāvaṇṇanā)

In the discussion on acts by sign, making a sign such as winking is rapid and lasts only a short time. Therefore, it is impossible to steal that property at that very moment. Because the effort to take begins immediately after the sign is made, it is said, "he steals by that very sign."

If it is impossible to steal in this way, does the argument that "this is only a pre-meal effort (purebhattappayoga)" reach a valid status? It does not. This is because an act by sign (nimittakamma) is not associated with a specific period of time like an act by signal (saṅketakamma). An act by signal is stated by way of time, while an act by sign is stated by way of gesture. This is the distinction between the two. The statement, "If one steals that property before or after that sign, there is no offense for the original commander," refers to...
196:
...the monk who takes before the sign is made, or the monk who, even after the sign is made, does not begin to take it but takes it later of his own accord.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Command (Āṇattikathāvaṇṇanā)

In the discussion on command, "asammohatthaṃ" (for the sake of non-confusion) is said because a person making signals or signs does not merely make a time-signal such as "pre-meal" or a sign such as winking. Rather, he also specifies the property, saying, "Take property of such color and shape." He also commands through a sequence of persons, such as "You tell so-and-so, and let him tell another." Therefore, when a command is given by way of time (such as morning), by way of gesture (such as winking), and by way of the property and the sequence of persons, confusion (sammoha) can arise due to a deviation from the signal (visaṅketa) in these acts of signal and sign. "Asammohatthaṃ" is said to remove that confusion.

"What was spoken by the commander as a sign-perception" refers to the property mentioned by the one commanding to take it during the morning or upon a wink, having made a sign-perception for such taking, characterized by such color, shape, etc. "This logic applies everywhere" refers to the Vinaya logic regarding the occurrence of pārājika and other offenses at the very moment of command in all matters related to command, whether mentioned below or to be mentioned above. This is called "logic" (yukti) because it proceeds by way of reasoning: at the moment the commanded person completes the action, the commander no longer possesses the effort (payoga) and the intention to steal (theyyacitta); thus, only a single offense occurs at the moment of command.

Because it is said, "a thullaccaya for the original person," even if Saṅgharakkhita receives [the item], Buddharakkhita and Dhammarakkhita incur only a dukkaṭa. Why does the teacher (ācariya) incur a thullaccaya in this case? It is said, "Mahājano hi," etc. "Mahājano" is said in reference to Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, and Saṅgharakkhita. "Dukkaṭa for the original person only" refers to the dukkaṭa of Buddharakkhita. This is said in reference to the dukkaṭa at the initial moment of command to show that the teacher who stands at the root does not have a thullaccaya [in that specific sense], but it does not refer to the occurrence of another dukkaṭa due to Saṅgharakkhita's act of receiving. Indeed, he does not incur two dukkaṭa offenses through a single effort.

However, some teachers say, "Because of the deviation from the signal, the Pali does not specifically say 'for the original person' but says generally 'he receives, there is an offense of dukkaṭa'; thus, this is said in reference to Saṅgharakkhita's dukkaṭa." Although this does not agree with the Commentary, it appears appropriate according to the Pali. This is because an offense does not fail to occur during his effort of receiving. By this [Pali], in the sections that come below...
197:
It should be understood that for the monks who receive [stolen goods], an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred. Some teachers say: "If one writes 'theft should be committed' on a leaf or a stone slab, etc., it is indeed a pārājika." However, it should be investigated [as follows]: this is appropriate only if written with a specific instruction such as "steal the property in such-and-such a person's house"; it is not appropriate if written without such a specification.

By the words "they are like the Fruit (phala) that occurs immediately after the Path (magga)," it is shown that just as for noble persons (ariya-puggala), when the Fruit-consciousness arises immediately after the Path, the task of meditation (bhāvanā-kicca) ending in the subsiding of defilements is said to be accomplished; likewise, when this volition (cetanā) that accomplishes the purpose arises, the task of commanding (āṇatti-kicca) is indeed accomplished. Therefore, it is said: "For that reason, this monk becomes a pārājika at the very moment of the command." The meaning is that he becomes a pārājika at the very moment of the volition that originates the vocal effort (vacī-payoga) of commanding.

## The method of the explanation of the discussion on command (Āṇattikathāvaṇṇanā) is finished.

## Explanation of the Classification of Offenses (Āpattibhedavaṇṇanā)

In that [explanation], "tattha tattha" refers to objects situated on the ground, objects situated on dry land, and so forth. In the Pāḷi, "property possessed by another" is said with reference to property taken possession of by humans. By these three terms—"he touches," "he causes to shake," "he moves from its place"—the fifth factor of theft, together with the preliminary effort, is stated. And this phrase "he moves from its place" is merely an illustration. It should be understood that all efforts such as commanding, as well as the laying down of the burden (dhura-nikkhepa), are also included here.

"Moving from its place" is stated according to the sequence of the Pāḷi, because the laying down of the burden must also be included. This method applies everywhere hereafter as well. Therein, by the phrase "not perceiving it as one's own," the state of being possessed by another is stated. By the phrases "not taking on trust" and "not taking temporarily," the perception of it being possessed by another is stated. Or rather, it should be understood that by these three [phrases], both the state of being possessed by another and the perception of it being possessed by another are stated. "Anajjhāvutthaka" (unoccupied) refers to things like wood, grass, leaves, etc., in the forest that have not been used by way of possession as "this is mine." "Chaḍḍita" (discarded) refers to anything that was first possessed and later discarded because it was no longer wanted. "Chinnamūlaka" (severed root) refers to property where, after searching for the lost item and not finding it, the root known as attachment is severed. "Assāmika" (ownerless) refers to ownerless objects shown by the three modes such as "unoccupied" (anajjhāvutthaka), etc. "Ubhaya" (both) means both ownerless property and one's own property.
198:
## Explanation of the Classification of Non-offenses (Anāpattibhedavaṇṇanā)

"Arisen in that very existence" means arisen as a peta in that very dead body. The statement "there is nothing to be said regarding a cloth hung on trees, etc." is said with reference to what is not guarded by humans. However, if that cloth is something guarded and protected by men appointed at a shrine (devālaya), a cetiya, a tree, etc., it is not proper to take it. The statement "if a little has been eaten... pe... it is proper to take" is said with reference to the absence of theft (adinnādāna). Taking and eating meat that is being eaten by a hungry creature is indeed unseemly (asāruppa) due to the lack of compassion and due to greed. For that very reason, those who practice the noble lineage (ariyavaṃsa) do not threaten and stop dogs, etc., even when they are eating the food in their own bowls. It should be understood that just as there is merit in giving material gifts (āmisa-dāna) to animals, there is indeed demerit in snatching away the material things of those animals. Therefore, it will be said later: "It should not be taken out of compassion for others."

## Explanation of the Miscellaneous Discussion (Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā)

When many people do not lift a single heavy object such as wood together, the phrase "sāhatthika-āṇattika" (by one's own hand and by command) is used with reference to the occasion where there should be physical effort (kāya-payoga) along with the vocal effort (vacī-payoga) "Take it! Lift it!" However, in a theft occurring thus: "You take this object, I will take another," the object taken by oneself is only "by one's own hand" (sāhatthika), and the object caused to be taken by another is only "by command" (āṇattika). Therefore, even if the combined value of those two objects amounts to five māsakas, there is no pārājika. There is only an offense such as thullaccaya according to the value of each individual object. For it is said: "The 'by one's own hand' is not a factor of the 'by command,'" and so forth. One who, not wishing to give back a deposited object or an object to be compensated, delays by saying "I will give it, I will give it," or one who harasses by remaining silent, causes the other to lay down the burden (dhura-nikkhepa) through various bodily gestures and so forth; therefore, it is said "and by the origination of action" (kiriyāsamuṭṭhānañca).

## The method of the explanation of the Word-Analysis (Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) is finished.
