## Explanation of the Vinītavatthu
In the Vinītavatthu (Decided Cases), language (nirutti) itself is called the 'path' (patha) because it is the means for grasping the respective meanings. For this very reason, it is said: "vohāravacanamatte" (in mere conventional speech). By the phrase "yathākammaṃ gato" (gone according to his kamma), it shows the death from that state of being a peta (hungry ghost). By the word "abbhuṇhe" (still warm), it shows the presence of heat in the body because of being on the verge of death. For this very reason, it is said: "allasarīre" (in a moist/fresh body). Even if it has reached a state of decay, it must be said to be 'broken' (destroyed) because it has deviated from the moist/fresh state. "Visabhāgasarīre" refers to a female body. The phrase "sīse vā" (or on the head) etc., is said with reference to the occurrence of mental perversion in the regions below the collarbone and above the kneecaps. If one acts without touching any specific limb indiscriminately, it is only 'well done' (sukata). In fact, they say that for a monk who touches even a dead corpse, incited by an indiscriminate manner, only an offense of wrongdoing for touching what should not be touched (anāmāsa-dukkaṭa) is incurred. That statement is appropriate. If a dukkaṭa offense can occur even regarding a female image which is not a basis for a pārājika, then it cannot be exempt from offense regarding a dead female body which is a basis for a pārājika.

## Explanation of the Case of Shifting the Lot (Kusasaṅkāmanavatthu)
"Balasā" means by force (violently). The future-tense statement "It will be a robe, I will take it" is said to show the preconception (parikappa) that arose even before grasping the bag. At the moment of grasping, however, the intention should be understood here as: "If it is a robe, I take it," while grasping the bag. It should not be understood as meaning he will take it only after taking it out and knowing it is a robe. Therefore, it is said: "Pārājika is incurred just by lifting it up." Otherwise, for a monk who takes it thinking, "I will not take it yet; I will take it later when it is dark or when I can distinguish it; for now, I will just get it into my hand as if I am looking at it," theft (avahāra) cannot occur at the moment of grasping. That such an avahāra does not occur is also appropriate. This is because at the time of such grasping, there is no final decision (to steal). Only when there is a decisive intention (saññiṭṭhāpaka-cetanā) is there an unwholesome act, just like in the case of killing (pāṇātipāta) and so on. Just as for one who catches a living being intending to "kill it later," even if that being dies at the moment of being caught, it does not constitute pāṇātipāta because the effort with the intention to kill has not yet been made; so too in this case (of theft), even if one moves an object from its place by planning the time, such as "I will steal when the sun sets," avahāra does not yet occur at that moment of moving, similar to the planning of location (okāsaparikappe). However, when the planned location and time arrive, for one who goes with the intention to steal without putting the goods on the ground, it is considered that avahāra occurs at every single step. Therefore, there are three types: planning regarding the goods (bhaṇḍaparikappa), planning regarding the location (okāsaparikappa), and planning regarding the time (kālaparikappa)...
200:
...planning (parikappa) should be understood. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, planning regarding time (kālaparikappa) is not mentioned separately, being combined within planning regarding location (okāsaparikappa); this is our view, and it should be accepted after investigation. The phrase "avahāra should be caused by the step" is said because of investigating without putting the goods on the ground. "Pariyuṭṭhita" means following (obsessed).

"Parikappa is evident" means that at the moment of taking, the specific planning is evident, showing that according to those teachers, avahāra does not occur at that time. "Because of carrying after seeing, parikappāvahāra is not evident" means that later, after investigating outside and knowing it is a robe, if one carries it away with the intention to steal, the planning made previously no longer serves as a factor for avahāra; it would be just theft (theyyāvahāra), like carrying it away after knowing it is "thread/cloth." Therefore, parikappāvahāra is not evident. Since the planning such as "If it is a robe, I will take it" no longer exists at the time of taking, it is purely avahāra and not parikappāvahāra; this is the meaning. By that, it shows that the theft involving planning the goods (bhaṇḍaparikappāvahāra) occurs only at the moment when one does not yet definitely know the goods, such as "If it is a robe, I will take it." Therefore, it is said: "For one who lifts the planned goods while they are still in the state of being planned and unseen, avahāra occurs."

If this is so, one might ask: why does okāsaparikappāvahāra become parikappāvahāra for one who steals after seeing the goods? This is not a fault, because that planning (parikappa) does not have the goods as its object. Indeed, okāsaparikappa is stated only for goods already seen and known. Although this Pali text, "Thinking it is that goods, he steals," is stated by the power of one who takes it definitely thinking "This is that very goods," even in this planning occurring as "If it is that goods, I will take it," there is a definiteness in the taking as "I will take it," which fulfills the meaning of avahāra; thus it is extracted. For this very reason, it is said: "it agrees."

"Keci" (Some teachers) refers to certain teachers within the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā itself. By the phrase "But in the Mahāpaccari..." etc., it shows that the view of 'Keci' is to be criticized and that the view of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is more appropriate.

"Alaṅkārabhaṇḍa" refers to ornaments such as rings and so on. "Kusaṃ pātetvā" means dropping a mark (lot) made of bamboo strips or palm leaves and so on. It is said "he protects during the lifting" (uddhāre rakkhati) to mean that even if the lot is lifted from another's portion, the exchange of the lot has not yet occurred. By the phrase "Pārājika just by being released from the hand," it shows that this is a distinct type of avahāra called shifting the lot (kusasaṅkāmana), which does not include moving from the place (ṭhānācāvana) and dropping the burden (dhuranikkhepa). All...

Thefts (avahāra) are accomplished through one's own action, by command, by intention, and by effort; in terms of meaning, they should be understood as being comprised of three types: removing from a place (ṭhānācāvana), laying down a burden (dhuranikkhepa), and transferring a lot (kusasaṅkāmana). The statement 'Another person takes his portion; in taking it, he commits a Pārājika' is said because the original owner has not yet relinquished attachment (ālaya) to his portion. If there is no attachment at all, it does not constitute theft; therefore, it is said, 'There is no theft even for one who takes what remains after selection.'

In the phrase 'even knowing that this is not mine,' the word 'pi' (even) includes one who takes with a mind of theft while being in doubt about the ownership of another's property. 'Siveyyaka' refers to cloth produced in the Sivi kingdom.

140-1. 'Having it made allowable' means having it cooked. In the phrase 'in that case, there is a Pācittiya,' it should be understood that a Dukkaṭa is not mentioned because there is no concurrent effort (sahappayoga) in the form of taking what is not given. 'By those commanded' means by those commanded by an authorized monk (sammuti). 'By the one commanded' means by the one commanded by the owners. 'Bhaṇḍadeyya' (property to be returned) is so called because, although it does not become a Pārājika since it was given by an authorized monk and others, it is called bhaṇḍadeyya because it was taken by referring to a person who does not actually exist. 'What is given by another' refers to taking what is given by someone other than the four, such as the authorized monk. A person who takes by saying 'Give the portion of another' without pointing to a non-existent person, or by saying 'Give another portion,' or by counting deceptive statements—if it is the property of laypeople and is given by the owner himself or by one commanded by the owner, it does not even become bhaṇḍadeyya. However, in the case of property belonging to the Saṅgha, it does become bhaṇḍadeyya. To show this distinction, it is stated again: 'by one who is not authorized or not commanded,' and so on. 'What is given by others' means what is given by an authorized monk or one who is commanded. 'One who takes in this way' refers to one who takes by saying 'Give another portion as well' or by counting deceptive statements. In the phrase 'but the owner,' the word 'pana' (but) indicates a special meaning. By that word 'pana,' it means that there is a distinction if the owner himself gives or causes it to be given when one takes by saying 'Give another portion as well' or by counting deceptive statements. 'Well given' (sudinna) means it does not become bhaṇḍadeyya. Below, however, for one who takes lay property given by the owner or by one commanded by him, saying 'Give the portion of another,' it becomes bhaṇḍadeyya because it remains the owner's property since the other person does not exist. Here, however, for one who takes property given by the owners themselves, saying 'Give another portion as well' or by counting deceptive statements, saying 'Give'...

Because it was said 'Give,' excluding the mere act of requesting from a non-relative, it does not become bhaṇḍadeyya (property to be returned) but is said to be 'well given.' However, some say that for one who takes property given by one who is not the owner or not commanded by the owner, it is indeed bhaṇḍadeyya; as in the section on the four bowls (pattacatukka), the status of theft (avahāra) is appropriate here. In the case of property belonging to the Saṅgha, even if one says 'Give,' because there is no individual owner, it should be understood that it is bhaṇḍadeyya even if given by an authorized person.

146-9. 'If they cause it to be brought, it is bhaṇḍadeyya' is said because, according to the statement 'If taken, he is pleased,' property taken from one who is not pleased must be returned. According to the statement 'It should be distributed by those present,' the goods to be distributed reach only those monks staying within the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā). Therefore, it is said, 'It is proper to take only for those staying within the precinct boundary.' Bhaṇḍadeyya means that even if there is attachment (ālaya) on the part of both the thief and the owner, it must not be given to the thief but only to the owner, because even the thief must give it back only to the owner. 'In this very way' means that if taken with the perception of discarded cloth (paṃsukūla), it is bhaṇḍadeyya, but if taken with a mind of theft, it is a Pārājika.

'When they depart' means when they flee, abandoning the village. 'Without distinction' means generally, without examining specifics such as whether there was effort. Because the owners' property is delimited, the mere presence of effort is the measure for the occurrence of an offense. 'From there' means from the property belonging to a group (gaṇasantaka), etc. 'Gives for the sake of favoring a family (kulasangaha)' means taking and giving with the perception of it being discarded cloth or property of an acquaintance. In that case, due to the cause of corrupting a family (kuladūsana), there is a Dukkaṭa offense and bhaṇḍadeyya. If there is a mind of theft, however, it is a Pārājika even for one who takes for the sake of favoring a family. For items worth less than five māsakas, there are Thullaccaya and Dukkaṭa offenses along with the Dukkaṭa of corrupting a family. 'Designated for the sake of lodgings'—this is said to show the Thullaccaya offense for one who gives by way of exercising authority. Even for property given for the sake of other requisites, if one gives it to relatives or for the sake of favoring a family by way of exercising authority without a mind of theft, there is a Dukkaṭa offense and bhaṇḍadeyya. 'By way of exercising authority' means by one's own sense of power, thinking, 'Who will stop me if I give? I alone am the authority here.' Thullaccaya means that for one who gives, whether for favoring a family or for another reason, there is a Thullaccaya offense and bhaṇḍadeyya because it is heavy property (garubhaṇḍa) designated for the sake of lodgings. 'Neck' (gīvā) here should be understood as: in the case of property designated for lodgings, there is a gīvā offense along with Thullaccaya; in the case of other property, it is a gīvā offense along with Dukkaṭa. 'Is well eaten' is said because one stays within the precinct boundary, distributes it, makes it one's own property, and then eats it. For property belonging to the Saṅgha...
203:
Goods connected to the monastery, which are to be distributed and are located outside the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā), must be distributed only by the monks staying within the precinct boundary; they must not be distributed by monks staying outside the precinct boundary.

There is an offense if a monk, who spoke because he was told to do so by his teacher (saying, "I speak because the teacher instructed me"), is later accused of Pārājika or other faults by the monk who told him to speak (saying, "Speak because I instructed you"), or if lay devotees criticize them, saying, "Venerable sirs, you speak without limit."

153-5. Chātajjhatta means consumed or oppressed by the internal fire (udaraggi) due to that hunger. Dhanuka is a small bow-shaped stick used for snagging (prey). In the case of "going while treading, one must give the value of the goods," if one pig is caught, since other pigs are not caught in that trap, one must only pay the value of goods equivalent to one pig. Adūhala is a mechanical stone; because they are crushed by that stone, deer are unable to flee. Pacchā gacchati means going later of one's own accord, not because of the effort made by that person. Therānaṃ means of the visiting elders. Tesampi means also for the resident monks. Paribhogatthāya means for the purpose of using after performing the prescribed procedure for communal (saṅghika) property. The remaining word "gahaṇe" (in taking) should be added and understood. Yattha means in whichever monastery. Aññesaṃ means to other visiting monks.

In that matter, "visiting monks have no authority" means they have no authority to distribute and consume because the lay donors or monks have designated and offered it for the sake of robes for the monks who reside permanently in the monastery. Visiting monks who wish to do so should also take it for the sake of robes after entering for the rainy season retreat, etc., in that monastery. "Must abide by the agreement of those resident monks" means that without distributing all the large and small fruits, the resident monks who are managing well might say, "We will distribute and consume the fruits from this many trees; with other large and small fruits, we will repair the lodgings," or "We will provide for requisites such as alms-food," or "Without distributing anything, we will set it aside only for the four requisites." Visiting monks must abide by such agreements of the resident monks. The meaning shown in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā by the word "anissarā" (having no authority) is explained in detail in the Mahāpaccariya starting with "of the four requisites." In the phrase paribhogavaseneva, the word "eva" is used in an inappropriate place; it should be connected as "distributing only that (fruit) by way of consumption." Senāsana-paccaya (lodging requisite) refers to the monastery itself and the property specifically designated for that monastery. To show the previously mentioned meaning "excepting one or two excellent lodgings" in a negative way, it is said, "one should not take it by cutting off the original property." This means one should not abandon all lodgings by cutting off the root of the property known as lodging. Here, some teachers say, "Even if one abandons starting from the inferior lodgings while keeping one or two excellent lodgings, the ground of the lodging should not be abandoned." This statement is also appropriate, as this meaning must certainly be stated. Otherwise, some might think it should be abandoned along with the ground.

"Having posted a notice" (paṇṇaṃ āropevta) means posting a notice saying, "Having protected this many trees, this much should be taken." "Having made a sign" (nimittasaññaṃ katvā) means making an agreement. "Children" (dārakā) refers to any guardians such as the sons and grandsons of those tree-guardians; all are called "children" here. "From there" (tato) means from the aforementioned timber materials. "Having asked permission" (āpucchitvā) means having asked the executive Saṅgha. "Having taken all that" (taṃ sabbampi āharitvā) means taking it temporarily even without asking permission. "Only this monk has authority" etc., means that because he had it built with his own timber materials, etc., because he repaired it, and because of his share in the communal (saṅghika) lodging, only this monk is the one in authority. It means that monk should not be removed from that lodging. "Worship with water" (udakapūjā) refers to offerings such as sprinkling water on the courtyard of a stupa. "By the power of duty" (vattasīsena) means purely out of faith, and not for the sake of wages, etc. "Together with the property" (savatthukaṃ) means together with the land. "Wall" (kuṭṭaṃ) refers to the wall of a house. "Enclosure wall" (pākāraṃ) is the surrounding enclosure wall. "From there" (tato) means from the abandoned monastery. "Having taken from there, a lodging is made" means a lodging is made by taking timber materials, etc., from a monastery abandoned by monks living in nearby villages.

To clarify the meaning "consumes as personal property," it is said, "he does not give to the elders who arrive." "Mixed with one-fourth water" means mixed with a fourth part of water. In the Pāḷi, the statement "Monks, there is no Pārājika offense" is said because the owners gave it into the hands of Thullanandā specifically for her, and because she used it without the intention to steal (atheyyacitta). Even if she used it with the intention to steal, since it is equivalent to deposited property, she would only have to return the goods to that nun. In the case of the distribution of boiled rice (odanabhājanīya), in the story that comes as "give a share to another" (it is meant).
205: By the words "out of compassion for that family, for the sake of protecting their faith," etc., it is shown that he did not act for the sake of favoring the lay supporter. Because he made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) by determining the time beforehand, saying, "As long as the children are ascending the palace, let the palace remain near them," it stayed there only for that determined duration. After that, the palace returned to its original place by itself. Regarding that movement, it is said, "The Elder withdrew his psychic power," as if it occurred through the release of psychic power. Since there are no bodily or vocal efforts for one who acts through the knowledge of psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa), and there is no intention to steal (theyya-citta) because he only directed the palace, it should be understood that the Elder Pilindavaccha acted thus, thinking, "There is no theft here." Alternatively, although the palace was brought solely out of compassion to carry the children—just as one might move pigs caught in a snare by showing them bait—there is no theft here because the intention was compassionate, even when the children brought from the battlefield ascended the palace and the power was later withdrawn. There is also no liability for restitution (bhaṇḍadeyya) because of the absence of bodily and vocal effort. Indeed, an offense or liability for restitution occurs only when there is bodily or vocal effort. Therefore, the Blessed One did not say, "Monks, there is no offense for one without the intention to steal," but said only this: "Monks, there is no offense for a possessor of psychic power in the domain of his psychic power" (Para. 159). In the term "iddhividhaye" (in the domain of psychic power), the meaning should be taken as: there is no offense in the domain of the psychic mind, which does not trigger bodily or vocal effort to take another's property, and which exists purely at the mind-door without the intention to steal. Regarding the objection, "Since the display of psychic miracles is forbidden, why is it allowable to perform them?", he said, "There is no offense in performing such a resolution-based psychic power (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi)." Indeed, by this very sutta—"Monks, there is no offense for a possessor of psychic power in the domain of his psychic power"—it is established that resolution-based psychic power is not forbidden. Showing external forms such as elephants without abandoning one's natural appearance, and the power mentioned as "being one, he becomes many," is called resolution-based psychic power (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi) because it is accomplished by the power of resolution. The power mentioned as "he, abandoning his natural appearance, shows the form of a child, or the form of a nāga... or various army arrays," is called transformation-based psychic power (vikubbana-iddhi) because it proceeds by the power of altering and abandoning the natural appearance. Merely showing elephants and so on externally while keeping one's natural form as it is, is not called transformation-based psychic power. It should be understood that transformation-based psychic power is the creation of one's own body into the form of an elephant and so on.
206:
Parājitakilesena means one who has conquered defilements, or one who is free from defilements. In this Dispensation (Sāsana), it should be construed that there is no other training rule like this second Pārājika training rule, which is interspersed with many methods and possesses profound meaning and decision. In that verse, 'meaning' (attha) refers to the meaning of the Pali text, and 'decision' (vinicchaya) refers to the decision outside the Pali text (pālimuttaka). A training rule that has such profound meaning and decision is called 'gambhīratthavinicchaya'. 'Vatthumhi otiṇṇe' means when a case of taking what is not given (adinnādāna) has been brought into the midst of the Saṅgha, either by way of accusation or by way of one's own reporting of one's transgression. 'Ettha' refers to that case which has been brought. 'Vinicchaya' means the determination of offence and non-offence. 'Kappiyepi ca vatthusmiṃ' means even in the property of parents and others which is suitable for one to take oneself.

## Paṭhamapaññattinidānavaṇṇanā
Below, it has been stated starting with 'That city was a city during the time of the Buddha and during the time of the Cakkavatti King,' showing how the city of Rājagaha reached prosperity only at the time of the Buddha's appearance. To show that this prosperity is the same here in the city of Vesālī, it is said 'This city also.' By saying so, it shows that it is not only Rājagaha and so on. The words starting with 'Mahāvanaṃ nāma' are spoken according to the view of the Majjhima-bhāṇakas and Saṃyutta-bhāṇakas. However, the Dīgha-bhāṇakas say, 'The forest that stands continuous with the Himavantā is called Mahāvana.' 'Haṃsavaṭṭakacchadanena' means covered by a swan's circle, having the shape of a swan's whirl. 'Kāyavicchandaniyakathā' means talk that produces detachment from the physical body (karajakāya). 'Chanda' means weak passion (rāga). 'Rāga' means strong passion. To show in detail the meaning stated in brief as 'hair, body hair, etc.,' the words starting with 'Ye pi hi' are spoken. In this term 'pañcapañcappabhedena,' there are fivefold divisions in this method...
207:
In this context, it is called 'pañcapañcappabheda' because it has fivefold divisions of five. Because of these fivefold divisions, it should be understood as a qualifier (visesana) of the word 'pariyāya' by way of a Bahubbīhi compound (bāhiratthasamāsa).

'Asubhāya' refers to the matrix (mātikā) of impurity. The feminine genitive case (sāmivacana) is used in reference to the matrix to be explained. Therefore, it is said, "having laid down the matrix (mātikā)," etc. 'Taṃ vibhajanto' means analyzing the matrix. 'Phātikamma' means bringing about accomplishment (nipphattikaraṇa).

In the term 'pañcaṅgavippahīna', it should be understood as being rid of the five factors (pañcaṅgavippahīnata) due to the absence of the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) such as sensual desire, and being endowed with the five factors (pañcaṅgasamannāgatata) due to the arising of the five jhana factors such as initial thought (vitakka) that has reached absorption (appanā).

In the phrase 'tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ', one should understand the state of having threefold goodness (tividhakalyāṇata) by way of the beginning, middle, and end of the jhana, and the state of being endowed with ten characteristics (dasalakkhaṇasampannata) by way of the characteristics of those same beginning, middle, and end. In the Commentary, however, it is said "tatri māni," etc., considering that by demonstrating the ten characteristics, the threefold goodness of the jhana, which is the basis of those characteristics, also becomes clear.

'Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi' means this is the Pali text in the context of explaining those ten characteristics. 'Paṭipadāvisuddhi' is the purity of the jhana from obstacles such as the hindrances, through the preliminary practice ending with change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). Since that purity is primary as a condition for the cultivation of equanimity, etc., and is accomplished by the preceding cause, it is said "paṭipadāvisuddhi is the beginning."

'Upekkhānubrūhanā' is the repeated cultivation through the accomplishment of the function of specific equanimity (tatramajjhattūpekkhā) because there is no longer anything to be purified. Although this cultivation of equanimity occurs at the same time as the purification from obstacles, it is said "upekkhānubrūhanā is the middle" to show that it is accomplished only because of that purification.

'Sampahaṃsanā' is the purification by way of the accomplishment of the function of knowledge that effects the non-transgression of associated states, etc. Since that gladdening (sampahaṃsanā) is said to be accomplished only upon the completion of all tasks to be done, it is said "sampahaṃsanā is the end."

Although these three types of goodness (kalyāṇa) can be obtained in a single moment, they are spoken of as beginning, middle, and end to show how they proceed by way of condition and conditionally arisen states, etc., and not because they are obtained sequentially in the three moments of arising, presence, and dissolution of the jhana.

In the words "majjhimaṃ samādhinimittaṃ paṭipajjati," etc., the absorption concentration (appanāsamādhi) that occurs evenly is called the 'middle sign of concentration'. Indeed, that concentration is 'middle' (majjhima) because it does not approach the two extremes known as sluggishness (līna) and restlessness (uddhacca). It is called 'concentration' (samādhi) because it especially establishes the mind on a single object. It is also called the 'sign of concentration' (samādhinimitta) because it is the cause for higher distinctions. 'Paṭipajjati' means he attains it.
208:
Because of practicing in this way, the mind rushes into and stands fixed in the object of absorption (appanā), which is the single object there, by means of the middle sign of concentration. A person who does not strive further in purifying that mind, because there is no longer anything to be purified in such a purified mind, is said to 'observe the purified mind with equanimity' (vissuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati). One who has practiced tranquility (samatha) by reaching the state of tranquility, and does not strive further in composing the mind, 'observes the practice of tranquility with equanimity'. Because of practicing tranquility, one who has thus abandoned association with defilements and stands fixed in oneness, and does not strive further to establish that oneness, is said to 'observe the establishment in oneness with equanimity'.

In the words "tattha jātānaṃ," etc., the gladdening, cleansing, and purifying of the coupled states (yuganaddhadhammā) known as concentration and wisdom, which have arisen in that jhana-mind cultivated by equanimity, occur through their nature of not overstepping one another. Also, there is gladdening through the single taste of the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa) because the faculties (indriya) such as faith are liberated from defilements. Furthermore, there is gladdening by way of the exertion (vīriya) that is suitable for those states of non-overstepping and single taste, in the sense of carrying or proceeding. And at that moment, gladdening and purifying should be understood as being accomplished by way of the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge that purifies, through the sense of repetition (āsevana) of the aforementioned states. The words "evaṃ tividhatthagataṃ cittaṃ," etc., are words of praise for that very mind. "Vitakkasampannaṃ" means having reached a state of excellence through the factor of initial thought (vitakka). "Cittassa adhiṭṭhānasampannaṃ" means being endowed with concentration, which is the continuous occurrence of the mind on that very object; this is spoken of by way of the jhana factors. "Samādhisampannaṃ," however, should be understood as being spoken of by way of the faculties (indriya).

"Paṭikuṭati" means it shrinks. "Paṭivaṭṭati" means it turns back. "Nhārudaddulaṃ" means a bundle of sinews. "Payutta-vācaṃ" means speech employed in seeking requisites. "Daṇḍavāgurāhi" means by nets known as long nets attached to sticks.

"Samaṇakuttako" means one who performs the duties of a recluse, such as wearing the saffron robe. In the term "vaggumudā," the author says "vaggumatā" to show that worldly people used the word "mudā" for what should be called "vaggumatā." It is called "puṇyasammata" because it is designated as "vaggū," meaning it is considered pure. That river is called "puṇyasammata" because it purifies by removing the evils of beings.

The place, object, or dwelling of Mara is called 'Māradheyya'. In essence, these are the states of the three planes, but here the five cords of sensual pleasure are intended. Regarding that realm of Mara, [the deity] thought and said, "This venerable one will not be able to transcend it by becoming a monk based on the samvega (spiritual urgency) that has arisen." He did not say it thinking, "He will not be able to transcend that realm of Mara because there is no more rebirth in the three planes through the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship." Why? Because the deity held the view that beings are liberated from saṃsāra only by dying. In fact, that deity did not desire rebirth in any plane for those who die. In this sense, only depriving others of the life-faculty would constitute the nature of liberation from saṃsāra. Because it is said, "They kill themselves, and they also kill one another," the statement "he killed all those five hundred monks" is spoken in a general sense (yebhuyya).
209:
The 'realm of Māra' (Māradheyya) refers in meaning to the dhammas occurring in the three planes of existence, but in this context, it specifically refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure. That deity (Māra) thought and said, "This pseudo-monk (samaṇakuttaka) will not be able to transcend [my realm] by entering the monkhood based on the root of a sudden sense of urgency (saṃvega)." He did not say it thinking, "He will not be able to transcend it by reaching Arahantship and having no further rebirth in the three planes." This is because that deity holds the view that beings are liberated from Saṃsāra only through death. That deity does not wish for the rebirth of the deceased in any realm. In this sense, when it is said, "It must be just so," it means that depriving others of life (killing) must be the nature of liberation from Saṃsāra in this way. Since it is stated, "They deprive themselves of life, and they deprive each other of life," the statement "he deprived all those five hundred monks of life" should be understood as a general statement. Therefore, it should be understood that, excluding the worldling monks (puthujjana) who killed themselves or each other, this [Migalaṇḍika] deprived of life (killed) the remaining worldling monks and all the Noble Ones (ariyas).

"Ekībhāvato" means from seclusion. "Uddesaṃ paripucchaṃ gaṇhanti" means they learn in the presence of their own teachers. After learning, they attend to the Blessed One together with their teachers. At that time, the teachers who gave the recitations and so on approached the Blessed One with a diminished number of monks; referring to that, the Blessed One asked.

## Explanation of the Discourse on Concentration through Mindfulness of Breathing
Mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) is included among the ten recollections (anussati), but it is mentioned again here to show its suitability for many monks at that time. Indeed, the Blessed One taught it to those monks. It should be understood that the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā) is not taken here because it is similar to the meditation on foulness (asubha), and the four formless states (āruppa) are not taken because they are unsuitable for beginners (ādikammika). "Aññaṃ pariyāyaṃ" means another reason for the attainment of Arahantship. "Atthayojanākkamaṃ" means the sequence of meaning and construction. "Assāsavasena" means by way of the out-breath as the object. "Upaṭṭhānaṃ sati" means the establishment of mindfulness by approaching and staying with that very out-breath and in-breath without forgetting; the state of staying thus is called mindfulness (sati). Now, wishing to describe the person by way of mindfulness, it is said, "He who breathes out," and so on. Therein, the meaning should be taken as: "He who breathes out, his mindfulness stays having approached the out-breath," and so on. "Akosallasambhūte" means...
210:
"Avijjāsambhūte" means [the moment] arisen from ignorance. "Khaṇeneva" means by its own moment of occurrence. This concentration, which is the foundation of the Noble Path, increases gradually and becomes as if it has reached the state of the Noble Path; hence it is said, "ariyamaggavuဍ္ဎippatto" (one who has reached the growth of the Noble Path). In the term "opammanidassanaṃ," the simile itself is called "opamma," and "nidassana" is the illustration of that simile.

Outsiders (non-Buddhists) who know mindfulness of breathing only know the first four modes; they do not know all sixteen modes. Thus it is said, "sabbappakāra," and so on. In the phrase "evamassetaṃ senāsanaṃ," "evaṃ" means that only when there is the binding of the mind to the object with meditative mindfulness in the manner described, does it exist; otherwise, it does not. By this, it is shown that for one who is unmindful (muṭṭhassatī), living in the forest is useless and unsuitable. "Avasesasattavidhasenāsanaṃ" refers to the seven types of lodgings mentioned as: "a mountain, a cleft, a mountain cave, a cemetery, a forest grove, the open air, a heap of straw." [The lodging] must be suitable for the three seasons such as summer, the three humors such as phlegm, and the three temperaments such as delusion. By sitting cross-legged, the stability of sitting is indicated; by keeping the upper body erect, the ease of the occurrence of in-breaths and out-breaths is indicated; and by establishing mindfulness in front (parimukhaṃ), the means of grasping the object is indicated. "Na paṇamanti" means they do not bend. "Pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satiṃ" means having established mindfulness which is thoroughly grasped and called "niyyāna" (leading out/liberation) because it is the opposite of forgetfulness; it means having established supreme mindfulness and circumspection. "Sato va" means being endowed with mindfulness. "Bāttiṃsāya ākārehi" refers to the thirty-two modes described by dividing the sixteen terms such as long and short breaths found in the four tetrads into two parts by way of out-breathing and in-breathing. "Dီghaṃ assāsavasena" means by way of a long out-breath; this is a description without dropping the case-ending (dīghaṃ), or it means by way of the long out-breath taught by the Blessed One. "Cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ" refers to one who knows the one-pointedness of mind, which has received the name "avikkhepa" (non-distraction) because it is the opposite of distraction. "Paṭinissaggānupassī assāsavasena" means being one who contemplates relinquishment by way of the out-breath. There is also a reading "paṭinissaggānupassiassāsanavasena," which means by way of the out-breath of one who contemplates relinquishment. Among those breaths, the breath that first goes outward is called "assāsa" (out-breath), and the breath that then goes inward is called "passāsa" (in-breath); thus it is said, "assāso ti bahinikkhamanavာto," and so on. However, in the Suttanta commentaries, it is stated in the reverse order: breathing in by way of pulling is "assāsa," and breathing out is "passāsa."
211:
The word "Tattha" (therein) in the context of the outgoing and incoming breaths is connected with the statement, "First, the internal breath goes out." Some teachers say that based on the developmental process of infants, as stated in "Sabbesampi gabbhaseyyakānaṃ" etc., the outgoing breath should be taken as "assāsa." In this matter, the Sutta method alone should be understood as being in accordance with the Pali: "For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath with mindfulness, if the mind is distracted internally, both the body and the mind become agitated, trembling, and disturbed. For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath with mindfulness, if the mind is distracted externally, both the body and the mind become agitated, trembling, and disturbed."

"Addhānavasena" means by way of duration (time). This word "addhāna" denotes both time and space. Between these two, the spatial duration is shown by way of a simile starting with "Yathā hi." Now, to clarify the long and short (dīgha, rassa) nature of the in-breaths and out-breaths by way of temporal duration, which is distinct from spatial duration, the statement beginning with "Evaṃ" is made. They are "pulverized" (cuṇṇavicuṇṇā) because they consist of many groups of materiality (rūpa-kalāpa). In this context, it should be understood that the long and short nature of the in-breaths and out-breaths in the bodies of animals such as elephants and dogs is stated only by way of temporal duration as distinct from spatial duration. This is because of the statement, "Having slowly filled the long duration called the physical body (attabhāva)," etc.

"Tesaṃ" refers to those beings. "Te" refers to the in-breaths and out-breaths. "Ittaramaddhānaṃ" means for a short time. "Navahākārehi" (by nine modes) refers to the three modes stated initially by way of mere duration for a person practicing meditation who has not yet attained distinction from the previous state to the subsequent state. These modes are stated by way of three types of persons: to some, only the in-breath (assāsa) appears; to some, only the out-breath (passāsa) appears; and to some, both appear. Similarly, there are three modes by way of zeal (chanda) and three by way of joy (pāmojja), making these nine modes. "Ekenākārena" means by one mode among the long in-breaths, etc.

"Addhānasaṅkhāte" means in the physical body (attabhāva) called the long spatial duration, or in the long temporal duration. The same applies to the term "ittarasaṅkhāte" above. "Chando uppajjati" (zeal arises) means that because of the relief obtained through the meditation that brings distinction from the previous to the subsequent stages, a wholesome desire (kusalacchanda) characterized by an intense wish to act arises in that meditation. "Chandavasena" means by way of the zeal that has thus arisen. "Pāmojjaṃ uppajjati" (joy arises) means that because the in-breaths and out-breaths become subtler, the object becomes more peaceful, and the meditation enters the path, joy (pāmojja) associated with the meditative mind arises as tender rapture (pīti) of the minor (khuddaka) variety, etc. "Cittaṃ vivaṭṭati" means [the mind turns away] in the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta)...
212:
When the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) arises, the mind turns away from the natural in-and-out breaths. "Upekkhā stands" means that when concentration (samādhi) of the access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā) variety arises in that counterpart sign, equanimity (ajjhupekkhanam) occurs because there is no longer any need for effort (byāpāra) to produce further jhāna. This equanimity should be understood as equanimity-in-the-middle-of-states (tatramajjhattūpekkhā). "Anupassanā-ñāṇa" (contemplative knowledge) is the knowledge that repeatedly contemplates the sign by way of serenity (samatha), and repeatedly contemplates the mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) based on the in-and-out breaths by way of insight (vipassanā).

"The body is the foundation (upaṭṭhāna)" means that mindfulness stands near the body called the in-and-out breaths, hence it is called the foundation (upaṭṭhāna). It does not mean mindfulness itself is the foundation; however, mindfulness is both the foundation and mindfulness because it stands near and remembers by its own nature. In the phrases such as "Therefore it is said," the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) is the contemplation of the aforementioned collection of in-and-out breaths and the physical body (karajakāya) which is its basis, not as permanent, etc., nor as a woman, man, being, or soul, but only as a collection of in-and-out breaths and as having the nature of impermanence, etc. The development and increase of the foundation called mindfulness through that contemplation of the body is called "the development of the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in the body" (kāye kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna bhāvanā). This is the summary of the meaning.

"Ittaravasena" means by way of a short time. "Tādiso" refers to being long or short. "Vaṇṇā" refers to the modes such as being long, etc. "At the tip of the monk's nose" means at the tip of the nose, or by the word "vā" (or), it means on the upper lip.

"Therefore" means that because one breathes in and out making the entire body of in-and-out breaths clear and evident through the mind associated with knowledge that subsequently arises by way of the prior attention (ābhoga) which was: "I will make the entire body of in-and-out breaths clear and evident by way of the beginning, middle, and end," such a person who is "experiencing the whole body" (sabbakāyapaṭisampavedī) is said to "train" (sikkhati) with the thought "I will breathe in, I will breathe out." It does not mean that one is said to train merely by thinking, "I will do this in the future." For one who thus makes the beginning, middle, and end evident, "restraint" (saṃvara) is mindfulness or even energy. "Not anything else" is said in reference to the prior attention such as "I will make the whole body evident." By the word "ādi" (etc.) in "in the arising of knowledge, etc.," one should include the calming of the bodily formation and the experiencing of rapture, etc. "Bodily formation" (kāyasaṅkhāra) refers to the in-breath and out-breath. Although it is mind-produced, it is called the bodily formation because its activity is tied to the physical body (karajakāya) and is conditioned by it. "At the time of not grasping" means the time when the meditation subject has not yet been started, meaning the time when the body and mind have not yet been grasped for the purpose of starting that meditation. "Sits" refers to the grasping (comprehending) of the body by the passage "sitting cross-legged and keeping the body erect," and the grasping of the mind by the phrase "setting up mindfulness in front."
213:
By the phrase "pallankaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya" (having sat down cross-legged, having set the body erect), the comprehension of the body (kāyapariggaha) is meant; and by the phrase "parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā" (having established mindfulness in front), the comprehension of the mind (cittapariggaha) is meant. "Adhimattaṃ" has the meaning of strong or gross, and it is spoken with a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa). In truth, it refers to the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra). Alternatively, in the sentence "adhimattaṃ hutvā pavattati" (it proceeds excessively), this word "adhimattaṃ" is an adverb (kiriyāvisesana). "Sabbesaṃyeva" means both of the teachers.

The statement "mahābhūtapariggahe sukhumo" is spoken with reference to insight attention (vipassanā-manasikāra) based on the four elements. "Lakkhaṇārammaṇika-vipassanā" refers to the comprehension of groups (kalāpasammasana). Starting from the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā), it is called strong insight (balava-vipassanā); below that contemplation of disenchantment, in the lower stages, it is called weak insight (dubbala-vipassanā). "Pubbe vuttanayena" (by the method previously mentioned) refers to the method stated in the way of serenity (samatha), starting with "apariggahitakāle" (at the time when it is not yet grasped) and so forth.

"Codanāsodhanāhi" means by way of questioning and clarifying. "Kathaṃ" etc., is the Pāḷi of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, where it should be connected as "kathaṃ sikkhati" (how does he train?). "Iti kira" etc., are the words of the objector (codaka), meaning "if it were so." The objector's intention is that if the in-breaths and out-breaths come to a total absence, meditation cannot occur. "Vātūpaladdhiyā" means that because of the absence of the air of in-breaths and out-breaths, there is no arising or development of the meditative mind that is obtained by taking that air as an object. In the phrase "na ca naṃ," the word "naṃ" is merely a particle (nipāta). Again, "iti kira" etc., is the answer to the aforementioned objection, meaning "if one trains in the manner I have stated." "Pabhāvanā hoti" means that although the gross bodily formations have subsided, because the subtle bodily formations still exist, the development of meditation indeed occurs. "Kaṃse" means in a bronze vessel. "Nimittaṃ" means of the sign, or of the manner in which those sounds occur. "Sukhumakā saddā" refers to the subtle sounds (reverberations). "Sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇatāpi" means that the subtle sound itself is the sign, and it also occurs because of taking that sign as an object.

In the term "ābhisamācārikasīlaṃ," "abhisamācāra" means noble conduct, and that noble conduct itself is called "ābhisamācārika-sīla" (virtue of noble conduct). This is a designation for the virtue included in the duties of the Khandhakas. The statement "I shall protect my virtue" is spoken with reference to the virtue included in the Ubhatovibhaṅga. "Āvāsa" refers to the impediment of the dwelling (āvāsa-palibodha). The same method applies to "kula" (family) and so forth. "Kamma" refers to new work (navakamma). "Iddhi" refers to the psychic power of worldlings, and that power is an impediment (palibodha) to insight. It is stated in the Visuddhimagga that such an impediment should be severed...
214:
The various impediments (*palibodha*) should be cut off by means of severing them. '*Yogānuyoga*' means repeated exertion in the practice (*yoga*) of meditation (*bhāvanā*). '*Aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu*' (among the 38 objects) refers to the eight *kasiṇas* mentioned in the Pāḷi texts, excluding the light *kasiṇa* and the space *kasiṇa*; however, in reality, there are forty meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). By the phrase '*yathāvutteneve nayena*', it points to the meaning: "because it is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the work of devotion to practice." '*Iminā kammaṭṭhānena*' means "by this mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) meditation subject." '*Mahāhatthipathaṃ nīharanto viya*' is like showing the path of the meditation subject by making it like the path of a great elephant.

'*Vuttappakāraṃ ācariyaṃ*' refers to the kind of teacher mentioned below, such as "one who, by this very meditation subject, has attained the fourth *jhāna*, developed insight (*vipassanā*), and reached Arahantship..." They also speak of the kind of teacher described in the *Visuddhimagga* as "lovable, venerable, and worthy of cultivation," etc. '*Pañcasandhikaṃ*' means having five joints or five parts. Learning the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) means learning the texts of the meditation subject. Inquiring and discussing the meaning of that meditation subject is called "inquiring about the meditation subject"; it is also inquiring about doubts regarding that meditation subject. The manifestation (*upaṭṭhāna*) of the meditation subject means the noting by one who exerts in meditation that "in this meditation subject, such a sign (*nimitta*) appears." Similarly, noting "in this way, one attains *jhāna*" is called the attainment (*appanā*) of the meditation subject. The characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of the meditation subject means noting the nature of the meditation subject, such that reaching the peak by means of establishing and exerting in meditation through counting (*gaṇanā*), following (*anubandhanā*), and touching (*phusanā*) is called meditation in this context. Therefore, it is said, "It means noting the nature of the meditation subject."

"Free from the eighteen faults of a dwelling" means a dwelling free from these eighteen faults: being too large, being new, being old, being near a main road, having a pond, leaves, flowers, or fruits, being a famous place desired by many, being near a city, wood-gathering area, or fields, having incompatible persons, being near a port, being in a remote border village, being on the border of two kingdoms, being unsuitable, and not finding a good friend (*kalyāṇamitta*). A dwelling endowed with five factors means:

"Monks, here in this Dispensation, a dwelling is not too far (from a village) and not too near, and is accessible for coming and going; by day it is not crowded with people, and by night it has little sound and is free from noise; there is little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, snakes, scorpions, and lice. For a monk living in that dwelling, robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites arise without difficulty. In that dwelling, senior elders reside... Monks, thus a dwelling is endowed with five factors." This refers to a dwelling endowed with the five factors spoken by the Blessed One. Among these five factors: (1) not being too far or too near, etc., is one factor; (2) not being crowded by day, etc., is one factor; (3) having few mosquitoes, gadflies, etc., is one factor; (4) ease of obtaining robes, etc., is one factor; (5) the residence of senior elders is one factor—thus these five factors should be understood. '*Upacchinnakhuddakapalibodhena*' means that monk who has cut off minor impediments (*palibodha*) by cutting long hair, etc., or by baking, sewing, or dyeing the bowl and robes, etc. '*Bhattasammada*' is the drowsiness or fatigue caused by having eaten a meal. Learning from a teacher is called '*ācariyuggaha*'. One learns the entire procedure of the meditation subject. It is not merely the learning mentioned previously. From what is learned from that teacher, '*ekapadaṃ*' means even a single part. '*Anuvahanā*' is the continuous occurrence of mindfulness by means of following after the out-breaths and in-breaths. Because, like the attention by means of counting (*gaṇanā*), etc...
215:
“Senior monks reside in the lodging ... Monks, in this way, a lodging is endowed with five factors” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.11) — in a lodging endowed with the five factors spoken by the Blessed One, the five factors should be understood as follows: (1) not being too far, etc., is one; (2) not being crowded during the day, etc., is one; (3) having few gadflies and mosquitoes, etc., is one; (4) the acquisition of robes, etc., is one; and (5) the residence of senior elder monks is one.

“Upacchinnakhuddakapaliibodhena” means that minor impediments (paliibodha) have been cut off by a monk through removing long hair, etc., and through performing tasks such as firing the bowl, and sewing or dyeing the robes, etc. “Bhattasammada” is the fatigue caused by food. Learning from a teacher is “ācariyuggaha”; it refers to the acquisition of the entire meditation procedure (kammaṭṭhāna-vidhi), not just the mere learning mentioned previously, but the procedure beyond that. “Ekapadampi” means even a single group.

“Anuvahanā” is the continuous maintenance of mindfulness by way of following the inhalations and exhalations. Because there is no separate mental attention by way of contact (phusanā) as there is by way of counting (gaṇanā), etc., and because counting, etc., should be done only at the place where contact occurs, he said, “Phusanā is the place of contact,” to show that phusanā is taken here in this mindfulness of breathing. “Ṭhapanā” is proper placement (samādhāna); however, since the concentration characterized by such placement is absorption (appanā), he said, “Ṭhapanā is appanā.” Insight is called “sallakkhaṇā” because it marks [phenomena] by their characteristics such as impermanence. The Path is called “vinivaṭṭanā” because it turns away from occurrence (pavatta) and signs (nimitta). The Fruit is called “pārisuddhi” because it is the state of the subsiding of defilements. “Tesaṃ” means of those two, vinivaṭṭanā (Path) and pārisuddhi (Fruit).

“Khaṇḍa” is a break in counting by way of skipping one, such as “one, three, five.” Or else, “khaṇḍa” means that a limit or boundary should not be shown in the interval by counting again after not counting for a certain period in between. For one who shows such a break, distraction may occur as the investigation arises: “Is my mind inclined toward the meditation subject or not?” Therefore, he said, “Has my [mind] reached the peak?” etc. This was said regarding one who attends to counting for a long time after showing such a break. Such a person might think so based on the mere lack of distraction thus obtained.

“Whichever [breath] appears, taking that breath” — this statement is made with reference to a person for whom only one breath appears first among the inhalations and exhalations. If both appear to someone, he should count by taking both. By this very statement, “whichever appears,” [it is meant that] whichever breath is distinct among the winds of the two nostrils, that breath...
216:
...should be taken; it should be understood that this meaning is also indicated. Even if they appear one by one at first, both breaths become distinct for one who counts while noting them in succession; therefore, he said, “The inhalations and exhalations become distinct.” It should be understood that “in this way, one should count very quickly” is the connection. To show the opportunity for beginning such fast counting, he said, “For this person also, who counts according to the previous method,” etc.

In that context, “according to the previous method” refers to the method of slow counting. By the words “having become distinct,” he shows that at the time of starting the slow counting, the subtle inhalations, etc., are indistinct due to the lack of clarity of the mind, and they become distinct later when the mind is clear; and when they are distinct, one should abandon slow counting and perform fast counting. The continuous occurrence of fast counting, in the primary sense, exists only in the process of absorption (appanā-vīthi); it cannot occur continuously in the sensuous-sphere process (kāmāvacara-vīthi) because it is interrupted by the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Therefore, he said, “as if occurring continuously.” “According to the previous method only” refers to the method of fast counting. One who attends to the wind entering inside is said to “send the mind inside.”

“Etaṃ” refers to this group of inhalations and exhalations. “Anugamana” is only the act of attending at the place of contact, not the following after the inhalations and exhalations. Therefore, he said, “And that, indeed, is not by way of following the beginning, middle, and end.” By the statement that there is no separate mental attention by way of contact and fixing, he shows that just as one attends to counting and contact, so too there is no mental attention to fixing and contact alone without following (anubandhana). It is indicated that after setting aside counting, one attends by way of following and contact until absorption (appanā) arises; but when absorption has arisen, one is said to attend by way of following and fixing. However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it should be understood that only this much was said: “It is said that one attends by way of following, contact, and fixing,” in order to show that there is no mental attention to fixing without following.

That meaning which is not determined with absolute certainty is near to the determined meaning. This is an illustration of achieving the goal through a well-known similarity, like “the gayal is like a cow.” “Paṅguḷa” means a lame person (pīṭhasappī). “Dolā” means a swing (peṅkhola). “Kīḷataṃ” means of those who are playing. The phrase “at the foot of the post for binding” is said with reference to the sign at the tip of the nose and the sign at the mouth (upper lip). “From the beginning onwards” means starting from the illustration of the meaning of the object of comparison (upameyya). “Nimitta” refers to the sign for binding, which is the sign at the tip of the nose or the sign at the mouth. “Not the object of a single mind” means that because inhalations and exhalations do not occur at the same moment, all three cannot be the object of a single mind; only two, either inhalation or exhalation along with the sign, [can be the object] at a single moment...
217:
It means they become objects. In the sentence 'For one who does not know the three things (ajānato ca tayo dhamme),' namely the sign, inhalation, and exhalation, by way of making them objects, the word 'ca' expresses the sense of contrast (vyatireka). By that word 'ca,' it shows the contrast that if it were so, it would lead to this undesirable fault. 'Bhāvanā' refers to the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-bhāvanā).

'How are these things not known... how is distinction attained?' This statement is the setting up of a question to explain the meaning already stated in the answer verse by using the simile of the saw (kakacūpama). There, the word 'kathaṃ' (how) should be applied to each: 'How are these things not known... how is distinction attained?' 'Padhāna' means the effort (vīriya) that accomplishes the development (bhāvanā). 'Payoga' means the application to the development that removes the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). 'Visesa' means the distinction ending in Arahantship. In the simile, 'padhāna' means the effort to cut the tree. 'Payoga' means the exertion (the act of sawing) to cut that very tree. Although it is not directly said in this simile that 'one attains distinction,' it should still be construed by way of meaning. 'Yathā rukkho' and so on is the comparison with the simile. In the phrase 'at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth,' a person with a long nose should focus at the tip of the nose; another (with a short nose) should focus at the upper lip, which is named 'mukhanimitta' because the mouth is covered by this lip.

'This is padhāna' means that by the exertion of which effort, both body and mind become fit for the work of development; it shows the cause by way of the result, saying this exertion of effort is called 'padhāna.' 'Upakkilesa' means the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). 'Vitakka' means wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) such as sensual thoughts; or, having shown the attainment of the first jhāna by abandoning the hindrances, it speaks of the attainment of the second jhāna and so on by way of the reason of the subsiding of thought (vitakka). 'This is payoga' means the application known as the devotion to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), which is the cause for attaining jhāna. 'Fetters are abandoned' means the ten fetters are abandoned by way of total eradication through the sequence of the paths (magga). 'They disappear' means likewise the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya) also disappear without any remainder, even of a fragment. 'This is distinction' means this abandoning of fetters and so on, which is obtained gradually depending on this concentration (samādhi), is the distinction of this concentration. 'Thus these three things' and so on is the concluding statement. 'Is fulfilled' means it is entirely full due to the fulfillment of the sixteen bases (vatthu). 'In order' means gradually. 'Is practiced' means is developed. 'This world' means one illuminates the world of the aggregates (khandha) and so on with the light of wisdom (paññā).

'Here' means in this place. It should be construed that there is a purpose in bringing the saw which serves as the simile. 'Nimitta' means the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta). 'Adorned with the remaining jhāna factors' means they say it is adorned with the remaining jhāna factors such as vitakka.
218:
Because vitakka (applied thought) is essentially appanā (absorption), it is said "with vicāra (sustained thought) and so forth." This vitakka is indicated as "appanā byappanā" (absorption, fixed absorption). When it is said thus (as vicāra and so forth), the word "avasesa" (remaining) becomes appropriate. Alternatively, considering samādhi (concentration), which is the principal factor among the jhāna factors due to its association with vitakka, as appanā, it is said: "The fixed absorption (ṭhapanā) known as appanā, adorned with the remaining jhāna factors, is accomplished." In some ancient manuscripts, the text to be mentioned later, "From the time of attention by way of counting... in sequence... as if reached," is found. Therefore, this passage should also be written here; it should be understood that it was omitted due to the error of scribes.

The words beginning with "When the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased" are brought in to show the method of investigating the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) which has reached the state of being investigated by the method previously mentioned. "By way of location" means from the location previously grasped by way of touch. "The sign should be established" means the perception (saññā) that grasps the sign with the previously grasped characteristics should be established at the point of touch. This is said in reference to this cause, known as the method of the appearance of the object for one to whom the object is not clear. "From here" means from the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). Because it is a meditation that is respected due to the difficulty of development, it is called "weighty development" (garuka-bhāvanā). "Having frequented" means having taken the object of resort. "The sign" (nimitta) means the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) or the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). Here, both are mentioned together. For, the three similes such as cotton wool are appropriate for the learning sign, while the remaining similes are appropriate for both.

"Like the appearance of a star" means like the color and appearance of a star. "Due to the difference in perception" means due to the difference in perceptions that occurred prior to the appearance of the sign. "Born of perception" means it is something imagined by the perception of development; it does not arise [as a physical reality] because it does not [actually] exist. Therefore, it is said, "It appears differently." It appears thus to one devoted to development. "Thus" means, in this sense, when the mind is established only on the sign in the manner mentioned.

"From here onwards" means starting from the arising of this counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). "In the sign" means in the counterpart sign. "Establishing" means establishing the mind by way of fixed absorption (ṭhapanā). "Various aspects" means the various aspects mentioned as "the four colors" and so forth. "Making them vanish" means making them disappear or making the beginning disappear. From the time the sign arises, for one who does not attend to those aspects, they become as if they have vanished. Making the various aspects present in the in-breaths and out-breaths vanish, or establishing the mind in the sign produced by the in-breaths and out-breaths, one binds one's own mind.
219:
"Nāma" is a grammatical connection (yojanā). Some teachers, however, state the meaning of the word "vibhāvayanti" as "vibhāvento—making clear what is known." That meaning would be appropriate in terms of the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). The meaning here is: making clear and knowing the various modes of the in-breath and out-breath, and placing the mind on the sign (nimitta) obtained therein, one gradually binds or fixes one's mind.

"Kilesā" refers to the remaining defilements. "Sannisinnāyeva" means subsiding and remaining quiet because of not obtaining the companionship of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). "Upacārabhūmiyaṃ" means at the moment of access (upacāra). "Lakkhaṇato" means by way of characteristics such as suppression (vikkkhambhana) or by way of characteristics such as impermanence (anicca).

"Gocara" refers to the alms-resort village. A village where it is difficult to obtain suitable alms-food is an unsuitable (asappāya) village. The other is a suitable (sappāya) village. "Bhassa" refers to speech based on the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu); that speech is suitable. Other speech is unsuitable. Among the remaining places such as dwellings, whatever place an unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated is a suitable place. Other places should be understood as unsuitable.

For a monk who, despite avoiding these seven kinds of unsuitable things and frequenting only suitable ones, does not yet attain absorption (appanā), the ten kinds of skill in absorption (appanākosalla) are mentioned, beginning with "vatthuvisadakiriyā" (making the basis clean), to show what should be accomplished. Among those ten, "vatthuvisadakiriyā" means making the internal physical basis clean by cutting hair, trimming nails, etc., and making the external basis clean by washing and repairing robes, dwellings, etc. By making things clean in this way, the wisdom also becomes clear and capable of accomplishing its task. "Indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā" means balancing the faculties such as faith (saddhā). "Nimittakusalatā" means skill in protecting the sign obtained through meditation (bhāvanā).

In the passages such as "at which time the mind should be restrained," when the mind becomes restless due to causes such as over-exertion and needs to be restrained, one restrains the mind not by developing the three enlightenment factors such as investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga), but by developing the three enlightenment factors such as tranquility (passaddhi). When the mind is sluggish due to causes such as excessive laxity of energy and needs to be exerted, one exerts the mind not by developing the three factors such as tranquility, but by developing the three factors such as investigation of states.

When the mind is listless due to the weakness of wisdom and application, etc., then there is the stirring up (saṃvejana) known as gladdening the mind through the contemplation of the eight bases of urgency (saṃvegavatthu). When, however, through such practice, the mind is not sluggish, not restless, not listless, but proceeds evenly on the object and has entered the path of serenity (samatha), then there is equanimity (ajjhupekkhanā) by attaining a state of non-interference in the exertion, restraint, and gladdening of the mind.
220:
"Tadadhimuttatā" means resolution toward concentration (samādhi), the state of being inclined, sloped, and bent toward concentration. "Ettha" means in this contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā). "Pārisuddhiṃ pattukāmo" means desiring to attain the fruition (phala) or desiring to enter into it. In that text, it should be understood that one first desires to attain the fruition immediately following the path (maggānantara-phala) by way of noting the characteristics and turning away from the round of existence (vivaṭṭana). Thereafter, one also desires to enter the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) by way of noting the characteristics.

In the phrase "āvajjana... vasippatta" (mastery in adverting, etc.), for one who has emerged from the attained jhana and reflects on each of the jhana factors such as initial application (vitakka), when the sense-sphere impulsions (kāmāvacara-javana) having the reflected jhana factor as object occur continuously, interrupting the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) immediately after the adverting (āvajjana) that arose, then the mastery in adverting (āvajjana-vasī) is accomplished for him. The ability to attain that jhana quickly, immediately after the desire to attain it, is called mastery in attaining (samāpajjana-vasī). The ability to maintain the jhana for a moment, such as the duration of a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps, is called mastery in resolving (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī). Likewise, the ability to emerge from jhana by way of the arising of the life-continuum after being endowed with jhana for a brief moment is called mastery in emerging (vuṭṭhāna-vasī).

The masteries of resolving and emerging are distinguished here by the difference in the prior preparation (parikamma) such as "I shall attain for only this much time" and "I shall emerge from jhana after being endowed with jhana for only this much time," but they are not different in their intrinsic nature. That mastery which is called "skill in attainment (samāpatti-kusalatā)" is also called "skill in emerging (vuṭṭhāna-kusalatā)." Mastery in reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-vasī) is mentioned only by way of mastery in adverting. Indeed, in the process of reviewing, mastery in adverting is the quick arising of adverting, and mastery in reviewing is the arising of the impulsions (javana) immediately following it; thus, it should be understood that by the accomplishment of mastery in adverting, mastery in reviewing is also accomplished.

"Jhānaṅgāni pariggahetvā" means having comprehended the jhana factors associated with the jhana-consciousness by way of their characteristics, etc. "Tesañca nissayaṃ" means the support of the [great] elements which are the support for those physical bases. This is stated according to the Suttanta method, as the support of the elements for the decads of physical bases (vatthu-dasaka) of the born body (karajakāya), and not according to the Paṭṭhāna method. Indeed, elements belonging to one group (kalāpa) do not serve as support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) for elements belonging to another group; however, according to the Suttanta method, they should be understood as decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya). It should be understood that all conditions not included in the Paṭṭhāna are included in the decisive support-condition according to the Suttanta method. "Tannissitarူပါနိ" means derived matter (upādā-rūpa). In the phrase "yathāpariggahitarūpavatthudvါရာရမ္မဏံ ဝါ," it means having as object the material objects such as hair as they were comprehended, or having as object the physical basis (vatthu) in the manner previously mentioned...
221: It should be understood by connecting the consciousness associated with the mental states together with the eye-door, etc., which have become manifest through the grasping of the physical body (karajakāya) that is the support of that heart-base (hadayavatthu). 'Kammāragaggarī' refers to the bellows of smiths. 'Tajjaṃ' means a state corresponding to that. 'Tassa' refers to mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa). 'Taṃ disvā' means having seen the causes such as ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā). 'Kaṅkhaṃ vitarati' means one overcomes the sixteen types of doubt (vicikicchā) occurring in such ways as 'Was I in the past?', etc. 'Kalāpasammasanavasena' means by way of comprehension by groups; 'comprehension by groups' (kalāpasammasana) is the comprehension of the five aggregates by taking each group of past, future, and present, etc., in terms of impermanence (anicca), etc. 'Pubbabhāge' means in the preceding stage of the contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā) which is included in the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi). 'Obhāsādayo' refers to illumination (obhāsa), knowledge (ñāṇa), rapture (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), happiness (sukha), resolution (adhimokkha), exertion (paggaha), equanimity (upekkhā), mindfulness (upaṭṭhāna/sati), and attachment (nikanti/taṇhā). Among these ten, resolution (adhimokkha) is faith (saddhā). Mindfulness (upaṭṭhāna) is sati. Equanimity (upekkhā) is specific neutrality (tatramajjhattatā). Here, the nine starting with illumination are called 'defilements' (upakkilesa) of insight because they are the objects of craving (nikanti), which is a cause of defilement. Attachment (nikanti) is called a defilement because it defiles and because it is the object of that defilement. 'Nibbindanto' means being disenchanted through the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā) preceded by the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā). One becomes dispassionate and liberated from all formations (saṅkhāra) by the path knowledge (maggañāṇa) that arises immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhūñāṇa), which arises at the end of the practice of the knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa), the knowledge of reflective contemplation (paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇa), the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa), and the conformity knowledge (anulomañāṇa). Indeed, at the moment of fruition (phala), one is called 'liberated' (vimutta), and at the moment of the path (magga), one is called 'being liberated' (vimuccanto). 'Ekūnavīsati-bhedassa' refers to the nineteen types of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) by way of the five objects to be reviewed—path, fruition, Nibbāna, abandoned defilements, and remaining defilements—which arise respectively after the four path-processes (magga-vīthi). For an Arahant, there are only nineteen because there are no remaining defilements. 'Assa' refers to the person practicing the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). 'Sappītake dve jhāne' refers to the first and second jhānas accompanied by rapture according to the fourfold method. 'Tassa' refers to that yogi. 'Samāpattikkhaṇe' means at the moment of attainment. 'Ārammaṇato' means rapture is experienced because the object is manifest through the grasping of the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta), since the object is experienced. When the object is known, the mental states (citta and cetasika) that take that object as their domain are said to be self-experienced because there is no doubt in subsequently grasping them by their individual characteristics and common characteristics. 'Vipassanākkhaṇe' means at the moment of seeing the object through the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā). Thus, the very grasping of rapture in terms of impermanence, etc., is called 'experiencing rapture' (pītipaṭisaṃvedana) without delusion.
222:
"By way of a long breath" means that for one who knows by way of a long breath which is the object, that rapture (pīti) is experienced; this is the connection. "For one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind" means for one who knows, through the wisdom associated with it, the one-pointedness of mind included in jhāna which has reached non-distraction. Just as rapture is experienced by way of the object, so too the states associated with it are also experienced. "Mindfulness is established" means when mindfulness associated with jhāna is established in its object by way of a long breath, it is also said to be established in the jhāna that has that breath as its object. In the passages beginning with "by way of a long out-breath," the meaning should be understood in this very same way. To show the experiencing of rapture thus shown, by way of the object and by way of non-delusion through analysis, the words beginning with "for one who adverts" are said. Among those terms, "for one who adverts" means for one who adverts to the jhāna. "That rapture" is the rapture included in that jhāna. "For one who knows" means for one who knows by way of the object at the moment of attainment; the connection is that for him, that rapture is experienced. "For one who sees" means for one who, having emerged from jhāna, sees with the knowledge that constitutes seeing. "For one who reviews" means for one who reviews the jhāna. "For one who resolves the mind" means for one who resolves the jhāna thought, "I shall be possessed of jhāna for this much time." Thus, by way of knowing the jhāna through the five masteries (vasībhāva), the experiencing of rapture by way of the object is shown.

"For one who is resolved" means for one who has faith, in the sense of by way of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). The same method applies to "for one who exerts energy" and so forth. "To be known by direct knowledge" (abhiññeyya) means the Four Noble Truths which are to be known by distinguished wisdom; the construction is: "for one who knows by direct knowledge through path-wisdom preceded by insight-wisdom," and so forth. Similarly, in "to be fully understood" (pariññeyya) and so forth, the construction should be understood as "for one who fully understands," and so forth. In that passage, "to be fully understood" refers to the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The remaining terms are the phrases "one experiencing bliss" and "one experiencing the mental formation."

In the phrase "feelings and so forth," perception (saññā) is included by the word "and so forth" (ādi); therefore, he said "two aggregates." "To show the ground of insight" is said by way of showing miscellaneous formations (pakiṇṇaka-saṅkhāra) headed by bodily bliss and so forth, because there is no bodily bliss in serenity (samatha). "That" refers to cessation (nirodha) mentioned by way of calming (passambhana). "By the method mentioned" means by the method mentioned regarding the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) in the passage beginning with "at the time not previously grasped by this monk." "Feeling is mentioned headed by rapture" means feeling is mentioned by way of the designation of rapture.
223:
The meaning is that by grasping pleasure, it leads to the inclination towards the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā). This refers to these two groups: 'Experiencing the mental formation, calming the mental formation.' Feeling associated with perception is mentioned because it is the contemplation of feelings. The statement 'the experiencing of the mind should be known' is said with reference to the previously mentioned method, such as by way of the object and by way of non-delusion. 'Mind' (citta) refers to the mind associated with jhāna and the mind associated with insight (vipassanā). 'Āmodeti' means to gladden with the associated rapture (pīti) that has jhāna as its object.
