By the words 'at the moment of insight,' etc., the moment of contemplating dissolution (bhaṅga) is meant.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Concentration through Mindfulness of Breathing is Finished.

Although noble persons (ariyas) do not deprive themselves or each other of the life-faculty, nor do they incite others to do so, it is said 'due to being mixed with noble persons' (ariyapuggalamissakattā) because there were noble persons among the worldlings who died in the three ways mentioned above, having been killed by Migalaṇḍika (the pseudo-ascetic). Alternatively, it should be understood that this is said because there are those who, while still worldlings, kill themselves but develop insight at the time of death, attain the noble path, and then die.

## Word-by-word Analysis (Padabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā)

'Without paying attention to the phrasing' (vyañjane ādaraṃ akatvā) is said because it was not stated in accordance with the phrasing such as 'knowing, perceiving,' etc. The phrase 'knowing it to be a living being' (pāṇanti jānanto) is said to show that it is a Pārajika offense even if one does not know it is a human, but merely has the perception of it being a living being. 'Having willed by the power of the intention to kill' (vadhakacetanāvasena cetetvā) means having thought with the intention to kill, 'I will kill this person.' 'Having planned' (pakappetvā) means having determined in the mind, 'I will kill him.' 'Having decided' (abhivitaritvā) means having made a resolution; therefore, it is said 'having sent forth a mind free from doubt' (nirāsaṅkacittaṃ pesetvā). 'The meaning has reached its peak' (sikhāppatto attho) means that although it is stated by the power of the preceding action 'intentionally' (sañcicca), it is the meaning that has reached the climax by showing the connection with the subsequent action of transgression. 'Jāti-uṇṇā' refers to the wool of a goat born on that very day. 'Thus having a similar appearance' (evaṃ vaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ) means having such a color and shape. The phrase 'or beyond that' (tato vā uddhaṃ) is said with reference to reaching the stage of foetal foam (abbuda), etc., in the second week and so on. The cause of the continuity whose momentum has diminished...
224:
'Is' (hoti) means it is a co-operating cause (sahakārī-paccaya), not a productive cause (janaka-paccaya). For kamma alone is the productive cause of the karma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) arising moment by moment. And that productive cause, kamma, can only produce (karma-born matter) during its occurrence if it obtains the co-operating cause of the fourfold continuity of matter (catusantati-rūpa) which has arisen previously and remains unimpaired; it cannot do so otherwise. Thus, it is established that for persons whose eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), etc., has been destroyed by some opposing cause, kamma, even though it exists, is unable to produce the eye-sensitivity and so forth.

'One who causes to fall' (atipātento) means one who destroys. 'Exactly as described' (vuttappakāram-eva) means the method of destroying the life-faculty is exactly as described. 'Atipāta' is the causing to fall excessively or rapidly, without allowing the life-faculty, which naturally tends to fall, to fall slowly by its own nature. The rapid falling of life (pāṇa) is 'pāṇātipāta' (taking life). 'Atharvanists' (āthabbaṇikā) are those who are proficient in the Atharva Veda. 'Atharva' (athabbaṇaṃ) is the science prescribed by the Atharva Veda. 'They employ mantras' (mantaṃ payojenti) means they recite mantras through practices such as eating saltless food, sleeping on grass, and going to cemeteries, etc. Through such recitation, the desired results such as the killing of living beings occur; therefore, that recitation of mantras is included in bodily and vocal actions. 'Īti' means affliction. 'Upaddava' means an even greater affliction than that. 'Pajjaraka' means a fever. 'Sūcika' means a piercing pain as if being pierced by needles. 'Visūcika' means dysentery with piercing pain. 'Pakkhandika' means bloody diarrhea. 'Having recited the science' (vijjaṃ parivattetvā) means having recited and chanted one's own learned science, such as the Gandhāra science, according to the method of reciting mantras. 'By those' (tehi) means by those objects. 'Purpose' (payojanaṃ) means bringing about. 'Oh, may this one' (aho vatāyaṃ) means this one who is in the womb. 'The fetus' (gabbhaṃ) means this fetus in the womb. 'Of the family' (kuluṃbassa) means of the fetus, or of the lineage, or of the household. 'By the power developed through meditation' (bhāvanāmayiddhiyā) is said with reference to the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāniddhi). The point that it is merely their wish does not agree with the meaning of the Sutta. For in the Sutta, when it says 'one who has psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind,' it should be understood as being said only by the power of Atharva psychic power, and not by the power developed through meditation.

'Otherwise' (itarathā) means if the meaning of the word 'should search' (pariyeseyya) were merely searching according to the literal sound, then it would mean that an offense is committed merely by searching and obtaining weapons, etc. It is called 'sattha' (weapon) because one harms or kills with these stones, ropes, etc. Therefore, intending it to be the name for all instruments of killing such as stones, ropes, etc., he said 'clubs' (laguḷa), etc. 'Laguḷa' is a name for a mallet. 'The collection of weapons' (satthasaṅgaho) refers to the weapons included in the taking of a weapon mentioned as 'satthahāraka' in the Matika. Because of the method to be mentioned later...
225:
This is because there is a method to be mentioned in the word-by-word analysis (padabhājana) of the second term, which is stated by way of a concluding summary later on. The reason for stating this to explain the meaning of the word 'citta' is that since the word 'citta' has many meanings, such as 'variegated' and so on, it is stated to exclude other meanings and restrict it to the meaning of 'consciousness' (viññāṇa).

'Kammunā bajjhati' means one is bound by the kamma of taking life; the meaning is that the kamma is accomplished for that person. 'Ubhayathāpi' means by way of being directed (uddisaka) or undirected (anuddisaka). By the words 'pacchā vā tena rogena' (or later by that disease), it shows the occurrence of taking life (pāṇātipāta) by taking as an object the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) that will exist in the future. This being so, because of the command, 'When you are able, then deprive him of life,' even if it is fulfilled after a long time, the act of taking life occurs at the very moment of the command. In permanent efforts (thāvarapayoga) such as digging a pit and so on, even if a being takes conception after the effort has been made and then dies, the act of taking life is established as having a future object.

In the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga, the statement 'the five precepts have only present objects' should be understood as being said with reference to the abstinence (virati) from taking life and so on, and not with reference to the kamma of taking life itself. 'Aññacittena' means with a mind that does not desire to kill. 'Dုtiyappahārena marati' means the person dies by the second blow alone, without the first blow. 'Paṭhamappahāreneva' means only at the moment of the volition (cetanā) that originated the first blow. Although the first blow by itself is not able to kill, when it receives the second blow and becomes able, it becomes the cause for the destruction of the life-faculty. Therefore, because death cannot be accomplished without the first blow, and because it accords with the statement 'the effort and the death because of that effort,' it is appropriate that the kamma is bound by the first blow alone, and not by the second, because that second blow was given with a different mind. Just as in this case of one person striking twice, it should be understood similarly in cases where another person gives the second blow and so on. If, however, the person giving the second blow also has the intention to kill, it should be understood that since the death occurs also because of his own effort, the act of taking life occurs at the moment of his effort.

'Kammāpattibyattibhāvatthaṃ' means for the purpose of making clear the distinction of kammas such as the ānantariya-kamma and the distinction of offenses (āpatti) such as the pārājika. Even if one wrongly perceives 'I will kill a goat,' because one actually takes 'this being' (the one lying there) in the ultimate sense, the kamma is bound according to the actual object; thus it is said 'imaṃ vatthuṃ' and so on. 'Ghātako ca hoti' means one is bound by the kamma of taking life. With reference to those of great virtue such as a mother...
226:
Because the intention to kill that arises toward those of great virtue, such as a mother, is a grave fault, it is said: "In this case, the intention is cruel."

'Lohitaka' means one who is smeared with blood. 'Kammaṃ karonte' means while performing the act of battle. 'Yathādhippāyaṃ gate' means that when shooting at a soldier, if the father is hit, or if the soldier is not hit and only the father is hit, there is no mistake in the target because the intention to kill also exists toward the father. Even if only the soldier is hit, this same method applies. 'Ānantariyaṃ pana natthi' means the kamma of taking life with the father as the specific object is not accomplished.

'Evaṃ vijjhā' (shoot like this) means commanding by way of teaching the manner of shooting, such as "standing on the ground with both feet like this, holding the bow like this, and drawing it like this." 'Evaṃ pahara' (strike like this) means "hold the sword firmly and strike like this." 'Evaṃ ghātehi' (kill like this) means "kill by performing such tortures." The phrase 'tattakā ubhinnaṃ pāṇātipātā' is said because both made an effort to kill unspecified persons without directing it at anyone in particular. If the commanding monk commands "shoot like this," perceiving that "if he shoots like this, so-and-so will die in this way," they say the commander is bound by the kamma only if the specified person dies. If the commanded person targets a specific individual and shoots the arrow, but the commander gave the command without specifying anyone, the commander is bound by the kamma regardless of who dies. However, it should be understood that the commanded person is bound by the kamma only if the person they specified dies.

'Majjhe' means in the middle of the elephant's back. 'Etena' refers to the Pali words such as "commanding after having determined (adhiṭṭhahitvā)." 'Tattha' refers to the effort of command (āṇattikappayoga).

Although specific actions (kiriyāvisesa) are not directly mentioned in the commentaries, because specific actions are referred to in the Pali text as "shoot like this, strike like this, kill like this," the teacher (the author) states "aparo nayo" (another method) and so on, showing the specific actions handed down through the lineage of teachers by correlating them with the Pali. 'Vijjhāna' means piercing with arrows, spears, and so on. 'Chedana' means cutting off hands, feet, and so on with swords and the like. 'Bhedana' means splitting the head and so on into two with clubs and the like. 'Saṅkhamuṇḍaka' (the shell-shave) means the torture called saṅkhamuṇḍaka, performed by peeling off the scalp along with the hair and rubbing the skull with coarse gravel until it becomes white like the color of a conch shell. In the word 'evamādi,' the word 'ādi' includes tortures such as bilanga-thālika (the gruel-pot torture). Specifications such as "strike the chest, strike the back, strike the neck" are also included under specific actions (kiriyāvisesa). This is because in the commentaries, even the killing that takes a body part as its object, such as the shell-shave...
227:
Because it is included in that specific manner of action (kriyāvisesa), the explanation in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Pārājikakaṇḍa 2.174, Payogakathā-vaṇṇanā) regarding the Commentary passage "strike from the front and kill," etc., which states: "Since the front, sides, etc., are similar in nature to the object (vatthu), they are included by the mention of the object itself; thus it says 'strike from the front,' etc."—this explanation is inappropriate. This is because the Commentary mentions the infliction of harm on body parts such as the shaven head (saṅkhamuṇḍaka) in the context of the specific manner of action (kriyāvisesa). Indeed, only the killing of a person other than the one ordered, by letting the ordered person go, is called a discrepancy regarding the object (vatthu-visaṃvāda); a discrepancy regarding the body part not ordered to be struck is not called a discrepancy regarding the object. Therefore, it is said: "Having caused a discrepancy regarding the object... he kills another instead. Or, 'strike from the front and kill'... there is no karmic bond (kammabaddha)." This phrase "strike from the front and kill," etc., should be understood as being stated to show the absence of a karmic bond due to a discrepancy in the specific manner of action, even when the object is the one ordered. Thus, instead of saying only "they kill without a discrepancy regarding the object," the requirement of the specific manner of action is also shown by the phrase "as ordered" (yathāṇattiyā). Otherwise, the word "as ordered" would be meaningless. In the description of the object, it is only said: "The object (vatthu) is the being to be killed"; it is not said: "The body part ordered to be struck is also the object." Therefore, it is our preference (khanti) that striking from the front, etc., are included only within the specific manner of action (kriyāvisesa); this should be accepted after careful consideration. "By the distinction of the object" (vatthu-visesena) means by the distinction of the being to be killed, such as a mother. "Distinction of action" (kamma-visesena) means the distinction of actions such as the ānantariya-kamma. "Distinction of offense" (āpatti-visesena) means the distinction of offenses such as pārājika.

"On any morning" (yadā kadāci pubbaṇhe) means on the morning of any day other than the day of the command. In the phrase "the one standing in this village," the "village" is mentioned to specify the person, not to specify the location. Therefore, it is said: "Kill him wherever he may be; there is no discrepancy." By this, it is made known that for a commander who does not wish to specify the time, place, weapon, posture, or specific manner, but only desires death by any means, even if there is a discrepancy in the time, place, etc., mentioned by word of mouth, he is still karmically bound. If a person, though only desiring death by any means, time, or place in his mind, specifies the time, etc., as a pretext (lesa) because he wishes to be free from the unwholesome act or from accusation through a discrepancy in time, etc., it should be considered that he is still karmically bound even if there is a discrepancy in time, etc., because he is not figuratively released from the pārājika of killing a human being (manussaviggaha). Some teachers do not accept this view; it should be investigated.
228:
"With the tip" (tuṇḍena) means with the point of the sword. "With the hilt" (tharuṇā) means with the handle of the sword. In the phrase "kill this one who is walking," the person is specified by the act of walking, not the posture (iriyāpatha); therefore, it is said: "There is no discrepancy."

Even if it is said, "Kill the tall one," because there are many people with a tall stature, and because he is not pointed out by a unique characteristic that distinguishes him from others, such as "the tall one with such a name and such a nature," it is said: "He commands without specifying." For this reason, it is said: "I will kill any such person." In this case, even if one person among many tall ones is specified in the mind, but not specified by speech, teachers say there is no discrepancy if another such person is killed. Excluding oneself, because the factor of perceiving a being as a living being in another's life is absent, there is no act of taking life (pāṇātipāta); thus it is said: "The commander is released from the offense." Regarding oneself, when specifying the location as "the one sitting in such a place," since the intention to kill arises by taking as an object the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) of whoever is sitting in that place, it is said: "Neither the killer nor the commander is released." This is because the one who specifies the location intends to kill the one sitting in that location, but he himself is not there at that time; therefore, the life-faculty of the one sitting there along with the location is the object, not his own life-faculty. However, if he himself is sitting in that very place and specifies his own sitting place saying "Kill him," and another person sitting there is killed, the intention to kill arises by taking as an object both that person's life and his own life; it should be understood that if another is killed there, the commander is karmically bound (guilty of the offense). The specification of the mental process in such cases is the domain of the Buddhas (Buddhavisaya), not the domain of others; therefore, it is said: "In this matter, one should not be disrespectful (one should pay heed)."

In the statement that the teacher who commands in this way first incurs a dukkaṭa offense: if the one commanded does not go according to the intention, the teacher incurs a dukkaṭa at the moment of the command. If he goes according to the intention, the thullaccaya offense mentioned later is incurred at the moment of the command. If he definitely kills, as stated later: "The pārājika offense applies to all," then this commander incurs the pārājika at the very moment of the command, not the dukkaṭa or thullaccaya. "A dukkaṭa offense for them as well" means a dukkaṭa is incurred by Buddharakkhita and others because of the act of informing. This is appropriate if Saṅgharakkhita is not yet deprived of life according to the command; if he is deprived of life, they also incur the pārājika at the very moment of informing. The phrase "merely by accepting" is stated to illustrate the nature of definite acceptance, not to mean the offense occurs at the very moment of acceptance.
229:
It is stated to show the *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If that person will certainly accept [the command], but the act of killing will not be completed, it should be understood that the *thullaccaya* offense is incurred by the teacher at the very moment of the command.

"The original instigator incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense." This statement merely shows the method found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakatha*; it is not his [the author's] own preference. Therefore, he says "If it is so," and so on. This means that the meaning is according to the method stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakatha*. If it were said that there is no offense at all in accepting, then there would be no *dukkaṭa* offense even in accepting death by saying "Good, very good" to the killer. To show that if a *dukkaṭa* occurs even in such a non-gross matter, how much more so in accepting death, the acceptance of acting as a messenger (*sañcaritta*), etc., is shown. To show the delight in death such as "It would be good if such-and-named person were to die," the meaning is that if there is a *dukkaṭa* in accepting the role of a messenger, how much more so in accepting death by saying "I will kill him."

By the word of restriction (*eva*), "This *dukkaṭa* occurs only to the one who accepts," it shows that the original instigator monk does not incur an offense due to the acceptance [by the other]. Because of the deviation [from the original command], only the *dukkaṭa* of the initial command occurs to him. Some teachers say, "The original instigator also incurs only a *dukkaṭa*." That statement is not appropriate, because two *dukkaṭa* offenses cannot occur through a single effort (*payoga*). "In the previous method" refers to the immediately preceding explanation of the messenger who does not deviate. "This" refers to the *dukkaṭa*. "Due to the lack of opportunity" means that because the *thullaccaya* for the original instigator will be mentioned, the *dukkaṭa* for the one who accepts is not mentioned due to lack of space, not because there is no offense.

Because he himself was the Elder of the Saṅgha, it is said "at the time of attendance (*upaṭṭhāna*)." "An offense of *dukkaṭa* is incurred due to the speech" means that it is said not with the intention "Let whoever hears my words kill this person," but only by way of delighting in death; thus, even in words such as "Even thieves do not kill that person," only a *dukkaṭa* is stated. "Referring to two" means either referring to two persons or referring to the death of two. Even if the intention (*cetanā*) that motivates the effort of one who praises death referring to both is single, it reaches a powerful state that should be called "two acts of taking life" (*pāṇātipāta*). Because it has great results in rebirth (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*), it is called a "mass of unwholesome states" (*akusalarāsi*). This same method applies when praising death referring to many. "That many acts of taking life" means as many as will die after hearing the praise; the intention, having taken as its object the entire present and future life faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of that many people...
230:
...because of its occurrence, there are that many acts of taking life. That single intention alone can give the functional result (*pavatti-vipāka*) given by that many intentions. However, it should be understood that the rebirth result (*paṭisandhi-vipāka*) can be given only one by one by itself and the preceding and succeeding intentions.

"From whose hands" (*yesaṃ hatthato*) means from the hands of relatives, those who have invited (*pavārita*), etc. This is said in reference to the absence of money (*rūpiyamūla*) among monks. If it is one's own property, one takes the price oneself and releases [the manuscript]. Even if one does not take the price, the standard here is bringing the manuscript (*potthaka*) into the ownership of the manuscript owner. "Those curious to see the writing" (*lekhādassanako-tūhalaka*) refers to those who wish to look either because they see beautiful characters or [wondering] "What kind of book is this?"

"Because it is an effort of taking life" (*pāṇātipātassa payogattā*) means because it is an effort that completes the separation of the life faculty from the body. However, for a monk who destroys unallowable soil (*akappiya-pathavī*) to produce iron for tools like hoes to dig a pit, or who destroys vegetation (*bhūtagāma*) for hoe handles, etc., it is only a *pācittiya* because it is not an effort of taking life. Just like the preliminary effort of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), in seeking a companion, etc., for digging this pit, it should be understood that a *dukkaṭa* occurs where a *dukkaṭa* is appropriate, and a *pācittiya* occurs where a *pācittiya* for false speech (*musāvāda*), etc., is appropriate. "In the measure" (*pamāṇe*) means in the measure marked by oneself. "Having shaved" (*tacchetvā*) means having shaved the raised area. "The last basket of earth" (*paṃsupacchiṃ*) refers to the very last basket of earth. The intention that completes the final effort with the desire to finish, thinking "This much is enough," is called the concluding intention (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*).

In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakatha*, it is said: "The final concluding intention is stated in reference to completing the digging with unremitting effort in a single day. In other commentaries, however, it is stated in reference to completing it by digging a little on one day and a little more on subsequent days with the intention 'Let them fall into this pit and die'." Thus, the mutual contradiction between the commentaries should be understood. "By its own nature" (*attano dhammatāya*) means either through ignorance or by slipping. "Even Arahants go into the collection" means it is said that the death of Arahants can occur even if they do not wish to die when they are thrown down by others. "In the previous method" refers to the method stated as "Those who wish to die will die here." "Deviation" (*visanketo*) means that because the pit was dug specifically for those who wish to die and those who wish to kill, there is no karmic bond (*kammabandha*) in the death of those who do not wish to die.
231:
“Taking out the one who has fallen into that pit” is said because death occurs due to the cause of falling into that pit. Even if one catches and kills a person who has come out after staying in the pit for a short while, or if a person dies from injuries sustained by falling into the pit—such as by stumbling and hitting stones while walking—it should be understood that the monk who dug the pit is not exempt from the offense. Because the intention “even if they do not wish to die” is possible, if a spontaneously born being (opapātika) dies because they are unable to climb out of the pit, it is said that a Pārājika offense is incurred. If it is argued that falling is not seen because the word “arising” (nibbattitvā) is used, there is no contradiction because arising in that pit is itself the falling.

The reason is that if a mother falls into a pit and dies after changing her gender (into a male form), that monk is still a matricide (mātughātaka), not merely a killer of a human male. Therefore, with the intention that the offense is determined by the form at the time of falling, it is said, “The form at the time of falling is the criterion.” However, this point is not the actual reason (for taking the form at the time of falling as the criterion). This is because even if the gender changes, it does not deviate from being the same continuity (santāna); for it is stated in the Commentary, “One who deprives of life a mother or father who is a human being, even if they have changed gender, commits an Ānantarika-kamma.” Beings are born with a certain nature (species); they die with that same nature. That nature remains the original nature even when those beings take on another form. Therefore, it is said, “The form at the time of death is the criterion; thus, it is a Pācittiya offense.”

The latter view is the criterion. If so, one might ask why it is stated in the Pāḷi: “If a Yakkha, a Peta, or a being in animal form or human form falls into that pit, there is an offense of Dukkaṭa. If painful feeling arises due to the fall, there is an offense of Dukkaṭa. If they die, there is an offense of Thullaccaya.” This is not a fault. In saying “a Yakkha or a Peta,” it refers to those Yakkhas and Petas who first show their original form and then remain even after taking another form; thus it says, “in animal form or human form.” Therefore, the construction (yojanā) here should be: “a Yakkha or a Peta in animal form or human form.”

Some teachers, however, say, “It seems as if animals existing in human form are treated separately and assigned a Thullaccaya offense.” That is not appropriate. This is because it is stated as “an animal or one in human form,” and because this distinction is not mentioned in the Commentaries. By the statement, “Even if they die in the form of a Yakkha or Peta, the method is the same,” it refers to the Thullaccaya offense because the form at the time of death is the criterion.

“Mudha” means without price (for free). Such a purchase is blameless because the buyer has made no effort regarding that pit. To show that if the purchasing monk also makes some effort regarding that pit, he is not exempt from the offense, the text says, “If they fall in this way,” and so on. In that passage, “in this way” means “if I have acted in this way.”
232: The meaning is: ‘They will not disappear’ means they will not go out of sight, they will not flee. ‘They will be easy to extract’—this statement shows the benefit of filling a deep pit. The meaning is that if the pit is made shallow, they will be easy to extract so that we can quickly catch and kill them. The phrase ‘When remorse (vippaṭisāra) arises’ is said with reference to the original person. If a later person also acquires that pit, does something as described, and then remorse arises and they act in this way, the same method applies to them as well. The phrase ‘When it has become natural earth’ is said to show that when another person digs such a pit again, one is freed from the offense at the time it had become natural earth. It should be understood that even if it is made like natural earth, well-pounded and filled more firmly, one is still freed. ‘More tightly’ means tying it together with another snare-post for the sake of making it firm, or tying that same loose snare more tightly. ‘Stump’ (khāṇuka) refers to the stump to which the snare-post is tied. The statement ‘One is freed by cutting the branch that grew there’ is said because if a branch existing in the forest is made suitable for tying a snare without cutting it from the base, and if someone else ties a snare there, the original person is not freed. However, it is said to show that if one cuts it from the base and breaks it into pieces, one is freed. ‘In small ropes’ refers to small ropes twisted once with bark fibers. ‘Twisted by oneself’ means a thin twisted string made into double or triple strands by oneself. ‘By undoing’ means by making it back to its original state. ‘Even if protecting’ means even if keeping it by shredding it into fibers. ‘Or a supporting tree’ is said with reference to a tree growing there. ‘Having made it for that purpose only’ means having a weapon such as a billhook made by smelting iron ore etc. specifically for the purpose of killing. ‘Natural’ means the original person obtains and keeps a natural weapon made by others. ‘Is freed’ means the original person is freed from the offense. ‘Uneven circle’ (visamaṇḍala) refers to a circle of poison smeared on beds, chairs, etc. In the phrase ‘Having spoken, he places a sword nearby,’ the same method applies even if he does not speak with his mouth but only thinks with his mind and places it. ‘By the previous method’ refers to the method such as ‘from whose hands the capital was taken,’ etc. ‘Dissimilar disease’ (visabhāga-roga) refers to the occurrence of leprosy etc. due to the disfigurement of the physical appearance, or the occurrence of boils, pustules, etc. because they are inimical to the continuation of life. By the phrase ‘The same method applies to a pleasant object,’ in the context of ‘he brings a pleasant form near,’ it should be understood by combining it with: whatever pleasant form there may be, placing that form nearby, or remaining oneself having made oneself endowed with a pleasant form, etc. ‘Having decorated, he brings it near’ means...
233:
"Endowed with a pleasing appearance and stands," etc., should be applied accordingly. "Adorning and bringing near" means bringing near with the intention, "Let them die by drying up without food." Therefore, it is said, "If they die of fright, it is a deviation (vi-saṅketa)." In the phrase "dies by drying up without food," the missing words "it is a Pārājika" should be understood. Mahākacchu is a specific type of creeper fruit, shaped like a cat's paw, which is rough to the touch and has fine hairs. "Haṃsapuppha" refers to the feathers of swans and similar birds. "If one dies by natural causes, there is no offense" is said in reference to Pārājika, because one is not exempt from a Dukkhaṭa offense.

"Unintentionally" refers to not noticing the effort that leads to death, as indicated by "with this effort," etc. "To one who does not know" refers to not knowing the act of using poison, etc., that leads to death, as indicated by "this person will die," etc. "Not having the intention to kill" refers to not having the intention to kill even if one knows the effort causes suffering, as indicated by "to one who does not desire death," etc. "Because there is no continuity" means because there is no continuous occurrence of the processes of displeasure (domanassa-vīthi).

## The method of the explanation of the Word-by-word Analysis is finished.

## Explanation of the Decided Cases

"By way of common usage" means by way of usage in the preliminary stage. Since there is no compassion at the moment of volition that decides the intention to kill, it is not like releasing a pig caught in a snare out of pity. The meaning expressed as "according to life" (yathāyunā) is also expressed by another synonym "according to the connection" (yathānusandhinā). Because one takes a fold of a robe when something is underneath, it is said, "where a fold is not apparent." It should be understood that such reflection applies only to the property of laypeople. In the Pali, "when pestles are stood up" means when two pestles are supporting each other and placed without leaning against a wall. "Mortar-related utensil" refers to wooden material brought for making a mortar. "Obstruction" means an obstruction to eating, which is to say, a danger to eating.
234:
In the word aggakārika, since the word kārika is in the sense of state (bhāva), although it means aggakiriya (making the first), because the act of making the first cannot be "given," only the alms-food associated with the first act of giving is to be taken here as aggakiriya by way of metaphorical usage. This is what is meant by "the alms-food first received," etc.

182-3. In the phrase daṇḍamuggaranikhādanavemādīnaṃ vasena, daṇḍa refers to a long staff. Muggara refers to a short one (a large mallet). Vema is a weaving tool (shuttle/beater) used by weavers to strike the woven threads. Vibhattibyattayena means by changing the case ending. Visesādhigama refers to concentration and insight. Visesādhigama means the attainment of supramundane states. Byākaritvā means having informed; this is said to show the state of having attained distinction. Indeed, conscientious (lajjī) monks definitely announce their attainment so that others may follow their example. Even if a monk has attained distinction, it is not proper to cut off food without announcing it. Since cutting off food is permitted only to remove obstacles to attainment, once that is attained, it should not be done. To the question of why it is not proper to announce attainment, the text says "to those of the same class," etc. "Washing goods" means washing robes. "Washing stick" is a stick for washing robes.

"Causing to be trampled and fall, it is a deviation (vi-saṅketa)" is said because it was not done as ordered. If the orderer, using common usage, says "trample and make it fall" referring to both trampling and causing to trample, it should be understood that there is no deviation. Because it is said, "or should praise the beauty of death," it is stated "there is no such thing as a pretext (pariyāya)." This means one is not released from an offense by a pretext. If a monk gives medicine before conception to prevent birth, with the intention "let the fetus perish if it arises in the womb," and it dies, he is bound by the act (kamma-baddha). If it is given with the intention "let no fetus arise in the womb," then whether it dies after arising or not, he is not bound by the act.

Sahadhammikānaṃ refers to those practicing together under the dispensation of the same Teacher, or those engaged in practicing the training rules (sikkhāpada). By the words "those of equal virtue and faith," etc., it is shown that one may refrain from treating those without virtue or those of different views.
235:
"Ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato" means (obtaining medicine) from the place of one's own relatives or from the place of those who have given an invitation. An intimation (viññatti) that is not appropriate for Noble Ones and has not been made before is called "akataviññatti" (unmade intimation).

"Paṭiyādiyati" means it is prepared or fulfilled. Regarding the phrase "It is not proper not to do it" (akātuṃ na vaṭṭati), some say a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. However, it should be understood here that the prohibition against not doing it is simply because it is inappropriate, not because of an offense (āpatti). "As far as the relatives see" (yāva ñātakā passanti) means as far as the relatives of the person performing the service can see. A father's sister is called a paternal aunt (pituccā). A mother's brother is called a maternal uncle (mātula).

"Nappahonti" means they are unable to perform (medical treatment). "Na yācanti" means they do not ask due to shame. Because it is said "having made an intention" (ābhogaṃ katvā), an offense is indeed incurred by a monk who gives in another way (without intention). Some teachers say, "It is allowable to give even without making an intention," but that is not appropriate. This is because, regarding medical practice, the Pāḷi text generally prohibits it by showing an intermediate offense: "There is no pārājika offense for the monk, but there is a dukkaṭa offense." It should be understood that an offense is established by the Sutta (Pāḷi) itself for one who acts in a manner not mentioned in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). For this reason, the Commentary also states, "Only the property of those [relatives]," and so on.

"Aññesaṃ" refers to those who are not blood relatives. Therefore, it was said, "To the succession of their sons," and so on. "Kulaparivaṭṭa" refers to the succession of relatives within a family. "For a monk who performs medical treatment" refers to one who does so according to the aforementioned method. For a monk who gives while thinking, "I will give it temporarily," without making a firm intention (to treat), no wrong livelihood (micchājīva) or corruption of families (kuladūsana) occurs, except for the intermediate dukkaṭa offense. Therefore, it is said: "Neither medical practice (vejjakamma) nor the offense of corrupting families occurs." This is because it is allowable to take the property of relatives even by asking for it. Thus, faults like corrupting families cannot occur among those relatives. "Sabbapadesu" refers to all terms such as "by the mother's younger sister" (cūḷamātuyā), etc.

"We bring it for the preceptor" (upajjhāyassa āharāma) is said to show the method to be followed by disciples who are ordered by their preceptor, "Bring medicine for my relatives." By this, it is shown that performing medical treatment for strangers is not allowable, even for novices (sāmaṇera) and others, even if they do not desire gain. "Seeking by the aforementioned method" refers to the meaning stated as "either by the practice of alms-round" or "by novice relatives." "Without desiring" (apaccāsīsantena) means that even a monk who treats visiting thieves and others does not expect to receive gain from them for himself, thinking, "Humans are indeed helpful." However, the intention is that for a monk who treats with the expectation of gain, faults such as medical practice (vejjakamma) and corrupting families (kuladūsana) occur. "When such a favor is done..."
236:
There is no fault in providing medical treatment with the intention of inspiring faith through the virtues of the Dispensation (Sāsana) or to make people helpful to the Saṅgha. Some say, "It is allowable to give medicine even to excluded persons such as visitors and thieves if one does not expect gain," but this is not appropriate. This is because it would lead to the pointlessness of the distinction between what should and should not be done. It would be enough to say, "It is allowable to give and treat everyone if one does not expect gain." The phrase "without expecting gain" is mentioned only to prohibit faults such as wrong livelihood and corrupting families (kuladūsana). It should be understood that one is released from this intermediate offense known as medical practice only by giving to those permitted, such as visiting thieves, etc. For this reason, even for one who does not expect gain, the phrase "a faithful family" (saddhaṃ kulaṃ), etc., is said to show where it should not be done. By the word "they ask" (pucchanti), it is shown that it is inappropriate to wander around speaking indirectly to every patient one sees. They say that even for one who is asked, indirect speech (pariyāyakathā) is not allowable if one expects gain.

"He conversed" (samullapesi)—how does one who does not expect gain initiate such mutual conversation? "The teacher's portion" (ācariyabhāgo) means the role of a medical teacher by pointing out medical treatments without violating Vinaya conduct. Since gold and silver received for the purpose of offering flowers becomes a nissaggiya offense if kept as one's own property, it is said, "having it accepted by a proper means." This means rejecting it by saying, "Gold and silver are not allowable for us; flowers are allowable for the purpose of offering flowers," and having it accepted through a proper act by a kappiya (attendant).

If one is told, "Please make a paritta," and one does so, it is said "it should not be done" because it becomes like a lay task or medical practice. However, if one is told, "Please recite a paritta," it is an invitation to teach the Dhamma; since the Dhamma should be recited even when not invited, it is even more so when invited. Thus, it is said "it should be done." "Shaking and stroking the paritta-thread" means that if one does this with the thought, "I am instilling the power of the paritta here," then the power of the paritta is indeed said to be instilled there. "From the monastery... a dukkaṭa offense"—they say this is said in reference to laypeople who are not relatives.

"Pouring water on the feet" is said according to the custom of that region. It is said that in that region, they pour water on the feet of the monks sitting in order to appease illness, etc., place the paritta-thread, and say, "Please recite the paritta," before leaving. While this is being done, if the monks withdraw their feet, people will think it is inauspicious or that the disease will not be appeased. Therefore, it is said, "The feet should not be withdrawn." Just as when seeing a corpse, even when seeing a cemetery alone, the perception of death (maraṇasaññā) can arise, thinking, "This is the place of destruction for all born beings."
237:
Regarding the viewing of a cemetery, it is said: "This cemetery is the place where beings who have arisen come to an end." Because the perception of death (maraṇasaññā) can arise, it is appropriate to go with meditation as the primary objective, as stated: "Starting with the viewing of the charnel ground... one will obtain the mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) meditation." Even if one is invited with a pure mind that has arisen naturally, without any ulterior motive (lesakappa), saying, "Please come for the sake of being an entourage," it is appropriate to go.

Anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāta means alms-food that has not yet been taken from or consumed. By the phrase "kahāpaṇagghanako hoti" (it is worth a kahāpaṇa), it is shown that the donors prepared it with many side dishes and offered it respectfully. Thālake refers to a bowl made of bronze or similar materials belonging to the Saṅgha; here, the alms-bowl is also included. By the words "na vaṭṭati" (it is not appropriate), it indicates that an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred. Dāmarikacorassa refers to a well-known robber who aspires to kingship. The connection should be made as: even if not given, they get angry, saying, "They do not give."

Closing the gap or opening that arises between oneself and others due to not obtaining material things or the Dhamma is called hospitality (paṭisanthāra). That hospitality is of two kinds: spiritual hospitality (dhamma-paṭisanthāra) and material hospitality (āmisa-paṭisanthāra). Between these two, regarding material hospitality, it is asked: "To whom should it be shown, and to whom should it not be shown?" To clarify the meaning stated briefly as "To a guest... it should indeed be shown," the words beginning with "āgantukaṃ tāva" are spoken. By the word "khīṇaparibbayaṃ" (one whose provisions are exhausted), it shows the state of not being biased and being an object of compassion. By that same word, it is established that it is not appropriate to give to wealthy donors and such who are the opposite of those with exhausted provisions, even if they are guests. When there are items like rice to be given, it is said: "At an improper time... it should not be said." Having said "apaccāsīsantena" (by one not expecting anything in return), the words beginning with "manussā nāma" are spoken to show the manner of expecting. However, it is not appropriate to give to those who are not permitted, even if one does not expect anything, because it amounts to wasting a gift given out of faith (saddhādeyya). If there is expectation, it also constitutes corrupting families (kuladūsana).

Ubbāsetvā means having caused the people who were plundering within a three-yojana radius to flee. Varapotthakacittattharaṇaṃ refers to a splendid rug decorated with various excellent figures such as women and men.

Among the group of seventeen monks (Sattarasavaggiya), because one monk had previously died due to being poked with a finger, it is said of the remaining sixteen: "The remaining fifteen persons as well," excluding the one who sat on top of the belly. Adūhalapāsāṇā viya means like stones placed on an unstable place. Kammādhippāyā means having the intention to perform a formal act such as the act of censure (tajjanīyakamma).
238:
Āvāhetvā means causing (a spirit) to enter. "Having made a figure, they cut off the hands, feet, etc." means causing a non-human (amanussa) to enter that figure made of flour or similar materials and then cutting off the hands, feet, etc., of that figure. The statement "He could even kill Sakka, the king of devas" is spoken by way of hyperbole (sambhāvanā). In reality, such powerful non-humans are not liable to be killed by weapons, for even in the war between the devas and asuras, there is no death among those devas caused by the striking of weapons.

The connection is "a blow should not be given." For a monk who strikes a non-human with a mind of anger, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For one who strikes with the intention of medical treatment (cikicchādhippāya), it should be regarded as improper conduct (anācāra). The words "A palm leaf... should be tied" are spoken considering that non-humans flee when a palm leaf is tied. Such tying of palm leaves and so on is also not appropriate for a monk to perform as medical practice (vejjakamma) for laypeople.

Regarding what should be said in the passages beginning with "One who is even crushed by a tree does not die," the teacher himself will explain in the commentary on the Bhūtagāma training rule; that should be understood there.

"Dabbūpakaraṇāni" refers to building materials (property) that have an owner and have been cut and placed by someone. In such a case, because there is no displacement from the original position, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated for one who intends to destroy them. The statement "khiḍḍādhippāyenapi dukkaṭaṃ" (even with the intention of play, it is a wrong-doing) refers to setting fire to dry grass and such. However, for a monk who sets fire to green grass even with the intention of play, it is a pācittiya offense. A fire that is opposite to or facing another fire is called a counter-fire (paṭaggi). Setting such a counter-fire is permitted even in green grass and such. A monk setting it, upon seeing a forest fire (dāvaggi) approaching from afar, should not set fire all around the monastery at once. Instead, starting from one part, he should let it burn slowly around the monastery so that even a large fire cannot reach the monastery. Having thus created an open space around the monastery, the counter-fire should be set. That counter-fire goes to meet the forest fire, merges with it, and is extinguished along with it. "Parittakaraṇaṃ" means providing protection such as cutting trees and grass around the area or digging a moat. Therefore, it is said: "Scraping the ground around small grass huts," and so on.

"Because of entering the field itself, it is a pārājika" means that since one stroke is included within the two strokes (specified for killing), a pārājika is incurred just by the first stroke falling within the specified area (khetta). However, some say that if it is specified, "Kill with two strokes only, not with one," and one kills with only one stroke, there is no pārājika. This same principle applies to cases like "only two men," and so on. Apart from the previous action (payoga) of cutting off the head, no other action that cuts off the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is found. By the first action...
239:
It is said, "Only for the one who cuts off the head (is the kamma bound)," because that person's life faculty (jīvitindriya) is severed by the first effort (payoga). The reason stated in the Sāratthadīpanī, "because the life faculty no longer exists," is an inappropriate reason. This is because the act of walking, which occurs through lifting, lowering, and stepping, is impossible without the mental continuum (cittasantati) that is dependent on the life faculty. The body does not move like a leaf or a cloth blown by the force of the wind. Nor can it be said that the mind-produced intimation (cittaja-viññatti) and others that occur during the lifting of the foot are the causes for the lowering of the foot and so on, because those movements occur in discrete, separate segments.

In fact, although they may not have had prior momentum, when certain types of reptiles are cut into two pieces, both parts move in two directions for a few moments immediately after being severed. In those two parts, the five-door adverting consciousness (pañcadvārāvajjanacitta) situated in the part where the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) remains, arises by taking as its object the tangible object (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa) that strikes the body-sensitivity (kāyappasāda) in both parts. Subsequently, the body-consciousness (kāyaviññāṇa), taking that same tangible object as its object, arises alternately, sometimes in one part and sometimes in the other, as appropriate. Then, only in the part containing the heart-base, the process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta) such as receiving (sampaṭicchana), and the mind-door process-consciousnesses (manodvāravīthiviññāṇa) which produce intimation (viññatti) and are separated by the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), arise. It is only because of the presence of the mind that produces such intimation that both parts perform the acts of going, moving, or quivering. Due to the rapid arising and passing away of the mind, it appears as if both parts are moving simultaneously. For example, just as a being submerged entirely in the Ash-pit Hell (Kukkuḷa-niraka) feels the suffering associated with body-consciousness throughout the entire body in a single moment, this case should be understood in the same way. Thereafter, in whichever part the life faculty ceases along with the remaining kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa), body-consciousness no longer arises in that part. Consciousness continues to arise only in the part with the heart-base until the cessation of the life faculty.

One might ask: "Let the alternate arising of body-consciousness throughout a single connected body in hell and such places be appropriate; but how can it be appropriate in two parts that are severed and separated?" This is not a flaw. What is called "connectedness" (ekābaddhatā) in the body is not something separate from ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma), like the "whole" (avayavī) asserted by external teachers. Connectedness is simply the simultaneous arising of many phenomena due to being dependent on a common cause such as kamma. In such a connected body, even if it is divided by encountering opposing causes like being cut with a weapon, the dependence on common causes like kamma is not yet severed. As long as that dependence is not severed, the occurrence of consciousness in that body will continue without interruption. However, the severed kamma-born matter and the other remaining matter of the three continuities (tisantati-rūpa) cannot persist for long because they lack mutual support. Yet, as long as they persist, they serve as conditions for consciousness. Because of consciousness,
240:
the occurrence of moving, going, and so on in different locations arises for those two parts. Therefore, even at the moment a decapitated trunk runs, the life faculty together with consciousness certainly exists. And that life faculty falls rapidly due to the effort of decapitation. Since the task is accomplished by the first effort before any subsequent effort can produce a specific effect in the body, it should be understood that the kamma is bound only to the one who performs the decapitation. "Evarūpāni" means objects similar to the case of the decapitated trunk. "Imassa vatthussa" refers to the meaning of the object of killing. "Atthadīpane" occurs in explaining the meaning called death, characterized by being killed by a single person or by a single effort.

It is connected as "allowable by drinking or consuming." Because it is stated as allowable by drinking or consuming, some teachers say, "The medicine loṇasovīraka (salted sour gruel) is yāmakālika (to be consumed within a watch)." However, other teachers say, "Since it is stated that it is allowable as it is for sick monks, but mixed with water for non-sick monks, it is sattāhakālika (a seven-day medicine) like molasses (guḷa)."

## Thus ends the method of the explanation of the Third Pārājika
## in the Vimativinodanī, the Sub-commentary to the Samantapāsādikā Vinaya Commentary.
## 4. Fourth Pārājika
## Explanation of the Story of the Monks on the Banks of the Vaggumudā River

"Adhiṭṭhema" means we arrange or manage. "Iriyāpathaṃ saṇṭhapetvā" means having acted in accordance with the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). In the phrase "anāgatasambandhe pana asati," by supplying the remaining words "bhāsito bhavissati" (it will be spoken), the objection is raised: "If there is no connection to the future, how can the past-tense word 'bhāsito' be connected with a future-tense word?" To answer this, the author said "lakkhaṇaṃ pana" and so on. Indeed, in such a case, experts in linguistics say that by the rule (lakkhaṇa) "dhātusambandhe paccayā," when there is a connection with the meaning of the root, suffixes may be valid even if not applied according to the literal time.

By the word "vaṇṇavā," the state of having a newly arisen complexion is expressed. By "pasannamukhavaṇṇā," the extreme excellence and beauty of the facial complexion is expressed. By "vippasannacchavivaṇṇā," the clarity of the natural body complexion itself is expressed according to the aforementioned method. Since the sense faculties such as the eye faculty are derivative matter (upādā-rūpa), their fullness occurs only through the power of their physical support (nissaya); therefore, it is said, "due to the fullness of the supporting space." Just like the five sensitive matters (pasāda-rūpa), the fullness of the heart-matter (hadaya-rūpa) is also certainly expressed.
241:
It is said even of what was already mentioned: 'the sense faculties with the mind as the sixth.' It should be connected that even though they constantly strive in teaching and questioning the Pali and Commentaries, they do not attain this physical beauty. In the phrase 'yathā taṃ,' 'taṃ' is merely a particle. In the word 'catucakkaṃ,' the four postures are called 'wheels' (cakka) because of the sense of moving and functioning.

'Upalabbhanti' means they are evident or known. 'Pacanto' means oppressing, or burning houses etc. oneself, or causing others to burn them. 'Uddhate' refers to those of a restless nature. 'Unnaḷe' refers to those possessed of uplifted empty conceit, like a reed held high. 'Capale' refers to those possessed of frivolity such as decorating the bowl and robes. 'Mukhare' refers to those of harsh speech. 'Pākatindriye' refers to those whose faculties remain in their natural state as in their time as laypeople, due to lack of restraint. In the word 'iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanādīni,' by the word 'ādi,' one should understand the use of requisites and speaking in the vicinity of requisites. Monasteries inhabited by monks of extremely scrupulous livelihood and established in the noble Ariyavaṃsa are called monasteries recognized by the world. 'Paripācetum' means to incline the mind by way of causing wonder. The phrase 'bhikkhācāre asampajjamāne' should be connected with 'wandering through the countryside,' not with 'teaching Pali' etc. Those words such as 'teaching' etc. are spoken to show the duties to be performed both in their permanent residence and in the countryside. Those monks perform teaching etc. as a duty; they do not do so for the sake of gain. Therefore, 'they' etc. is said. The word 'kicchena' is a synonym for 'kasirena' (with difficulty). Both refer to the effort of fulfilling the perfections (pāramī). 'Sādhāraṇaparikkhārabhāvena' means as communal property (saṅghika). Because it is communal, it is theft due to being non-transferable (avissaggiya) and non-divisible (avebhaṅgiya), not in the sense of moving it from its place. Therefore, it is said 'he commits a dukkaṭa offense of corrupting families.' For the word 'asantaṃ,' 'abhūtaṃ' is the reason; it means non-existent because it has not arisen. 'Kitavassēva' is like a deceitful hunter catching birds. 'Kerāṭikassa' means of a deceitful person. 'Samaṇo' means they are lineage-members (gotrabhū) because they only enjoy and bear the appearance of a monk; they are monks in name only. 'Dujjānaparicchedaṃ' means because suffering is endless, it is difficult even for Omniscient Knowledge to know by defining it with a number as 'this much suffering,' but it is not difficult to know by its nature, as that is not beyond the scope of Buddha-knowledge.

## Adhimānavatthuvaṇṇanā
'Arahatte' refers to the highest fruit, Arahatship. 'Ñāṇacakkhunā' means with the eye called reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa), or with the eye of knowledge associated with the fruit-consciousness (phala-citta). With one's own...
242:
By means of knowledge associated with oneself, without confusion, it is called 'seeing for oneself'; this means even without seeing that Fruit of Arhatship. Because one knows by the power of abandoning all defilements, or knows from all sides or in all ways, the Path of Arhatship is called 'Aññā' (Highest Knowledge). By way of metaphorical usage for that Path, its result, the Fruit, is also intended as 'Aññā'; therefore, it is said, 'They declared Aññā means they declared Arhatship.' 'Antarā ṭhapeti' means that overestimation (adhimāna), thinking one has attained while still in the stage of a trainee (sekhabhūmi), causes one to stop. The phrase 'not seeing the manifestation of defilements' is spoken only in terms of those defilements abandoned by the three preceding paths, not in terms of the craving for existence (bhavarāga) and so forth.

## Commentary on the Training Rule with its Analysis (Savibhaṅgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)
The Dhamma attained by noble persons such as the Buddha, which is superior to ordinary humans, is called 'Uttarimanussadhamma' (superhuman state); thus it is said, 'Uttarimanussānaṃ,' etc. In the Pali text, in the phrase 'Atthi ca me ete dhammā mayi,' the word 'me' is merely a particle to complete the sentence. Asking about jhānas and so forth, which are called 'attainments' (adhigama) because they are to be attained, is called 'asking about attainment' (adhigamapucchā). That inquiry about attainment generally occurs regarding jhānas and so forth. Now, in that inquiry about attainment, whether one has attained the first jhāna, or any one among the second jhāna and so forth; and among those, which object-based jhāna such as the kasinas; or among the supramundane states, whether one has attained the Path of Stream-entry, or any one among the Path of Once-returning and so forth; and among those supramundane states, whether one has attained the Emptiness liberation (suññatavimokkha), or any one among the Desireless liberation (appaṇihitavimokkha) and so forth—to show the manner of questioning by extracting each distinction, this question is shown in the Pali text: 'Again, which of these states have you gained?' Thus it should be understood. Therefore, it is said, 'Among the first paths,' etc. The practice by which the supramundane attainment comes in due order is the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapaṭipadā), also called the 'path of arrival' (āgamanapaṭipadā). 'Na sujjhati' means that when questioned, one speaks by bypassing the order of practice. 'Apaneatabbo' means that one should be removed from the overestimation of thinking one has attained, by saying, 'This state cannot be attained by the order you have described.' Because of not clinging to the four requisites that are allowable and present nearby, it is said, 'With a mind like a hand in the sky.' The construction is: 'It is a declaration similar to what was said.' Because defilements have been well-suppressed, the practice is similar to the practice of an Arhat (khīṇāsava). This is spoken in terms of one who claims Arhatship; therefore, it is said, 'Of the one whose taints are destroyed,' etc. Thus, the claim of a trainee's state by a monk whose defilements are well-suppressed cannot be tested by such frightening or by the watering of the mouth upon seeing sour fruit, etc. Therefore, that claim should be believed based on that monk's word alone. This monk... the phrase 'sampannabyākaraṇo' is not intended only for one who is simply fearless. Why? Because some worldlings (puthujjana) who are brave by nature are also not afraid. It should be understood that it refers only to being well-purified in all ways, being free from the arising of craving such as the watering of the mouth even when objects of desire like jujube or sour and spicy things are brought near. 'Evil desire' (pāpicchā) has the characteristic of pretending to have qualities one does not possess; therefore, it is said, 'Yā sā idhekacco,' etc. By the word 'ādi,' the text beginning with 'assaddho' is included. 'Sāmaññaṃ dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ' refers to the state of a monk called 'monkhood' (samañña).
243:
The term "Sampannavyākaraṇo" is not intended to refer only to one who is fearless. This is because some worldlings of a courageous nature are also fearless. It should be understood as referring only to being thoroughly purified, being free from the occurrence of craving such as salivation even when sour things like jujube or mango are brought near.

"Pāpicchā" (evil desire) has the characteristic of pretending to possess qualities that do not actually exist, as stated in the passage beginning with "Yā sā idhekacco". By the word "ādi" (etc.), the text beginning with "assaddho" is included. "Sāmaññaṃ dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ" means that asceticism, known as the practice of a recluse, which is wrongly handled (grasped) due to broken virtue and so forth, drags that person to the suffering of hell and causes rebirth there. "Sithilo" (lax) refers to that which is done with a loose grasp due to performing it slackly, or that which is taken up with deceit. "Paribbajo" means the state of a recluse. "Bhiyyo" (more) means scattering further dust on top of the dust of lust and so forth that already existed before. "Bhikkhubhāvo" (monkhood) is the state of a monk achieved merely by an unrighteous claim. In the term "Ajānam-eva", the word "eva" is used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), meaning "only while not knowing". There is also a reading "Ajānam-evaṃ", in which case it should be construed as "I know thus, I see thus".

## Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

By the word "Evaṃ", there is the reflection on the first jhāna and so forth, meaning "I know the first jhāna, I know the second jhāna, etc." In the term "Asubhajjanādīni", the word "ādi" includes the jhāna of mindfulness directed to the body, kasina jhānas, and the formless jhānas based on kasinas. "Vimokkho" (liberation) refers to the four paths. Desiring to show the names such as "Suññata" (Void) by way of the path's own qualities, he said "So panāyaံ", etc. Indeed, the Path receives its name through five reasons: by its own nature (sarasa), by its opposite (paccanīka), by its quality (saguṇa), by its object (ārammaṇa), or by its arrival (āgamana). If the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) emerges into the Path after contemplating formations as impermanent (anicca), the Path is liberated through the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha). If it emerges after contemplating them as suffering (dukkha), it is liberated through the desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha). If it emerges after contemplating them as non-self (anatta), it is liberated through the void liberation (suññata-vimokkha). This is the name received by its own nature. Because this Path has come about by abandoning the sign of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence in formations, it is called "Animitta" (Signless). Because it has come about by abandoning the perception of pleasure and longing (paṇidhi) through the contemplation of suffering, it is called "Appaṇihita" (Desireless). Because it becomes "Suññata" (Void) by way of seeing the voidness of self after abandoning the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self, this is the name received by way of the opposite.
244:
Furthermore, this Path is called "Suññata" because it is void of lust and so forth. It is called "Animitta" because of the absence of the signs of form, etc., or the signs of lust, etc. It is called "Appaṇihita" because of the absence of longing (paṇidhi) such as the longing of lust. This is its name by way of its own quality (saguṇa). It is called "Suññata", "Animitta", and "Appaṇihita" because it takes Nibbāna—which is void of lust etc., signless, and desireless—as its object. This is its name by way of the object (ārammaṇa). Arrival (āgamana) is of two kinds: arrival through insight (vipassanā) and arrival through the Path (magga). Among them, in the Path, there is only arrival through insight. In the Fruit (phala) immediately following the Path, there is arrival through the Path. In the attainment of the Fruit (phala-samāpatti), there is also arrival through insight. By way of the contemplation of non-self, the Path is called "Suññata". By way of the contemplations of impermanence and suffering, it is called "Animitta" and "Appaṇihita". In this way, insight gives its own name to the Path, and the Path gives its name to the Fruit. This is the name by way of arrival (āgamana).

"Suññatā" means being secluded (vivitta). Because lust and so forth are called "paṇidhi" in the sense of being a basis (for rebirth), he said "of the longings of lust, hatred, and delusion". By the phrase "of this knowledge (vijjā)", they speak referring to each individual knowledge such as the knowledge of the divine eye. The intention in the Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā is that even if one does not mention the name of even one knowledge, but speaks referring to those very knowledges, saying "I am a possessor of knowledges", one becomes defeated (pārājika). However, if one speaks referring to the knowledge of sites (vatthu-vijjā) and so forth, one does not [become defeated]. "By way of each individual group" means, according to the method stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, saying simply "I am a possessor of the foundations of mindfulness" by way of each individual group, without making it specifically supramundane. "Therein" means in those groups. Although the abandoning of defilements is merely an absence, it is called supramundane because it is a supramundane function; to establish this, he said "But that [abandoning]", etc. The state of the mind being free from lust means the state of the mind being free from hindrances due to lust; because of being liberated from that lust, it means the state of being free from the hindrance of lust; this should be construed with the words "which are the five knowledges". In this Word-by-Word Analysis, because it is said "Knowledge means the three knowledges", it means the remaining five knowledges are not included. "Because of being the absolute supramundane" means it is the true supramundane, entirely unmixed with mundane things, because of the absence of conditioned things common to mundane states. "Other [texts]" refers to the Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā and others; it should be connected as "that statement is also rejected in that very [commentary]".

In the passage "having brought it back again, it should not be construed with the first jhāna and so forth", some say "the reading should be 'with the first jhāna'". That is indeed appropriate. By the word "ādi"...
245: It is because of the absence of the jhāna to be attained. Indeed, there is only one khaṇḍacakka (broken cycle) rooted in the first jhāna. Since the word 'bhaṇita' can also be an agent noun (kattu-sādhana), he said 'atha vā' and so on. It is not possible to know 'I am lying' with the very same mind that utters the lie. However, it is meant that one knows 'I am lying' through other intervening mind-door processes (manodvāra-vīthi); thus it is said, 'while speaking, the knowledge "I am lying" arises.' In this context, the meaning of musāvāda (false speech) endowed with three factors is shown. 'Dava' means speaking hastily (recklessly). 'Rava' means a slip of the tongue where one intends to say one thing but says another. Knowing that speech is called 'taṃ-ñāṇa' (knowledge of that). The state of that knowledge is 'taṃ-ñāṇatā'. It means self-awareness through the relationship of the object and the subject of knowledge. 'Ñāṇa-samodhāna' means the convergence or simultaneous arising of many knowledges in a single moment. The phrase 'knows with the mind "I shall lie"' is said by combining the preceding volition (pubba-bhāga-cetanā) and the deciding volition (sanniṭṭhāna-cetanā). With the mind that is the preceding and deciding volition, one knows the beings to be deceived; with that mind, one knows 'I shall lie.' With that very mind... [pe] ... should be abandoned: this means the monk knows by taking that very lying mind as an object, thinking 'Thus I am lying' or 'I have lied.' Thus, the view of 'taṃ-ñāṇatā'—that a person knows both the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself simultaneously with a single mind during the three moments of preceding, succeeding, and deciding volition—should be abandoned. This is because at that time, it is due only to the manifestation of the object. Therefore, he said 'na hi' and so on. If the nature of knowledge itself is not known, how can the subsequent mind know that knowledge? Thinking thus, he said 'purimaṃ purimaṃ' and so on. In that context, it means the preceding mind arising in the three periods (such as 'I shall speak') becomes the condition (paccaya) for the arising of the subsequent mind which takes the preceding mind as its object. For this reason, the minds in the three moments must be known by minds other than those [lying] minds, and those [knowing] minds certainly arise because of the preceding minds. Therefore, when the mind 'I shall speak' exists in the preceding stage, there is no such thing as the two thoughts 'I am speaking' and 'I have spoken' not occurring. Although the moments are distinct, because of their continuous arising, he speaks with reference to the state where they are grasped as 'this [subsequent mind] is that [preceding mind].'
246:
Balava-dhamma-vinidhāna-vasena means by the power of hiding a strong view. Dubbaladubbalānaṃ means (by the power) of very weak views. Sakabhāva-pariccajana-vasena means by the power of relinquishing one's own state of possession.

Uttāsitattā means because of being driven out as if by creating fear. Referring to the fact that once driven out in this way, one does not return to that place, he said: "by the power of showing the state of not associating again." Since scholars of linguistics read the word 'kheṭa' in the sense of terror, he said "that meaning..." and so on. Aṇu eva means only a subtle defilement is called aṇu-sahagata, or it means associated with the state of being subtle.

## Commentary on the Section on the Desire to Speak (Vattukāmavāra-kathā-vaṇṇanā)
In the word kevalaṃhiyaṃ, it should be understood by adding "this section is only...". The phrase "knows at that very moment" is said with reference to knowing immediately after the natural speech. However, even without making such a vocal utterance, if an agreement is made: "Whoever leaves this monastery first, we shall know him as an Arahant," and a certain monk leaves the monastery first with the intention "Let them know me as an Arahant," then even if the moment has not passed, he incurs a Pārājika offense as soon as he has just stepped out. This is like the story mentioned: "A certain monk, [thinking] let them know me as an Arahant..." and so on. Viññattipathe means in a place suitable for perceiving bodily and vocal intimations. Therefore, if someone standing beyond the range of intimation knows through the divine eye seeing the bodily movement or through the divine ear hearing the vocal utterance, it is shown that no Pārājika is incurred. In this section on comprehension (paṭivijānana-vāra), where the Pali states "there is a Pārājika offense for one who comprehends," it should be understood that if another person understands the meaning such as "this monk has attained the first jhāna" only when a certain syllable is uttered or a certain bodily action is performed, then a thullaccaya (grave offense) is incurred for the preceding efforts like uttering syllables, and the Pārājika is incurred only at the final moment of the effort of comprehension. This is because here, the thullaccaya is in the vicinity of the Pārājika. For this reason, the teacher Buddhadatta said:
"The dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense is described only in the vicinity of the first Pārājika; however, in the vicinity of the remaining three, the thullaccaya offense is mentioned."

It should be understood that this meaning is also included by this Pali: "there is a thullaccaya offense for one who does not comprehend." By the phrase "by the power of learning, questioning, etc.", it is shown that even if one does not know the exact meaning upon hearing because of not having previously studied the meanings of terms like jhāna and samādhi, if another person understands "this monk has attained some noble state of a monk," it is still a Pārājika.

## Commentary on the Classification of Non-offenses (Anāpattibheda-kathā-vaṇṇanā)
Anullapanādhippāyassa refers to a monk who speaks without the intention: "By speaking thus, I am displaying a superhuman state (uttari-manussa-dhamma)"; for instance, a monk who says "Friend, I am not afraid of death" and so on (incurs no offense). Since such a speaker is, in terms of conventional usage, a monk who answers something other than the fruit of Arahantship, he said "to one who answers something else." Bhāyanto means...
247:
This meaning should also be understood as being included by this rule: 'There is a grave offense (thullaccaya) for one who does not fully understand.' By the phrase 'by way of learning and questioning' etc., it shows that because of a lack of prior familiarity with the meanings of words like jhāna and samādhi, even if one hears them but does not know 'this is the meaning,' yet others understand that 'this monk has attained some distinguished quality of a recluse (samaṇaguṇa),' it is still a Pārājika offense.

## Anāpattibhedakathāvaṇṇanā
'Anullapanādhippāyassa' refers to a monk who speaks words such as 'Friend, I am not afraid of death,' without the intention: 'By saying this, I will be making known a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma).' Such a monk, by his speech, is one who answers with something other [than an attainment of the fruit of Arahantship]; therefore, it is said 'aññaṃ vyākarontassa' (for one who answers something else). 'Bhāyanto' means fearing 'Will they despise me if they know?'

## Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

## Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā
By the word 'sekkhabhūmiyaṃ' (in the stage of a trainee), the stage of jhāna is also included. 'Tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ' refers to the three seclusions: bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka), and seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhiviveka). Because going for alms ends with the meal, it is said 'yāva bhojanapariyosānaṃ' (until the end of the meal). For a monk who returns after eating in the village, if he arranges his robes etc. with the desire to be praised according to the method already mentioned, it is only an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). However, in the Pali text, regarding cases like 'difficult to do' (dukkara), the statement 'there is no offense for one without the intention to boast' is said to show that there is no offense even of a grave nature (thullaccaya). Indeed, even for one who intends to boast, if it is said 'Friend, it is not difficult to answer something else,' it should be understood as only a grave offense (thullaccaya) because there is no personal attribution (not claiming it for oneself).

'Na dānāhaṃ tattha gamissāmi' means 'I will not go to that dwelling place again.' The intention is that if this is so, others will think, 'This monk went there first and has not returned; therefore, he must be an Arahant.' 'Taṃ ṭhānaṃ' refers to the place previously defined by words like 'dwelling' (āvāsa). Because the agreement was made with reference to going on foot, the words 'yānena' (by vehicle) etc. are used. 'Iddhiyā' is said with reference to psychic power consisting of knowledge (vijjāmayiddhi). This is because for one who intends to boast, supernormal power (abhiññiddhi) is impossible. 'Aññamaññaṃ rakkhanti' means...
248:
Even if there is an intention to boast, they are protected (from an offense) because not even a single monk was the first to go. However, if among monks who have made an agreement, one or two are left behind and the rest go together with the intention to boast, then for all those who went, it is a Pārājika offense. Among them, for whichever monk there is no intention to boast, there is no offense for him. 'Etaṃ' refers to all the agreements mentioned below. 'Nānāverajjakā' means inhabitants of various districts. 'Saṅghalābho' refers to the portion received according to seniority. This rejection is made with reference to doing so without distinction; however, if one makes a distinction, saying 'this much is to be given to such a person,' and gives it after seeking permission (apalokana), it is proper.

'Dhammadhātū' refers to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) or the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammānaṃ sabhāva). The word 'upapattī' is spoken with reference to the individual existence (attabhāva). The phrase 'dussaddhāpayā honti' (they are difficult to make believe) is said with reference to worldlings (puthujjana), not to noble persons (ariyapuggala) like the Elder Lakkhaṇa. 'Vituḍenti' means they fly through, piercing; they make holes between the ribs and go through them—this is the meaning by way of the ablative case (nissakka). In the reading 'vitudenti,' the word 'phāsuḷantarikāhi' is the ablative case used in the sense of the locative (ādhāra). 'Lohatuṇဍေဟိ' means with beaks made of black iron. 'Acchariyaṃ vata' means it is of a nature suitable for snapping one's fingers in blame because it is contemptible.
