'Cakkhubhūtā' means those who have become like the eyes of the world; it also means those who are similar to eyes.

In the phrase 'tasseva kammassa' (of that same kamma), if the meaning is taken as 'due to that same cattle-slaughtering kamma, he was reborn in hell; due to that same [kamma]...', it would follow that many rebirths occur from a single volition (cetanā). This is not appropriate, just as it is impossible for many sprouts to arise from a single mango seed. Therefore, to resolve this point, the statement 'tassa nānācetanāhi āyūhitattā' (because it was accumulated by various volitions) etc. is made. According to this, at the moment of performing the act of cattle-slaughtering, there are many volitions even in a single act of killing—preceding volition (pubbacetanā), subsequent volition (aparacetanā), and the concluding volition (sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā). In the case of various acts of killing, it goes without saying. Among those many volitions, after suffering in hell due to one volition, he is reborn in this state of a hungry ghost (peta) due to another subsequent volition (aparāpariyacetanā) among the remaining volitions. Therefore, the phrase 'avasesakammaṃ vါ kammanimittaṃ vါ' (the remaining kamma or the sign of kamma) etc. is said. Here too, the kamma and the sign of kamma (kammanimitta) are taken with reference to the arising of a result similar to the kamma, not the sign of the destination (gatinimitta). Therefore, it is said, 'The heap of bones alone was the sign.' In the Pali, 'vitacchenti' means they pluck as if carving with their beaks. 'Virājenti' means they scratch.
249:
*Vallūravikkayena* means by selling dried meat. *Nippakkhacamme* refers to a creature with skin devoid of wings and feathers. *Ekaṃ migaṃ* refers to a single deer, specifically a barking deer. *Kāraṇāhi* means by means of killing or torturing. *Ñatvā* means having known the meditation subject (or the place of torture).

One is called *maṅguli* because of appearing in an ungraceful manner; it means existing in an ugly and loathsome state. *Cittakeḷiṃ* means playing with improper conduct according to one's own mind.

*Nissēvālapaṇakakaddamo* refers to a river free from moss (*sevāla*) the size of sesame seeds, algae (*paṇaka*) that makes the water surface look like the back of a dark frog, and black mud (*kaddama*). Because it warms with heat, a river having *tapa* (warm) *udaka* (water) should be called *Tapodaka*, but the letter 'ka' is dropped and it is called *Tapodā*. *Petaloka* refers to the collection of those who have gone from a happy state to a miserable state due to manifest unwholesome kamma, or their place of residence. *Katahatthā* means those with hands well-trained in the art of archery, meaning those who can shoot a target without missing. Those who approach the assembly of kings at royal houses to demonstrate their skill and practice archery are called *katūpāsanā*. It means those who have demonstrated their skill in all places. *Pabhaggo* means destroyed or defeated.

*Āneñjasamādhi* (Imperturbable Concentration) refers here only to *rūpāvacara* concentration which is susceptible to being disturbed by the 'thorn' of sound, even though sound is ceased in the *arūpa* attainments; thus it is said "unshakable (*anejaṃ*)," etc. It is said with reference to initial thought (*vitakka*) and so forth, which are obstacles to concentration. Although this story occurred during the early period after enlightenment (*pathamabodhi*), when the monks accused him of mere improper conduct (*anācāra*), the Blessed One declared, "Monks, there is no offense for Moggallāna." This was a decision made even then, in accordance with the *Pārājika* rule he himself would later prescribe. Therefore, it should be understood that the Elder Recorders of the Dhamma (*Dhammasaṅgāhaka*) included this in the Council as a decided case (*vinītavatthu*) of this training rule prescribed later. To show the inability of disciples to recollect out of order (by skipping), it is said "not out of order." "A difficult deed has been done" is said because it is difficult for disciples to perceive, through inference, the causal connection between the death-consciousness seen in the third existence beyond and the rebirth-consciousness of the present life, without being confused even though the continuity of consciousness was not seen during the intervening five-hundred-aeon lifespan (of the non-percipient beings).
250:
*Paṭividdha* means similar to being pierced. For example, as if one standing at a distance were to pierce the tip of one strand of yak-tail hair, which has been split seven times, with the tip of another strand of hair as if threading it; in this same way, it means this Elder Sobhita has done a difficult deed. *Etadagga* means this Elder Sobhita is foremost. *Yadidaṃ* means "that is to say, this" Elder Sobhita.

## Nigamanavaṇṇanā

*Idha* means in the *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga*. *Uddiṭṭhapārājikapari dīpana* means the explanation of the *Pārājikas* shown by way of the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* in the training rules. It does not mean the explanation of all offenses occurring in the entire *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga*, because *thullaccaya* (grave offenses) and so forth also occur there, and because the *Vibhaṅga* already mentioned is indicated by that word *uddiṭṭha* (recited). The four *Pārājikas* unique to bhikkhunīs are: the *Pārājika* of touching above the knee (*Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā*), the *Pārājika* of concealing a fault (*Vajjappaṭicchādikā*), the *Pārājika* of following an expelled monk (*Ukkhittānuvattikā*), and the *Pārājika* of eight grounds (*Aṭṭhavatthukā*). This means these are *Pārājikas* prescribed only for bhikkhunīs and not shared with bhikkhus. *Vatthuvipanna* means the status of being a basis for going forth and ordination is called *vatthu* (basis); it means being defective in that basis alone, or having a defective basis. By the words *ahetukapaṭisandhika* (one with rootless rebirth), the cause for the non-arising of the Path is stated. Although the Path does not arise for two-rooted (*duhetuka*) individuals either, those two-rooted individuals, remaining in the state of a monk, are able to fulfill the causes for the Path in the future. Rootless (*ahetuka*) individuals, however, even remaining in the pure fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), are unable to fulfill them; therefore, those rootless individuals should be known as *vatthuvipanna* (defective in basis) also because of their inability to remain in that purification of virtue. *Pārājika* means they reach defeat at the very moment of rebirth due to the failure of action (*kammavipatti*). Although those who live by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) and so forth strive in insight while remaining in the state of a layperson, it is said "the Path is barred" because there is no arising of the Path in that existence. A male organ that hangs down because of its length is called *lamba*; one who has such an organ is a *lambī*. He does not become a *Pārājika* by this much; he becomes a *Pārājika* only if he inserts that long organ into his own mouth or his own anus with the intention of indulging. Here, only insertion into the anus is intended, because insertion into the mouth is mentioned only for a monk with a flexible back (*mudupiṭṭhika*). Indeed, even that monk with a flexible back becomes a *Pārājika* only when, having a back made flexible through preliminary practice (*parikamma*), he bends over and takes his own organ with his mouth; not by the organ alone. As for a monk who takes his own anus, or the opening of another's anus, or the urinary passage of women with his mouth; or for a monk who touches a male organ with a male organ—even if he brings organ to organ, he does not become a *Pārājika*. Only by bringing the male organ into another passage...
251:
Because of the term 'sexual intercourse' (methunadhamma), 'sitting on another's organ' means sitting on top of another person who is lying on their back, inserting one's own anus into their functional organ. This is merely an illustration; if one consents to the insertion of another's organ into one's own anus, it is also a Pārājika. However, if one is forced and another person forcibly inserts it into the anus or the mouth, if there is no consent, there is no offense. In this case, not consenting is difficult because one must be free from lust. Among these excluded persons (abhabba-puggala), those who kill a mother, father, or an Arahant while still a layman, or who defile a nun, are shown to be unable to even attain novicehood (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā); thus, the four types such as matricides are mentioned separately. It should be understood that their offenses are included within the third and first Pārājikas. Just as with these four, one who causes the shedding of the Buddha's blood while a layman should also be regarded as a lohituppādaka (one who sheds the blood of a Buddha). 'Etena pariyāyena' means by the reason described as the obsession of lust in both. In the second alternative, the word-analysis 'kacci atthā' should be understood.

## 2. Saṅghādisesa Section
## 1. Explanation of the Sukka-vissatthi Training Rule
'Terasakassa' means of the section (kaṇḍa) called Terasaka, because it consists of thirteen training rules in extent. In this first Saṅghādisesa, 'anabhirata' (discontented) refers to the lack of delight in either Samatha (tranquility) or Vipassanā (insight). Since it does not mean discontent with monkhood, it says 'one with a distracted mind' (vikkhittacitta). To show the cause of distraction, it says 'kāmarāga' (sensual lust), etc.

'Abbohārikā' (negligible) is said because it does not deserve to be called a failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti). However, in terms of being unwholesome (akusala), its negligibility does not exist.

236-7. To show that the prefix 'saṃ-' has no separate meaning from the word 'cetanā' and that the suffix '-ika' is meaningful, the second alternative 'sañcetanā vā', etc., is stated. 'Sikhāppatto attho' (the meaning that has reached the peak) is said with reference to the intended meaning. 'Āsayabhedato' means by way of the distinction of the four locations: bile, phlegm, pus, and blood. 'Dhātunānattato' means by way of the diversity of the seven elements such as plasma (rasa) and blood (ruhira), or the four elements such as earth (pathavī). 'Vatthisīsaṃ' refers to the upper part of the bladder. Since the rut of elephants is called 'sambhava' (semen), it says 'sambhava (semen) is emitted'. 'Sambhavavegaṃ' refers to the impulse of bodily agitation caused by the semen moving from its place and descending toward the urinary tract. 'Bāhusīsaṃ' refers to the shoulder region. In the word 'dassesi', the word 'iti' has a causal (hetu) meaning. Therefore, the connection of the sentence should be understood as: 'Because semen is emitted from both ear-lobes... etc... and he showed the semen, therefore the speech of the third teacher is well-spoken'. 'Dakasoṭaṃ' means the region of the male organ, which is the path for urine to exit from the bladder.

This so-called semen (sukka) is the middle element (majjhima-dhātu) among the seven bodily elements such as plasma and blood. It is produced from four causes and is included in the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) like bone marrow. It exists throughout the entire body of those who live depending on nutriment, even in very young infants. That semen moves from its place due to the sensual lust that arises in beings from the age of fifteen or sixteen. Once moved, it becomes a mind-produced (cittaja) form in the nature of the water element (āpo-dhātu) and descends to the urinary tract. From the urinary tract onwards, it becomes a temperature-produced (utuja) form caused by the mind, like mucus dripping from the brain. For those whose obsession with lust [is abandoned] by means of eradication (samuccheda) or suppression (vikkhambhana)...
253:
There is no oppression by lust, so for them, the emission of semen is not possible. Thus, the emission of semen from its place is caused only by a mind of lust, not by natural physical form (pakati-rūpa). Therefore, in the Kathāvatthu Commentary, it is said: "What is called emission of semen is caused by lust." This refers only to emission caused by lust, not natural physical form.

In the six sensual-sphere heavens (kāmāvacara-deva), although the semen element exists, it does not flow from its place even with lust aroused through mutual union. Staying in its place, it undergoes some change, bringing about the subsiding of momentary feverish heat, thus completing the sexual act. Some teachers say: "The pleasure of bodily contact alone is the sensual act for those devas." For Arahants and Anāgāmīs, because of the total absence of sensual lust, it should be understood that the semen element does not even undergo change. For Rūpa-brahmas, because sensual lust has been suppressed and they do not live on physical food, the semen element does not exist at all.

"In the same way" refers to making an effort with the sexual organ while delighting in the release, etc. Since it is stated in the Padabhājanī that "vissaṭṭhi means displacement from its place," why is it said "merely upon entering the water stream"? To answer this, it says "entering the water stream here," etc. In all three views, "having endured" means having made an effort with the sexual organ and then, when remorse (vippaṭisāra) arises, dispelling the delight in the release. "To prevent in between" means not allowing the semen, which has been displaced from its place due to one's effort on the sexual organ, to descend into the water stream (dakasota) but preventing it in between. For one who performs actions like rubbing with the hand while delighting in the release, even if semen is emitted, it is only a dukkhaṭa offense; because there was no effort made on the sexual organ itself, it is not a saṅghādisesa offense—thus it says "with the hand... no offense." Referring to the decision stated by "entering the water stream here," etc., it is said: "This is a decision common to all teachers."

"Khobhakaraṇa-paccaya" (cause of disturbance) refers to causes such as incompatible medicine, lodging, food, etc. "Various dreams" means dreams consistent with disturbed elements like wind, etc. "Previously experienced" means what has happened before or what has been previously imagined by the mind. This is said to include heaven, hell, other regions, etc. "Because of desiring benefit or desiring harm" is said to show the helpful or harmful intentions of devas. "For benefit or for harm" refers to the naturally occurring good or bad results.

Considering the objection: "If the objects brought by devas do not exist in the ultimate sense, how does a man see those objects, or how do devas bring those non-existent objects?" it is said: "He [sees] those of the devas..." etc. By those words, it means that just by the devas thinking "Let him think thus," the mind of the sleeping person is cut off from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and arises thinking according to what the devas thought. Thus, it is said that the objects thought of by that man are brought by the devas. It is shown that the man sees those objects through the power of the devas. In the words "Like the mother of the Bodhisatta, the sign of obtaining a son," etc., on the day the Bodhisatta descended into his mother's womb, Queen Mahāmāyā dreamed that a noble white elephant entered her womb through her right side; this is called a dream that is a cause for obtaining a son. For our Bodhisatta, on the night of the fourteenth day of the fortnight, when it was said "Tomorrow he will become a Buddha," at dawn, he dreamt of using the Himālaya mountains as a pillow, with his hands in the eastern and western oceans...
254:
To show that deities desire what is harmful, He spoke the words beginning with 'So tāsaṃ'. By these words, it is shown that just by the deities thinking, 'Let this person imagine thus,' the mind of the sleeping person falls from the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-santati) and arises imagining exactly in the manner the deities intended. In this way, the objects imagined by that person are said to be 'brought forward by the deities.' And that person is said to see those objects through the power of the deities.

In the words beginning with 'Like the mother of the Bodhisatta, the sign of obtaining a son,' the dream seen by Queen Mahāmāyā on the day the Bodhisatta descended into her womb—seeing a noble white elephant entering her womb through her right side—is called a dream that is a sign of obtaining a son. For our Bodhisatta, however, at the time of dawn on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, thinking 'Tomorrow I shall become a Buddha,' there were these five great dreams: (1) sleeping on the great earth, making Mount Himavanta his pillow, and placing his left and right hands in the eastern and western oceans, and his feet in the southern ocean; (2) a type of grass called tiriya, known as dabba grass, with a red stalk the size of a plow-handle, growing from his navel and reaching the sky many thousands of yojanas high in an instant; (3) white worms with black heads crawling up from his feet and reaching as far as his kneecaps; (4) four birds of various colors coming from the four directions and becoming white at the soles of his feet; (5) the Bodhisatta walking upon a great mountain of dung without being soiled. These five great dreams should be understood as the precursors, respectively, to: the realization of the Four Noble Truths (Sambodhi), the proclamation of the Noble Path to deities and humans, the taking of refuge by laypeople, the four castes such as the Khattiyas ordaining and attaining Arahatship, and being unsoiled when receiving the four requisites.

The sixteen dreams are well-known. They are said to be 'certainly true' because the results invariably occur. However, the seeing of a dream is perverted (vipallattha) in all instances. Among the four root causes such as the disturbance of the elements (dhātukkhobha), dreams are sometimes seen due to two or even three causes; this is intended by the phrase 'saṃsaggabhedato' (due to a variety of combinations). The 'variety of dreams' refers to the distinction between truth and untruth.

In the term 'rūpanimittādi-ārammaṇa,' a visible object (rūpārammaṇa) other than kamma-nimitta and gati-nimitta is the cause of consciousness, and thus it is called 'rūpa-nimitta.' The bhavaṅga-mind that has such objects as its object—starting with rūpa-nimitta and including the seven signs—is called 'rūpanimittādi-ārammaṇa.' 'Of such a nature' means having objects such as rūpa-nimitta and being associated with lust (rāga) and so on. 'By the common conventional mind' (sabbavohārika-cittena) refers to the normal process-mind (vīthi-citta) of one who is awake. 'Who sees?' means that since there is no occurrence of mind that is not associated with either sleeping or waking, there can be no 'dreamer' as such. Therefore, He said, 'It reaches the state of non-existence of the dream.' By the phrase 'kapimiddhapareto,' it is shown that one dreams through a mind-door process (manodvāra-vīthi), either wholesome or unwholesome, which is interrupted by the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurring by the power of drowsiness. Therefore, He spoke the words beginning with 'yā niddā.' 'Free from the two extremes' means being free from the two extremes called wholesome and unwholesome.
255:
The meaning is that there can be no 'dreamer' because there is no occurrence of mind that is dissociated from the states of being asleep or awake. Therefore, He said, 'The non-existence of the dream itself follows.' By the phrase 'kapimiddhapareto,' it is shown that one dreams through a mind-door process (manodvāra-vīthi), either wholesome or unwholesome, which is interrupted by the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurring by the power of sleep. Therefore, He spoke the words beginning with 'yā niddā.' 'Free from the two extremes' means free from the two extremes known as wholesome and unwholesome. 'In the moment of adverting and registration' (āvajjana-tadārammaṇa-kkhaṇe) is said by taking what is fit to arise in the mind-door, since there is no five-door process in a dream.

In this context, because of the mention of registration (tadārammaṇa) even within a dream, the sense-sphere resultant states (kāmāvacara-vipāka) that occur pervertedly by imagining visible objects and so on—which were previously experienced or heard—as they occurred before, are called 'having a limited object' (parittārammaṇa) because they occur by imagining based on limited (sensual) things. It should be understood that it is not only because they take limited things in their own nature. If this is so, for the states that have results such as lust (rāga) occurring by attributing the forms of women, men, and so on, and for the resultants such as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) that arise by taking the objects of those lustful states, the status of 'having a limited object' and 'having a kamma-nimitta as object' is indeed appropriate. However, the mental states (citta and cetasika) that arise by taking a counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) of a kasiṇa and so on—which is a concept (paññatti) dissociated from ultimate reality (vatthu-dhamma)—and which occur by way of access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā), should be understood as 'having an indescribable object' (navattabba-ārammaṇa) in the Paritta Triad.

That dream is called 'having a weak basis' (dubbalavatthuka) because it has a limited object imagined pervertedly. The meaning is that it does not occur according to one's will in a non-existent object. Therefore, He spoke the words beginning with 'avishaye uppannattā.'

The phrase 'āpattinikāyassa' is spoken in accordance with the masculine gender of the word 'Saṅghādiseso.' 'Assa' means of that group of offenses, of the group of offenses from which one wishes to be rehabilitated (vuṭṭhāpetuṃ). Therefore, He spoke the words beginning with 'kiṃ vuttaṃ.' In the phrase 'ruḷhīsaddena,' 'ruḷhī' here refers to the renown of a word that is produced for a whole but is also applied to a part of that whole. A word endowed with that conventional usage is a 'ruḷhī-sadda.' By that conventional term (He speaks). He states the reason for the conventional usage with the words beginning with 'avayave.'

'Kālañca' refers to the time shown by the words 'rāgūpatthambhe' and so on. When 'rāgūpatthambhe' is said, it is understood that he emits (semen) at that time when there is the support of lust.
256:
In terms of meaning, the time should be understood. The ninth intention refers to the intention to investigate (vīmaṃsādhippāya). The term 'vatthu' refers to the object (visaya). Because those creatures have hair, they are called 'lomasa' (hairy insects).

'Mocanena' means by the effort of emission. In the phrase 'mocanassādasampayuttāya', the desire to emit itself is called 'mocanassāda' (enjoyment of emission). The volition associated with that desire to emit is called 'mocanassāda-cetanā'. One should not interpret it as a volition longing for the pleasure of emission. If interpreted that way, an offense would only be incurred by a monk who emits seeking pleasure, and not by a monk who emits for the sake of health, etc. Therefore, one should interpret it as the volition with the desire to emit for any purpose, such as health, etc.

'Vāyamato' means by physical exertion on the male organ with the body. 'Two thousand offenses' is stated without including the khaṇḍacakka (broken cycles), etc. If desired, one can also count them by dividing them into khaṇḍacakka, etc. 'Ekena padena' refers to the term 'household-based affection' (gehasitapema).

Similarly, it is meant that if one falls asleep without giving up the effort of intense squeezing, etc., with the volition of the desire to emit, and emission occurs, a saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. 'Suddhacitto' (pure-minded) is said with reference to giving up the effort made with the thighs, etc., and the enjoyment of emission. Therefore, it should be understood that even if one does not contemplate foulness (asubha), there is no offense in emission due to the absence of effort (payoga).

'Emission by that effort' means that apart from the semen being emitted, other semen also moves from its place. If, despite the effort, only the semen being emitted descends to the urinary tract, only a thullaccaya (grave offense) is incurred because there is no emission of semen by effort. 'Jagganatthāya' means that it is permissible to hold the male organ with the hand to prevent staining the robes, etc.; the meaning is that such effort does not constitute an effort (for emission). 'Anokāsa' refers to the region of the male organ.

'Supinantena kāraṇena' means due to the cause of effort occurring within a dream. This 'no offense' is stated even in a situation where an offense could occur, because it is beyond one's control. Therefore, it was said: 'If it were within one's power, one should remain still,' etc.
257:
In the Aṇḍakaṇḍuvana story of the Vinītavatthu Pali, a saṅghādisesa is stated because by moving the testicles with the intention to emit, the male organ also moves, thus constituting an effort on the organ. However, if the male organ does not move and one touches only the testicles to relieve itching, there is no offense even if emission occurs, because the testicles are not the male organ (anaṅgajātattā).

'Vatthi' is the skin covering the tip of the male organ (the prepuce). In the statement 'For a monk warming his belly... there is no offense,' it means that although the male organ becomes warm due to warming the belly, such warmth does not constitute an effort made on the organ.

In the story 'Come here, novice,' when commanding another, if a monk enjoys the movement of the male organ performed by that other person with the enjoyment of emission, that movement is also considered to have originated from the monk's mind of enjoyment. Therefore, only the enjoyment-volition (assāda-cetanā), which is the cause of the movement of the male organ that leads to emission, is the factor for the offense. The words of command are not a factor for the offense because a saṅghādisesa is not completed at the moment of speaking those words, and because no offense occurs for a monk who, despite having given such a command, removes the enjoyment of emission through wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). Thus, this training rule should be understood as anāṇattika (not by command), kāyakamma (bodily action), and kiriyasamuṭṭhāna (originated by action). However, a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) is incurred for the words of command.

If a monk enjoys the effort performed by another who was not commanded but used force, and emission occurs, he incurs a saṅghādisesa just as in the first pārājika; if there is no emission, a thullaccaya is incurred. The teachers say that if there is no volition for the enjoyment of emission, even if one enjoys it with lust for physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggarāga), there is no saṅghādisesa even if emission occurs. This is indeed appropriate.

In the Kāyatthambhana story, it is stated that an offense is incurred by stretching the body, just as an effort on the male organ occurs through movement.

In the Upanijjhāyana story, 'male organ' (aṅgajāta) refers only to the urinary tract (passāvamagga) of living women, not to any other organ.

'Pupphāvalī' is a specific type of game. It is said that those playing that game make a broken riverbank slippery with water and mud, and sit there with both legs extended...
258:
They slip down; there is also a reading as "Pupphāvaliya". The word "pavesentassa" is in the causative sense and, because it takes two objects, the accusative case is applied to both words "vālikaṃ" and "aṅgajātaṃ". In this training rule, these three factors should be understood: intention (cetanā), effort (upakkama), and emission (muccana).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Emission of Semen is finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Physical Contact

In the opening of the second training rule, it is said, "even though certain windows are open, because it is pitch dark outside, light cannot enter; because the open door-leaf blocks the light coming from elsewhere, there is only thick darkness behind the door-leaf," referring to such windows, it is stated, "those windows which, though open, are dark," and so forth.

When the Brahmin woman's limbs, large and small, were touched, she was compliant with the improper conduct (anācāra) and did not say anything; she only spoke when the monk spoke words of praise. Therefore, it is said, "perceiving that he likely wishes to go forth (as a monk)"; it means perceiving him as if he were one wishing to go forth. For women of good family, such mistreatment by others is an extreme insult; therefore, it is called "treating oneself with perversity."

Regarding the term "otiṇṇa," referring to the passive sense (kammasādhana), it is said, "by yakkhas and so forth"; referring to the active sense (kattusādhana), it is said, "into wells and so forth." "In that object" means in the object known as the female body.

"To him" refers to all modes such as grasping the hand and so forth.

"Of these words" refers to words such as amasana (touching) and so forth. "Perceiving as a woman" means perceiving as a human woman. The word "naṃ" acts as an adjective to "kāya" to show the meaning "this body"; thus, it is said, "alternatively," and so forth. The statement "touching... only one offense" is said with reference to an unclothed woman, not a clothed woman. For a monk who slides his hand down from the head of a clothed woman, if the hand reaches above the garment she is wearing, he commits an offense of thullaccaya (grave transgression). If he slides his hand from the garment and touches from the calf onwards, he again commits an offense of saṅghādisesa.
259:
"Yathāniddiṭṭhaniddesa" refers to the previously mentioned explanation of physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggiya-niddesa). "Tena" means for that reason by which the perception of the object (vatthu-saññā) and so forth occur. The construction is: "one should show or make clear to the monk the heavy offense (saṅghādisesa) mentioned in the previously stated explanation of the training rule."

"Saññāya virāgitamhi" means when the perception is mistaken. The phrase "such and such an object" is said with reference to the absence of non-offense (i.e., an offense is committed) for a monk who touches any conscious or unconscious object, whether mentioned in this training rule or not.

"Sāratta" (lustful) means being infatuated specifically with the lust of physical contact. "Viratta" (dispassionate) is said with reference to those such as one's mother towards whom one is free from the lust of physical contact. "Dukkaṭa" (wrongdoing) is said with reference to a monk who grasps out of affection for his mother and so forth. However, for a monk who grasps even a woman who is not lustful, but does so with the lust of physical contact, it is indeed a saṅghādisesa offense. It is stated that this is in accordance with the Pali text. If it is asked, "How is it in accordance?"—If, when the thought "I will grasp an object connected to a woman's body" arises, the perception of her as a woman should disappear, then even in grasping the object connected to the body, there should not even be a thullaccaya offense. Why? Because in the Pali text, a thullaccaya is stated only when there is the perception of her as a woman. Therefore, for a monk who grasps the body with the thought "I will grasp an object connected to a woman's body," the perception of her as a woman is not considered to have disappeared. Thus, the view stated by the Elder Mahāsumma—that a monk who grasps the body with the thought of grasping an object connected to the body, because of the presence of the perception of a woman, the lust for physical contact, and the act of grasping the body, falls into a saṅghādisesa offense according to the object—is in accordance with this Pali text. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) also, a thullaccaya is stated for a monk who, with the perception "I will grasp many women by encircling them with my arms," grasps them, in respect of those women in the middle. Truly, that monk does not have the perception "I will grasp the women in the middle with an object connected to the body." Therefore, it should be understood that it is also in accordance with the Commentary. A "Kāḷitthī" (dark woman) is so called because she is difficult to distinguish due to her dark clothing.

"Sevanādhippāya" means the desire to enjoy the pleasure of touch (phassasukha). In the section on touching an object connected to the body (kāyapppaṭibaddhāmasanavāra), the enjoyment of touch by means of the object connected to the body should be understood. The statement "no offense" (anāpatti) due to the mere arising of a thought is said with reference to the absence of effort (payoga) even for a monk who consents to the movement of the body performed by a woman, because no movement of his own body occurs through the mere lust for physical contact. In the first Pārājika, however, because there is no exertion by others, when the desire to indulge arises, with that intention...
260:
The arousal (stiffening) of the sexual organ occurs naturally; it is stated in the Pārājika that such an occurrence is considered to be caused by that monk. Similarly, in the first Saṅghādisesa, it should be understood that an offense is committed if arousal of the sexual organ occurs while consenting to the effort made by another.

In this fourth section (vāra), 'neither exerts with the body nor perceives the touch,' the word 'api' in the phrase 'perceiving the touch also' indicates that, as in the third section, there is no exertion (vāyāma). The statement 'as if handling a nissaggiya with a nissaggiya' should be understood as merely illustrating the absence of perceiving the touch, not the absence of effort. Regarding the 'intention for release (mokkhādhippāya),' because of the mind's nature to change rapidly, even if lust for physical contact arises intermittently, there is no offense as long as the intention for release remains unbroken. However, if that intention is broken, an offense is committed.

## The Method of Explaining the Padabhājanīya

In this context, the instruction 'do not say "take it"' is stated with reference to a dukkaṭa offense for touching something connected to the body with household-based affection (gehasitapema). However, there is no offense for a monk who says 'take it' to a woman who is unable to hold clothes etc. out of compassion, nor for a monk who, out of compassion for a disabled woman drowning in water, pulls her by the hair etc. with the intention of saving her, without considering her as 'untouchable' (anāmāsa). In truth, it is not even proper to lift one's own dying mother. This same rule applies to women who are not relatives. The word 'mother' is used to show that touching even one's noble mother is not proper. There is no offense in performing necessary duties for her or for other women, as there is no difference in the nature of being anāmāsa.

Tiṇaṇḍupaka (grass coil) refers to a coil (cumbaṭaka) made of radish-grass roots etc. for hair decoration. 'Turning around' means removing it from its state as one's own garment etc. Touching it temporarily for the purpose of worship etc. is allowable. The phrase 'head ornament, toothpick, needle, etc.' should be applied in two ways: head ornaments made of cloth pieces etc. for hair decoration, and toothpicks (hairpins) etc. It shows the meaning in order: the head ornament is to be taken for the purpose of a razor-case accessory, and the toothpick (hairpin) for its own accessory use. Alternatively, the toothpick (hairpin) made to be inserted crosswise after tying the hair bun is itself called the 'head-ornament toothpick'; being a needle carried inside a razor-case, it is the accessory for various tasks, and thus it can be construed as 'razor-case-needle accessory.'
261:
The construction should be made accordingly. Potthakarūpa refers to a figure made of lime etc. Even a figure made in the likeness of female animals that are subjects of Pārājika is considered an untouchable object (anāmāsa). It is allowable to use cloth, walls, etc., on which female figures etc. are displayed, provided one does not touch the female figure itself. There is no fault for a monk who touches such untouchable objects with something connected to his body, provided there is no lust for physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggarāga).

Regarding the word 'bhinditvā' (breaking), it is considered no fault because the Commentary states that even untouchable objects may be broken with a stick, stone, etc., and the Pali text also states there is no offense in touching with the intention of escaping from danger. To free creatures caught by a female snake, wild beast, etc., it is allowable to hold that snake etc. by surrounding it with cloth, a stick, etc. It is also allowable to hold a dying mother etc. in water with cloth etc., or if unable, to pull her out by the hair etc. out of compassion. This meaning should certainly be accepted. As for the statement in the Commentary, 'but she should not be touched,' it is our preference to consider that it refers to a situation where she is not in immediate danger of death.

'Determining the path (maggaṃ adhiṭṭhāya)' means giving rise to the perception, 'This is the path.' The phrase 'they prepare and give' is said in terms of proper conduct (sāmīci). If those laypeople do not prepare a seat but say 'Please sit,' it is allowable to prepare it oneself and sit. 'Grown there (tatthajātaka)' refers to grass etc. that remains in the state of vegetation (bhūtagāma) without being cut. Because it is said 'by way of playing,' there is no offense for a monk who touches them for a specific reason. However, objects belonging to monks that are fit for use should not be touched in any way because they might be handled improperly. The phrase 'I will give to the unordained' refers to taking something by force without it being offered. There is no fault in taking something for oneself after it has been offered, as it does not have the nature of anāmāsa.

Maṇi (gem) refers to all types of gems such as jotirasa, other than beryl (veḷuriya). Veḷuriya is a gem the color of moist bamboo; some say it has the color of a cat's eye. Silā refers to a very smooth black stone the color of beans; some say that very smooth stones of red or white color, which are called rubies, are also anāmāsa. By the word 'rajata' (silver/money), all forms of currency (rūpiya) are included, starting from those made of lac such as kahāpaṇa and māsa coins, and including all others not yet mentioned. Lohitaṅka refers to a dark red ruby. Masāragalla is a variegated gem; some call it an emerald. Because pearls ground and mixed for medicinal purposes lose their status as precious gems (ratana) and are not regarded as gems at the moment of handling, it is said, 'But for the purpose of medicine, it is allowable.' As far as...
262:
As long as those pearls remain in the form of gems, they are not to be touched. Like these pearls, other precious stones may be taken for the purpose of grinding and mixing into medicine. However, gold and silver may not be accepted even for the purpose of grinding and mixing into medicine. Even if laypeople mix them and offer them, if the gold etc. remains in its visible form within the medicine and can be separated, such medicine is not allowable. If it has reached the state of being unreckonable (abbohārika) [by being ground and mixed], it is allowable. Because it is said, "starting from jātiphalika," high-quality stones such as suriyakanta and candakanta should be included under the category of rubies (maṇi). One should connect the terms: a shell for blowing, a polished and perforated shell, and a shell mixed with gems. "Perforated" (viddha) means having a hole made in it, as is done with rubies and so on.

"Mixed with gems" (ratanamissa) refers to a conch shell decorated with gold creepers or inlaid with gems like pearls. By this term "mixed with gems," it is shown that conch shells other than those used for blowing are untouchable (anāmāsa) only if they are mixed with gems. The same principle applies to crystal. By the term "water-conch" (pānīyasaṅkha), it is established that it is allowable for monks to accept conch-shell vessels made in the shape of bowls and so on. "The rest" (sesā) refers to the remaining conch shells, excluding those associated with gems.

"Starting from the seed" (bījato paṭṭhāya) means starting from the ore-stone from which silver is refined. The word "rejected" (paṭikkhipi) is said because of the nissaggiya offense incurred by making a gold relic casket, a Buddha image, etc., into one's own property. Because it is said, "in the place of a disposer of silver," it is clear that it is allowable for a monk who is a disposer of silver (rūpiyachaḍḍaka) to touch and discard gold and silver. "To cause to be moved" (keḷāpayituṃ) means to touch and move it from here to there. "It is said" (vuttaṃ) refers to what is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Regarding the statement "it is allowable only to remove rubbish," some say that whether it be a guardian or someone else, it is allowable to wipe away rubbish with the hand and remove it, and it is also allowable to wipe away dirt. That view does not agree with the Commentary because such wiping is similar to moving (keḷāyana). Ārakūṭaloha (brass) is a specific type of artificial metal with a color like gold. Artificial metal is of three types: kaṃsaloha (bronze), vaṭṭaloha, and hārakūṭaloha. Among them, the metal made by mixing tin and copper is called kaṃsaloha. The metal made by mixing lead and copper is called vaṭṭaloha. The metal made by mixing mercury and copper is called hārakūṭaloha. Regarding that hārakūṭa, some teachers say that because it is said to be "in the category of gold," a nissaggiya offense is incurred for the monk who accepts it. Since it is not counted among silver (rūpiya), it is not a nissaggiya; it should be understood that there is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in touching and accepting it. "All allowable" (sabbakappiyo) means...
263:
The meaning is that the use of monastery requisites made of the aforementioned gold and so on, in terms of touching and guarding them, is allowable in every way. Therefore, he said "Therefore" (tasmā) and so on. Because it is said, "in the explanation of the Dhamma-Vinaya of the monks," it should be understood that only monastery buildings and requisites made of gold etc. that belong to the Saṅgha (saṅghika) are allowable; those that are personal (puggalika) are not allowable.

"Having broken" (bhinditvā) means that without touching it first, one makes a slight break with a stone or similar object, and afterwards, intending it to be an allowable object (kappiyabhaṇḍa), it is allowable to take it with the hand. Therefore, it is said, "Thinking 'I will make it an allowable object,' it is allowable to accept it all." In this case too, it should be touched only after slightly breaking or separating it.

In the phrase "shields, nets, etc." (phalakajālikādīni), kiṭikāphalaka (shield) refers to what is held by the hand to protect against the danger of arrows, and jālikā (mask/netting) refers to that which is made in the form of a net with iron, bronze, etc., to protect the eyes and is worn on the head and so on. By the word "etc." (ādi), armor and so on are included. "Untouchable" (anāmāsāni) is said with reference to items that obstruct others, such as fishing nets; it does not refer to protection against arrows, because that is not a weapon. For this reason, he will say later, "for the prevention of obstruction by others," and so on. "Of the seat" (āsanassa) refers to the perimeter (paribhaṇḍa) made around a cetiya. "I will bind" (bandhissāmi) means "I will bind so that crows and so on cannot destroy it."

"Drum-assembly" (bherisaṅghāṭa) is a drum with skin attached; "lute-assembly" (vīṇāsaṅghāṭa) is a lute with skin attached—so it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī. Since there is no distinction from the statement in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, "lutes, drums, etc., covered with skin," and because in the Kurundī, the author begins to state a distinction with "But in the Kurundī..." and so on, the collection of materials used for covering drums and so on should be known as bherivīṇāsaṅghāṭa (called saṅghāṭa because they are joined together). "Empty cavity" (tucchapokkhara) is the hollow body of drums or lutes that have not yet been covered with skin. "Attached skin" (āropitacamma) refers only to the skin of the drum-head that was previously attached and later removed from the drum and kept separately, not including the remaining parts. If it is with the other parts, it is called saṅghāṭa; this is the distinction. "To cover" (onahituṃ) means to place the skin on the drum-body etc. and bind it with all the accessories like leather thongs.

In the Pali, "of the paṇḍaka" (paṇḍakassa) means "by the paṇḍaka." "At the time when it is capable of a pārājika" (pārājikappahonakakāle) means at the time when the corpse has not yet decayed. If there is lust for physical contact and so on, in all circumstances, a woman's...
264:
If the form of a woman is visible, it should be understood that one is not free from the dukkaṭa offense of anāmāsa (touching what should not be touched). Since bridges and such cannot be moved from their place, they are not designated as 'connected to the body' (kāyappaṭibaddha); therefore, it is stated to be a dukkaṭa offense.

Ekapadikasankama means a small bridge. Because it is said, 'pulling' (āviñchanto), a thullaccaya (grave offense) occurs only with a rope that is suitable for moving. Regarding other ropes that are not suitable for moving, such as walls, pillars, etc., it is said, 'whatever is a great rope' (yā mahārajju hoti), etc., meaning [a thullaccaya] does not occur. Therefore, it should be understood that even touching a small rope or a small staff suitable for moving without actually moving it results in a thullaccaya offense. Paṭicchādetabbā refers to things that should be hidden by covering, etc. The five factors of this training rule are: being a human woman, perceiving her as a human woman, having lustful intent for physical contact, making an effort, and touching the hand, etc., through that effort.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Physical Contact (Kāyasaṃsagga-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) is Finished.

## 3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Lewd Words (Duṭṭhullavācā-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

In the third training rule, asaddhammapatisaṃyutta means words connected with sexual intercourse. Bālā refers to one who does not know good or bad speech; women who do not know due to intoxication from liquor, or due to reasons such as insanity, are also included here. 'It does not yet reach the head' (na tāva sīsaṃ eti) means it has not yet reached the limit or completion that constitutes the cause for a saṅghādisesa offense. This is because it is not connected with the [sexual] path or intercourse. However, a dukkaṭa offense does occur.

Apasādeti means speaking words that are not pleasing. Dosam deti means causing anger to arise. 'By three' (tīhi) means that because terms such as animittāsī are also suitable for being interpreted with non-lewd meanings, there is no absolute rule that they must be connected with the urinary tract, etc. However, it should be understood that with those eight terms, a thullaccaya offense is incurred, as in the case of the female wanderer (paribbājikā).

Kuñcikapanāḷimatta means merely the size of a keyhole. Sukkhasotā means the disappearance of the red color because the urinary tract is dry.

Suddhāni refers to terms that occur even when not associated with words like 'intercourse'. The phrase 'only those connected with the practice of intercourse' (methunadhammena ghaṭitāneva) is a mere illustration (upalakkhaṇa). Even with the birth canal, the urinary tract, or the signless...
265:
Even if one speaks by connecting [the words] as 'your birth canal or urinary tract is like this,' etc., it still constitutes an offense.

Garukāpatti (grave offense) refers to the pārājika offense of a nun involving the area above the knees (ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika).

The phrase 'laughing, laughing' is a mere illustration (upalakkhaṇa). Even if not laughing, if one speaks while manifesting one's perverted mind to a woman in any manner, it is an offense.

Kāyacittato means the offense arises from body and mind for a monk who makes jokes or gestures with hands and feet.

Therefore, 'a dukkaṭa offense is incurred' means a dukkaṭa occurs because [the woman] does not understand. If she does understand, it is only a thullaccaya offense because it is not a direct term (khettapada), as in the case of the female wanderer (paribbājikā). In the case of a direct term, if she understands, it would be a saṅghādisesa offense, as in the two cases of asking for intercourse. Although those two cases are mentioned in the fourth saṅghādisesa because of asking for intercourse, it should be understood that they are mentioned here [in the third] because they occur merely through the enjoyment of lewd words. What offense occurs for a monk who speaks with a direct term if the woman does not understand? Although it is not explicitly stated in the Pali or Commentaries as 'such-and-such an offense,' it should be a thullaccaya offense here. This is because it is stated that for an indirect term (akhettapada), it is a dukkaṭa if she does not understand and a thullaccaya if she understands. In the case of a direct term, a saṅghādisesa is stated if she understands; thus, it is appropriate that it be a thullaccaya if she does not understand, not a dukkaṭa. This should be accepted to avoid the consequence of there being no distinction from an indirect term. Just as in this [third] training rule, in the fourth training rule also, it should be understood that for an indirect term, it is a thullaccaya if she understands and a dukkaṭa if she does not; but for a direct term, it is a thullaccaya if she does not understand. In the Pali, 'navāvutaṃ' means that which is not spoken (not preached).

'Referring to the ignoble dhamma' (asaddhammaṃ sandhāya) means speaking with reference to sexual intercourse. For that intercourse receives the name 'sowing' (vappa) because it is the dropping of the seed for the arising of children.

'Saṃsīdati' means it sinks or it carries. 'Saṃsarīyati' has the same meaning. The five factors here are: being a human woman, having such a perception, having lustful desire for the enjoyment of lewd words, speaking lewdly with that lust, and her understanding at that moment.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Lewd Words (Duṭṭhullavācā-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) is Finished.
266:
## 4. Explanation of the Attakāmapāricariya Sikkhāpada

In the fourth Saṅghādisesa training rule, a collection of almsfood placed in a bowl by others is called 'piṇḍapāta' (almsfood) because it is gathered early in the morning. Due to its similarity to food obtained through alms-round, any other food obtained by monks is also simply called 'piṇḍapāta'. It is called 'paccaya' (requisite) in the sense of 'patikaraṇa' (remedy/support) because it occurs depending on that requisite. Alternatively, it is called 'paccaya' because it arises as an opposite to the suffering of diseases.

'Sappāyassa' means beneficial (hita). 'Nagaraparikkhārehi' means with things that surround and protect a city. These seven—the royal residence, the moat, the palace, the wall, the gatepost, the crossbar, and the watchtower—are called the city's appurtenances (nagaraparikkhāra). 'Setaparikkhāro' is the ornament of pure virtue (sīla). Here, the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is intended by 'chariot' (ratha), and its factors such as Right Speech are called 'parikkhāra' (requisites/ornaments) in the sense of being ornaments. 'Cakkavīriyo' means having the wheel of energy (vīriyacakka). 'Jīvitaparikkhārā' are the causes for the continuation of life. 'Samudānetabbā' means should be well brought up or sought after.

'Upacāre' refers to being in such a place where one is able to make oneself understood. In the Pali text, among these four terms: 'one's own desire, one's own reason, one's own intention, one's own service,' the terms 'kāma' (desire), 'hetu' (reason), and 'pāricariyā' (service) are called 'attha' (meaning) because they indicate the meaning of the formal definition (viggahavākya) in the first alternative interpretation (atthavikappa) mentioned in the Commentary. The remaining single term 'adhippāya' (intention) is merely 'vyañjana' (phrasing/letter); it means it is just a word because it is not applicable to the first alternative interpretation. The same method applies to the second alternative interpretation.

To show the aforementioned meaning in conjunction with the word-by-word analysis (padabhājanī), the Commentary begins with: 'If one says: one's own desire, one's own reason, one's own service, the wise will understand,' and so on. The meaning is this: when 'one's own reason (attano hetu)' is said, the meaning 'for one's own sake' is understood. When 'one's own desire, one's own service (attano kāmaṃ attano pāricariyaṃ)' is said, the meaning 'service with sensual desire' is understood. Therefore, the wise will understand through these three terms this alternative interpretation: that 'attakāmapāricariyā' is service with sensual desire for one's own sake.
267:
When 'one's own intention' (attano adhippāya) is said, since the word 'adhippāya' has the same meaning as the word 'kāmita' (desired), the wise will understand this alternative interpretation: 'service with the sensual desire intended by oneself' in the sense of what is desired by oneself.

'This is supreme' (etadaggaṃ) means this service is excellent. In the Duṭṭhullavāca Sikkhāpada (Pārājika, 285) also, asking for sexual intercourse appears as: 'he begs and he entreats.' However, in that training rule, it is spoken by the power of lust that delights in lewd words, whereas in this training rule, it is spoken by the power of lust that delights in one's own sexual intercourse—this is the distinction.

In the Vinitavatthu cases, the statement 'Give the supreme gift' is spoken for one's own sake. In the Duṭṭhullavāca Sikkhāpada, even if spoken for another's sake, it should be understood that it reaches the head (the major offense). 'Subhagā' refers to a woman endowed with excellent auspicious marks such as power (issariya). There are five factors here: being a human woman, perceiving her as a human woman, having lust for service with one's own sensual desire, requesting service with sensual desire through that lust, and understanding at that moment.

## The Explanation of the Attakāmapāricariya Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Sañcaritta Sikkhāpada

In the fifth training rule, 'paṇḍicca' means knowing through natural wisdom. 'Gatimanta' means being endowed with the course of natural wisdom. 'Veyyattiya' means knowledge learned in the duties to be performed by women. 'Medhā' means wisdom that arises according to the situation even in those duties of women that have not been learned. 'Cheka' means being skilled and clever in cooking and so on by oneself.

Taking a maiden is 'āvāha,' which is the receiving of a maiden. Sending her to another's family according to custom is 'vivāha,' which is the giving of a maiden.

'Randhāpana' means causing rice to be cooked. Completing the preparation of curries and so on is 'pacāpana.' 'Na upāhaṭa' means not given. Buying is called 'kaya.' Selling is called 'vikkaya.' Combining both of these, it is called 'vohāra' (trade).

By the statement 'A wonder (abbhuta) should not be performed,' it shows that a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense is committed. Because it is said 'The loser must give,' one who does not give should be made to do so by relinquishing the burden (of the offense).
268:
Matchmaking (sañcaritta) is called "acirakālādhikārika" because it involves excessive exertion (adhikāra) in a short period of time. Alternatively, there is a variant reading "acirakālācārika." It should be understood as having transgressing conduct (ācāra/ajjhācāra) in a short period of time.

Although monks ordained by the "Ehi Bhikkhu" method and others may commit prohibitional offenses (paṇṇattivajja) such as matchmaking, because such monks are not present at all times and are few in number, the word-analysis (padabhājanī) beginning with "yvāyaṃ" is spoken with reference to those ordained by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma). Going back and forth is called sañcaraṇa; one who has this going back and forth is a sañcarī; the state of such a monk is sañcaritta. Therefore, it is said to be "the state of a person who goes back and forth." It means the state of going back and forth between a woman and a man.

"Jāyābhāve" means for the state of a wife (bhariyābhāva). "Jārabhāve" means for the state of a husband (sāmibhāva). It means for the purpose of making them husband and wife. In this context, the locative case is used in the sense of cause (nimitta). Although in the word-analysis of the term "jārattane," the word-analysis is stated in the feminine gender as "jārī bhavissasi" (you will be a mistress), yet in the description of the phrase "sañcarittaṃ samāpajjeyya," it is stated as "sent by a woman, one goes to a man; or sent by a man, one goes to a woman." Thus, to show the manner of speaking to a man, and because the description "jārattane" is common to both women and men, it is said: "One who informs a man of a woman's desire speaks for the state of a husband (jārattana)." In the Pali text, however, both terms are linked only by the manner of informing a woman of a man's desire, but following that sequence, the manner of informing a man of a woman's desire can also be understood.

Now, wishing to show the meaning according to the method taught in the Pali text, the commentary says "apica" and so forth. The phrase "pati bhavissasi" (you will be a husband) is spoken as a synonym for a man because the word jāyā is fixed only in the feminine gender. It means "you will be a permanent husband" (nibaddhasāmika). "Jāro bhavissasi" means "you will be a husband who approaches through misconduct (micchācāra)."

"Serivihāraṃ" means living according to one's own will (sacchandacāra). "Attano vasaṃ" means one's own authority. Because the word gotta (clan) applies to those who have a lineage, and the word dhamma applies to those who practice the Dhamma, it says "sagottehi" and so forth. In that context, "sagottehi" means with those of the same clan. "Sahadhammikehi" means with those who have practices that should be practiced together in the teaching of the same Teacher.
269:
Or (one should associate) with those of the same family customs. For this reason, it is said "ekaṃ satthāraṃ" and so forth. "Those belonging to the same group" (ekagaṇapariyāpannehi) refers to those included in the same group, such as florists and the like.

Women who have husbands are called sārakkhā (protected). If the king has established a penalty for going to a certain woman, she is called saparidaṇḍā (with a penalty). For the last two types, the protected (sārakkhā) and those with a penalty (saparidaṇḍā), just like the men who go to them, those women also commit misconduct (micchācāra) because they have husbands. For the other eight types of women, such as those protected by a mother (māturakkhitā), misconduct does not occur because they have no husband. Misconduct occurs only for the men who go to them because they are protected by mothers and others. Indeed, men are not allowed to go to a woman guarded by any others. Women, however, are only disallowed from going to another man if they are taken as a wife by a certain man. Other (unmarried) women are masters of their own touch. Mothers and others do not guard them for the purpose of enjoying that touch themselves; they merely prevent the approach of men. Therefore, because their touch is not possessed by another, and because it is their own touch, women do not commit misconduct. For men, however, it should be understood that misconduct occurs because they enter a place that does not belong to them and is forbidden by others.

"Bhogena" means by reason of wealth. A woman taken after touching a water bowl is called odapattakinī. Since the word dhaja (flag) signifies only an army, it says "ussitaddhajā" and so forth.

"Bahiddhā vimaṭṭha" means communicated in another place. The phrase "he/she will accomplish that matter" is spoken with reference to the capability to accomplish that task, whether or not that task is actually completed after informing the woman. Even if parents send a message to other parents without the knowledge of the boy or girl, if the three factors consisting of acceptance, inquiry, and reporting back are fulfilled, it should be understood that a Saṅghādisesa offense indeed occurs.

To show that even if one informs the mother or others of the person intended, it still falls within the scope (of the offense), the example "Buddhaṃ paccakkhāmi" (I renounce the Buddha) is cited. It should be understood that this is cited because, although the reversal of words and the reversal of reasons are different, the general nature of reversal is the same. To remove the fault of that example and show conformity with the Sutta, it says "taṃ pana" and so forth. It agrees with this statement.
270:
In the following words, this is the meaning: Just as there is no misalignment (visaṅketa) for a monk who, without informing [the woman] himself, speaks to others such as disciples to have them investigate and then brings back the news; likewise, for a monk who, without informing her himself, speaks to the mother and others for the purpose of informing her, whether those mothers and others complete that task or not, if he brings back even the fact of their silence, there is no misalignment.

She is called a housewife (gharaṇī) because she carries out household duties. The misalignment for a monk speaking to a certain person is like the misalignment of the object (vatthu-saṅketa) in an order (āṇatti) concerning theft (adinnādāna) and so forth. In the phrase 'mūlaṭṭhānañca vasena' (by the power of the original place), the mother and others of the man are called 'mūlaṭṭha' (original source) because they are the primary source in sending the message.

In the Pali, regarding the woman guarded by her mother (māturakkhitā), the phrase 'the mother sends the monk' should be understood as: she sends the monk to her own or her daughter's presence saying, 'May she be the wife of a man of such-and-such a name,' or she sends him to that man or his relatives saying, 'May my daughter be the wife of a man of such-and-such a name.' This same method applies to the rest. Because the method has been stated previously, it is the same as the method stated in the first Saṅghādisesa.

'Ante ekena' means with a single word. 'Ettova pakkamati' means departing from that very place without bringing back the news. The word 'anabhinanditvā' (not delighting) is said in reference to one who practices in such a manner. However, a monk who, even if there is delight, does not inform [the woman] of the message, is said not to be investigating. In the third phrase, 'by the method stated' refers to the method stated as 'he, not delighting in her words,' and so forth. In the Pali, 'having a disciple investigate' means having the disciple investigate, thinking, 'This disciple is capable of speaking to them.' If that disciple, having taken that word, remains silent, for the teacher monk who brings back that news, it should be understood that a Saṅghādisesa is incurred, just like the monk who brings back the silence of the mother and others when they remain silent.

In the fourth round of the Pali, it is stated that 'in the fourth, there is no offense' because it is already implied by the meaning that a monk who goes without mindfulness completes the task, but upon returning, causes a misalignment, there is no offense.
271: 'Kāruka' refers to the five types of workers among carpenters and so forth: the bronze-smith, the weaver, the laundryman, and the barber. Because this kind of work related to the Saṅgha is not the service (veyyāvacca) of laypeople, it is said, 'By such work... there is no offense.' 'Originates from the body' (kāyato samuṭṭhāti) means that for a monk who does not know the regulation (paṇṇatti), or the state of separation (alaṃvacanīyabhāva), or both, the offense originates only through the body. In the remaining two origins (samuṭṭhāna), it is the same way. 'They are separated' (alaṃvacanīyā honti) means that whether it is a woman, a man, or both, because they have abandoned their desire for the status of wife and husband and are completely separated, they are called 'alaṃvacanīya' because it is appropriate to say to them, 'Do not do this,' etc., for the sake of reuniting them again. Or, they are called 'alaṃvacanīya' because it is appropriate to speak words of reconciliation to those women and men. The meaning is that they have already given up and do not approach each other without the word of a reconciler. In the phrase 'knowing the regulation,' one should also say 'knowing the state of separation.' Therefore, in the Mātikā Commentary, it is said, 'knowing both,' etc. If a monk is given a letter (paṇṇa) where one's desire is written without letting the monk know, and he is told, 'Give this letter to such-and-such a person,' the act of being a go-between (sañcaritta) does not occur for the monk carrying it. This is because this training rule is 'asittaka' (without specific intent) only in terms of not knowing the regulation and the state of separation. It is not 'asittaka' in terms of being completely ignorant of the act of being a messenger. In the Pali and the Commentaries, only the act of informing is shown. Therefore, it should be understood that an offense occurs only for a monk who, knowing the meaning, informs by showing the letter, or by body, or by speech. 'In whatever manner in whatever districts' shows the fixed methods in various regions, such as giving a letter or informing relatives and authorities, to make the state of separation clear. This is said regarding those taken as permanent wives. For women who associate by their own choice and for prostitutes who associate for a moment, the mere turning away of the mind (dispassion) from the man is to be understood as the cause for the state of separation. In the word 'duṭṭhullādīsu,' the word 'ādi' includes 'attakāma' (desire for one's own pleasure) and 'sañcaritta.' Here, although the Pali does not specifically show human women and human men by saying 'a woman means a human woman, not a female yakkha,' etc., since only human women are shown by 'ten types of women protected by their mothers,' etc., the men suitable for them should also be included.
272:
In this context, only human women and men are intended. Therefore, for those among whom the act of acting as a go-between is performed, these five factors are present: their being of human birth, not being a person who should be rejected (na nālaṃvacanīyatā), acceptance, investigation, and reporting back.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Acting as a Go-between is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Building a Hut

In the explanation of the sixth training rule, the Kuṭikāra Sikkhāpada, the word "ettakena" means 'with this much wood and so forth.' "Aparicchinnappamāṇāyo" means 'having unmeasured quantities of wood and so forth.' "Mūlacchējjāya" means 'by way of making it one's own property by severing it from the ownership of others.' For a monk who asks in this way, there is an offense of wrong-doing for intimation from a non-relative (aññātakaviññatti dukkaṭa) and an offense of wrong-doing for accepting a slave (dāsapaṭiggahana dukkaṭa). This is because it is rejected in the Commentaries based on the Sutta passage: "He abstains from accepting female and male slaves."

"Sakakammaṃ" refers to the act of killing living beings (pāṇātipāta). Asking for such an act is stated to be a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) to avoid the fault of killing living beings, not to avoid the fault of intimation (viññatti). The phrase "aniyametvāpi na yācitabbā" (should not be asked for even without specifying) is said to show proper respect (sāmīci). There is no offense for a monk who asks for manual labor with a pure mind. "Yadicchakaṃ kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati" means it is allowable to have it done even without asking, such as by saying, "I ask for manual labor, please give it."

For one who has work done by someone already engaged in their own business, there is no fault of intimation at all; it is only explained analytically to show proper respect. "Sabbakappiyabhāvadīpanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of showing suitability in every respect. Since it was first said, "We will give the price," it is allowable to say, "Give the price." Although the word 'viññatti' or 'price' (mūla) is a general term related to both allowable and unallowable things, it is said because there is no delighting in unallowable things (akappiya-vatthu) when making payment to those whose hired work is finished. "Anajjhāvutthakaṃ" means unpossessed (apariggahita).

In the passages such as "one who wishes to have a bed... etc... or robes made," for one who wishes to have a robe made, if he has it woven by asking for manual labor from non-relative and uninvited weavers, although there is no wrong-doing due to intimation, it should be understood that offenses of pācittiya and dukkaṭa occur as appropriate according to the Cīvaravāyāpana Sikkhāpada (Training Rule on Robe-weaving). "Akappiya-hirañña-suvaṇṇādi na dātabbaṃ" means that even if obtained through allowable means, for the sake of performing manual labor...
273:
It is said that saying "Give money to this person" and giving it is not allowable. Even if no fault is apparent in giving for work already done, they say it is still inappropriate (asāruppa). There is no fault for a monk who has a fee paid indirectly through allowable speech (kappiya-vohāra) for work already done or for work to be done. "Vatta" means conduct; the meaning is that no offense occurs.

"Kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā paṭiggahetabbāni" (having made it allowable, it should be accepted) is said for the purpose of avoiding the destruction of the seed-group (bījagāma) by cutting leaves when making a fly-whisk from a branch, and for avoiding the dust and so forth clinging to that branch which has not yet been formally accepted. If there is no doubt regarding these two, there is no fault in not doing so (as described in the Commentary). Since water in rivers and such is unpossessed, it is said that it is allowable to say, "Bring it." Because of the statement "one should not use what has been brought [improperly]," even if one confesses the wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) incurred through intimation (viññatti), a wrong-doing occurs every time that object is used; it is not allowable for any of the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika).

Because it is stated generally that "manual labor should not be caused to be done by shameless (alajjī) monks or novices," it is not allowable to have any manual labor done for one's own sake. However, if a shameless person performs acts like fanning even when forbidden, there is no fault. It is allowable to have them perform work for a Cetiya and so forth. Here, because it is said "by shameless novices," it should be understood that the characteristic of being shameless, such as "intentionally falling into an offense," is stated as a general description (upalakkhaṇa) primarily with reference to ordained monks. Therefore, for novices who lack those specific offense-characteristics, and for those who claim to be monks but are of bad conduct (dussīla), including those who have stolen the signs of a monk or are merely monks by name (gotrabhū), the characteristic of being shameless should be understood as intentionally not abiding by the prescribed practice (paṭipatti).

"Wrong-doing for one who causes it to be brought" means a wrong-doing due to intimation at the moment of asking, and a wrong-doing due to delighting in the oxen at the moment of receiving. Even if oxen are obtained without intimation for one's own sake, it is not allowable to delight in them, because it is said: "He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares." For this very reason, it is said: "It is not allowable to ask for ownership even from relatives or those who have invited him." In this case, although there is no wrong-doing for intimation, there is still a wrong-doing in asking for and accepting an unallowable object (akappiya-vatthu). "Rakkhitvā" means having protected from dangers like thieves; "jaggitvā" means having nurtured by giving grass and so forth.

However, in the case of relatives or those who have invited him, it is allowable to ask for ownership because a cart is something that may be accepted. Asking for temporary use is allowable in both cases.
274: The meaning is: personal items such as axes (vāsī) and so forth are also permissible; therefore, he said, "This method applies to the axe," and so on. In the case of creepers (valli) and so forth possessed by others, this same method should be applied and understood. The phrase "only in matters sufficient to be heavy property (garubhaṇḍa)" was said with reference to making a request (viññatti). However, regarding the taking of what is not given (adinnādāna), starting from a blade of grass or a stick, for one who takes property possessed by another with the intention to steal, it is indeed theft (avahāra); it should be decided by the value of the property. In the phrase "in creepers and so forth," the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes bamboo (veḷu) and others mentioned in the Pāḷi. In a region where substances like orpiment (haritāla), realgar (manosilā), and cinnabar (hiṅgula) are expensive even in small amounts, in that place, even if the item is smaller than the size of a ripe palm fruit (tālapakka), it is indeed heavy property (garubhaṇḍa), and it is not permissible to request it. "Sā" refers to making a request (viññatti). Among indirect talk (parikathā) and so forth, speaking by way of a roundabout meaning such as "The monastery is very cramped" is called indirect talk (parikathā). Speaking in a way that makes one's desire clear without speaking directly, such as "Is a palatial dwelling not permissible for monks?" is called hinting (obhāsa). Making a sign to bring about the four requisites by performing tasks such as preparing the ground for a monastery and so forth is called making a sign (nimittakamma). "Ukkamanti" means they depart. Because there was a jewel in the neck of that Naga, he is called Maṇikaṇṭha. "Devavaṇṇaṃ" refers to the celestial physical form. In the Pāḷi, in the statement "I have need of the bowl (patta)," the Blessed One caused the monk to speak thus even though he did not need the bowl, by the power of a protective mantra for the sake of well-being. That monk also said, "I shall speak the words commanded by the Blessed One"; therefore, there is no falsehood (musāvāda) for him. Alternatively, this statement "I have need of the bowl" should be understood as having the same meaning as "Give the bowl." This method also applies to "I have need of the jewel (maṇi)." Therefore, it should be understood that there is no fault of speech for others who speak or cause others to speak in such a manner. Plastering with the face turned upwards is called "ullitta"; this is because those who plaster the inside of a roof mostly plaster with their faces turned upwards. Therefore, he said, "plastered inside." Plastering with the face turned downwards is called "avalitta"; this is because those who plaster the outside mostly plaster with their faces turned downwards. Therefore, he said, "plastered outside." "Byañjanaṃ vilomitaṃ bhaveyya" means that because the simple agent term "karontena" (by one doing) is not a synonymous term for the causative agent term "kārayamānena" (by one causing to be made). Therefore, if the explanation (niddesa) were made by expressing the meaning of the term only with the instrumental case as "karontena vā kārāpentena vā" (by one doing or by one causing to be done) in accordance with the heading term (uddesa) "kārayamānena," the wording would be contradictory. Instead of showing it by the power of the term's literal meaning, in order to show the meaning that is established by implication (sāmatthiya), it is stated in the word-by-word commentary (padabhājana) using the nominative case as "karonto vā kārāpento vā" (one doing or one causing to be done). This is the intention. Therefore, he said the words beginning with "atthamat-tam-eva" (only the meaning itself). It means only the meaning obtained by the literal sense of the word and by implication. It should be understood here that the implication (sāmatthiya) is: the duty that should be practiced by a monk who wishes to have something made must also be practiced by a monk who does it himself. "Uddeso" refers to that which is pointed out by way of ownership. "Setakammaṃ" (whitewashing) refers to the act of making a white appearance by applying a thin layer of white clay or lime (sudhā).
275: (That) is not the case; therefore, if the explanation (niddesa) were made by expressing the meaning of the term only with the instrumental case as "by one doing or by one causing to be done" to be consistent with the multiple heading terms (uddesa), the wording would be contradictory. Instead of showing it by the power of the term's literal meaning, in order to show the meaning established by implication (sāmatthiya), it is stated in the word-by-word commentary (padabhājana) using the nominative case as "one doing or one causing to be done." This is the intention. Therefore, he said "only the meaning itself" and so forth. It means only the meaning obtained by the literal sense of the word and by implication. It should be understood here that the implication (sāmatthiya) is: the task that a monk who wishes to have something made completes, must also be completed by a monk who does it himself. "Uddesa" refers to the person pointed out by way of ownership. "Setakamma" (whitewashing) refers to the thin application of white clay or lime (sudhā) to create a white appearance. To prevent doubt as to whether the measurement is exceeded when measured along with that whitewashing, he said "abbohārika" (negligible/not counting). The meaning is that because the whitewashing is not a constituent part of the hut (kuṭi), it does not come under the designation of exceeding the measurement. Desiring to show the method mentioned for the meaning already stated, he said "For it is also said thus" and so forth. In that Pāḷi, instead of saying "by length and by width," the word "vā" (or) which has an alternative meaning is used, saying "either by length or by width"; the intention is to show that an offense is committed even if only one side is increased. "Tihattha" (three cubits) means three cubits by the natural cubit (pakati-hattha). Some also say, "three cubits by the carpenter's cubit (vaḍḍhakī-hattha)." That statement contradicts this Pāḷi: "In which place... it does not come to be counted as a hut." The reason is that even in a hut of three cubits by the carpenter's cubit, a standard-sized bed (mañca) can be easily turned around.
