The statement "or less than four cubits" was also said with reference to the fact that it is not suitable to turn a bed of the smallest standard size. If even in a hut of four natural cubits, a standard-sized bed cannot be turned, then that building is simply not a hut (kuṭi). Therefore, the measurement should be understood as just enough to turn a bed. A standard-sized bed refers to a bed of the very smallest standard size. That bed is either nine spans (vidatthi) or eight spans by the natural span. A bed smaller than that is not sufficient to lie down with a pillow (sīsūpadhāna) and stretch out one's legs. "Less than the measurement" means less than the maximum measurement. This was said to remove doubt as to whether the site designation (vatthudesanā) should be performed even for a hut of the smallest standard size.
276:
The smallest couch, in comparison with the lowest measure, is indeed nine spans or eight spans by the standard span. A couch smaller than eight spans is not sufficient for sleeping with a pillow and stretching the legs. The phrase "even less than the measure" is stated to dispel doubt as to whether the site-marking (vatthudesanā) should be performed for a hut (kuṭi) that meets the minimum measure.

"Kalalalepa" means smearing with some kind of resin, or smearing with red clay and the like to produce colors such as white or red. Therefore, it was said, "only if there is no smearing." By this, it is shown that thick smearing with hardened mud in tanks and the like is included only under the smearing of fine clay, as it falls under the term "smearing." "Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa" refers to the square wooden frame known as the doorpost. In that doorway, the door leaf, along with the upper ring, is leaned upon to close the door.

"Oloketvāpi" means having asked permission, or by the power of the act of asking permission. It should be understood that the sound "apa" has been changed to "o."

In the term "nibaddhagocaraṭṭhāna," the regular path of elephants going to find food is also included. "Etesaṃ" refers to lions and so forth. "Gocara-bhūmi" means the place where meat is obtained. "Na gahitā" means not taken in the sense of being prohibited, or not forbidden. In fact, the feeding grounds of lions and the like are not permanent like those of elephants; wherever there are animals such as cattle and buffaloes, those lions go quickly even to distant places to take food. Therefore, their feeding grounds are not forbidden; only the regular path from their dwelling is forbidden because the path from the lair is permanent. "Other wild animals" refers to wild buffaloes and so forth. "For the sake of health" means to be free from danger. "The remaining places" refers to the sixteen places, such as those dependent on crops. These places should be known as being accompanied by dangers such as being crowded with people, extreme congestion, destruction of the hut, and physical exhaustion. Because of the meaning "they kill in this place," it is called "abbhāghāta." To clarify the meaning already stated as "the house of enemies," it is said "a place made for the purpose of killing thieves."

"Dhammagandhikā" is a chopping block where hands, feet, and so forth are cut off according to the law (daṇḍanīti). "Gandhikā" refers to a piece of wood or a plank on which hands and so forth are placed and cut; it also refers to the place marked by that chopping block. In the Pali, "dependent on the main road" means depending on a large road. "Dependent on a crossroads" means depending on the junction of four main roads. "By cart" means by a cart carrying materials such as bricks and lime.

"Pācīnaṃ" refers to the foundation or base of the dwelling, starting from the ground up to the top, where the structure is to be built. Upon that foundation, walls, pillars, and so forth are established. Therefore, it was said "starting from that," and so forth. Although in this Kuṭikāra Sikkhāpada there is no distinction between preliminary effort (pubbapayoga) and simultaneous effort (sahapayoga) as there is in Adinnādāna, to analyze them, it is done here to show the extent of the destruction of the hut in the phrase "even if destroyed, it should be made again." "For that purpose" means for the purpose of scraping. "Thus made" means making it without the Sangha's approval or exceeding the measure. "Leaf-roofed hut" (paṇṇasālā) refers to smearing the inside and outside of a leaf-roofed hut to prevent grass and leaf dust from falling. With this intention, the word "leaf-roofed hut" is used. Therefore, it will be said later, "he smears the leaf-roofed hut."
277:
In this phrase "even if destroyed, it should be made again," it is said to show the extent of the destruction of the hut. "For that purpose" means for the purpose of scraping the wood. "Thus made" means making it without the Sangha's approval or exceeding the measure. "Leaf-roofed hut" (paṇṇasālā) refers to smearing the inside and outside of a leaf-roofed hut to prevent grass and leaf dust from falling. Therefore, it will be said later, "he smears the leaf-roofed hut."

Intending to complete it only with internal smearing, the phrase "or in internal smearing" and so forth was taught. In the phrase "or in external smearing," the same method applies. "In that hole" should be connected as "when it is placed in the door frame or in the window." "The place of that" means the hole that is the place for that door frame and so forth. "Having enlarged again" means if the previously placed space is small, it is enlarged again by breaking the opening for the door or window. "If it is placed" means having brought the door frame or the window frame and placing it in that hole, whether enlarged or not. "Not connected with the smearing" means the smearing applied all around does not connect with the door frame or window thus placed; it means it does not become one piece. "That" refers to the door frame or the window. "A Saṅghādisesa offense is committed from the beginning" means because the smearing all around was already connected and completed before, the Saṅghādisesa offense is committed even before the door frame and window are placed.

"Only by connecting with the smearing" means that, excluding windows and the like made of bricks, an offense is committed only by connecting with the smearing all around. This is because windows and the like are not places for smearing, or because they are made of bricks. Some also interpret that in windows and the like, an offense is committed only by the smearing connecting with the wall smearing. "In that" means in the leaf-roofed hut. "Smears leaving about eight finger-breadths for light" means that as long as he smears the gap of about eight finger-breadths between the timbers of a wooden wall, he leaves it for light and smears the rest of the wall and the roof; the intention is that there is no offense if he leaves it thinking, "I will smear this gap later." However, if he does not do this but leaves it permanently as a window for light, when the window or door frame is connected, the smearing also becomes connected; to show that in such a case, a Saṅghādisesa offense is committed from the beginning, he said "sace" (if) and so forth. Only a mud wall falls under the category of mud smearing; therefore, he said, "If he makes a wall with mud, if it connects with the roof smearing, an offense is committed." "No offense for both" means because the first monk's smearing was not yet connected, and for the second monk, the state of being intended for himself (attuddesikatā) is not possible.
278:
"āpattibhedadassanatthaṃ" means: "In a place where there is danger, or in a place where there is not enough room for a cart to turn (if one builds), because the site was not announced, and because the measurements were exceeded, a Dukkaṭa offense or a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred." This is for the purpose of showing the classification of the offense.

"aniṭṭhite kuṭikamme" means when the work on the hut, which ends with plastering, is not yet finished even by a single lump of clay. "aññassa puggalassa vā" is said to show that there is no offense for the monk who originally established it. However, for whichever monk receives it, if he finishes that hut, he indeed incurs an offense because of the statement: "If one finishes by oneself what was left unfinished by others, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense," and so on. Even if the work was done previously, from the time it is received, it is considered as being done for one's own benefit. Therefore, the monk who receives it later should have it finished by giving it to the Saṅgha or to novices, etc. "aññassa vā" should be understood as referring only to an unordained person (anupasampanna). Some teachers, however, say: "There is no offense in finishing a hut received from another, because it was not made for one's own benefit from the beginning."

"apacinitabbā" means it should be destroyed down to the dust. "bhūmisamaṃ katvā" means making it level with the original ground.

"leṇaṃ" means a mountain cave. Since there is no plastering of the roof in this cave, it is said: "plastering is not applicable here." Or it is because it is allowed separately. If one applies plaster inside or on the upper part of the cave for the purpose of making paintings, etc., it does not fall under the category of a plastered hut (ullittakuṭi) and is indeed allowable. A specific type of dwelling made of bricks, etc., with a square peaked roof, bound by a single pin, and not too high, is called a "guhā." Even if such a cave-dwelling is large, there is no offense for a monk who plasters it inside and out. "bhūmiguhaṃ" means a tunnel cave.

"aṭṭhakathāsu" means in the commentaries such as the Kukkuṭacchikageha (house shaped like a bird's wing), a grass hut is called a kukkuṭacchikageha; the commentary teachers who further explain that statement say: "the roof with sticks..." and this should be understood by connecting the words. There, "daṇḍakehi jālabaddhaṃ katvā" means making it like a net with sticks placed lengthwise and crosswise, tied with creepers, etc. That state of being plastered inside and out refers only to the roof. It refers only to the plastering of the inside and outside of the roof. It should be understood that the plastering of the roof is the primary factor, because even if there is no plastering on the mud walls, an offense can occur just by the connection of the wall and the roof plastering.
279:
It should be understood that the plastering of the roof is the primary factor because an offense can occur even by the mere connection of the roof plastering. Although the roof plastering is primary in this way, nevertheless, because of the words, "If one lays stones below only for the purpose of being free from termites and plasters above without plastering those stones, it is not called connected plastering; there is no offense," one must certainly desire the plastering of the entire wall in order to connect the roof plastering. This is because if even a part of that wall is not plastered, the roof plastering is not connected. Therefore, it is said, "the plastering is not connected." Here (ettha) refers to the grass hut. Not only in a grass hut, but also in caves (leṇa), guhās, etc., there is no offense even on account of the open space for circumambulation (saparikkamana). By this method, it is also shown by implication that for one who builds a hut for the sake of another, there is no offense even on account of hazards (sārambha), etc.

In that context, to resolve the contradiction with the Pali text, the phrase "yaṃ pana" etc., is stated. The intention here is: for one who builds for the sake of another, such as a preceptor (upajjhāya), etc., there is no offense even on account of hazards, etc. As for the statement in the Pali, "there are three dukkata offenses for the builders," etc., it is not stated to show an offense for one building for another on account of hazards, etc. Rather, it is stated to show an offense on account of not building the hut according to how it was assigned and instructed. In that context, "yathāsamādiṭṭhāya" means: "The monk gives instructions and departs; he instructs, 'Build a hut for me,' and says, 'Let the site be pointed out, let it be without hazards, and let it have an open space for circumambulation.'" The meaning is that the offense is due to building while disregarding the sequence of instructions of the one who ordered it. In some books, after the passage "even if it reaches the characteristics of a hut, for one building for another... there is no offense," the passage "yaṃ pana āpatti kārukānaṃ" etc., is seen; that is more appropriate. If it is so, the intention therein becomes clear.

In saying "there is no offense," it means there is no offense because it is not designated specifically as a dwelling-hut. "For one who builds without having the site pointed out" refers to even one who builds according to the measurements. "Acittaka" means being without intention because of not knowing the regulation (paṇṇatti). There are seven factors: being one of the types such as an internally plastered hut, meeting the minimum measurements, having a site not pointed out, exceeding the measurements, being for one's own use, being a dwelling-hut, and having connected plastering. Or, there are six factors including those such as being in accordance with the measurements.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Building a Hut is Finished.
280:
## 7. Vihārakāra-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the explanation of the seventh training rule on building a monastery, regarding the usage of the word "pūjita," it is stated as "gāmassa vā pūjitaṃ" because the genitive case is desired even in the sense of the agent. The phrase "kāyindriyaṃ sandhāya" (referring to the body faculty) is mentioned to state the existence of a single faculty by referring to the faculty present among the physical faculties. Those teachers also desire the mind faculty (manindriya) for vegetation (bhūtagāma).

"Kiriyato samuṭṭhānābhāvo" means that it does not arise solely from action (kiriya), excluding the non-action (akiriya) which is the failure to point out the site for the monastery. This is because this training rule arises from both action and non-action. In this training rule, in the phrase "bhikkhū vā anabhineyyā," the word "vā" has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya). By that word "vā," it combines both action and non-action, saying, "he should build a large monastery, and he should not bring the monks."

## Vihārakāra-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 8. Paṭhamaduṭṭhadosa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the explanation of the eighth training rule, the phrase "pākārena ca parikkhittaṃ" (and enclosed by a wall) should be connected. In the phrase "gopuraṭṭālakayuttaṃ," a special structure built on walls for the purpose of battle, having a curved shape and provided with arrow-slits, is called a "watchtower" (aṭṭālaka).

"Soḷasavidhassa" refers to the sixteen-fold tasks consisting of full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriya), and development (bhāvanā), which are to be performed respectively regarding the Four Noble Truths through the four paths. "Te gāravena" means that those exhausted monks, showing their tired bodies in front of the monks assembled at the place of food-allocation, did so out of respect (meaning, out of shame). "Terasapi" means there are thirteen types by virtue of the appointments (sammuṭi) of: food-allocator (bhattuddesaka), lodging-assigner (senāsanagāhāpaka), storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), robe-receiver (cīvarapaṭiggāhaka), robe-distributor (cīvarabhājaka), congee-distributor (yāgubhājaka), fruit-distributor (phalabhājaka), food-distributor (khajjabhājaka), disposer of minor items (appamattakavissajjaka), undergarment-assigner (sāṭiyagāhāpaka), bowl-assigner (pattagāhāpaka), attendant-sender (ārāmikapesaka), and novice-sender (sāmaṇerapesaka).

In the Pāḷi, the word "apisu" is a particle with the same meaning as "apica." "Evaṃ sabbapadesu" means it should be understood that he causes them to speak by determining each individually in all lodgings such as benches, etc., and in times of agreement, entry, and exit, etc.
281:
It should be understood thus. The statement 'This is the nature of created forms (nimmita)' is spoken by way of created forms that are not specifically determined. However, if one specifically determines them, saying, 'Let this many forms speak this and that matter, let this many remain silent, let them perform various postures and actions, and let them have various colors, shapes, ages, and origins,' and then performs the preliminary work, enters into concentration, emerges, and determines it, then they become exactly as desired, in various forms, even differing from one another. "Avatthukavacana" means useless speech.

"Ekacārikabhatta" refers to food that is to be reached individually according to seniority so that all monks may receive it, as it is very desirable. "Taddhitavohārena" means by way of derivative usage, such as 'it is called a quartet (catukka) because it has four measures.' "Bhavo" has the meaning of 'that which should be' (bhavitabba). "Atītaṃ divasabhāgaṃ" (the past part of the day) is spoken referring to the moment of drawing lots on that very day. The meaning of the word "hiyyo" (yesterday) is just "ajja" (today). For that reason, they said, 'Tomorrow we,' and so on. "Padhūpāyantā" means fuming by virtue of repeatedly arising anger. In the Pāḷi, "kissa maṃ" means 'for what reason, me?'

Making 'Do you remember?' (sarasi tvaṃ) into one sentence, and making 'doer' (kattā) into a word ending in the -tu suffix in the sense of the agent, and making it into one sentence with the added word 'are' (asi), the phrase 'of such a nature' (evarūpaṃ) and the phrase 'as this nun said' (yathāyaṃ bhikkhunī āha) should be applied respectively to the two sentences; to show this, he said 'Alternatively' (atha vā), etc. 'Straightforwardly indeed' (ujukamevāti) means that taking the meaning first by virtue of the word ending in the -tvā suffix is straightforward (appropriate).

To show that the second word 'dabba' is a synonym for 'wise' (paṇḍita), etc., he said, 'Dabba, are you not wise (dabba)?' "Nibbeṭhenti" means they release from fault. It means placing the text (tanti) in the domain of the characteristics of Vinaya judgment. In the Pāḷi, in the words 'From the time I was born,' etc., the meaning should be understood as: 'From the time I was born, I have never known sexual intercourse even in a dream, nor have I been a practitioner of that sexual intercourse.' Therefore, he said 'even in a dream' (supinantenapi), etc. Now, to show the connection by virtue of a single sentence, he said 'Alternatively' (atha vā), etc. "Na ghaṭati" means that because the word of this nun does not agree with the word of the Arahant, and because such inconsistency occurred only because of her extremely bad conduct which was well-known among the monks since before, the meaning is: 'Expel (destroy) the nun Mettiyā from the Dispensation.'

"Cara pire" means 'Go, you unloved one, you outsider.' "Vinassa" means 'Go to where you cannot be seen.' "Akārikā" means one who is not made (guilty) by a groundless accusation. "Kārako" (means)...
282:
If she is expelled by this confession, 'I have been corrupted by the noble one,' then the Elder becomes the perpetrator of that fault because the fact of him being a corrupter of a bhikkhunī is established. 'He is not the perpetrator' means he is not the perpetrator because the Blessed One, without regarding the confession made by her, said generally, 'Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiya.' For if the Elder were the perpetrator, [the Blessed One] would certainly have said, referring to that very fault, 'Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiya for such and such a reason.' Since He did not speak thus, and since He did not say 'Investigate the Elder Dabba' but said 'Investigate these monks,' it is established by implication that the bhikkhunī Mettiya deserved expulsion for another fault, that the case was groundless, and that the Elder was not the perpetrator.

'One's own Sutta' refers to the fraudulent (fabricated) Sutta accompanied by this inserted phrase, 'by one's own confession.' In the phrase 'the Elder is the perpetrator,' the meaning is this: In your view, the Elder is the perpetrator because the expulsion of that bhikkhunī was enjoined only in the context of the incident that occurred, where [the Blessed One] said generally 'Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiya' without saying 'by one's own confession.' However, if it is said 'by one's own confession,' then in our view, the Elder is not the perpetrator because it is established that she should be expelled by her own confession for a pārājika offense already established previously. In the view of the Mahāvihāra dwellers also, when it is said 'by one's own confession,' the expulsion of that bhikkhunī is enjoined only in the context of the incident that occurred, and not generally.

'Herein' means in these two views or in the Suttas. 'That which was said later' means the statement made by the Mahāvihāra dwellers is appropriate. 'This has been investigated' means the appropriateness of this latter view has been investigated; it is decided by the method to be mentioned: 'Therein, the saṅghādisesa is one that leads to rehabilitation... she was expelled only because of impurity.' The view of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is shown by the words: 'If one accuses a bhikkhunī, there is a dukkaṭa.'

'Therein' means among those dukkaṭa and pācittiya offenses. Having shown the meaning of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā view which says 'dukkaṭa,' the phrase 'also in the latter method' etc. is said to show the meaning of the Kurundī view which holds it to be a 'pācittiya.' 'By the authority of the word' means that although the intention to deceive is the same, it is by the power of the word prescribing saṅghādisesa etc. in specific cases such as accusation. 'A dukkaṭa for a monk because of a bhikkhunī' means a dukkaṭa offense for a monk who accuses a bhikkhunī.
283:
Having thus clarified the meaning in both Aṭṭhakathā statements, the phrase "But therein" etc., is said to point out the fault in the later pācittiya view and to establish only the earlier dukkaṭa view. In that statement, "separately" (visuṃ) means a separate pācittiya from the pācittiya mentioned in the rule on deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda); the meaning is that it is included within that musāvāda-pācittiya. "Therefore" means because a separate pācittiya is prescribed for groundless accusation, therefore the earlier method, the dukkaṭa view, is correct. Having thus shown the dukkaṭa and pācittiya views that intervened, the phrase "Likewise the nun" etc., is begun to clarify the evident meaning. In that phrase, "likewise" means just as saṅghādisesa and dukkaṭa are mentioned for a monk who accuses a monk or a nun. "There is no expulsion by these" is said generally; the meaning is that there is no expulsion for this nun by an offense of wrongdoing. "Immoral" (dussīlā) means one who has committed a pārājika.

"By the difference in manner" means by the difference in the manner of being corrupted and the manner of the corrupter. "Dissatisfied" (anabhiraddho) means one who is not pleased. Therefore, it is said "not happy" (na sukhito). "Not appeased" (na pasādito) means one whose confidence has not been inspired. The word "khīla" (obstruction) expresses a state of hardness and is also a synonym for rubbish; therefore, it is said "mental... obstruction." "Not satisfied" (nappatīto) means not reached or approached by joy, happiness, etc. Therefore, it is said "not approached" (na abhisaṭo).

In the phrase "by which he is malicious and by which he is angry," it should be connected as: "that by which he is said to be malicious and that by which he is said to be angry" is mentioned both in the Mātikā and the Padabhājana. "By two" means by the two words "anger" (kopa) and "malice" (dosa) mentioned as "by that anger and by that malice"; however, in terms of meaning, only hatred (dosa) is shown by both; therefore, it is said "it shows only the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)." "By which" (yāyā) means by the state of being displeased.

"Not by way of the accused" means if "groundless" were intended also by way of the accused, the Padabhājana would say "groundless means not having committed [the offense]." "Which pārājika" means any one of the nineteen pārājikas suitable for a nun. However, in the Padabhājana, taking only those that appear in the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga, it is said "by any one of the four." "This is not the standard here" means the fact of whether this offense is committed or not is not a factor in this context.
284:
In this matter of groundless accusation (anuddhaṃsana), whether an offense is committed or not is not the factor; rather, the intention to cause a fall (cāvanādhippāya) from the Dispensation is the factor here, whether the person has committed an offense or not, based on the perception of purity such as 'this person has not committed an offense, he is pure,' or based on doubt.

By the word 'tatheva' (likewise), it refers to the meaning of hearing with a clear ear (pasādasota) or with the divine ear (dibbasota). Suspicion that arises from following what was seen is called diṭṭhapariśaṅkita. The same applies to the remaining types, such as sutapariśaṅkita. The phrase 'even without seeing' is spoken by way of the highest case (ukkaṭṭhavasena); there is no fault even for those who depart after seeing. 'Imesaṃ' means 'by these monks.' The phrase 'they will do' shows the manner of occurrence at that moment; later, however, one accuses (codanā) with suspicion, thinking, 'What did they do during this much time?' There is no such accusation as 'they will do.' The phrase 'the ariṭṭha medicine should be drunk' shows the sign or reason for the smell of liquor in the mouth. Ariṭṭha is an allowable medicine with a color and smell similar to liquor.

In the passages beginning with 'diṭṭhaṃ atthi samūlakaṃ,' it shows the presence or absence of grounds for the possibility or impossibility of transgression (ajjhācāra). The passage beginning with 'atthi saññāsamūlakaṃ' shows the presence or absence of grounds for the possibility or impossibility of the perception of what was seen. In the phrase 'accuses with the perception of having seen only after seeing,' it also includes one who, seeing someone other than the person they are accusing committing a transgression or emerging from a concealed place, accuses them with the perception that 'this is that person.' The same method applies to hearing (suta) and so on. In the phrase 'either with grounds (samūlaka) or based on perception (saññāsamūlaka),' one who accuses a person who has committed a pārājika with grounds such as seeing, and with the perception of impurity thinking 'this person has committed an offense,' is said to accuse with grounds (samūlaka). Since non-offense (anāpatti) is possible only when it is based on perception (saññāsamūlaka), one who accuses a person—whether they have committed an offense or not—with the perception that they have, or who has the perception of seeing or hearing regarding grounds that were seen or not seen, and accuses that person based on those grounds of seeing etc., is said to accuse based on perception (saññāsamūlaka). For these people, there is no offense. The meaning in the case of an offense (āpattivāra) should be understood by the reverse of what has been stated.

'Standing nearby' means standing within the range (upacāra) of sight and hearing where hand gestures and vocal sounds made for the purpose of accusation can be perceived. Some teachers say, 'standing within twelve cubits,' but that is not appropriate. When showing non-offense by the opposite later on, it is only said, 'by sending a messenger, a letter, or a message.' It is not said, 'there is no offense for one who accuses beyond twelve cubits.' 'Vācāya vācāya' (word after word) means that for a person who has been commanded once and speaks the whole day, an offense occurs for the commander for every single word. And that person who was commanded, without saying 'I myself have seen' etc., but knowing it is groundless and with the intention to cause a fall...
285:
For every word spoken by the person who speaks all day having been commanded once, the offense falls only upon the monk who gave the command to accuse. That commanded monk also (incurs an offense). Even if that commanded monk does not say 'I myself have seen' etc., but knowing it is 'groundless' and with the intention to cause a fall, says 'You have committed a pārājika dharma,' speaking generally as if it were not another's words, he still incurs a saṅghādisesa. However, even if there is the intention to accuse, if he merely repeats what another said, saying 'Such-and-such a person said this,' there is no saṅghādisesa for that monk. If he says that another person said it when they did not, then an offense is indeed committed.

In the phrase 'sambahulā sambahule sambahulehi vatthūhi,' by specifying the plurality of the accused (cuditaka) with 'sambahule,' it is intended to show that in the previous three rounds (vāra), there can also be different rounds due to the plurality of the accused. Indeed, this fourfold set (catukka) is taught based on the distinctions of the accused, the matter, and the accuser in a single case. Because another fourfold set can be obtained through the plurality of the accused, it becomes an eightfold set (aṭṭhaka).

In connection with groundless accusation, the section beginning with 'But who is allowed to accuse?' (codetuṃ pana ko labhati) is started to show the characteristics of an accusation with grounds. In the sutta beginning with 'Having heard from a monk, he accuses,' those who reveal the failure (vipatti) of others to the accuser also reveal it while standing in the position of an accuser at that moment. Having taken their words, another accuser is allowed to accuse himself and to make the one who does not admit it confess by confronting them with those first accusers, ending with the disciples of other sects. Therefore, it should be understood that they are brought forth here as witnesses.

In the phrases such as 'a messenger or,' it refers to one who is able to accuse by sending a messenger, saying 'You go and accuse in this way,' or by sending a letter or a verbal message. 'Samayena' means at the moment of knowing naturally.

'Of the two grave ones' (garukānaṃ dvinnaṃ) refers to the pārājika and saṅghādisesa offenses. Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is the ten-based view occurring in the manner of 'there is no result of giving' and so on. The view that holds to an extreme, known as eternalism and annihilationism, is called antaggāhikadiṭṭhi. 'The six prescribed for the sake of livelihood' (ājīvahetu paññattānaṃ channaṃ) are the six training rules that might be transgressed for the sake of livelihood. These are: the pārājika regarding superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), the saṅghādisesa regarding acting as a go-between (sañcaritta), the thullaccaya incurred by saying indirectly 'The one who lives in your monastery is an Arahant,' the pācittiya incurred by a monk requesting superior food...
286:
The pāṭidesanīya offense for requesting fine food from a bhikkhunī, and the dukkaṭa offense for requesting soup and rice (supodana-viññatti)—these six training rules mentioned in the Parivāra are not laid down solely for the sake of livelihood (ājīva), because they can also be committed through other means such as acting as a go-between (sañcaritta), etc. This statement is made with reference to committing these offenses for the sake of livelihood; the meaning is that they are also laid down for the sake of livelihood. Not only these six, but there are also other offenses to be committed for the sake of livelihood through theft (adinnādāna), corrupting families (kuladūsana), killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), practicing medicine, and so on. However, it should be understood that those offenses are not mentioned separately because they are included within the six classes of offenses such as pārājika, etc., by way of being of the same nature.

The phrase "the head does not come this far" is said with reference to the saṅghādisesa offense; however, the accusation (codanā) has indeed been made. "Tiṃsāni" means that among those three hundred, there are thirty; it means there are more than thirty. In the word "navutāni," the same method applies.

In the phrase "attādānaṃ ādātukāmena," the accusation is called "attādāna" because it is taken up by oneself, because it is taken up based on grounds such as what is seen (diṭṭha), etc., and because it is held firmly without giving the other person a chance to struggle. "Ādātukāmena" means desiring to take up that accusation, or desiring to make an accusation.

"Ubbāhikāyā" means the ubbāhikā-committee, which is so called because it removes (ubbahanti) the threats or disputes of shameless persons (alajjī) by means of this authorization; it refers to the authorization of the Saṅgha. "Settlement" (vinicchaya) means the settlement by the monks authorized by that committee. In a gathering where shameless persons are numerous, two or three monks endowed with the ten qualities mentioned in the Samathakkhandhaka should be authorized by the formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiya-kammavācā) as stated in that same Samathakkhandhaka. Those authorized monks should settle that legal process (adhikaraṇa) either by sitting separately or by announcing to that assembly that "no one else should say anything."

"Kiṃhi" means on what basis, or in what failure (vipatti). The phrase "kiṃhi naṃ nāma" is a question for one who is unable to understand, due to lack of skill in the Vinaya, even when asked in any easily understood language, "By what failure do you accuse this person?"—thinking, "Is he asking me whether it is a failure of virtue (sīla-vipatti), a failure of conduct (ācāra-vipatti), a failure of view (diṭṭhi-vipatti), or a failure of livelihood (ājīva-vipatti)?" It is not a question for one who does not know the mere literal meaning of the words such as "kiṃhi." Indeed, an investigator (anuvijjaka) does not question a foolish accuser in an unfamiliar language by saying "kiṃhi naṃ." This statement, "Do you not even know 'kiṃhi naṃ'?" is also not said with reference to the mere words...
287:
When it is said, "By what failure (vipatti) do you accuse?", it should be understood as referring only to the meaning of the statement that one does not know how to say, "I accuse by such and such a failure." Therefore, it will be said later, "A method should be given to a foolish but conscientious (lajjī) person." Having said that, the giving of a method is mentioned only to clarify the meaning, such as "In what do you accuse him? I accuse him in the failure of virtue (sīlavipatti)," and so on. It is not merely to show the synonyms of the words "kiṃhi naṃ."

Indeed, even if a foolish accuser knows the meaning of the question "In what failure do you accuse him?", he is unable to know the different types of failures or the specific nature of the failure he is accusing. Therefore, only by such ignorance should the shameless person (alajjī) be subdued. This phrase "kiṃhi naṃ" is also a mere illustration (upalakkhaṇa). One should be released only after demonstrating one's lack of skill through any other indefinite manner.

Because it was taught, "For the restraint of ill-behaved persons (dummaṅkūnaṃ)," etc., it is said, "It is laid down... for the sake of restraining the shameless (alajjī)." In the word "ehiti," the syllable "hi" should be understood as an augment (āgama); it means "he will come." "Diṭṭhasantānena" means by the way of what is seen (as perceived).

"It should be done only with the confession of the shameless person" means that even if the fault is evident through the sequence of questions and answers, the disciplinary action for the offense should be taken only with the confession (paṭiññā) of the shameless person, admitting "I am impure."

Some teachers, however, say, "The meaning that 'the offense is not committed only with the pure confession that the shameless person does not have this fault' is included here." That is not appropriate, because the role of the investigator (anuvijjaka) would then be useless, and the accuser himself would have to rely on the confession of the shameless person. Here, "confession" (paṭiññā) is intended only as an admission of the fault. Therefore, it will be said later, "He does not give a confession that 'I do not have this [fault] either'," and so on.

"Tadattha-dīpanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of showing that even if the fault of the shameless person is evident, the action must be taken only upon his confession of the fault. Those who are opponents in the matter known as a dispute (vivāda-vatthu) are called "atthapaccatthikā." "Giving a sign" means making a sound for the purpose of interrupting their talk or for the purpose of making them face [the assembly].

"Unfit to settle" is said with reference to the inability to investigate because one has entered the side of the accuser with the perception that "he is impure," thereby being outside the status of an investigator (anuvijjaka). Indeed, investigation is possible only when there is doubt. If there is a fixed view that "he is impure," everything said by the accused (cuditaka) appears as if it were untrue; in such a case, how could there be an investigation?
288:
With the words "He will be one destroyed in that way," it is shown that, without giving a decision, separating him from the Saṅgha is a type of destruction (nāsana), similar to the destruction of the marks (liṅganāsana). "Viraddhaṃ hoti" means falling into an offense suddenly while knowing it. "From the beginning, there is no such thing as a shameless one (alajjī)"—this statement is the reason for the occurrence of the characteristic of a shameless one, namely, "he does not give his acknowledgment in order to protect his faction." From the time he conceals the offense, he is indeed called shameless; it means he no longer protects his previous state of being conscientious (lajjī). Not giving acknowledgment means he does not give his consent, thinking, "If I speak of the fault I have committed, the monks who follow me will be divided." "Ṭhāne na tiṭṭhati" means he does not stand in the place of conscientious persons; the meaning is that there is simply transgression by body and speech. Therefore, it is said, "A decision should not be given." Even if a legal issue was previously settled by the acknowledgment of the factions, because it was poorly settled, the meaning is that this monk will also be one destroyed in that way.

"Knowing the practice regarding the accused and the accuser" means knowing the procedure to be practiced by the inquirer (anuvijjaka) towards the accused and the accuser, as stated in words such as "Will you be satisfied with our decision?" and so forth. "Vinicchayo majjhe" means in the middle of the inquiries that will end with a decision of either an offense or no offense.

Because they speak of what is groundless as if it had a ground, it is said, "two grounds." In words such as "I will speak at the proper time," a monk who speaks after asking for permission is said to speak at the proper time. A monk who accuses in places such as where voting tickets are given, where congee is served, or where alms are collected, is said to speak at an improper time. A monk who speaks with the desire to make one rise from a fault is said to speak words connected with benefit. "Dosantaro" means having a mind of anger. "In the fifteen factors" refers to: having pure bodily conduct, pure verbal conduct, a mind of loving-kindness towards fellow celibates, being very learned, well-mastering the two Pātimokkhas, and the five factors taught as "I will speak at the proper time," etc., along with compassion (kāruññatā), desiring benefit (hitesitā), sympathy (anukampatā), making one rise from an offense (āpattivuṭṭhānatā), and placing the Vinaya at the forefront (vinayapurekkhāratā). These are the fifteen factors. Among those fifteen, by the word "kāruññatā," compassion (karuṇā) is shown. "Hitesitā" means seeking benefit. "Anukampatā" means connecting one with that benefit; by these two, loving-kindness (mettā) is shown. "Āpattivuṭṭhānatā" means establishing one in a state of purity. Accusing regarding the matter, reminding, obtaining acknowledgment, and performing the legal act according to the acknowledgment is called placing the Vinaya at the forefront (vinayapurekkhāratā).
289:
"Adhikaraṇaṭṭhena" means a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) in the sense of being something that must be dealt with excessively, or in the sense of being something that must be settled by means of settlement (samatha). The phrase "taṃ nānattaṃ dassetuṃ" (to show that distinction) is used to show that distinction by way of extracting the meaning, even if it is not required in this training rule. This is the intention. Therefore, it will be said later, "The remaining ones are stated by way of extracting the meaning." By the words "yaṃ adhikicca," etc., the state of the word "adhikaraṇa" as a passive derivative (kammasādhana) is stated.

"Gāha" (grasping) means the taking up of the manner of accusation with the mind, as in "I will accuse such and such a person." "Cetanā" (intention) means the mental action known as the exertion of the mind that has arisen, thinking "I will accuse." "Akkanti" (intolerance) means the inability to endure the anger that has arisen upon seeing the failure of the accused, or any group of mental states (citta-cetasika) that occurs in that manner. "Vohāra" (usage/expression) means the speech occurring by way of accusation. "Paññatti" (designation) means the name-designation conceived by the mind occurring by way of accusation. "Attādānaṃ gahetvā" means taking up the accusation with the mind. "Taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ" refers to that legal issue characterized by grasping (gāha).

Since intention (cetanā) is momentary and ceases, that intention reaches settlement (samatha); thus, the connection with an undesirable consequence in this context should be understood. Similarly, further on, by the words "he remains silent," the cessation of the expression of speech is shown. Therefore, it is said, "That legal issue will reach settlement." Having shown the conclusion made in the Commentaries that "Therefore, designation is a legal issue," and now showing how that very conclusion is rejected by some teachers, and then again refuting that rejection to establish the fact that only the designation mentioned in the Commentaries is a legal issue, the words "taṃ panetaṃ," etc., are said. In that text, "taṃ panetaṃ" is connected with the idea that "this view that designation is a legal issue is contradictory." With the recognition that an offense such as a Pārājika is strictly of an unwholesome nature or an indeterminate (avyākata) nature, the Sutta text such as "the Pārājika offense of sexual intercourse" is cited to show that it contradicts the doctrine that designation is a legal issue. Therefore, it is said, "na hi te... accanta-akusalattā," etc. "Te" refers to the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariya).

In the phrase "amūlakañceva taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ," the words "yañcetaṃ," etc., are said to show that by the word "adhikaraṇa," only a groundless Pārājika is intended. The words "yasmā pana," etc., are undertaken to show that it is appropriate for only the groundless Pārājika offense intended here to be a designation (paññatti). In that text, "yāya paṇṇattiyā" refers to the name-designation produced by the accuser as "one who has become a Pārājika," etc., even towards a person who is pure by nature. "Paññatto" means stated. "Because of occurring in a legal issue" means...
290:
Because it occurs as a verbal expression in the āpattādhikaraṇa (legal issue of an offense), which is merely attributed by the mind even though it does not [physically] exist. Having thus shown the nature of āpattādhikaraṇa as a designation by way of name-designation (nāmapaññatti) in this training rule, the phrase beginning with 'Yasmā vāyaṃ' is now stated to show it by way of meaning-designation (atthapaññatti). 'Paññattimattameva' means it is merely a meaning-designation attributed by the mind to a non-existent object as if it were existent. 'Tañca kho idheva' means that the status of the designation as a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) in the manner described occurs only in this very training rule.

'Eke' refers to certain teachers. 'Taṃ na yuttaṃ' means that the detailed explanation given by some teachers in the commentaries—starting with 'Taṃ panetaṃ methunadhamma-pārājikāpatti'—to establish the ultimate reality (paramattha) such as wholesome states (kusala), while rejecting the status of the legal issue as a designation, is not appropriate. The reason for this inappropriateness is stated starting with 'Ādikammikassa'. By that statement, if an offense were indeed either unwholesome (akusala) or indeterminate (abyākata) in that view, how could there be 'no offense' (anāpatti) for the first offender? For unwholesome states and so on would have arisen for that first offender as well. From the time the Blessed One laid down the training rule, it cannot even be said that 'it is an offense,' because unwholesome states in sexual intercourse and so on occurred even before the training rule was laid down. For that very reason, it would follow that unordained persons (anupasampanna) would also incur an offense, and for sick monks and others, there would be no 'no offense' (anāpatti) through the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti).

If it is argued, 'It is not merely unwholesome states etc. that are offenses; rather, only those unwholesome states etc. arising in one who knows they are prohibited by the Blessed One are called offenses,' that statement is also baseless. This is because it would follow that there is no offense for one who transgresses sexual intercourse etc. without knowing the laid-down training rule. Furthermore, for an offense characterized by unwholesome states etc., there would be no singularity etc. in a single effort (payoga). It is not that only a single unwholesome state arises for a monk who touches a woman without releasing her from his body for the whole day; nor is it that many unwholesome states arise for a monk who touches many women and then leaves, by which the singularity or plurality of the offense would be determined. Thus, it should be understood that such inappropriate points are summarized and shown.

In that text, 'vatthu' refers to the transgression (vītikkama). That transgression is called 'vatthu' (basis) because it serves as the ground for the conventional designation of an offense. 'Gotta' (lineage/category) refers to a conceptualized commonality (sāmaññākāra) created by excluding the notion of other things like taking what is not given. 'Nāma' (name) refers to the name-designation of what does not [physically] exist. It should be understood that the offense, which is the meaning of the name 'Pārājika,' is indeed a meaning-designation (atthapaññatti).
291:
It should be understood thus. Those [teachers] have cited sutta passages such as 'A dispute-legal-issue (vivādādhikaraṇa) may be wholesome' and 'An offense-legal-issue (āpattādhikaraṇa) may be unwholesome.' Regarding those statements, what should be said here—that the wholesomeness etc. of disputes etc. is taught in a figurative sense (pariyāya)—has already been stated in detail in the Sāratthadīpanī, the commentary on the origin of the first Pārājika, for the purpose of correcting erroneous points. Therefore, that statement should be taken from that very commentary on the first Pārājika. The view of the author of the Sāratthadīpanī is that 'an offense is indeed of an unwholesome nature etc.' For that reason, even in this training rule, he showed his own view as if it were the view of the Commentator, disregarding the contradiction with the texts, by saying: 'Therefore, having shown the conclusion in the commentaries that it is a designation-legal-issue (paññatti-adhikaraṇa), now, to show that this [conclusion] is also inappropriate, he said "Taṃ panetaṃ" etc.' In truth, in this training rule, Venerable Buddhaghosa did not begin the passage 'Taṃ panetaṃ' etc. to show that the commentary's view is inappropriate. Why? Because he himself says later: 'It should be understood that the offense-legal-issue is merely a designation.' Rather, seeing the distorted view of some people with wrong views on that matter, he began [the passage] wishing to refute that view once more. Therefore, it should be understood that 'Eke' (some teachers) is mentioned at the end.

If disputes etc. were wholesome etc., then the settlements (samatha) that pacify them would also partake of that nature. This is because it is not appropriate to settle ultimate realities (paramattha) by means of a designation. Therefore, it is said, 'by wholesome settlements etc.' Only the four legal issues (adhikaraṇa) which are of the nature of designations are to be settled by settlements. However, those [legal issues] that are of the nature of ultimate realities like wholesomeness etc. are not to be settled. This is because those ultimate realities, being momentary (khaṇika), reach settlement on their own. Thus, wishing to show the meaning established below as a conclusion, it is said: 'Thus, because of this meaning of legal issue.' The meaning of that statement is: because of the state of being settled by settlements in the manner already described. By the phrase 'Here, a certain person,' he refutes unnecessary disputes in this matter.

'Anuvāda' (accusation) consists of both reproaching (upavadanā) and charging (codanā) with failures (vippatti). Among those two, 'upavadanā' means blaming and reviling. The phrase 'the five also' is said with reference to the offenses included in the Mātikā. 'Kiccayatā' means the state of what is to be done. In the term 'Sapadānukkamaniddesassa,' 'padānukkamaniddesa' refers to the word-by-word commentary (padabhājaniya). The meaning is: of the training rule together with that word-by-word commentary.

The word 'assa' is a genitive case used in the sense of the agent (subject); thus it is said, 'by that accuser' etc. The phrase 'But in what is based on what is seen' is said with reference to the canonical section beginning with 'Ajjhāpajjanto'. In that text, that accuser sees the person committing a Pārājika offense merely by seeing [the act of] sitting in a secluded place with a woman etc. He does not see it by way of seeing [the act of] inserting his own organ into the other's organ etc. If that accuser had seen that person in such a manner, this accuser would certainly have the perception that the person is impure. Having the perception of impurity...
292:
## The word beginning with 'Ajjhāpajjanto'

This is stated with reference to the Pali passage beginning with 'Ajjhāpajjanto' (Pārājika Pali 387). In that Pali, the accusing monk sees the person committing a Pārājika offense merely by seeing them sitting in a secluded place with a woman, but he does not see it by way of seeing the insertion of the path into the path (sexual intercourse), etc. If the accuser had actually seen the person in such a manner, he would only be one who perceives that person as impure. For one who accuses a person, whether pure or impure, while perceiving them as impure, there is no Saṅghādisesa offense, according to the words: 'There is no offense for one who perceives the pure as impure, or for one who perceives the impure as impure' (Pārājika Pali 390).

Therefore, even if one only sees the sitting in a secluded place with a woman, if one who perceives that person as pure or is doubtful, thinking, 'This is a faithful son of good family, he would not commit a Pārājika,' yet accuses him definitively, saying, 'I heard he committed a Pārājika,' etc., then only for such an accusing monk is there a Saṅghādisesa offense; it is not so for a monk who perceives the other as impure. For that monk, it should be understood that there is only a light offense (lahuka āpatti) due to lying, such as saying he saw or heard.

If that monk, while perceiving the person as pure, intends to make him fall from the monkhood but speaks only of the seen sitting in a secluded place, and does not speak of the unseen Pārājika matter such as the insertion of the path into the path, or say 'You are no longer a monk,' etc., there is no offense for him. However, for one who speaks excessively, there is certainly an offense because it is said, 'He says he saw what was not seen' (Pārājika 386-387).

Some teachers say that if a monk, perceiving another as impure regarding the first Pārājika based on the seen sitting in a secluded place, etc., and with the intention to make him fall, says 'I saw' or 'I heard' that he committed the offense of taking what is not given (Adinnādāna), there is no Saṅghādisesa offense for him because he perceives the impure as impure. Other teachers, however, say, 'There is certainly an offense because he does not perceive him as pure regarding the specific Pārājika with which he accuses him.' This statement is appropriate. Thus, it is stated in the Mātikā Commentary (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Explanation of the Duṭṭhadosa training rule): 'Knowing that he has not committed the Pārājika with which he accuses him, and with the intention to make him fall... there is a Saṅghādisesa offense.' In this way, the decision should also be understood regarding the grounds of hearing, etc.

'Aññatra āgatesu' refers to words that appear in the Omasavāda (insulting speech) training rule, etc. 'Avassuta' (leaking/wet) refers to one who is wet with the oozing of misconduct that constitutes a Pārājika matter through the three doors. 'Kasambujāta' (become rubbish) means one who is like refuse, meaning one who is without essence.

'Koṇṭha' means a thief, an immoral person. 'Jeṭṭhababbatikā' is said to be an ascetic devoted to the practice of the goddess Kāḷakaṇṇī; that Kāḷakaṇṇī is said to be the elder sister of the goddess Siri. 'Yadaggena' means for which reason, or by as much reason as...
293:
The meaning is: in the word 'tadaggena', the method is the same. The Elder Mahāpaduma's intention is that the words beginning with 'no kappeti' are spoken only to show the state of being doubtful.

In this accusation (codanā), the intention of one who accuses with an offense, thinking 'I will perform the Tajjanīya-kamma (Act of Censure), etc.,' is called 'kammādhippāya' (intention for a legal act). The intention of one who accuses with an offense in order to make him rise from the offense through the sequence of giving Parivāsa (probation), etc., is called 'vuṭṭhānādhippāya' (intention for rehabilitation). The intention of one who accuses with an offense for the purpose of preventing him from performing Uposatha or Pavāraṇā within the Saṅgha is called 'uposathapavāraṇaṭṭhapanādhippāya' (intention to suspend Uposatha or Pavāraṇā). For one who accuses behind someone's back or for one who insults, there is a Dukkaṭa offense.

In all commentaries, because Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are formal acts of motion (ñattikamma), the suspension of Uposatha or Pavāraṇā can only occur while the motion (ñatti) is being recited, not when it is finished. And that motion is said to be finished when it reaches the syllable 'yya'. Therefore, it is said, 'When it reaches the syllable yya, it is no longer obtainable (to suspend).'

Some say that such a monk is not even a lay follower (upāsaka) because his taking of refuge has also been revoked. By the words 'for one who teaches Dhamma without specifically referring,' it is shown that one who teaches by specifically referring must ask for permission (okāsa). Having confessed the offense of not asking for permission, these five factors are present here: the one he accuses is ordained; he perceives that person as pure or is doubtful; the Pārājika with which he accuses is groundless in terms of seeing, etc.; the accusation or causing of accusation is made to his face, definitively saying 'You are a Pārājika,' etc., with the intention to make him fall; and the accused understands it at that moment.

## The Explanation of the First Duṭṭhadosa Training Rule is Finished.
## 9. Explanation of the Second Duṭṭhadosa Training Rule

In the ninth training rule, in the phrase 'the nun Mettiyā,' although she had been expelled by the destruction of her gender (status), it is spoken by taking her former designation. 'Aññabhāgassa' refers to a portion (category) other than the Elder's human monkhood, namely, the state of being a goat of the animal species. The word 'idaṃ' is spoken generally in the neuter gender.
294:
This ram is the meaning. *Aññabhāga* refers to another portion, which is the state of being a ram of the aforementioned animal species. "That which is connected with another portion is *aññabhāgiya*" is the meaning of the first derivation (*viggaha*). "That which has another portion" is the meaning of the second derivation. Both derivations refer only to the ram. Now, wishing to show in detail the meaning already stated by both derivations, [the commentator] says "Yo hi so," etc. In that Pali, it should be connected as: that ram which is mentioned belongs to another portion, and it receives the name *aññabhāgiya*. To show the meaning of the second derivation, "So vā," etc., is said. In the phrase "adhikaraṇanti veditabbo," here too, the ram mentioned as "named Dabba Mallaputta" should be brought in and connected. "Referring to that ram" means referring to the ram that is the basis for the naming as "Dabba." "Those bhikkhus" refers to those bhikkhus who are investigating. Since the offense also has a person as its basis, it is said, "it is only a hint (*lesa*) regarding persons."

Regarding the words "Yā ca sā avasāne...pe... codanā vuttā," it refers to the variety of accusations such as: "A bhikkhu is seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense; he has the perception of *saṅghādisesa* regarding the *saṅghādisesa*; and one accuses him of a *pārājika*," etc. Although the seven classes of offenses are similar in being *pārājika*, etc., respectively, there is also a state of dissimilarity (*visabhāga*) by way of the basis (*vatthu*) such as sexual intercourse or taking what is not given, and by way of nature (*sabhāva*) such as lust, hatred, or living beings; therefore, it is said, "Yasmā pana...pe... na hoti."

"Vuttanayeneva" means by the method already stated, such as "by way of similar and dissimilar bases (*sabhāga-visabhāga-vatthu*)." Because the characteristic of an action (*kamma*) and the attention to that action are the causes of an unimpaired action, it is called "action" by way of metonymy (*phalūpacāra*); thus it is said, "because it arises depending on that action." Because *mānatta*, etc., arise depending on *parivāsa*, etc., it is said, "the preceding and preceding," etc.

"Savatthukaṃ katvā" means speaking by making a person the basis (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). "Dīghādino" refers to the appearance or sign (*liṅga*) such as being long or short. "Diṭṭhādino" refers to things such as having been seen before.

"Evaṃ tathāsaññī" means seeing another person's act of sexual intercourse, etc., and having the perception that "this bhikkhu is that person." The factors (*aṅga*) are similar to those stated in the first *Duṭṭhadosa*; however, in this training rule, the clinging to even a slight hint (*lesa*) is additional.

## The explanation of the second Duṭṭhadosa Sikkhāpada is finished.
295:
## 10. Explanation of the First Saṅghabheda Sikkhāpada

In the tenth training rule, "*bahūnaṃ*" refers to those who are unable to make their minds concentrated due to weakness and by resorting to the forest, etc. Because they cannot make an end of suffering in that existence, and because the mere words and syllables, such as learning and memorizing the Buddha's words, are the highest [they can achieve] without attaining the Path, they are called "*padaparama*." "*Abhisambhuṇitvā*" means having accomplished. That which is apart from the Dhamma is called "*uddhamma*." "It is indeed rejected" is said because of the statement: "Bhikkhus, one should not enter the rains-retreat in a place that is not a dwelling." Referring to this very statement, it was also said in the Pali text as "for eight months," etc.

"By the three points" means by the three impure points. Here, because bhikkhus depend on alms-food already cooked among the four classes of families, and because families who do not eat fish and meat are rare, and because it is difficult to prevent the suspicion of fish and meat being mixed in the curries obtained from those families, even the mere maintenance of the bhikkhus' bodies would not be possible. Therefore, the Blessed One did not reject fish and meat entirely, but rejected only that which is impure by the three points. For if the Blessed One had rejected fish and meat entirely, bhikkhus would not eat food suspected of being mixed with fish, etc., even if they were about to die. Then, it would be necessary to allow them to receive and store rice, grain, etc., and to cook for themselves, and to certainly have servants, maids, mortars, pestles, etc., as their requisites, just like alms-bowls. If that were so, it would be a household life like that of the sectarians (*titthiyas*), and it should be understood that it would not be a dwelling for bhikkhus. "*Jāla*" is a net for catching fish, and "*vāgurā*" is a net for catching deer. "It is allowable" means if there is no suspicion because of their words, it is allowable; those words should not be made into a pretext (*lesa*). Therefore, it will be said: "Wherever one is free from doubt, all that is allowable."

"*Pavattamaṃsa*" is meat of a dead animal available for sale in shops, etc. In the phrase "not made specifically for the sake of bhikkhus," the word "*eva*" is merely an expletive without meaning, and it should be connected as "indeed not made for the sake of bhikkhus." Therefore, it should be understood that meat prepared by mixing for both bhikkhus and for weddings, etc., is also not allowable. Some teachers, taking the emphasis according to the Pali as it stands, say "it is allowable," but that statement is not good. By the word "*vatta*," it shows that there is no offense.

"*Kappa*" refers to an *asaṅkheyya-kappa* (incalculable aeon). Some say it is an "*āyu-kappa*" (life-span aeon). One-fourth of a *mahā-kappa* is an *asaṅkheyya-kappa*. One-twentieth of that *asaṅkheyya-kappa* [is said to be the life-span aeon of one who causes a schism in the Sangha].
296:
It is said that one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha (suffers in hell) for the duration of an aeon (āykappa). This statement does not agree with the explanation concerning the aeon (kappa) found in the Commentaries, such as the Vibhaṅga Commentary, which states, "He is released only when the aeon is destroyed (kappavināse)," and so forth. "Brahmam puññam" means noble merit. In the phrase "kappam saggamhi," it should be understood as remaining for an entire aeon through a succession of rebirths.

"Laddhinānāsaṃvāsakena" refers to following the views of one who has been expelled (ukkhittaka); in this definition, the state (bhāva) is the primary focus. "Kammanānāsaṃvāsakena" refers to the state of being an expelled person. Since it is stated separately as "he should strive for a schism," it should be understood that it is appropriate to perform the formal act of admonishment (samanubhāsana) for a monk who strives to cause a schism in the Saṅgha by seeking followers and so forth, even prior to the undertaking and promotion of the legal issue (adhikaraṇa) that leads to the schism. The phrase "yo cāyaṃ saṅghabhedo" is also a connection (of the preceding and following text).

"Kammena" means by way of a formal act such as an apalokana-kamma. "Uddesena" means by the recitation of the Pātimokkha. "Vohārena" means speaking by way of various reasons, such as "proclaiming non-Dhamma as Dhamma," and so forth; it has the meaning of making others understand. "Anusāvanāya" means repeatedly whispering and speaking into the ear for the sole purpose of making others accept one's own view. "Salākaggāhena" means by causing them to take voting tickets (salāka) as a sign of having joined one's own faction, after supporting their minds through such repeated persuasion. In this context, either the formal act (kamma) or the recitation (uddesa) is the primary cause of the schism in the Saṅgha; however, it should be understood that factors such as speech (vohāra) and so forth are the preliminary stages of the schism. "Abbhussitaṃ" means advanced or risen up. "Accheyya" means he should dwell.

Based on the statement, "The shameful one will protect (the rule)," reporting an offense out of fear of the offense is the responsibility only of shameful (lajjī) monks; thus it is said, "by shameful monks." Even for a shameless (alajjī) monk, if he does not report it, an offense is indeed committed. The statement that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for not giving up (the view) refers to the occurrence of a dukkaṭa offense according to the number of monks who speak individually. "Pahontena" means one who is able to go, meaning one who desires to go. The offense should be understood as applying to a monk who is not ill and is within half a yojana.

With reference to the occurrence of dukkaṭa offenses and so forth through the formal motion (ñatti) and so forth, it is said, "there is no offense of Saṅghādisesa." "Assa" refers to Devadatta. Since the formal act of admonishment (samanubhāsana) did not exist before the training rule was promulgated, it is said, "not for one who transgresses a promulgated training rule." This is because the formal act of admonishment was allowed only at the same time the training rule was promulgated. Regarding the phrase "allowed with reference to," it is said with reference to what was allowed specifically, such as, "Monks, I allow the ruminating (chewing the cud) for a ruminating monk..."
297:
...with reference to what was allowed specifically (uddissānuññāta), such as "Monks, I allow the ruminating for a ruminating monk" (Cūḷavagga, 273). "Anāpattiyam" refers to the section on non-offense. "Āpattiṃ ropeṭabbo" means he should be charged with a pācittiya offense through the formal act of admonishment. "Āpattiyeva na jātā" means the Saṅghādisesa offense simply does not arise.

It is called "release through perception" (saññāvimokkha) because one is released from the offense due to the absence of the perception "I do not give it up." "Sacittaka" means it occurs with the mind that knows "I do not give it up." If a monk is unconscious, frightened, or distracted, and does not know that "it should be given up" or that "the Saṅgha will perform a formal act," there is no offense for him. Striving for a schism, formal admonishment according to the Dhamma, the conclusion of the formal motion (kammavācā), and not giving up with the thought "I do not give it up"—these are the four factors here.

## The Explanation of the First Saṅghabheda Training Rule is Finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Second Saṅghabheda Training Rule

In the eleventh training rule, since it is appropriate to perform the formal act of authorization (sammutikamma) such as ubbāhikā even for many monks, it should be understood that the statement "The Saṅgha does not perform a formal act against the Saṅgha" is said with reference to a formal act performed for the purpose of punishment (niggaha). As for the factors here, they should be taken as similar to those mentioned below for the (first) Saṅghabheda training rule, but excluding "striving for a schism" and including "following (the schismatic)."

## The Explanation of the Second Saṅghabheda Training Rule is Finished.

## 12. Explanation of the Dubbaca Training Rule

In the twelfth training rule, "vambhanavacanaṃ" means scornful speech. The word "saṭa" has the same meaning as the word "patita" (fallen); since that qualifying word is placed at the end, it is said, "grass, wood, or leaves fallen here and there." "Kenāpi" means by anyone such as a preceptor who is like the wind.

Persistent anger that overwhelms and binds the mind is called a grudge (upanāha). An attachment to anger (kodhābhisaṅga) that is stronger than that and difficult to release is so named. "Paṭippharaṇatā" toward the accuser means...
298:
Standing in opposition to the accuser is called being hostile to the accuser. Disparaging the accuser (codakaṃ apasādanā) means attacking with words. Counter-accusation (paccāropanā) means charging the accuser with an offense, saying, "You too have an offense." Evasion (paṭicaraṇatā) means concealment. By one's conduct (apadānena) means by one's own actions and behavior. Not explaining fully when questioned (na sampāyanatā) means that when the accuser says, "I saw this person commit an offense," and one is asked about the conduct in such a way as, "What were you doing at that time? What was this person doing? Where were you? Where was this person?" and so on, one does not explain fully despite being questioned.

By this introductory phrase, "If there should be an offense for anyone," all offenses are included; thus it is said, "Yassa siyā," and so forth. In this training rule, the factors are similar to the first training rule on schism in the Saṅgha. However, the distinction in this training rule is that, just as there is an effort to cause a schism there, here, making oneself one who should not be spoken to (avacanīyakaraṇatā) should be understood.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Difficult to Speak to (Dubbaca-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 13. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Corrupting Families (Kuladūsaka-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

In the thirteenth training rule, Kīṭāgiri is the name of that market town. With reference to that market town, it is said later, "The monks Assaji and Punabbhasuka should reside in Kīṭāgiri." The expulsion is only from the village market town, not from the district. Because it is connected to that market town, the district is also counted as "Kīṭāgiri"; thus it is said, "in the district of this name."

"There" means in Sāvatthī. "In the vicinity" means in the place facing it, near the gate of the Jeta Grove; this is the meaning. "By two rains" means by the two rains: the rainy season rain and the winter rain. Because they were more than the six group-leaders, it is said "more than" (samadhika).

"Of water" means of unallowable water. Because "pouring allowable water" will be mentioned separately, and because it will also be said that "in the planting of trees for the sake of a monastery garden etc., even among unallowable expressions, the pouring of allowable water etc. is proper," here also, having made a distinction...
299:
The pouring of allowable water and so forth is shown separately. Just as physical actions such as pounding and digging are included in unallowable expressions, similarly, making a channel straight and so forth are included in allowable expressions; thus it is said, "making a dry channel straight." Here, the removal of old leaves and so forth is also included. Since only the Mahāpaccari view is taken as the standard, it is mentioned later. To show that even among unallowable expressions, some things are allowable, it is said, "not only the rest," and so forth. "Any channel" means whether it is dry or not dry. "Therein" means in the planting of trees for the sake of a monastery garden and so forth. "Likewise" is said with reference to having garlands made through allowable expressions and methods. By this, it is shown that making garlands etc. for the sake of favoring families (kulasangaha) is not allowable.

Wishing to question why making a garland oneself for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem is not allowable, it is said, "Is it not so?" and so forth. The intention of the questioner is: just as planting a tree oneself in allowable ground for the sake of a monastery garden is allowable, why is making a garland oneself for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem not allowable? The words beginning with "It is said" are the answer. If so, why is it said, "But it is not mentioned in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā"? Is not the word mentioned in the Mahāpaccari and others also a standard? This is not a contradiction. It is said because one wishes to establish that the act of planting oneself, which is not mentioned in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, is indeed a standard by way of showing the method of comparison with the pouring of water mentioned in that very Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. The word "should be thought" (maññeyyāsi) should be connected with the words "how is that" (taṃ kathaṃ). The meaning there is: although planting oneself is not mentioned in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, the act of pouring allowable water oneself is indeed mentioned. Therefore, just as pouring allowable water oneself for the sake of a monastery garden is allowable, why is making a garland for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem not allowable? That statement also does not contradict. The statement that rejects making garlands etc. for worshipping the Triple Gem but mentions planting and pouring water oneself for the sake of a monastery garden does not contradict what precedes or follows when compared with the Pāḷi.

When asked how that statement does not contradict, it is said, "Therein indeed," and so forth. "Therein" means in the matter of planting and pouring water. Since it is specified as "flowering shrub" (mālāvaccha) in connection with favoring families with flowers and so forth, it is understood that only planting for the sake of favoring families is intended; thus it is said, "saying flowering shrub," and so forth. "This is said" refers to the statement: "They both plant and cause to plant flowering shrubs, they both pour and cause to pour water." "But in another case" means in the case of planting flowering shrubs etc. for the sake of a monastery garden. "Method" (pariyāya) means the specific meaning of the expression consisting of doing it oneself and causing it to be done.
300:
The phrase 'obtained because there is no benefit of favoring families' is the meaning. In this context, when taking the meaning by way of the power of the word *pariyāya* (method/synonym) as 'doing' and 'causing to be done,' it excludes the stringing and causing to be strung that are prohibited in the Pāḷi text as 'they string and they cause to be strung.' Later, it refers to causing to be strung through allowable (*kappiya*) words such as 'know thus, if done thus it will be beautiful.' In such cases of causing to be strung through allowable methods, the state of being blameless is established. Why? Because 'causing to be strung' is intended only as causing to be done by the command 'string [them]!'

In the phrase 'knowing the presence of a method there and the absence of a method here'—in passages such as 'they plant flower bushes,' because there is the qualifier 'flower bush' which indicates the benefit of favoring families, there is the presence of the method known as doing and causing to be done. In these passages such as 'they string,' because there is no such qualifying word, one should know the absence of that method. The connection (*yojanā*) should be understood as: 'knowing this, that statement is indeed well-said.'

Regarding the phrase 'everything should be understood according to the method already stated,' it means that planting and so on, and causing to be strung and so on, should all be understood only by the method appearing in the Commentaries. The conclusion is: 'one should not have doubt in this matter.'

'In carrying and so on' refers to carrying and so on for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem. 'Because of carrying for the benefit of women and so on' means it is intended that carrying is prohibited specifically when it is for women and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'In the section on carrying,' etc. *Mañjarī* means a cluster of flowers. *Vaṭaṃsaka* is a specific flower arrangement made to be worn above the ear; that specific flower is called '*vaṭaṃsa*.' *Kaṇṇikā* is the name for many flowers or garlands bound together; they also call it an 'ear ornament.' *Hāra-sadisa* refers to something resembling a string of pearls.

'With allowable water' means with *kappiya-udaka*. 'Only of those two' means of the two types: favoring families and personal use. 'Wrongdoing' (*dukkaṭa*) means an offense of wrongdoing is incurred in watering by oneself for the sake of favoring families, or in causing it to be watered through either allowable or unallowable speech. For the sake of personal use, however, a wrongdoing is incurred in watering by oneself or in causing it to be watered through unallowable speech. 'Because of the abundance of effort' means because of the abundance of bodily effort in doing it oneself and vocal effort in causing it to be done.

A garland produced by stringing is called *ganthima*. This same method applies to the remaining types like *geṇṭhima*. 'Not allowable' means it is not allowable even for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem; the meaning is that it is an offense of wrongdoing. 'Allowable' means it is allowable for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem; however, for the sake of favoring families, even for a monk who causes it to be done with allowable speech, it is still only an offense of wrongdoing.
301:
The *Nīpa* flower is the *Kadamba* flower. 'In the same way as the previous method' means according to the method already stated as 'to a monk,' etc.

Regarding everything stated as 'on a banana trunk,' etc., it is said, 'that action is very coarse.' The meaning is that in all cases of doing it oneself or causing it to be done with unallowable speech, there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*). Some teachers say that because the statement 'it is not allowable even to bind a thorn for the purpose of piercing flowers' is an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*), binding with a rope for the purpose of hanging flower garlands, etc., is also not allowable. Other teachers, however, say that because it is specified as 'a thorn for piercing flowers,' it is only the binding of a thorn for that purpose that is not allowable; and that this prohibition should be understood by taking the Commentary as the authority. This point should be accepted after careful consideration.

*Puppha-paṭicchaka* (flower receptacle) is a flower stand made of sticks and so on. This flower receptacle, as well as the *nāgadantaka* (wall peg), should be taken only if they have holes. '*Asokapiṇḍiyā*' means in a cluster of Asoka branches or Asoka flowers. *Dhamma-rajju* (Dhamma rope) is a rope tied around a cetiya or similar object for the purpose of inserting flowers between the cetiya and the rope. It is also said, 'it is tied thus for the purpose of inserting flowers between the loops of a loosely twisted rope.'

*Matthaka-dāma* is a flower garland hanging above a Dhamma-throne (*dhammāsana*) and so on. 'Only of those things' means only of lotuses and so on. 'With fiber or with a stick' means with the fiber that remains attached to the flower after splitting the flower stalk, or by binding it together with a stick. In this way, because flowers are not included among the five types of seeds, they do not fall under the category of 'seed-group' (*bījagāma*), just like leaves. Therefore, there is no fault in destroying them even without making them allowable (*kappiya*).

The opening of a plucked flower bud is not a sign of growth because it cannot happen in a very young bud.
