It is only when the moisture in the petals of a mature bud is exhausted that they separate; this is what is called 'blooming.' Therefore, the blooming of a plucked bud is inferior to the blooming of an unplucked bud, or it is seen to be associated with wilting. The fact that a wilted flower becomes fresh again upon contact with water is not a sign of growth, as it is the same with betel leaves and so on. Furthermore, nowhere in the Pāḷi or Commentaries does it mention the act of making flowers allowable (*kappiya-karana*). Therefore, it is understood that flowers are not seeds (*bīja*) in any way. This point should be accepted after careful consideration.

Because it is said 'as in a bag,' it is established that it is allowable to put flowers in a flower bag, or in a bag-like binding, or in any robe. 'Not allowable to bind' is said with reference to binding with ropes and so on. However, it is indeed allowable to bind flowers with their own unsevered stalks or fibers.
302:
## Regarding the phrase "pupphapaṭe ca daṭṭhabbanti," it is stated with reference to the filling of a flower-garland cloth by a monk through the process of bringing and bringing back the flower garland longitudinally. Carrying it transversely is called a woven garland (vāyima), not a filled garland (purima). Since it is stated generally as "passing the previous spot," an offence is incurred by a monk who passes the previous garland by wrapping it, whether touching or not touching the end of the flowers. The phrase "it is proper to bind" means it is proper to bind at the ends of the threads that are without flowers. The phrase "whether carrying once or wrapping" is stated with reference to the previously mentioned wrapping of a cetiya and the like, as well as the making of a flower-garland cloth.

"Filled by others" means spread out longitudinally. "To weave" means to carry transversely; such carrying is not allowed even once. "A monk who places flowers" refers to placing unstrung flowers so that they touch each other. "Ghaṭikadāma-olambaka" refers to a flower tassel that has a pot-like shape at the bottom, or a hanging ornament in the shape of a wooden pot. The so-called "geṇḍuka" (ball) is made of thread. "In all cases" means in all cases such as knotted garlands (ganthima) and so on.

"Rēcaka" refers to a similar demonstration (abhinaya); it means showing the manner of dancing, saying "dance like this." Some also say it means "making oneself spin like a wheel." "They play only in the sky" means both play while speaking only with the mouth, saying "I have moved this piece to such-and-such a square." "Jūtaphalaka" refers to a gambling board. "Playing with dice" (pāsaka-kīḷā) refers to a gambling game played by making dots, such as one dot and so on, on the four sides of two dice (pāsaka) made of wood, ivory, etc., which are three finger-breadths in size, throwing them on the board, and moving the pieces according to the dots seen on the upper side.

Mañjaṭṭhi refers to the heartwood extract of the madder tree. "Salākahattha" is a name for a bundle of coconut fibers and the like. In the Pali, "tharusmiṃ" refers to a sword (khagga). "Ussēḷenti" means they release a whistling sound with the mouth; it means they produce a loud, indistinct sound. "Apphoṭenti" means they make a sound by striking the folded left arm with the right hand. "Mukhaḍiṇḍima" refers to mouth-drumming.

By the word "tesaṃ," the meanings that are subordinate in the compound are also referred to. "Bondō" means frivolous or of a weak nature. "Frowning" means making a particular movement of the eyebrows. "Nelā" means faultless.
303:
In the Pali, the word "Sāriputtā" is an address to both Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna by the method of ekasēsa (one word representing two); for this reason, it is expressed in the plural.

The eighteen duties (vatta) refer to the eighteen duties found in the Kammakhandhaka of the Cūḷavagga, beginning with "one should not ordain" and ending with "one should not associate with monks." "Na pannalomā" means their hair of pride has not fallen; it means they are those who do not behave compliantly.

The statement that giving another's property is only an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is said with reference to giving by taking on trust (vissāsagāha). In this context, "thullaccaya" (grave offence) can also occur depending on the value of the goods (bhaṇḍadeyya).

By the phrase "and that flower only for the purpose of worshipping the object," it is shown that even a monk giving flowers to his parents should give them only for the purpose of worshipping (the Triple Gem). As for giving for the purpose of decoration or for worshipping the Shiva-linga and the like, since only this much is stated, it is proper to give to parents with the intention that "they will live by selling these flowers"; however, to other relatives, it is proper to give only for temporary use. The phrase "only by novices who are relatives" is stated to free those novices from the work of laypeople. Other novices who are not relatives should also carry them as part of their duties toward their teachers and preceptors. "Cūḷaka" means half of a half (a quarter).

"Novices... place them" is said with reference to things that are not guarded or protected. "In various places" means either on the road or on the cetiya courtyard. The phrase "they are not allowed to have novices give them" is stated because it is like making novices do the work of laypeople; it does not mean giving flowers is allowed for novices, as it is also improper for them. And it has been stated, "by oneself," etc. By the phrase "stated without distinction," it is shown that it is improper for everyone (to give flowers to laypeople).

"To those whose provisions are exhausted" is said with reference to travelers (āgantuka). Even regarding trees that have an owner, a monk who says, "The fruits are good here," etc., is said to be currying favor with families (kulasangaha); therefore, it is said, "one should not speak thus."

"Rukkhasallī" means tree bark. It is called heavy property (garubhaṇḍa) because it is not to be distributed. "By the method stated" shows that giving leaves is also currying favor with families (kulasangaha) according to the method stated for flowers, fruits, and so on.

"Of the kind previously stated" refers to the kind of training rule first mentioned, such as "Worship the feet of the Blessed One with my words," and so on. The phrase "Let the venerable one depart" is...
304:
It is spoken by way of the pabbājanīyakamma (act of banishment). Again, the phrase 'Let the venerable one depart' is also spoken by way of the duties of one for whom the pabbājanīyakamma has been performed. In this training rule, the offenses to be prescribed regarding the many kinds of misconduct (anācāra) practiced by the monks Assaji and Punabbhasuka have already been prescribed in other training rules. Therefore, without prescribing those offenses again in this training rule, it should be understood that this training rule was laid down to restrain those who corrupt families by means of the pabbājanīyakamma, and to impose a saṅghādisesa offense through formal rebuke (samanubhāsana) by a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma) for those who, not conducting themselves properly in that very pabbājanīyakamma, harass the Saṅgha that performs the act by accusing them of being led by favoritism and so on. In the phrase 'It is just like the first saṅghabheda,' among the factors, just as there is effort in that schism, so here the accusation through favoritism and so on should be understood. The remaining factors are just like that schism.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Corrupting Families is Finished.

## Conclusion of the Commentary

The connection is: the other (nine) offenses should be understood as 'up to the third time' (yāvatatiyaka). For a fever that comes and goes in one day, does not arise in the following two days, but arises on the third day, is called a tertian fever (tatiyaka). But a fever that does not arise even on the third day but arises only on the fourth day is called a quartan fever (catutthaka). Referring to such a person, it is said 'as on the third day' and so on. By the words 'unwillingly and without power,' it is shown that because what is called 'not making amends for an offense' (appaṭikammakaraṇa) is a characteristic of the shameless (alajjī) and is an obstacle to heaven and liberation, therefore the person who has fallen into an offense is not allowed to delay, saying 'I will undergo probation later,' and the Saṅgha must give probation even to a monk who is unwilling. In the Pāḷi, 'A monk who has practiced the mānatta... abbhetabbho (should be rehabilitated),' the application of the two words 'monk' should be understood thus: 'The monk who has practiced the mānatta, that monk should be rehabilitated.' Those monks also, knowing the deficiency in the number [of the Saṅgha for rehabilitation], yet perform the rehabilitation; they are to be blamed because of the occurrence of a dukkaṭa offense. 'Proper conduct' (sāmīcī) means the duties of conduct.

305:
## 3. The Section on Indefinite Offenses (Aniyata-kaṇḍa)

## 1. Explanation of the First Indefinite Training Rule

Because the word “son” (putta) is a general designation, or by the method of ekasesa (inclusion of the other gender), it also includes daughters; thus it says “many daughters as well.” “Tad-anantaraṃ” means the period after offering food to the monks.

444-5. “That action” (taṃ kammaṃ) refers to the act of transgression such as sexual intercourse (methuna) and so forth. In the Pali, the phrase “seclusion from the ear” (sota-raho) is stated by way of extracting the meaning. Why? Because in the subsequent second indefinite training rule, by saying “not indeed screened” and so forth, the scope of this first indefinite training rule is excluded, and since it will be stated separately as “seclusion from the ear” which is a different scope, saying “it is sufficient to address a woman with lewd words,” here only “seclusion from the eye” (cakkhu-raho) is intended. Why? Because of the teaching “in a screened seat” and so forth, and because it is said “he is able to practice sexual intercourse.” Therefore, it says “even though” (kiñcāpi) and so forth. “Definition” (pariccheda) means the delimitation of the offense incurred by sitting in seclusion.

Now, to show the delimitation of the offense by seclusion from the eye alone, the phrase “even if” (sacepi hi) and so forth is stated. By the phrase “with the door not closed,” it shows that because of the screened state, only seclusion from the eye is intended here, not seclusion from the ear. Therefore, it says “with the door not closed... there is no offense.” Indeed, by opening the door, seclusion from the ear does not disappear, but only seclusion from the eye disappears. The phrase “even within twelve cubits” is stated to show that there is no offense in any way from the offense of lewd words (duṭṭhullavācā) incurred by seclusion from the ear as mentioned in the second training rule. Indeed, a person sitting outside twelve cubits cannot make it so that there is no offense of lewd words because there is seclusion from the ear in that second training rule. If one considers it in the manner of seeing the non-occurrence of the offense incurred by seclusion from the eye, one should not say generally “there is no offense,” but should say specifically “there is no offense regarding sexual intercourse or bodily contact.” Therefore, it should be understood that “twelve cubits” is mentioned to show that there is no offense in any way without saying it in that manner. Indeed, if it were said with reference only to the state of seclusion from the eye, one would not say “within twelve cubits,” because even if one sits further than twelve cubits in an unscreened place, there is no seclusion from the eye. Because a person who is sitting and nodding, oppressed by drowsiness, opens his eyes at some times and at other times...
306:
This is because there can be no seclusion of the eyes. For a person overcome by drowsiness (kapimiddha) while sitting and nodding may open their eyes at one time and close them at another. Therefore, it is said: "Even while asleep, it causes the state of no offense."

The phrase "one who has attained the fruit of Stream-entry" (Sotāpatti-phala) is stated as the minimum limit. "Admitting to sitting" means admitting to sitting in private with the potential for sexual intercourse, physical contact, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Whether by a Pārājika," and so on. "Not for one who does not admit" means that even if a person is unconscientious (alajjī), if they do not admit it, they should not be judged by the offense alone. In fact, as long as that person does not admit the fault, they should not be called "pure" or "impure," but should be judged only by the consistency of their statements (vattānusandhi). This is stated in the Parivāra: "A confession is made among the conscientious; such a confession does not exist among the unconscientious. Even if the unconscientious speaks much, one should judge by the consistency of the discourse."

In the passage "In sitting and so forth... that bhikkhu should be judged," the word "admitting" (parijānamāno), although not directly in the Pali text, is stated with the understanding that it is included by way of authority (adhikāra).

"Caused to speak" means that although the person was free from doubt due to the Arahant's psychic power, they spoke because they wished to admonish the Arahant. The meaning is: because of sitting in an unsuitable place without investigation, you have caused people like me to speak of your dispraise, saying, "The Elder sits in private on the same seat with a woman"; do not do this again. "He did so" means he did this only to demonstrate the attainment of this special state, which should otherwise be concealed, in order to make you believe. "Protect this Dhamma" means do not reveal this superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) to others.

"Pācittiya for sitting" means a Pācittiya offense is incurred if there is enjoyment of sitting in private. However, if that bhikkhu dispels the enjoyment of sitting in private and his mind is directed elsewhere, such as by attending to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), or if he falls asleep, there is no offense. Therefore, it is said: "When enjoyment has arisen." By the phrase "When the woman is seated," it shows the absence of enjoyment at the moment of sitting. Indeed, if enjoyment arises at the moment of sitting, he must get up. Otherwise, an offense is incurred, just as in the case of a woman repeatedly getting up and sitting down; in that case also...
307: There is no offense for a monk who stands up from his seat. It is said that because of such standing, the offense of sitting in private is also an akiriyasamuṭṭhāna (originating from non-action). Both this Aniyata training rule and the subsequent one are not prescribed separately by way of prescribing an offense, because the offense for sitting in private, etc., has already been prescribed in other training rules. They are prescribed by dividing them into two types based on the story (vatthu) to show the method of judgment for investigators when a monk is accused by someone of offenses such as Pārājika. It should be understood that these rules are not mentioned separately for Bhikkhunīs because they are sufficient for them to grasp the method of judgment. The breach of factors here should be understood according to the offense he confesses. Therefore, it is said, "This rule is indefinite (aniyata)." The three offenses—Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, and Pācittiya—mentioned here by way of being indefinite, are said to have "origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., similar to the first Pārājika" because they have mutually similar origins. ## The Commentary on the First Aniyata Training Rule is finished. ## 2. Commentary on the Second Aniyata Training Rule Instead of saying "He should not sit alone with a woman...", it is said "A woman is forbidden...", etc. To prove that the nominative case "eko" (alone) does not agree with the word "forbidden" and should be said as "ekassa" (of one), he said "itarathā hi" (for otherwise), etc. "Pariveṇangaṇa, etc." refers to the terrace (māḷaka) of the precinct. By the word "etc.", it includes the terrace of a stupa surrounded by a wall, etc. "Antogadha" (included) applies only to un-secluded places. In this training rule, it should be connected that a woman can also act so that there is no offense. Why can a woman act so there is no offense only in this training rule and not in the previous one? Because this training rule comes by way of lewd words (duṭṭhullavācā) other than sexual intercourse (methuna). Women conceal only sexual intercourse from one another, as in the case of the monk who fell asleep with the door open in the Mahāvana. However, they do not conceal lewd words. Therefore, in the Duṭṭhullavācā training rule, it is said, "Those women who are modest, they come out and complain about the monks."
308:
Therefore, it is said, "The woman also commits an offense." The reason is also stated as "because it is an unsecluded place." Since lewd gestures with the body are possible, in this training rule, seclusion of the eye and seclusion of the ear are intended; thus it is said, "one who is not blind, not deaf," and so on. However, some teachers say that in the Vibhaṅga, only this much is stated: "he is not able to engage in sexual intercourse" (Pārājika 454), and it is not stated that "he is not able to engage in physical contact." Therefore, seeing that there are no others in an unsecluded place, they consider that physical contact with a single woman is possible. For this reason, they say that even if a person is not deaf but is blind and stands within the twelve-cubit range of hearing, he cannot know whether there is physical contact or not. Thus, without considering the occurrence of lewd gestures with the body, it is said, "one who is not blind, not deaf," etc., to avoid the offense of physical contact (kāyasaṃsagga).

In the Sāratthadīpanī, the statement "one is said to be not blind by way of physical contact" (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.453) is made without considering the occurrence of lewd gestures with the body; it should be understood as "also by way of physical contact." For this very reason, it is stated in that same Sāratthadīpanī: "In this training rule, only seclusion of the ear is intended... some teachers say, 'Both types of seclusion are intended here,' but that statement should not be accepted."

The statement made to establish the absence of eye-seclusion, such as "In an unsecluded place, seclusion of the eye is not possible," is inappropriate. This is because a person standing at a very great distance cannot perceive lewd gestures with the body or actions such as taking the hand. Therefore, in the Pāḷi, it is called "seclusion of the eye," and it is not rejected in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). Not only is it not rejected, but it is explicitly stated: "one who is not blind and not deaf" and "one who is not blind or even one who is not deaf does not do so." Therefore, in this training rule, both types of seclusion should be taken.

By the phrase "within twelve cubits," it is shown that the seclusion of the ear is delimited by twelve cubits. As for the seclusion of the eye, it should be understood as being delimited by the distance at which bodily movements and such are no longer clearly visible. The phrase "one who is deaf but has eyes" is said with reference to the Saṅghādisesa offense of lewd speech (duṭṭhullavācā). The statement "the duṭṭhulla offense is mentioned" means that the duṭṭhulla offense is mentioned in a sense that exceeds the offenses mentioned in the previous training rule; it should not be taken as meaning only the duṭṭhulla offense, because physical contact (kāyasaṃsagga) is also to be taken here. For this very reason, "and the Pārājika offense..."
309:
...only this much is said: "parihāpetvā" (having given up). Otherwise (if physical contact were not to be taken), it should have been said, "kāyasaṃsaggañca" (and physical contact).

The phrase "tisamuṭṭhānaṃ" (three origins) and so on is said by way of the Saṅghādisesa of lewd speech, which exceeds the offenses mentioned in the previous training rule. Some also say that since physical contact and so on were already mentioned in the previous training rule, they are not mentioned in this training rule. This statement should be accepted after careful investigation.

## The Explanation of the Second Aniyata Training Rule is Finished.

## The Method of the Aniyata Explanation is Finished.

## 4. Nissaggiya Chapter
## 1. Cīvara Vagga
## 1. Explanation of the First Kathina Training Rule

Samitāvi means one whose evil is calmed (samitapāpa). The name Gotamaka-cetiya refers to a monastery built at the site of the Gotamaka yakkha's shrine.

In the phrase "navamaṃ vā dasamaṃ vā" (the ninth or the tenth), the accusative case (upayogavacana) is used in the sense of the locative case (bhūmmattha). "Sace bhaveyya" means if anyone should have a doubt. "Vuttasadisaṃ" is said because it is similar to the extent already mentioned as "dasamaṃ vā"; it is also written as "vuttasadisameva." In the word "dhāretuṃ," the remaining verb "āha" should be understood.

"Suciyā paṭisāmanaṃ" means storing away properly in a needle-case; this is said to show the completion of all sewing work. "Etaṃ" refers to the lost robe (naṭṭhacīvara). By the word "etessampi," reference is made to the lost robe and so on; by this, the absence of the robe-impediment (cīvarapalibodha) is shown. "Dutiyassa palibodhassa" refers to the residence-impediment (āvāsapalibodha). Here, by showing the absence of the two impediments with the two phrases "niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ" (when the robe is finished) and "ubbbhatasmiṃ kathine" (when the kathina is removed), it is indicated that for a monk who has spread the kathina, it is allowable to keep an extra robe (atirekacīvara) for as long as one of the two impediments—the robe-impediment or the residence-impediment—is not yet severed within the five-month period. "Pakkamantikā" means that which has departure (pakkamana) as its end; the remaining matikas should be understood in this same way. The detail of these eight matikas will become clear in the place where they occur (in the Mahāvagga, Kathinakkhandhaka).

In the phrase "dasāhaparamṃ kālaṃ," the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). This is what is said... [pe]... "dasāhaparamabhāvo"—this is just showing the meaning of the word "dasāhaparamatā." The construction here should be understood as: this means "the state of having ten days as the maximum." The phrase "ayamattho" and so on is said by way of showing the intended meaning of the word "dasāhaparama" itself. In that context, "ettako kālo" means the time which is called "dasāhaparamatā" is this much time.

"Khomaṃ" refers to a linen cloth or linen robe woven with linen threads; some call it a robe made of bark (vākamaya). A robe woven with cotton threads is called "kappāsika"; the rest are the same. "Kambalaṃ" is a cloth woven with threads made from the hair of animals such as sheep. "Bhaṅgaṃ" is a robe woven by mixing all or some threads like linen and so on. Some say that bhaṅga is also just a robe made of bark. As for these six types of robes: dukūla (fine cloth), pattuṇṇa (silk), somārapaṭa (cloth from the Somāra country), cīnapaṭa (Chinese cloth), iddhija (produced by psychic power), and devadinna (given by devas)...
311:
These six types of robes are not mentioned separately because they are merely conforming (anuloma) to those robes such as linen (khoma). To elaborate, the dukūla robe, being made of bark fibers, conforms to the hemp (sāṇa) robe. In the dictionary (Abhidhāna), it is stated: "The pattuṇṇa robe is a special kind of silk robe." Robes produced in the regions of Somāra and China are called somāracīnapata. The three types, including pattuṇṇa, conform to silk (koseyya) robes because they are made of threads produced by silkworms. The iddhija robe refers to the robe that arises for ehibhikkhu monks through the power of their merit. Robes produced from kalpavriksha trees and those given by devas conform to all [six types] because they are one of the six types such as linen (khoma).

Regarding the natural span of humans, it is said "two spans," etc. By this, it is shown that a robe with a length of one carpenter’s cubit (vaḍḍhakī-hattha) and a width of half that cubit reaches the state of being assigned (vikappanā). Thus, in the Commentary on the Kuṭikāra Sikkhāpada, it is stated: "A Sugata span (sugata-vidatthi) is equal to three spans of a middle-sized man of the present age, and it is one and a half carpenter’s cubits." Therefore, it is evident that 12 Sugata finger-breadths make one Sugata span, which is one and a half carpenter’s cubits. By this definition, it also agrees with the passages stating that "8 Sugata finger-breadths equal one carpenter’s cubit."

In the phrase "taṃ atikkāmayato," the word "taṃ" refers to either the robe or the time. "Tassa yo aruṇo" refers to the dawn that has passed on the day the robe was acquired. "Cīvaruppādadivasena saddhiṃ" means together with the past dawn which is the beginning of the day the robe was acquired. Since the Blessed One said "ten days at most" and then again "at the rise of the dawn on the eleventh day," this is stated as "together with the day the robe was acquired" to reconcile the preceding and following statements, although it is understood through the wording. Only if it is said "at the dawn of the tenth day" would it agree with the words "ten days at most." In reality, a day is considered passed only by the future dawn which marks the end-limit of the day. It is not considered passed by the dawn which is the beginning of the day, as this is not the case in practices like parivāsa (probation). However, in this training rule, because the Blessed One wished to show the limits of the beginning and end of the day, He said "at the rise of the dawn on the eleventh day." Therefore, in the Commentary, taking the dawn that is the beginning of that day and associated with it, it is said: "At the rise of the dawn on the eleventh day, it becomes a forfeiture (nissaggiya)." Here, "dawn" (aruṇa) should be understood as the special radiance that precedes sunrise, which increases and is thick and red.

"Vacanīyo" is a word regarding the Saṅgha. "Vacanabhedo" means the variety of speech to be uttered, such as "He remembers two offenses during the motion (ñatti)," etc.
312:
"In this case, perception does not protect" is said in reference to one who has doubt and one who perceives that [the ten-day limit] has not yet passed. "To that person who has such a perception" means to that monk who perceives that it has not passed or who has doubt. The distinction of not being lost or not being plundered is stated as "by way of taking by force." A robe taken by way of theft is also considered "lost" in this context.

The phrase "having regained what was made by another," etc., is said in reference to the sitting cloth (nisīdana). If a monk makes a new sitting cloth without taking a Sugata span from around the old cloth, that cloth becomes a forfeiture (nissaggiya) for him; however, for another monk who regains it from him and uses it, there is no offense. This meaning applies to all forfeitures (nissaggiya).

"To determine the triple robe (ticīvara)" means to determine it by names such as the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), etc. "Not to assign (vikappeti)" means not to assign it by this name. By this, a monk who assigns the three robes is no longer one who possesses the triple robe (tecīvarika). It shows that for him, the procedure to be performed, such as not being separated from the robes at night, as in the case of determined robes, is not to be done. It does not mean there is a fault in the act of assignment (vikappanā). "After that" means some teachers say that after four months have passed, it is allowed to assign and use it. Others say, "It is proper to keep it assigned only until the coming month of Āsāḷha." Yet others say, "There is no fault in assignment; a robe thus assigned should be determined by the name of accessory cloth (parikkhāracola) and used."

"Muṭṭhipañcaka" (five-fist) refers to a group of five cubits marked by a fist. It means measuring four cubits and making the fifth cubit a fist. Some teachers, however, say: "A group of five fist-cubits is muṭṭhipañcaka; therefore, all five cubits should be measured by making a fist." The same method applies to "muṭṭhittika" (three-fist). Since it is impossible to cover the three circles (the two knees and the navel) with an inner robe (antaravāsaka) of two cubits, the phrase "by way of wrapping," etc., is stated. "Atireka" (excessive) means exceeding the measurement of the Buddha's robe. "Ūnaka" (deficient) means less than the muṭṭhipañcaka, etc. It shows that the determination of the triple robe (ticīvara) does not take effect for such robes.

"I relinquish this outer robe (saṅghāṭi)" means "I cancel the determination of this outer robe, I give it up." "Performing a bodily action" means touching the robe with the hand or moving it. In the phrase "it should be determined by speech," it should be understood that determining by both body and speech—by moving it with the body and also uttering with speech—is included, because it is said "without touching with the body." "Twofold" means twofold by way of being within the reach (hatthapāsa) and outside the reach. There, "reach" (hatthapāsa) refers to two and a half cubits. Some say "twelve cubits," but that is not appropriate here. The phrase "in a nearby monastery" is said in reference to being in a place where the location of the robe can be noted. Even if it is in a further place, it can be determined by noting it. Noting the placement of the robe is the standard. It is not possible to note the location in every single detail. "It is not proper to place it in one monastery and determine it as being in another." Some say, "Even if the place is thus noted, there is no fault in determining it," but that statement does not agree with the Commentary and should be investigated. "With cloths kept by determination" means with cloths kept by determining them with the name of accessory cloth (parikkhāracola)...
313: Some say [it is twelve cubits]; this statement does not agree with the determination of robes here. The phrase "sāmantavihāre" is spoken with reference to being situated in a place where the location where the robe is kept can be recognized. Even for a robe situated further than that, if one can recognize the place where it is kept, it should indeed be determined. In that distant place as well, the recognition of the robe's presence is the standard. It is not possible to recognize the location in every single way. Having kept it in one monastery, it is not proper to determine it as being kept in another monastery. Some, however, say, "Even if one recognizes it in such a way and determines it, there is no fault"; this statement does not agree with the Commentary and should be investigated. "With cloths kept by determination" means cloths kept by determining them under the name of "requisite cloth" (parikkhāracola). For this very reason, the relinquishment (paccuddhāra) of the requisite cloth is shown by the words "I relinquish this cloth." By this, it is shown that a monk who observes the dhutaṅga of the triple-robe (ticīvarika), if he is unable to sew and dye a cloth obtained as a refuse-rag (paṃsukūla) etc. within ten days, must pass the ten days only after determining it as a requisite cloth; otherwise, a nissaggiya offense is incurred. For this very reason, it is stated in the Visuddhimagga: "From the time it is dyed, it is not proper to set it aside; he is called a dhutaṅga-thief." The phrase "they should be determined again" is spoken with reference to a monk who wishes to use them by determining them with the names of the triple-robe such as the saṅghāṭi (outer robe), etc. For another monk who wishes to carry it as a requisite cloth, the previous determination alone is sufficient. By the phrase "it should be determined again," it is shown that the smudge-mark (kappabindu) should also be applied. Because a boundary for non-separation (avippavāsasīmā) can be authorized within a formal boundary (baddhasīmā), it is not difficult to maintain [the robes] there; therefore, it is said, "It is difficult to maintain in an informal boundary (abaddhasīmā)." If it exceeds the [prescribed] measurement, there is a pācittiya offense involving cutting; therefore, it is said, "not exceeding the measurement." "Thereafter, having relinquished it, it should be shared (vikappana)" means that after the rainy-season months (vassāna) have passed, the determination should be relinquished and shared. By this, it is understood that the determination remains even beyond the four months of the rainy season, because it is only proper to relinquish it after that. The statement in the Mātikā Commentary, "The rainy-season robe is released from determination even by the passing of the rainy-season months, and the itch-covering cloth even by the recovery from the illness," is not found in the Samantapāsādikā. In the Parivāra Commentary, it is stated: "The offense is incurred in the winter, not in the summer." A monk who wears a rainy-season robe that was shared and kept on the first day after the full moon of Kattika incurs an offense in the winter. In the Kurundī, however, it is said: "If one does not relinquish the determination on the full moon day of Kattika and reaches the winter, an offense is incurred"; that statement is also well-spoken. "To determine for four months, and thereafter..."
314: ...it is said "it should be shared" in the Parivāra Commentary. Among those commentaries, the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā states that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to wearing the rainy-season robe during the winter, while the Kurundī Commentary states that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to the failure to relinquish (paccuddhāra). Therefore, by the method stated in the Kurundī, it is clear that the rainy-season robe does not lose its determination even when the rainy-season months have passed. Among the ways determination is lost, the loss due to the passing of the rainy-season months or the recovery from illness is not mentioned even in the Mātikā Commentary. Therefore, according to the method found in the Samantapāsādikā, it should be understood that the determination remains as long as it is not relinquished. Since it is permitted for the purpose of bathing, it is said, "This rainy-season robe is allowable even if its color is only slightly changed." By the phrase "but two are not allowable," it is shown that, as with the saṅghāṭi etc., a determination cannot be placed on a second rainy-season robe, and it becomes an extra robe (atirekacīvara). In the Mahāpaccarī Commentary, with reference to the absence of the function of using it as a robe, it is stated that there is no offense, as in the case of a bedsheet given for the purpose of monastery requisites. The statement "the bedsheet should also be determined" is not restricted to the monastery alone because it is included among the nine [types of] robes. Therefore, it should be understood that one should determine it in one's own name, store it, and use it as appropriate, just like a requisite cloth. Cloaks (pāvāro), rugs (kojavo), etc., are mentioned separately from bedsheets given for monastery requisites because they are commonly referred to as such in the world. "By returning to the lower life" is spoken with reference to one who, having committed an ultimate offense (pārājika), still claims to be a monk; one who has gone over to a heretical sect; and a nun who, having no regard for her status as a nun, takes up the appearance of a layperson or a heretic. Some say it refers to becoming a layperson without renouncing the training, but that is not appropriate because at that time he is still ordained and the robe has not been relinquished from his possession. "Measurement robe" (pamāṇacīvara) is spoken with reference to the minimum measurement. "One who wears two robes" refers to wearing the saṅghāṭi as a double layer when entering a village. By the phrase "this is the method," it encompasses the meaning that in robes that have the [proper] measurement, if a hole appears anywhere, the determination is lost, and so forth. "There is no other minimum measurement" means that there is no measurement mentioned in the Pāḷi [Canon]. Now, to clarify that very point, it is said "Which...", etc., but since the minimum measurement of the saṅghāṭi etc., such as the five fist-widths (muṭṭhipañcaka), is not found in the Pāḷi, it means it does not agree with that commentary statement. "Makes a large one small" means that when cutting an excessively large robe to match the minimum measurement such as the five fist-widths, the place being cut at the time of cutting...
315:
It does not reach the count of a hole and does not relinquish the determination (adhiṭṭhāna); this is the meaning. It also agrees with the statement: "He joins and cuts, but it is not broken."

However, if a utility cloth (parikkhāracola) is cut to a size smaller than the minimum required for assignment (vikappanā), it relinquishes the determination because it lacks a basis for determination. It should be understood that if those pieces are joined together again, the determination must be re-established. Some teachers say: "In the case of cutting a rain-robe (vassikasāṭika) into two pieces, even if each piece is sufficient for the minimum size, the determination remains only on one piece and not the other, because it is stated that 'two are not allowable.'" This same method applies to sitting cloths (nisīdana), skin-covering cloths (kaṇḍupaṭicchādi), and so on.

That which occurs in the presence is called "Sammukhā"; it is in the nominative case and is an adjective for assignment (vikappanā). Therefore, some interpret the word "Sammukhā" as having the sense of the ablative case in a locative meaning, signifying "in the presence." Alternatively, assignment performed by one's own speech is called Sammukhā-vikappanā (assignment in person). Assignment performed by another's speech is called Parammukhā-vikappanā (assignment in absence). This meaning should also be understood in the instrumental sense; this meaning alone accords with the Pali. "Sannihitāsannihitabhāvaṃ" refers to the state of being near or far. "It is allowable to store it with this much" means that the task of assignment is completed by this much assignment; thus it does not become an extra robe (atirekacīvara). Therefore, the intention is that even if ten days pass, it does not generate a forfeiture (nissaggiya) offense. "It is not allowable to use" refers to the fact that if one uses it without revoking (paccuddharaṇa) it oneself, a pācittiya offense is incurred; if one determines it or relinquishes it to others, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred.

"Usage and so on are also allowable" means that usage, relinquishing, and determination are also allowable. By the word "api" (also), it means that storing is also allowable. In this way, even when revocation is performed, the robe remains an assigned robe (vikappita-cīvara) and not an extra robe. A monk who wishes to determine that robe by a name such as "triple robe" (ticīvara) must determine it. It is shown that another monk should use it only as an assigned robe. However, some teachers say: "An assigned robe should be stored without being revoked as long as it is not yet used. Only when the time for use arrives should it be revoked, determined, and then used. If it were revoked before that time, the assignment would disappear due to the revocation, and it would become an extra robe; if ten days pass, a nissaggiya pācittiya offense is incurred. Therefore, only a robe that is to be kept without being used should be assigned. Once revoked, it must be determined within ten days. The statement in the Commentary such as 'From then on, usage and so on are also allowable' contradicts the Pali." This statement is merely the opinion of those teachers.
316:
In the Pali, it is stated generally: "Within ten days, he determines or assigns" (Pārājika 469), and "If he himself assigns a robe and uses it without revocation, there is an offense of expiation" (Pācittiya 373), and "There is no offense if the recipient gives it, or if he uses it on trust in that person" (Pācittiya 374). Furthermore, in the Commentary, the method of revocation is not shown directly as "I revoke this robe" or "I revoke the assignment," but rather it is stated as revocation through usage, etc., without releasing it from being one's own property, such as "Use my property or discard it." Since it is stated, "From then on, usage and so on are also allowable," referring to separate usage and storage even without determination, it appears that this is a distinct Vinaya procedure for using and storing a robe that is fit for assignment and is apart from the triple robes, by having it revoked immediately after assignment without determining it. Moreover, since it is mentioned for assigning and revoking many alms-bowls (patta), it is established that revocation serves to show the state of those bowls as extra bowls. This is because only one of those bowls can be determined. Therefore, it should be understood only according to the method found in the Commentary.

## Paññattikovido na hotīti
This means not knowing the Vinaya procedure that "immediately after assignment, it should be revoked in this way." Therefore, it says, "He does not know how to revoke." By this Pali, the decision that "revocation should be performed only immediately after assignment" should be understood.

## Avisesena vuttavacananti
This refers to a statement made in general terms pertaining to the triple robes and so on. In this context, having said "it seems to be contradictory," the statement "By way of the summary of the triple robes... the opportunity for assignment is given" is made to prevent the fear of such contradiction. Even though it is stated generally as "he determines or assigns," the meaning that "he also assigns the triple robes" is not established. This is because it is specifically stated: "The triple robes are to be determined, not assigned" (Mahāvagga 358). One determines the robe that should be determined. One assigns the robe that is apart from the triple robes and should be assigned; thus the meaning is established. Therefore, no contradiction between the preceding and following parts is seen here, because the general statement applies only to the remainder of what has been stated. In this context, in the statement "the triple robes by way of the summary of the triple robes..." etc., which is meant to show the method of assigning the triple robes, it is not allowable to revoke and assign even one of the robes being carried by way of the summary of the triple robes. For one who wishes to remove one or all from the triple robes and carry another triple robe by way of the summary of the triple robes, or for one who, having released the determination of the triple robes, wishes to treat all robes as utility cloths (parikkhāracola)...
317:
For a monk who wishes to use [a robe], or with the intention that 'it is allowable to assign the previously determined triple robe after withdrawing it,' the statement beginning with 'If one wishes to stay away with one robe among the triple robes' may exist; this statement is consistent with the Pāḷi. However, if it were said with the intention that 'one withdraws and assigns it for the sake of the comfort of staying away, wishing to determine that very triple robe again with the determination of the triple robe,' that statement would not be consistent with this Pāḷi passage: 'One should not assign the triple robe for the purpose of determination' (Mahāvagga 358). For if the triple robe, like the remaining robes, were to be assigned after being withdrawn, this statement 'One should not assign the triple robe for the purpose of determination' would be useless, as there would be no distinction between the triple robe and the remaining robes. Therefore, this word 'assigns' is said only in reference to robes other than the triple robe. It should be understood that it is not allowable to assign the triple robe. For this reason, in the section on non-offense (anāpatti-vāra) of the second Kathina training rule, this word 'assigns' is not mentioned. One should investigate and consider the meaning here in such a way that it does not contradict the Pāḷi.

In statements such as 'I give to you,' because it has been relinquished, even if it is not mentally accepted, it becomes the property of the recipient monk; that monk has the right to take it at any desired moment. The term 'to so-and-so' is said in reference to a monk who is absent. The statement beginning with 'to whomever it pleases' is said in reference to the state of being ownerless because it has been relinquished by both parties.

The statement 'That is not proper' is said because taking on trust (vissāsaggahaṇa) within only ten days is mentioned in the section on non-offense, and because in this context, the forfeiture (nissaggiya) robe is taken with a pretext to make it allowable. Some teachers, however, say, 'If others take it by force as a shared possession, or if it is taken on trust and then regained, there is no fault.' 'Anadhiṭṭhānena' means due to not making the determination that should be made by body and speech. These five are the factors here: the robe being one's own property, being of the proper kind and measure, the state of the impediments (palibodha) being severed, being an extra robe, and the lapse of ten days.

## The Explanation of the First Kathina Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Udositā-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, 'avippavāse' means when the state of not being away [from the robes] is to be accomplished, it is the formal act (sammuti) to be performed to achieve the state of being without the fault of staying away.
318:
'Paṭisiddhapariyāpannena' means the demonstration of metonymy (samudāyopacāra), using a part to represent the whole, with one robe included among the three robes forbidden for staying away from.

## 478-9.
'Ettāvatā' is indicated by the word 'parikkhitto.' After saying 'Sabhāyeti liṅgavyattayena sabhā vuttā,' the commentator, by using the word 'sabhāye' himself, shows that there exists the word 'sabhāya,' which is a synonym of the word 'sabhā' and is of the neuter gender. Alternatively, there is a reading 'Sabhāyanti liṅgavyattayena sabhā vuttā.' By the phrase 'liṅgavyattayena sabhā,' it should be understood that there is the word 'sabhāya,' a synonym of the word 'sabhā' associated with a different gender.

'Sabhāyaṃ gacchati' means one goes to the assembly hall. 'Vasitabbaṃ natthi' means there is no place to stay except within the reach of the hand (hatthapāsa) of the robe. 'Tassā' means of the street. In the phrase 'the hatthapāsa of the hall and the door should not be abandoned,' the streets and houses between the hall and the door are already included because the beginning and the end are taken.

A monk staying in those doors, streets, and houses must avoid the faults of entering a village, the fault of sleeping in the same place (sahaseyya), etc., and must live with proper concealment, etc. As for the assembly hall, if it is made like a rest house (water-pot shed) for all people to stay, it should be understood that it is allowable to stay as one pleases, as if within a monastery precinct. Intending to point out the state of being a single precinct (ekūpacāra) due to having an enclosure, and the state of being different precincts (nānūpacāra) due to not having an enclosure in houses etc., he said the words beginning with 'eteneva upāyena.' Houses and such should be understood as situated outside the village. This is because houses located within the village are already included by the word 'village.' 'Sabbattha' refers to the fifteen places such as villages, market towns, houses, etc. In the word 'parikkhepā,' only the lack of enclosure should be taken by the word 'ādi.' One should not take 'ekakula' (a single family/house) etc. This is because 'ekakula' etc. are not the causes for being a single precinct or different precincts. In this context, an enclosure is said to exist only for a group of traders (caravan) that has camped in a certain place for a few days, not for a moving caravan.

## 482-7.
A storehouse built by rulers on the seashore etc., outside the village, is called 'udosita.' Therefore, he said the words beginning with 'yānādīnaṃ.' 'Muṇ္ဍacchadanapāsāda' refers to a mansion that is not very high, is equipped with an open-air courtyard (balcony), and is devoid of peaked roofs or multiple tiers.

'Pariyādiyitvā' means having overpowered or covered. Regarding 'nadīparihāra' (river enclosure), some teachers say it is only the hatthapāsa of the robe because the river enclosure is not mentioned separately like the enclosures of villages etc. Other teachers say that by this commentary statement, the river enclosure is also separately established; therefore, the hatthapāsa of the river should not be abandoned. The word 'vihārasīmaṃ' is said in reference to the boundary for not being away from robes (avippavāsa-sīmā).
319:
It is said that one should not abandon the hatthapāsa (hand-reach) of the river. "Vihārasīmaṃ" refers to the avippavāsa-sīmā (boundary of non-separation). In this context, although the monastery may belong to various donors, since non-separation from the robes is possible everywhere within the limits of the avippavāsa-sīmā, that boundary is primary. Because the protection of a caravan cannot be obtained in that place, it is said, "One should go and stay in the monastery." The phrase "near the caravan" is spoken by way of the aforementioned internal limit (abbantara). In the Pāḷi, it is stated: "There is a caravan of various families; having placed the robes in the caravan, the hatthapāsa should not be abandoned." In this sentence, the hatthapāsa of the caravan group is taken.

The phrase "in the field of a single family" refers to a field that is not enclosed.

491-4. What is called a vihāra is an upacāra-sīmā (vicinity boundary). There, the phrase "in whichever monastery" is said with reference to the interior of the compound (pariveṇa) and so forth of that monastery. The ownership by a single family and so on in this monastery is by way of the donors who had it built. The phrase "of the place touched by the shadow" is said with reference to the area within the range of a stone thrown straight down.

"On a path that should not be traveled" means in the small islands in the middle of the ocean where one cannot go and return on the same day; this is how it should be construed. "In another robe" means in the robe that is in the eastern direction. By the words "at the time of Uposatha... etc... it increases," the Great Teacher shows the extreme difference between the seven abbantaras of being separated from the robes and the seven-abbantara-sīmā of the samānasaṃvāsa (communion). Indeed, when many bhikkhus sit together and keep their respective robes within the surrounding seven-abbantara limits, the seven-abbantara limit for each bhikkhu, starting from his sitting place, is different from one another and of many kinds; it does not become a single unit because it is not marked from the edge of the assembly. Therefore, in those seven abbantaras of being separated from the robes, there is no increase or decrease by way of the assembly. It is not so with the seven-abbantara-sīmā. That seven-abbantara-sīmā, even if the assembly is a league (yojana) in size, is only one, being defined by seven abbantaras all around starting from the edge of the assembly. Therefore, that sīmā increases and decreases by way of the assembly. Thus, it should be understood that the seven-abbantara-sīmā is one thing, and the protection against being separated from the robes in an open space defined by seven abbantaras is another. Whatever else should be said here, I will say in the Sīmākathā of the Khandhaka.
320:
"Descends into the river" means descending after releasing the hatthapāsa of the robe. "Having placed it outside the village" is said because it should not be worn (inside the village). "A vinaya-kamma (legal act) should be performed" means that one should first perform the vinaya-kamma on the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and on the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) placed outside the village, and then, after wearing the upper robe, perform the vinaya-kamma on the inner robe (antaravāsaka). In this matter of relinquishing robes, because the vinaya-kamma is mentioned even for the saṅghāṭi placed outside the village, it should be understood that it is proper to relinquish an object that is out of sight, and to give what has been relinquished. Because there is effort in the journey of young bhikkhus, it is said, "The nissaya (dependence) does not cease." The phrase "for a moment... it ceases" is said because the journey is interrupted even though there is effort. For those young bhikkhus who rise before dawn and travel with effort, even if dawn rises during the journey, the nissaya does not cease because it is said, "They sleep until the rise of dawn." For that very reason, it is said, "Having entered the village... it does not cease." In the passage beginning with "without taking the word of one another," the cessation of nissaya is not mentioned at the moment of traveling because there is effort. "Due to danger from a cow" means due to the danger of cows with young calves running forward and striking with their horns. In the phrase "the nissaya also ceases," it is said because those who stop due to danger from a cow etc. must stay until the danger subsides, and thus they cannot determine, "I will go only within the dawn." Where it is possible to determine thus, even if dawn rises during the journey, the nissaya does not cease, like the young bhikkhus who enter a village for the sake of medicine. "The village within the sīmā" refers to a village established after the avippavāsa-sīmā was authorized. This is because it must be authorized excluding the village and the village vicinity (gāmūpacāra). "Those who have entered" means that for teachers and pupils who have gone separately, because it is an avippavāsa-sīmā, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya), and because there is effort, the nissaya does not cease. "On the way" means on the way of the young bhikkhus who are returning after listening to the Dhamma.

By the words "here, non-relinquishment (apaccuddharaṇa)," it is shown that like determination (adhiṭṭhāna) and assignment (vikappanā), relinquishment (paccuddharaṇa) must also be done by body or by speech. Because of the failure to do what should be done by body and speech, this training rule is said to be produced by body and speech (kāyavācā-samuṭṭhāna). Having the three robes determined (adhiṭṭhita), the kaṭhina not being spread, not having obtained the consent (sammuti), and spending the night separated (from the robes)—these four are the factors here.

## The Explanation of the Udositasi Sikkhāpada is finished.
321:
## 3. Commentary on the Third Kathina Training Rule

In the Pāḷi of the third Kathina training rule, "cīvarapaccāsā nikkhipituṃ" means to keep [the robe] when there is an expectation of receiving a robe. In this phrase "niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā," the meaning of the third case ending (instrumental) should be understood only in the sense of possession (sāmī-attha), just as in the second Kathina training rule.

499-500. A robe given as "tuyhaṃ dammi" (I give to you) refers to a robe given in this way: "Venerable sir, I give this out-of-season robe (akāla-cīvara) to you." This also means it is a robe given with a specific reference during the robe-season. This statement is from the Commentary. In the Pāḷi, the phrase "kālepi ādissa dinnaṃ" (given with reference even during the season) is also spoken by way of extracting the meaning (atthuddhāra), just as the seclusion of the ear (sotassa raho) was mentioned in the first Aniyata, in order to show all robes obtainable due to the similarity of the term "akāla-cīvara."

Specifically, a robe given to the Saṅgha with a reference even during the robe-season is called an out-of-season robe (akāla-cīvara) because it is similar to a robe that arises out of season, in that it must be shared by all—both those who have completed the rains-residence (vuttha-vassa) and those who have not. Thus, it is stated in the Pāḷi as "kālepi ādissa dinnaṃ" by way of extracting the meaning. It is not stated to show that "a robe obtained by distributing that [robe], or a robe obtained out of season, does not receive the one-month protection or the five-month protection for monks who have completed the rains-residence, and that they receive only a ten-day protection if there is no expectation of a robe."

In the Commentary as well, it is stated: "It is given with reference to a single person, saying, 'I give this robe to you,'" in order to show all [robes] obtainable due to the similarity of the term "ādissa dinna" by way of extracting the meaning. It should be understood that this is not stated to show that such a robe, or a robe obtained out of season, must be determined (adhiṭṭhāna) within ten days by monks who have not spread the Kathina; for if the meaning were taken in any other way, it would contradict the Pāḷi and Commentaries. For this reason, in the Acceka-cīvara training rule, it is stated that even an urgent robe (acceka-cīvara) that arises out of season "should be kept until the robe-season time."

In the Commentary on that training rule, it is also stated: "For an urgent robe obtained on the fifth day of the waxing moon of the month of Assayuja (Thadingyut), if the Kathina is not spread, the protection is one month and eleven days; if the Kathina is spread, the protection is five months and eleven days." Referring only to that protection, it is stated: "From the sixth day of the waxing moon onwards, even a non-urgent robe (anacceka-cīvara) that arises, or a robe that is kept after being relinquished (paccuddharaṇa), also receives this protection."

Therefore, it should be noted that an extra robe (atireka-cīvara), however it is obtained, whether in-season or out-of-season, certainly receives the protection for the whole month or for five months, as is appropriate, for monks who have completed the rains-residence.

The connection is that the Padabhājanīya is taught without speaking in this manner. In that context, "evaṃ" refers to the meaning of the term "tato ce uttari" in the Commentary, which has a maximum of one month...
322: "Uttari" (beyond/more) has already been stated, and that same meaning is reviewed here. The intention is that in the Padabhājanīya, a different meaning is intended instead of this meaning. The phrase "tāva uppannaṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ" is in the nominative case (paccatta-vacana). This phrase "mūlacīvaraṃ" is in the accusative case (upayoga-vacana). "Making it like its own" means that the robe in expectation (paccāsācīvara) obtained on the second day, etc., in the interval, is not allowed to be kept as the original robe which has a one-month limit, but is made to stay within its own ten-day limit; this is what is meant by "making it like its own". In this context, "the original robe beyond that" (tato uddhaṃ mūlacīvaraṃ), "mūlacīvaraṃ" is in the nominative case. This is because that original robe, having exceeded twenty days, is sewn together with the robe in expectation obtained on the twenty-second day, etc. Not being allowed to go up to the ten-day limit, it is made like its own by the day of the nine-day limit. However, a robe in expectation that is kept separately without being sewn together has only a ten-day limit. In the Pali, "dasāhā" means "by ten days". In "if it arises on the eleventh", etc., it means if it arises on the eleventh day, etc.; or this reading itself should be taken. "If it arises on the twenty-first... should be made within nine days", etc., is stated by excluding the day the robe in expectation was obtained. Therefore, it is said, "On the thirtieth... it should be determined on that very day." This statement "Another robe in expectation... should be made" is said only when there is expectation. If the expectation ceases from the desired place, thinking "From today onwards, I will not get the robe," but expectation arises elsewhere by some means, the original robe should not yet be determined. Only when expectation has ceased in every way should the original robe that has exceeded ten days be determined on that very day. "The robe in expectation should also be determined as a small accessory cloth (parikkhāracola)" is said referring to a dissimilar (visabhāga) robe that arose earlier. "Aññamaññaṃ" means "each one" or "one by one"; or this is the reading itself. The factors in this training rule are the same as those stated in the first Kathina training rule. The only difference is that in that rule, it is an exceeding of ten days, whereas in this rule, it is an exceeding of one month. ## The Commentary on the Third Kathina Training Rule is finished. ## 4. Commentary on the Purāṇacīvara Training Rule 503-5. In the fourth training rule, in the Pali, "bhattavissaggaṃ" means the discharging of food into the stomach, the entering, the swallowing—the act of eating. By the completion of the meal, of the food...
323:
They also say "vissajjana" (relinquishment). In that phrase, "nāma tvaṃ" means "you by that name," or it means "you together with that unrelated bhikkhunī." Father and mother are called "pitaro." The father and mother of the parents are called "pitāmahā." Because they are in pairs, they are called "yuga" (pair/generation). Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as "pitāmahavaṭṭa" (lineage of grandparents) up to the seventh generation of grandparents. By taking the word "pitāmaha" in this way, the mother's father, the father's mother, and the mother's mother are also included. Beyond the seventh generation, they should be known as "unrelated" (aññātaka). "Yā" refers to a bhikkhunī. The father's mother is called "pitāmahī." The mother's father is called "mātāmaho."

"Payoge payoge bhikkhussa dukkaṭaṃ" (for every effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the bhikkhu) is said because by the single command "wash!", all subsequent efforts that are part of that washing are commanded.

Since washing cannot occur without those preliminary efforts, and because it is said, "having made a bodily movement" and "within the twelve-cubit precinct," there is no offense for a bhikkhu who gives, throws, or sends the robe without clearly showing the desire to have it washed by hand, or for a bhikkhu who stands outside the twelve-cubit precinct and commands by body or speech to throw or send it, etc.

"Ekena vatthunā" means with the object first acted upon. Because there are five hundred of those bhikkhunīs, they are called "pañcasatā" (the five hundred bhikkhunīs). A bhikkhunī who has changed sex from being a bhikkhu is also one who has received the single-sided higher ordination (upasampadā) in the presence of the bhikkhus.

"Tāvakālikaṃ gahetvā" means requesting and taking it temporarily for the purpose of wearing it for a few days. The three factors (aṅga) in this training rule are: being an old robe, commanding an unrelated bhikkhunī while standing within the precinct, and having her wash it, etc.

## The Commentary on the Old Robe Training Rule (Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
324:
## 5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Receiving Robes (Cīvarapaṭiggahanasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

In the fifth training rule, "apannatte sikkhāpade" means before the training rule regarding staying behind from the group (gaṇamhā ohīyana) was enacted. "Koṭṭhāsasampatti" means the beauty of the five parts, such as the hair, etc. By the phrase "showing only the palm of the hand," it indicates not showing the rest of the body except for the palm.

"Vihatthatāya" means because of being without folded hands, because of not being mixed, and because of being without refuge. Therefore, it is said "samabhitunnatta," which means because of being pained. An object to be exchanged is called "parivatta"; that same thing is called "pārivattaka," meaning an object given in exchange.

As in the previous Purāṇadhovāpana training rule, there is no twelve-cubit precinct restriction in this training rule; therefore, it says "leaving the precinct." "Except for exchange" means excluding cases where one takes an item in exchange, even by giving at least a piece of gallnut (harīṭaka) or by forming the intention, "I will give."

By the statement "that point is not consistent with being mindless (unintentional)," it reveals the state of being mindless through not knowing she is a bhikkhunī, etc., just as in not knowing she is a relative, etc.

513-4. Because it is a triad and also a pācittiya, it is called "tika-pācittiya," meaning a triad of pācittiya offenses. The phrase "alms-bowl bags, etc." is said in reference to items that do not require formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna). "What need is there to speak of alms-bowl bags, etc.?"—by this statement, it shows that if there is no offense even for a large rug (bhisicchavi) because it does not require determination, then what need is there to speak of alms-bowl bags, etc., which do not require determination because they lack the minimum size for assignment (vikappanā)? However, it is not proper to take alms-bowl bags, etc., that have the minimum size for assignment. Receiving is an action (kiriyā), and not exchanging is a non-action (akiriyā). The three factors here are: being a robe suitable for assignment, the absence of exchange, and receiving from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Receiving Robes is finished.
325:
## 6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Requesting from Unrelated Persons (Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

In the sixth training rule, only a clever person is called "paṭṭa." In the Pāḷi, "dhamma-nimantanā" means an invitation by virtue of the mere custom of conduct to be practiced toward monks; it does not mean an invitation made with the desire to give. For that very reason, it says "viññāpessati" (he will request). This is because requesting from an unrelated or uninvited person is called "viññatti" (requesting).

By this Pāḷi, "he should come covering himself with grass or leaves," it refers to the permission to damage vegetation (bhūtagāma), and thus it says "not for the sake of wanting to destroy vegetation," etc. Even if one first takes the monk's sign (robes) with a pure heart and later takes up a [wrong] view, he is still a "titthiyapakkantaka" (one who has gone over to sectarians); therefore, it says "even after dressing, the [wrong] view should not be taken."

In the phrase "whichever residence he first reaches," it means that even a monk entering for the sake of monastery robes, etc., must go only after covering himself with grass, etc.; he must not come naked. This is because a dukkaṭa offense is taught in general. "Cimilikāhi" means with coarse cloths. "Paribhogeneva" means by using it because no other robe was obtained. "Paribhogajiṇṇa" means worn out and shabby through use, becoming unsuitable.

In the phrase "for the sake of another," the statement "to relatives, to those who have invited" follows along; therefore, it says "to one's own relatives or those who have invited," etc. In this training rule, however, it should be understood that there is no nissaggiya offense for a monk who requests from unrelated or uninvited persons for the sake of another monk whose robes were snatched or lost. Otherwise, there would be no distinction made by the phrase "to relatives, to those who have invited." For that very reason, it will be said in the subsequent training rule: "In the commentaries, however, it is said that in the place of relatives and those who invited... only the [proper] measure is suitable; that statement does not agree with the Pāḷi," and "Since this training rule was enacted only in the case of requesting for the sake of another, 'for the sake of another' is not said here." There are four factors in this training rule: being a robe suitable for assignment, the absence of the [proper] time (emergency), requesting from an unrelated person, and obtaining it through that request.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Requesting from Unrelated Persons is finished.
326:
## 7. Commentary on the Tatuttari Sikkhāpada

522-524. In the Pāḷi of the seventh training rule, 'paggāhikasālā' refers to a cloth shop. It is called 'paggāhikasālā' because it is the place where merchants hold up (paggahitvā) cloths to show them. 'Assa cīvarassa' means the robe that is to be accepted. By the word 'ticīvarikena', it is shown that there are no robes stored in places such as monasteries, other than the three robes stolen by thieves. If there were, it is not proper to ask for one. One should borrow a robe temporarily and wear it, then take one's own robe. For a monk who cannot even get a temporary one to wear, just as it is proper to destroy vegetation (bhūtagāma) and cover oneself with grass and leaves, asking is also indeed proper. 'Anñena' refers to a monk whose entire set of robes was not stolen. 'Dve naṭṭhāni' means 'two [robes] to be accepted' (dve sāditabbāni) according to the context (adhikāra).

526. 'Pāḷiyā na sameti' means it does not agree with this Pāḷi: 'Anāpatti ñātakānaṃ pavāritānaṃ' (There is no offense for relatives or those who have invited). This is because it was taught only in the case of transgressing by asking for more than the [inner and upper] robes. The phrase 'Anñassatthāyāti na vuttaṃ' (It is not said 'for the sake of another') shows the meaning that a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred when asking for more than those robes for the sake of another. As for that Pācittiya offense, if one asks for the sake of those monks whose robes were stolen, would it be incurred by those monks or only by the monk who asks? It should not be incurred by those monks because they did not ask themselves; nor should it be incurred by the monk who asks because he did not ask for himself. Therefore, the Nissaggiya Pācittiya is not evident even for one who asks for the sake of another. However, in the Pāḷi, they say that 'anñassatthāya' is not mentioned in the section on non-offense because this training rule proceeds by way of being connected to one's own acceptance. That statement also seems appropriate; it should be accepted after investigation. These are the four factors here: being a robe more than those [inner and upper] robes, having a cause such as theft, asking from a non-relative, and obtaining it through that asking.

## The Commentary on the Tatuttari Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the First Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada

528-531. In the eighth training rule, 'yo kattā' is said with reference to the donor (dāyaka). A cloth (paṭo) is itself called 'paṭaka'. The phrase 'appagghaṃ cetāpeti' (causes a low-priced one to be acquired) is said with reference to not incurring a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense; however, a Dukkaṭa offense is indeed incurred due to the act of asking. Because [it is said], 'Pubbe appavārito' (Not previously invited)...
327:
...the reason for asking is taught in the Sutta. Also in the Mātikā Commentary: 'Great desire for robes, asking from a non-relative, and obtaining it through that asking—these are the three factors here.' Thus, the state of asking from a non-relative is shown. Some teachers, however, say: 'Even if the donor has not said to him, "I wish to give," it is indeed proper to have them bring a robe of the value that the donor wishes to give.' That statement does not agree with the Rāja Sikkhāpada Commentary either. This is because, even if a messenger or the donor reports, 'I have brought robe-fund intended for the venerable one,' the act of having it brought from an unnamed steward (mukhavivaṭaka-kappiyakāraka) and others is forbidden in that commentary.

For it is said there: 'These two are called unnamed stewards; one should act towards them as towards non-relatives who have not invited... nothing should be said. This statement, "He should send robe-fund by a messenger," is merely a teaching; the same method applies to those who, having brought it themselves, give it for the sake of alms-food and so on.' Indeed, because the donor has not specified, 'Take robes, alms-food, etc., from such-and-such a person,' even though the donor has relinquished the object, it is said 'nothing should be said' regarding unnamed stewards and others. It is not said because that object belongs to the unnamed steward and others. Therefore, in this training rule also, a monk who speaks without being invited by the donor or the messenger saying, 'Speak what you wish,' indeed incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. 'Agghavaḍḍhanaka' (increasing the price) means this training rule arose based on increasing the price for robes, not for alms-food and so on. This should be understood because increasing the price for those [alms-food etc.] is only a Dukkaṭa, and increasing the price for fine alms-food is a Suddha Pācittiya. For that very reason, the factor 'great desire for robes' was taught.

## The Commentary on the First Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Second Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada

In the ninth training rule, 'paccekacīvaracetāpannā' in the Pāḷi means robe-funds specified individually; it means robe-funds specified separately for each person. 'Ubhowa santā ekena' means both being together as one; it means both having become one together.

## The Commentary on the Second Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada is finished.
328:
## 10. Rājā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, the word 'ajjaṇho' is formed from 'ajja no' with the addition of the letter 'ha' and the change of the letter 'na' to 'ṇa'; therefore, it means 'today for us for the whole day.'

538-9. In the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, the statement 'Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, clothe the monk named so-and-so with the robe' is said to demonstrate the purity of the origin (āgamana-suddhi). If [the donor] had sent [the messenger] saying, 'Give this robe-fund to the monk named so-and-so,' then because the origin is impure, the monk should not even point out a voluntary attendant (kappiya-kāraka) regarding that unallowable object. That statement [in the commentary] refers to an unallowable robe-fund which is a matter for forfeiture (nissaggiya) and wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). When there is no purity of origin, such as saying 'Give [this fund] to so-and-so monk,' or when the messenger's speech is impure according to the method in the training rule, one should only refuse in every way. It is not proper to say, 'We accept the robe itself,' nor is it proper to follow that speech and point out a steward (veyyāvaccakara), because both the origin and the messenger's speech are impure.

However, according to the method in the Pāḷi text, it is stated to show that if there is purity of origin, even if the messenger's speech is impure, one should perform everything (such as pointing out a steward) according to the method in the training rule. Therefore, just as one should point out a steward when the origin is pure even if the messenger's speech is impure, this meaning is automatically established: that one should also point out [a steward] when the messenger's speech is pure even if the origin is impure. If both are pure, there is no need to mention it. It should be understood that the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā says 'a voluntary attendant should not even be pointed out' with reference only to the side where both are impure.

In this matter, the statement in the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭီkā, such as 'no distinct benefit is seen from the purity or impurity of the origin,' is said without grasping the intention of the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, because the purity of origin etc. is beneficial according to the aforementioned method. Here, the 'undesirable consequence' (aniṭṭhappasaṅga) mentioned—that 'even if the messenger speaks with unallowable terminology while the original owner sent him with allowable terminology, a voluntary attendant should be pointed out'—is not actually an undesirable consequence, because it is desired. For that very reason, in the training rule, to a messenger who speaks with unallowable terminology saying, 'Venerable sir, please accept this robe-fund'...
329:
...it is taught that a steward should be pointed out through an allowable act because the origin is pure. If the origin is impure, however, a steward should not be pointed out even through an allowable act. Therefore, there is indeed a benefit in the purity or impurity of the origin. How can the purity of origin be known through the messenger's speech? This is not a heavy burden. Only when the messenger speaks with unallowable terminology should the purity of origin be investigated; otherwise, it need not be. In that case, it can be known by questioning the sequence of his speech and through logic, etc. In this training rule as well, the fact that he was sent to buy and offer a robe is known by the messenger's speech itself: 'I have brought a robe-fund.' If the purity of origin cannot be known in any way, one should only refuse.

In the Pāḷi text, the words such as 'We accept the robe itself' are taught to show the procedure to be followed if there is purity of origin even though the messenger's speech is unallowable. The words such as 'He... should not be told "Give it to him"' are taught to free one from consenting to an unallowable object. The words such as 'one who is restrained' are taught to show that 'only when the messenger speaks again in this way should one prompt him, not otherwise.' The statement that one should not say 'Give me the robe... buy me the robe' is because [the person] is a voluntary attendant pointed out by oneself to receive the gold and silver brought by the messenger. Thus, a monk who says 'Give me the robe, buy it for me' would be engaging in monetary transactions (rūpiya-saṃvohāra) by exchanging that gold and silver, saying 'Give, buy' based on that money. Therefore, to avoid that fault from afar, it is taught as in the case of money that has been accepted and then forfeited in the midst of the Saṅgha. For it is said there: 'One should not say "Bring this one or that one."' Therefore, it should be understood that this is not taught to avoid the fault of intimation (viññatti). Otherwise (if it were to avoid intimation), it would lead to the consequence that one could not even say 'I have no need for this robe.' For that very reason, since there is no suspicion of monetary transaction with those pointed out by the messenger, it is taught that one may have it brought even by appointing another voluntary attendant. Even in that case, the intention should be taken that one should not say 'Buy a robe with the money placed by the messenger and bring it,' but simply say 'Bring a robe.'

In the phrase 'ṭhānaṃ bhañjati,' the word 'ṭhāna' is a name for both standing (ṭhiti) and cause/reason (kāraṇa). Therefore, by sitting on a seat, the 'standing' is broken, and the 'reason for coming' is no longer apparent to them. However, in cases such as accepting material gifts without breaking the 'standing,' it only spoils the 'reason for coming,' not the 'standing.'
