Therefore, it is said, 'It spoils the reason for coming.' Some teachers, however, say, 'By accepting material gifts etc., it spoils the standing as well.' That statement does not agree with the Commentary.
330:
The phrase beginning with “Yatassa cīvaracetāpannaṃ” indicates the procedure to be followed by the monk himself if the robe is not yet completed, even though he has designated a steward (veyyāvaccakara). When the monk speaks to the owners of the property in this manner, if those owners prompt the steward and give the robe, it is allowable (vattati), as it is stated in the section on non-offense (anāpatti-vāra) that “the owners give after prompting.” Because of this, if a monk does not prompt the steward himself but speaks to lay devotees and others using indirect means (pariyāya) to have them prompt the steward, and those devotees prompt the steward seven times (or many times) to have the robe given, the monk is free from offense. This is because this training rule (sikkhāpada) does not involve a command (āṇattika) to another.

One who, without being designated by anyone, takes on the responsibility of a steward (veyyāvaccakara) solely through his own speech is called a “mukhavevaṭika.” By the word “avicāretukāmatāya,” it is shown that even Noble Ones (ariyas), when they have property but do not wish to give it, may say “It does not exist” according to worldly convention, without any intention to deceive. The words beginning with “Santi, bhikkhave,” spoken in the story of the merchant Meṇḍaka in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka, are indeed the Meṇḍaka training rule. The phrase “kappiyakārakānaṃ hatthe” (in the hands of the attendants) is said with reference to attendants designated by a messenger, and not with reference to those designated or not designated by the monk. Therefore, it is said, “In this matter, there is no limit to the prompting,” and so forth.

“When they give, having brought it themselves” is the connection of the words. By the phrase “for the sake of almsfood and so forth,” it is shown that it is not only for the sake of robes. By the phrase “in this same manner,” it is shown that in the case of various attendants designated by the owner of the property, and in the case of donations for the sake of almsfood and so forth, all matters such as standing and prompting must be done according to the method already mentioned below.

Because it is said, “Without touching the Saṅgha... or...”, if people speak while touching upon the Saṅgha, saying “We give for the sake of the Saṅgha’s monastery,” etc., it must be rejected. The statement “The Saṅgha accepts” is said by way of the highest standard (ukkaṭṭha-naya); even in groups (gaṇa) and so forth, if they accept for the sake of the Saṅgha, there is a Dukkaṭa offense both in the act of receiving and in the act of using. In the Sāratthadīpanī, it is said, “There is a Pācittiya offense in receiving,” but that is not appropriate because it has been stated that there is a Dukkaṭa offense in receiving for the sake of the Saṅgha, shrines (cetiya), and so forth. “Prompts” (codeti) means that even though one knows the monk is without fault, one prompts him out of anger or greed, saying “Give the goods.” Such a monk indeed becomes one who has committed an offense, incurring Pācittiya or Dukkaṭa offenses due to false speech and so forth. However, for a monk who speaks with the perception that it is allowable (gīvāti-saññāya) but then desists upon realizing there is no fault, there is no offense.
331:
An embankment pond (taḷāka) is said to be “not to be accepted” because it has entered into a field (becoming part of the land). If it is donated with the intention “May the Saṅgha use the four requisites,” it is allowable. In this context, it is allowable to say, “I give this pond for the purpose of the Saṅgha’s use of the four requisites,” or “I give this pond so that the Saṅgha may use the four requisites,” or “I give the four requisites arising from this pond.” This is said specifically regarding donations for the Saṅgha’s use. However, such a pond or field given to an individual monk is not allowable. For a monk with a pure mind, wells, lotus ponds, and so forth, for the purpose of using water are allowable. Indeed, in all instances such as “The Saṅgha has a pond; how is that?” it is spoken only in terms of the Saṅgha. “Hatthe” means “at [one's] disposal.”

“Keep it” (ṭhapetha) is said as a polite expression; even if it is not said, there is no fault for the monk who keeps it. Therefore, it is said, “It is permissible to block the water.” Even during the crop season, it is allowable to scare away [animals] and let them go. For a monk who does not let them go, he is liable for the value of the goods (bhaṇḍadeyya). “Gives again” means that [the authority] gives it back after having seized it; the connection is that even in this case, it is allowable. By this, it is shown that “If any ruler, with the perception that ‘This has been abandoned by the monks and is ownerless,’ takes it himself and then gives it back, it is allowable.” We shall further discuss the decision regarding allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra).

“By way of water” means for the purpose of using water. The phrase “for those with pure minds” is said with reference to monks who perform the work with their own hands or who command using unallowable terminology. For the purpose of producing crops, even for such monks with impure minds, it is indeed allowable to command using allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra) without doing it themselves. The statement “It is not allowable to appoint an attendant (kappiyakāraka)” is said to be “unsuitable” because it is a pond made by one’s own hands. However, no offense is found for the monk who appoints an attendant, nor for the Saṅgha that uses the requisites obtained from there. Alternatively, an offense should be understood here by taking the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) as the authority. If even a conscientious monk (lajjī) [can incur an offense], then it goes without saying for a shameless monk (alajjī); the meaning is that an offense is incurred if they are made to perform tasks such as digging up clay. “New crops” refers to fields that have not been cultivated before. By the word “kahāpaṇa” (money), it is shown that in the production of grain, it is unallowable only for that [monk who exerts effort]. In the effort to produce grain, there is only a Dukkaṭa offense, just as in the effort to produce money.

Because saying directly “Plough! Sow!” would be unallowable for all monks, it is said “without saying [so].” In the phrase “this much of a portion,” it is said with the intention of “this much money.” Even if it is said with the intention of money, at that time the money...
332:
Because of the non-existence of coins, a requisite that arises in the future is indeed allowable for others. Therefore, it is said: "That [requisite] is unallowable for that [monk] alone." For that monk, however, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in all efforts (payoga) as well as in usage (paribhoga). Some teachers say: "There is an offense only in the usage of grain, not in the initial effort." That is not appropriate. Because, since an offense occurs in the subsequent usage of grain due to such efforts as measuring and guarding, it is inappropriate to say there is no offense in performing those efforts. In the case of indirect speech (pariyāyakathā), however, there is no offense in all instances. For that very reason, it is said to be unallowable in the case of a specific command (niyama) such as "Bring such and such a thing with this much grain." The same method applies to the management of coins (kahāpaṇa). The statement beginning with "Such a thing exists, but there is no attendant (kappiyakāraka)" is the evidence here.

In the passage "I give a forest... it is allowable," because it is a place of residence, it is allowable even for an individual to accept it with a pure mind. Because it is spoken with a general term such as "monastery boundary" (vihārasīmā) in the phrase "We give a boundary," it is said "it is allowable."

Even though it is said "attendant" (veyyāvaccakara) and so forth, it is allowable even for an individual to accept a servant (dāsa). This is because the Blessed One specifically allowed it, saying, "Bhikkhus, I allow a monastery attendant (ārāmika)." And that [acceptance] must be in the manner of acceptance and usage by the Venerable Pilindavaccha, not in the manner of a layperson's usage of a servant. However, fields and so forth are allowable only for the Saṅgha, as they are not allowed to be accepted individually in the Pāḷi. The statement "We give to the monastery" is said with reference to a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha (saṅghika). The prohibition found in the Suttas such as "He abstains from accepting fields and property" was made by the Blessed One as a cause for an offense; thus, the Great Elders who conducted the Council, knowing the intention of the Blessed One, stated all these decisions outside the Pāḷi (pāḷimuttavinicchaya) concerning the acceptance of fields and so forth. There are four factors here: (1) pointing out a kappiyakāraka, (2) entrusting through a messenger, (3) further effort, and (4) acquisition through that effort.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Kings (Rājasi kkhāpada) is finished.

## The First Chapter on Robes (Cīvaravagga) is finished.
333:
## 2. Kosiya-vagga
## 1. Explanation of the Kosiya Training Rule
In the first training rule of the second chapter, in the Pāḷi, "kosiya-kārake" refers to those who make clothes and so forth with silk thread called kosiya, which is produced from the cocoons of silk-producing insects. "Saṅghāta" means destruction.

Because it is taught as "avāyimaṃ" (not woven), there is no offense in making it by weaving. "Missetvā" means having mixed it with sheep's wool. "Paṭilābhena" means upon completion. Since it is taught as "He finishes it, [it is] an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya)", the three factors here are: (1) the state of being mixed with silk, (2) making or causing to make a rug for one's own use, and (3) acquisition.

## The Explanation of the Kosiya Training Rule is finished.

547-552. The second [training rule], Suddhakāḷaka-sikkhāpada, and the third, Dvebhāga-sikkhāpada, are quite clear in meaning. However, in that Suddhakāḷaka training rule, the state of being "without intention" (acittaka) should be understood when one makes a rug with pure black wool while perceiving it as mixed with white wool and so forth. In the third training rule, it is when one makes a rug while perceiving that the black wool does not exceed [the limit] when it actually exceeds two parts.

## 4. Explanation of the Chabbassa Training Rule
In the fourth training rule, the root 'had' is in the sense of defecation, and the root 'mih' is in the sense of sprinkling (urination). With reference to the meanings of these roots, it is said: "They perform both excrement and urine." In this training rule, the state of being "without intention" (acittaka) should be understood through such instances as perceiving [a rug] to be over six years old when it is actually less than six years old.

## The Explanation of the Chabbassa Training Rule is finished.
334:
## 5. Nisīdanasanthata Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule, the phrase "it will be evident there [in Sāvatthī]" means that the wise will know because of the improper conduct regarding their own agreement. In the Pāli, the three ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), such as the forest-dwelling practice, are taught by way of the primary factors of the three requisites, such as lodgings; it should be understood that those monks also undertook the remaining ascetic practices.

"Pihayantā" means desiring or longing for. Because a sitting rug (nisīdana-santhata) is not a woven item and because it is a lodging accessory, it is not something to be formally determined (adhiṭṭhāna) as a robe. Therefore, the statement "because of perceiving it as a fourth robe" means perceiving it with a distorted perception. Some teachers, however, say: "This so-called sitting rug is indeed the sitting robe (nisīdana-cīvara) among the nine robes, and no other. This is because in the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada, as in this training rule, it is said, 'What is called a sitting rug is said to have a border,' and also in the Commentary, it is stated, 'Having spread it like a rug, at one end, a portion about one Sugata-span is split in two places to make three borders; because of those borders, it is said to have a border.'"

That statement is not appropriate. This is because the measurement is not specified in this training rule, and because the rug is not a woven robe, the Commentary does not state that it is sufficient for formal determination. As for the sitting robe (nisīdana-cīvara), it is made like a rug by spreading out pieces of the six robes according to the proper measurement. For that reason, the term "similar to a rug" is used. Therefore, only that [sitting robe mentioned in the Ratanavagga of the Pācittiya] is both a robe and should be formally determined; this [sitting rug] should be understood as neither a robe nor sufficient for formal determination.

The state of being an acittaka offense (offense regardless of intention) in this training rule should be understood by way of perceiving that one has taken the Sugata-span measurement when one has not, and perceiving that it is not less than the Sugata-span when it is actually less. Since it is stated that there is no offense if it is made for the sake of a canopy (vitāna) and such, there is indeed an offense for one who makes it for the sake of lying down. The statement "it is not fit to use" is said because pure black items are unallowable among silk items. For that reason, it is stated in various places in the Pāli, "If one obtains and uses what was made by another, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)." However, in the other two training rules, it is stated, "There is no offense." Among those training rules, in the fourth rule, there is no offense even if it is made for another; in the fifth rule, however, it should be understood as a wrongdoing if one does so. There is no fault in taking a rug that has been relinquished and given back. In using it, there is no fault if it is unraveled and made in an allowable manner.

## The Commentary on the Nisīdanasanthata Training Rule is finished.
335:
## 6. Eḷakaloma Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the explanation of the sixth training rule, the phrase in the Pāli "for one who has set out on a journey" is taught by way of the case (vatthu). Even for sheep's wool obtained at a place of residence, it is not allowable to carry it beyond three yojanas. The phrase "when there is no carrier" is taught as a suitable condition. Even when there is a carrier, there is no fault for a monk who carries it himself. "There is indeed an offense" because it was carried without being commanded [to another]. In stating the reason for both sides, the phrase "because of being with effort" means because the desire to go has not yet ceased. The reason for the side of the pure mind is stated as "because of being done without intention (acittaka)." "Does not agree" is stated because the analysis was given only for the portion "there is no offense if one has another carry it." "Not going" refers to a stationary vehicle and such. "Below" means on the ground.

"For one carrying that wool" means for a monk carrying it beyond three yojanas starting from the place of first acquisition. While carrying it in such a manner, if robbers seize it and return it, it is allowable to carry it for three yojanas from the place where it was returned. Some teachers, however, say: "Since 'first acquisition' is mentioned among the factors in the Mātikā Commentary, there is no offense even if one exceeds three yojanas from the place of the second acquisition." That statement is not appropriate. The second acquisition is also an entry into a place of acquisition, similar to going again from a place where one went to reside. Wool placed between waistbands and such is similar to being placed in a bag, and thus it is called "not a finished good." Likewise, the opening of a bundle (nidhānamukha) is the same. In this training rule, there are these five factors: (1) not being a finished good, (2) first acquisition, (3) exceeding three yojanas, (4) carrying it to and fro, and (5) having no intention to reside.

## The Commentary on the Eḷakaloma Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Eḷakalomadhovāpana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the explanation of the seventh training rule, in the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra) in the Pāli, regarding the phrase "having an unused finished good washed," the washing of a used finished good such as a blanket can cause an offense according to the Purāṇacīvara-dhovāpana training rule; therefore, to preclude that offense, it is stated "an unused finished good." The remaining words have clear meanings.

## The Commentary on the Eḷakalomadhovāpana Training Rule is finished.
336:
## 8. Rupiya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

583-4. In the eighth (explanation of the Rupiya Sikkhāpada), since a gold-made coin is also counted under the name 'rajata' (silver/money), it is said, "whether it be a gold-made coin." "Whether it be a silver-made coin" refers to a coin made by shaping silver into a figure. "Pākatika" (natural/ordinary) refers to the common coins currently in use.

By the phrase "all this also," it indicates all the objects of forfeiture (nissaggiya vatthu) taught in the training rule and the analysis (vibhaṅga). This phrase connects only with the term "the fourfold objects of forfeiture," and not with the nearby term "rajata." Now, wishing to show those fourfold objects of forfeiture in their specific forms, the phrase beginning with "rajata" is stated. In that context, although only "rajata-māsaka" was mentioned below and not silver (rajata) alone, because it is mentioned in the training rule by the term "jātarūpa-rajata," this term "rajata" is stated separately to show silver itself. However, in the word-for-word analysis (padabhājanī), since it is already established by the matrix (mātikā) term, silver alone is not mentioned; instead, to show what is counted together with that silver, the phrase beginning with "rajata means a kahāpaṇa" is stated. "Jātarūpa-māsaka" refers to coins (māsaka) made of gold. "Of the stated varieties" refers to the varieties stated as "whether made of silver or ordinary," etc. "Paṭaka" means a cloth or garment.

"Only a dukkaṭa" means that for the monk who receives it, an offense of dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) is incurred due to the act of receiving. Regarding usage, if the five classes of fellow practitioners receive items such as pearls, excluding grain, all monks who use the requisites arising from those items incur only a dukkaṭa. Some teachers, however, say: "If grain is received by the five classes of fellow practitioners, it is unallowable for all monks to use, just like pearls or land; the statement 'that grain is unallowable only for that monk' refers only to the management of grain produced on Sangha land through allowable procedures (kappiya-vohāra)."

The phrase "whether one, a hundred, or a thousand," etc., is stated to show the manner in which gold and silver (rupiya) exist at the lowest limit, not to show that "one must practice in this way." Since saying "Put it here" constitutes causing someone to pick it up (uggaṇhāpana), it is said, "One should not say, 'Put it here'." "It is allowable... and so on" means that because one does not take delight in it, the requisites arising from it are allowable, and thus it is said to "stand depending on the allowable." If there is improper management, the requisites arising from it are also unallowable, and thus it should be understood to "stand depending on the unallowable."

By the statement "One should not purchase any allowable goods with that gold or silver," it means that if one does purchase them, there is no way to use them, because they were purchased with gold or silver that was received and not surrendered to the Sangha. It is shown that for such goods, one must perform the act of forfeiture (nissajjana) in the midst of the Sangha, and only after discarding them can one confess the pācittiya offense.
337:
Some teachers say: "Allowable goods purchased after receiving a nissaggiya object are similar to allowable goods brought by lay attendants (kappiya-kārakas) after exchanging the gold or silver surrendered to the Sangha; therefore, they may be distributed and used without special means." That statement does not agree with the discussion on the fourfold bowl (pattacatukka), etc. In that discussion on the fourfold bowl, it is only shown that a bowl exchanged for gold or silver is not to be used, and the procedure for forfeiture is not mentioned.

"Upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapetvā" refers to the act of lay attendants lending for the sake of interest. "Akappiyaṃ" (unallowable) is stated because it was obtained with that nissaggiya object.

The term "patitokāsaṃ asammannāharantena" (not attending to the place where it fell) should be understood as showing a state of indifference. "Asantasambhāvanāya" refers to the declaration of false superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) through pretense and such. "Theyya-paribhoga" (usage by theft) is stated because it is not permitted by the Blessed One, who is the owner of the requisites. "Iṇa-paribhoga" (usage as a debt) is stated because one uses the requisites without performing the required reflection (paccavekkhaṇā), even though they are permitted by the Blessed One; by such usage, it shows that the virtue dependent on requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla) is compromised.

"Paribhoge paribhoge" (at each use) means that in usage where one repeatedly puts on and takes off (the robe) from the body, one should reflect during the last watch of the night; this is how it should be construed. In the context of "standing in the position of usage as a debt," some say that past reflection (atīta-paccavekkhaṇā) such as "Yesterday this robe was used by me" is also valid. "Paribhoge paribhoge" also means one should reflect when entering indoors from a place where water drops, and when sitting or lying down. "Satipaccayatā vaṭṭati" means it is proper to obtain the state of having mindfulness as a condition for reflection. It shows that the mindfulness of reflection must not be omitted during both the receiving and the using. Therefore, it is said, "having established mindfulness," etc. Some teachers, however, interpret "satipaccayatā" as "when there is a cause for using medicinal requisites"; even in their view, "paccaye sati" should be understood as "when there is noting of the presence of the requisite," because virtue is not purified by the mere presence of the requisite.

By the text "An offense is incurred for one who does not perform usage," the breach of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is shown, not the breach of the virtue dependent on requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla), because that virtue can be purified by past reflection. In this medicinal requisite and in the other three requisites, the difference between these two types of virtue should be understood: that only the virtue dependent on requisites is broken by the mention of usage as a debt, etc.

Having thus shown the purity of the virtue dependent on requisites, the phrase beginning with "for purity is fourfold" is stated to show all types of purity in that connection. Therein...
338:
Purity (suddhi) is called the fourfold morality (catubbiddhasīla) because it is purified by means of confession (desanā) and so forth, or because it is cleansed by confession and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "Because of being purified by confession," and so on. Here, by including "confession," the rehabilitation (vuṭṭhāna) of monks who have committed a pārājika offense and the admission of no longer being a monk are also included. This is because even for those who have committed a pārājika, by rising from the pārājika offense, the monk's virtue previously guarded below is said to be pure; because of such purity, the attainment of the Path (magga) can also be fulfilled for them.

It is called inheritance (dāya) because of the sense of being given; they are called heirs (dāyāda) because they take that inheritance. In the phrase "of the seven learners (sekkhas)," noble worldlings (kalyāṇaputhujjanas) are also included. This is to be understood because their use [of requisites], which is not use as a debtor (iṇaparibhoga), is included in the use as an heir (dāyajjaparibhoga). The Dhammadāyāda Sutta is the discourse beginning with, "Bhikkhus, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.29). In that sutta, the meaning should be taken by bringing in the word "me" (my) as in "do not be my heirs in material things." Only by taking it this way will it be the achiever of the aforementioned meaning.

Use together with a conscientious (lajjī) person means the state of being mixed by way of Dhamma and material things (āmisa). In the case of use together with a shameless (alajjī) person, the method is the same. By the statement "From the beginning, there is no such thing as a shameless person," it is shown that one should not harbor suspicion toward every monk one sees; it should be done only when there is a cause such as seeing or hearing. Those who are one's own burdens refer to co-residents (saddhivihārikas) and so forth. "If he does not refrain" means not refraining from the use of Dhamma and material things through bias (agati). The statement "There is no such thing as an offense" is said with reference to requisites rightfully obtained by the shameless and to legal acts according to Dhamma (dhammakamma). For even those shameless ones, there is indeed an offense in using requisites obtained through corrupting families (kuladūsana) and so forth, or in performing schismatic acts (vaggakamma) and so forth.

Since it is said, "Rightful and unrightful use should be understood by way of requisites," it should be understood that the use by a conscientious person has already been mentioned below both by way of requisites and by way of performing a single legal act (ekakamma) and so forth. Therefore, in the commentary on the Duṭṭhullavācā training rule, two shameless monks who stand in the position of accuser and accused were told, with reference to the use of Dhamma, "Live as those having communal use" (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.385-386), because there is no conflict in their mutual use of Dhamma and material things. It is only for conscientious persons that both types of use together with a shameless person are improper.

Use of Dhamma (dhammaparibhoga) refers to communion (saṃvāsa) mentioned as "performing a single legal act, having a single recitation," and so forth, as well as all non-material use (nirāmisaparibhoga) such as taking and giving dependence (nissaya).
339:
It should be understood. Because it is stated, "He should not be made to undergo a penalty for an offense," it should be understood that an offense is committed if a conscientious person (lajjī) supports a shameless person (alajjī). "Itaropi" refers to the conscientious person (lajjī). It is shown that if this conscientious person supports a shameless person who praises himself—either out of regard for gains obtained through words of praise and so on, or out of worldly affection (gehasitapema)—then that conscientious person is one who causes the disappearance of the Dispensation (Sāsana). In this way, the shameless person, having received support from lay devotees and others, gains strength and oppresses the virtuous monks who love morality; before long, he makes the Dispensation contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya.

By the statement, "In that case, the use of the Dhamma (dhamma-paribhoga) is also allowable," it is shown that the use of the Dhamma is more significant than the use of material requisites (āmisa-paribhoga); therefore, the use of the Dhamma should be conducted in extreme seclusion from shameless persons. Because it is said, "It should be learned for the sake of supporting the Dhamma," when shameless persons are numerous and the Dispensation is declining, if there are insufficient conscientious persons, it is indeed proper to support the Dispensation by including even a shameless person (who has not committed a pārājika) to complete the quorum for performing acts such as higher ordination (upasampadā), or by supporting some shameless persons with the use of Dhamma and material requisites to suppress the remaining group of shameless persons.

However, some teachers say that because it is stated, "The scripture stands at the peak," only the learning of scriptures is called the use of the Dhamma, and single acts (ekakamma) such as Sangha-acts (saṅghakamma) are not the use of the Dhamma. Therefore, they say it is allowable to perform acts such as the Uposatha together with shameless persons and that there is no offense; however, that statement is not appropriate. This is because, among the many types of Dhamma-use such as single acts, the scripture is cited here only as an example to show the appropriate use of the Dhamma at a time when it must be done together with shameless persons. In fact, it cannot be said that procedures such as single acts are not the use of the Dhamma, because they are not material requisites. This is because there is no use (paribhoga) that does not fall under either Dhamma or material requisites (āmisa).

For this very reason, in the Atthasālinī commentary, in the discussion on Dhamma-hospitality (dhamma-paṭisanthāra), it is shown that Sangha-acts and so on also belong to the category of Dhamma: "Meditation subjects should be taught, the Dhamma should be recited... rehabilitation (abbhāna), penance (mānatta), and probation (parivāsa) should be given, those fit for novice ordination should be ordained, those fit for higher ordination should be ordained... this is called Dhamma-hospitality." Among those categories of Dhamma, if one performs the Uposatha out of consideration for shameless persons for reasons such as completing a quorum, or if one learns the Dhamma or takes dependence (nissaya) from them, it is called "the use of the Dhamma" (dhamma-paribhoga) because it is both Dhamma and a form of use. It is not allowable to engage in such use of the Dhamma without a suitable reason. For the monk who does so, it constitutes the use of a shameless person and he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Acts of suppression such as the act of censure (tajjaniya-kamma), acts of benefit such as probation (parivāsa), and the teaching of Pāḷi and commentaries, when performed without regard for shameless persons, are called only "Dhamma" and not "use" (paribhoga). It is allowable to perform such Dhamma for suitable shameless persons. Just like giving material requisites, there is no offense. Giving dependence (nissaya) and granting the thirteen types of formal authorization (sammuti) and so on are not allowable, because they are causes for "use," such as enjoying the performance of major and minor duties. If a prominent shameless person is presenting what is not Dhamma and not Vinaya as the Buddha's teaching, it is not allowable to perform acts of benefit such as higher ordination (upasampadā) or to teach Pāḷi and commentaries to his co-residents (saddhivihārika) and others. Only an offense is incurred. Only acts of suppression should be performed. For this very reason, supporting a shameless person is forbidden. In fact, one should desire only to suppress shameless persons by avoiding the use of Dhamma and the use of material requisites with them. Such suppression is for the sake of the comfortable living of monks who love morality, for the endurance of the True Dhamma, and for the support of the Vinaya.
340:
Whether it is a disciplinary act such as the act of censure (tajjaniya-kamma), or a helpful act such as probation (parivāsa), or the teaching of the Pāḷi and Commentaries, etc., these should be performed. Such performance is merely Dhamma and is not considered communion (paribhoga). It is proper to perform this Dhamma, which is not communion, for suitable shameless (alajjī) monks. Like the giving of material gifts (āmisa-dāna), there is no offense. However, giving dependence (nissaya) and the thirteen authorizations (sammuti), etc., is not proper because they are causes for communion, such as enjoying major and minor services.

If a monk is greatly shameless (mahā-alajjī) and treats the Teacher’s Dispensation as what is not Dhamma as Dhamma and what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, it is not proper to perform for him helpful acts such as higher ordination (upasampadā) for his co-residents (saddhivihārika), etc., nor the teaching of Pāḷi and Commentaries, etc. An offense is indeed incurred. Only disciplinary acts should be performed. For this reason, the favoring of shameless monks is also rejected. Indeed, by avoiding communion in Dhamma (dhamma-paribhoga) and communion in material things (āmisa-paribhoga), the intention is only to discipline shameless persons. Such discipline is for the sake of the comfortable living of conscientious (pesala) monks, the stability of the True Dhamma (saddhamma), and the support of the Vinaya. The prescription of training rules (sikkhāpada) is also for the purpose of having such benefits.

Therefore, whatever action serves to support the shameless, or causes discomfort to conscientious monks, or leads to the decline of the True Dhamma, etc.—whether it be communion or non-communion—it is not proper to perform. Those who act in this way cause the Dispensation to disappear and they also incur offenses. Among these communions in Dhamma and material things, only the communion in Dhamma, such as performing communal acts (kamma) together with the shameless, leads to the discomfort of conscientious monks and the decline of the True Dhamma, etc. Communion in material things is not like that. Conscientious monks do not suffer discomfort merely by using the requisites of the shameless; it happens only through the aforementioned communion in Dhamma. Only by avoiding that communion in Dhamma do comfortable living and other benefits arise.

For this reason, when shameless persons who have transgressed training rules enter for the Uposatha, etc., they should be addressed by the monks with words such as, "You have committed transgressions in bodily and verbal doors." If they do not abide by the Vinaya, they should be well disciplined by means of expulsion from the Saṅgha, etc. Monks who do not do so but continue to associate with those shameless ones also become shameless themselves, in accordance with the saying, "Even one shameless person can create a hundred shameless ones" (Pārājika Commentary 2.585). If they were not disciplined in this way, they would increase quarrels, etc., in the Saṅgha, cause discomfort to conscientious monks by obstructing communal acts of harmony such as the Uposatha, and gradually increase their following like Devadatta and the Vajjiputtakas. By presenting their own wrong practice as Dhamma and Vinaya, and by causing schisms in the Saṅgha, they would soon cause the Dispensation to disappear. However, if they are disciplined by means of expulsion from the Saṅgha, etc., all these dangers will not occur. Thus it is said:
341:
"Depending on an immoral person (dussīla), the Uposatha does not stand, the Pavāraṇā does not stand, communal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅgha-kamma) do not proceed, and there is no harmony... but when the immoral are disciplined, all these dangers do not occur, and then the conscientious (pesala) monks live in comfort" (Pārājika Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 39).

Therefore, communion in Dhamma (dhamma-paribhoga), such as performing a single communal act, should be performed with extreme seclusion from the shameless, even more so than communion in material things. It should be understood that it causes an offense because it is a cause for the decline of the True Dhamma.

Furthermore, this point is also evident because the Commentary explains that communal acts of the Saṅgha should not be performed with the shameless, stating, "The Uposatha does not stand, the Pavāraṇā does not stand, communal acts of the Saṅgha do not proceed." Similarly, regarding the conduct of a monk whose gender has changed (parivatta-liṅga) and who goes to a nunnery: "If there are conscientious (lajjinī) nuns who are pleasing and hospitable, one should not leave for another place after upsetting them. If he does go, he is not free from offenses such as traveling between villages (gāmantara), crossing a river (nadīpāra), staying away from requisites overnight (rattivippavāsa), and leaving the group (gaṇa-ohīyana)... If the nuns are shameless (alajjinī) but still provide hospitality, one is permitted to leave them and go elsewhere." Thus, for the sake of avoiding the offense of communion (saṃvāsa-āpatti) that would arise from living with shameless nuns, the teacher permits situations involving heavy offenses (garuka-āpatti) such as crossing a river. From this, it is understood that the offense arising from association with the shameless is even heavier because it is a cause for the decline of the True Dhamma. Indeed, teachers do not permit the commission of a heavy offense just to avoid a light offense (lahuka-āpatti) or a non-offense situation.

Likewise, in the commentary on the word "asaṃvāsa" (non-communion): "Because one must train in harmony with all conscientious (lajjī) persons, it is called 'equality in training' (sama-sikkhātā). Here, since all conscientious ones live together in these communal acts, etc., and not even one is seen outside of that, therefore, taking all of them together, this is called 'communion' (saṃvāsa)." Thus, it is explained that communion such as performing a single communal act is proper only with the conscientious.

If that is so, why are the shameless not counted among those who are "non-communal" (asaṃvāsika)? This is not a contradiction. This is because only those who are not of good standing (apakatatta), such as those who have fallen into Pārājika and whose presence as a quorum-filler (gaṇa-pūraka) would invalidate a communal act, are taken as "non-communal." There are shameless ones who are still of good standing (pakatatta). Although they can complete a quorum and fulfill a communal act, they cause an offense to those monks who perform the act solely out of favoritism (agati).
342:
Monks who have fallen into an offense of the same nature are like those who commit offenses with one another. This is because the state of being unconscientious (alajji) and conscientious (lajji) in worldlings (puthujjana) is connected only to a moment of consciousness (cittakkhaṇa) and is not permanent. When a mind intending to transgress arises with volition, they become unconscientious. Again, with the thought, "I will not do such a thing again," they become conscientious. Among those unconscientious monks of normal status (pakatatta), only those who do not desist even when admonished by monks who love virtue (pesala) and who transgress repeatedly should not be associated with (asaṃvasitabba). Others who desist upon being admonished are not to be avoided, as they have entered the state of being conscientious (lajji-dhamma). For this reason, it was allowed to perform the Uposatha and so forth only after purifying [the assembly] to avoid those unconscientious monks, without counting them among those excluded from communion (asaṃvāsika).

Thus, the inappropriateness of performing the Uposatha in an impure assembly was shown by such words as, "Venerables, announce your purity; I shall recite the Pātimokkha" (Mahāvagga 134). The manner of performing the Uposatha by establishing even an unconscientious monk in the state of conscientiousness was also taught: "If any monk has an offense, let him reveal it... if he reveals it, it will be well for him" (Mahāvagga 134). In the Uposatha of purity (pārisuddhi-uposatha), the purity of the monks performing the Uposatha was shown by: "Are you pure in this assembly?... Venerables, you are pure herein," and "Venerable, I am pure; may you sustain me as one who is pure" (Mahāvagga 168). The procedure for suspending the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā for those unconscientious monks who do not desist even when spoken to was also taught. Because it is improper to associate in any way with unconscientious monks who do not enter the state of conscientiousness, the refusal to give or receive dependence (nissaya), the performance of acts of punishment such as the act of rebuke (tajjaniya-kamma), and the procedure for bringing an unconscientious monk along with his followers to the state of being excluded from communion (asaṃvāsika) by performing the act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) were also taught. Therefore, according to the aforementioned methods of the Suttas and the words of the Commentaries, it is not proper to perform communal acts (kamma) or associate with any unconscientious monks, whether they are of normal status (pakatatta) or not (apakatatta); for those who do so, there is only an offense. This conclusion should be reached here because all training rules were laid down only for the purpose of restraining ill-behaved persons. For this very reason, in the Second Council, the Vajjiputtaka monks, though of normal status (pakatatta), were unconscientious, and thus Elder Yasa and others separated them from the Saṅgha with great effort. Among those Vajjiputtaka monks, there were no those excluded from communion (asaṃvāsika) such as those who committed Pārājika, because the ten points they presented were only within the scope of light offenses (lahuka-āpatti).

"Tassa pana santike" means in the presence of Elder Mahārakkhita. "Kharapatta" refers to an object resembling gold called 'khara'. When donors give gold or silver unintentionally, and then take it back thinking it is their own property, it is not proper to refuse to give it back, nor is it proper to give it by saying, "Take this forfeiture object (nissaggiya-vatthu)." ... that money object ...
343:
(When the donors take it back thinking it is their own property), it is not proper to refuse to give it back, nor is it proper to give it (as a forfeited object); therefore, he said, "Look at your piece of cloth." Even if given after speaking thus, although there is no object to be forfeited as in the case of a lost item, the offense must still be confessed. In truth, if one takes that money object with one's own hand along with cloth etc. out of forgetfulness and gives it saying, "I give this," it becomes a gift because the nature of relinquishment exists at the time of giving, just as when one intends to give a low-value item but gives a high-value one. For the monk who receives it, even if he knows it is given out of forgetfulness, it does not constitute theft (adinnādāna) because the donors gave it; therefore, it is only a forfeiture offense (nissaggiya) due to consenting to the gold or silver. Some teachers, however, say, "Such a gift is not called a gift; that is why it is said here, 'Look at your piece of cloth'." We do not approve of that statement; it should be investigated.

The word "Ekaparicchedāni" is said with reference to sometimes being an action (kiriya) and sometimes being a non-action (akiriya). There are three factors here: being gold or silver, being for one's own sake, and being one of the acts such as receiving.

## The Explanation of the Rūpiya Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Rūpiyasaṃvohāra Training Rule

In the ninth training rule, the four types of forfeiture objects such as gold (jātarūpa) are included here by the word "rūpiya" itself; therefore, he said, "Exchange of gold and silver (jātarūparajataparivattanaṃ)." "Paṭiggahitaparivattane" means exchanging gold or silver that has been received through either allowable or unallowable terms.

In the Pali, "ghanakataṃ" refers to things made of bricks and so forth. In the passages such as "Rūpiyaṃ nāma satthuvaṇṇo," although silver alone is not taken, it should be understood that it is included by the word "rūpiya" itself. It should be understood by adding that it refers only to pure trading with gold and silver. In the passage "Rūpiye rūpiyasaññī" etc., the remaining text is "I shall speak the decision."

In the Pali, "Rūpiye rūpiyasaññī" is said with reference to one's own property that is being given. "Rūpiyaṃ cetāpeti" refers to another's property. This method applies to the rest as well. Therein, by the word "arūpiya," objects of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) are also included. In the last triad, the application in all places should be understood by this method: "If one perceives non-money as money and buys non-money, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)." In this triad, however, only allowable objects are taken by the word "arūpiya," not objects of wrongdoing such as pearls. Because at the end, "Together with the five..."
344:
## 
Because it is stated as "Anāpatti" (no offense), even if a dukkaṭa object is not taken, for a monk who exchanges a dukkaṭa object for another dukkaṭa object, or a kappiya object for a dukkaṭa object, a dukkaṭa offense is established by way of method. This dukkaṭa offense occurs for the monk who exchanges it whether with a correct perception, an incorrect perception, or with doubt regarding the dukkaṭa object, because this training rule is acittaka (an offense that occurs regardless of intention). "Pañcannaṃ saha" means together with the five classes of co-religionists.

Now, to show that the meaning of "exchanging a nissaggiya object for a dukkaṭa object or a kappiya object" is obtainable by way of method, although it does not appear directly in the Pāḷi text, the words beginning with "Yo hi ayaṃ" are stated. In this training rule, an arūpiya object (a kappiya or dukkaṭa object) exchanged for gold or silver (rūpiya) does not become nissaggiya even if forfeited, because it is unallowable for all monks. This is because only an object that is fit to be used by other monks after being forfeited should be forfeited according to the Vinaya procedure. Simply by discarding this arūpiya object exchanged for gold or silver, the monk who made the exchange must confess only a pācittiya offense. Therefore, the Blessed One did not teach the triad beginning with "One who perceives gold and silver as gold and silver causes a non-monetary object to be acquired; there is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense." In all three cases, it is because the object being exchanged is arūpiya, which is inconsistent with the term nissaggiya, and because only the gold and silver (rūpiya) itself must be forfeited.

The Pāḷi text shows the procedure for how monastery attendants and others should handle only the gold and silver that has been forfeited, but not for the arūpiya object. Therefore, in the Commentary, it is stated, "Although this triad is not taught, it should be understood," in order to show that only a pācittiya offense occurs in this exchange of an arūpiya object for gold and silver; it is not stated to show the nissaggiya status of that arūpiya object. For this very reason, in the Pattacatukka-kathā, it is stated, "It cannot be made kappiya by any means," and so on. This is our (the Vimativinodanī-ṭīkā author's) preferred view. The words beginning with "Attano vā hi" are stated to support the fulfillment of the third triad in accordance with the second triad. The meaning there is: just as the second triad was taught stating "a transaction involving gold and silver (rūpiyasaṃvohāra) is indeed committed" because gold and silver is involved on one side for a monk who causes another's gold and silver to be acquired with his own arūpiya object, so too should a third triad be taught for a monk who causes another's arūpiya object to be acquired with his own gold and silver. However, that third triad is not separately taught in the Pāḷi text because it is fulfilled by the second triad itself, due to the common factor of gold and silver being involved on one side. In that sentence, "ekantena rūpiyapakke" means being included in the category of gold and silver on one side. Alternatively, there is a reading "ekato rūpiyapakke".

Now, in order to show the different types of offenses in exchanging gold and silver etc. for a dukkaṭa object, among the dukkaṭa and kappiya objects which are the meanings of the term "arūpiya" in the second triad...
345:
## 
The words beginning with "Dukkaṭavatthunā" are commenced. However, the words beginning with "Dukkaṭavatthunā dukkaṭavatthu" are stated to show that the meaning, although not directly taught in the Pāḷi text regarding exchange with a dukkaṭa object, is obtainable by way of method. In that text, "iminā" means by this Rūpiyasaṃvohāra (trading with gold and silver) training rule; through that training rule, it also shows the acittaka nature of the dukkaṭa offense. The words "aññatra sahadhammikehi" are stated because of the statement "there is no offense together with the five classes of co-religionists"; by those words, it also establishes that the Kayavikkayasikkhāpada (trading training rule) is indeed based on allowable (kappiya) objects. This... (omitted)... and regarding the exchange of gold and silver should be connected with the original text. "Idha" means in this training rule. "Tattha" means in the Kayavikkayasikkhāpada.

Having thus shown the different types of offenses in exchanging gold and silver etc. for a dukkaṭa object, the words beginning with "Kappiyavatthunā pana" are now commenced to show them regarding allowable (kappiya) objects as well. In that text, "teneva" means only with a kappiya object. The words "having accepted gold and silver" are stated by way of the highest case. A bowl caused to be made by accepting dukkaṭa objects such as pearls is also certainly unallowable for the five classes of co-religionists. "Samuṭṭhāpeti" means he causes it to arise either by going himself or by commanding another, saying, "Give this money (kahāpaṇa) etc. to the workmen and cause the seeds to be produced." "Mahā-akappiya" (greatly unallowable) is stated because he himself has spoiled it from the seed stage onwards, and thus there is no other original owner.

That bowl (made from the seed onwards) is not allowable for any monk who knows about it, even if it is stolen by thieves and then recovered. If it were allowable, the teachers would have said it is allowable even if stolen, as in the case of tank embankments and dams. "Cannot be done by any means" means it cannot be made allowable (kappiya) by forfeiting it to the Saṅgha, or by it being stolen by thieves, etc. This statement is made regarding its existence in that form (as a bowl) and its existence in the form of the cloth, pearls, etc., which were the price of that bowl. It is not possible by any means to make the dukkaṭa object or the kappiya object that was the price of that bowl allowable in that same form. However, it should be understood that if that monk causes gold and silver to be acquired again with that kappiya or dukkaṭa object, it would be possible to make it allowable for others after having that gold and silver forfeited.

In the phrase "buys a bowl", it should be understood that causing monastery attendants and others to buy it, saying "Go and buy a bowl from the blacksmith's family with this money (kahāpaṇa) etc.", is also included. For this very reason, in the Commentary on the Rājasikkhāpada, it is taught: "If one says, 'Bring a robe with this much money; prepare gruel etc. with this much money,' the item they bring is unallowable for all monks. Why? Because the money has been managed and used."
346:
This has been stated. However, the statement in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā that the Rūpiyasaṃvohāra Sikkhāpada is 'anaṇattika' (a training rule not requiring a command) does not agree with this (Vimativinodanī) statement. Not only does it disagree with this statement, but it also disagrees with the Pali text. In the Pali text, when one wishes to have attendants (ārāmikas) and others exchange relinquished gold and silver for ghee and so on, it is stated that one should say, 'Friend, know this gold and silver.' If that person asks, 'What should be brought with this gold and silver?', one must not say, 'Bring this or that.' One should only point out allowable items (kappiya), saying, 'Ghee...' and so forth, thus speaking in a way that avoids gold and silver trading (rūpiyasaṃvohāra). Even if one says 'Bring this' to a person asking 'What should be brought with this gold and silver?', it effectively becomes a command by the monks to 'Bring this with this gold and silver' due to the context. Therefore, to avoid such gold and silver trading, the prohibition was made: 'One must not say, "Bring this or that."' In the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra), it is also not stated that 'one informs the kappiyakāraka.' However, it is stated so in the Kayavikkaya Sikkhāpada. Therefore, this (Rūpiyasaṃvohāra) training rule is only 'sāṇattika' (involving a command), and only the Kayavikkaya Sikkhāpada should be understood as 'anaṇattika'.

'Mūlassa anissaṭṭhattā' means that because the price (gold/silver) with which the bowl was bought has not yet been relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha. By this, it is shown that only the gold and silver must be relinquished, and there is no need to relinquish the non-monetary object that was the price of that gold and silver. If one had exchanged that gold and silver for other gold and silver, it should be relinquished just as described in the Rūpiyasaṃvohāra Sikkhāpada, and then the remaining monks may use it. By the phrase 'mūlassa asampaṭicchitattā', it is shown that the price belongs to a layperson, and therefore, no fault of gold and silver trading arises regarding the bowl. This is because the fault of gold and silver trading occurs only when the property belongs to the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika). In such a case, a pācittiya offense is incurred for one's own property, and a dukkaṭa offense for another's property.

'Nissajji' (relinquishes) is said in the sense of giving, not in the sense of a formal Vinaya act (vinayakamma). That is why it is said, 'having filled it with ghee.' In exchanging with one's own property, there are two factors here: the property being gold or silver, and it being one of the acts of exchanging or causing to exchange.

## The Description of the Rūpiyasaṃvohāra Sikkhāpada is finished.
347:
## 10. Description of the Kayavikkaya Sikkhāpada

593-5. In the Pali of the tenth training rule, 'know' means 'investigate right now; it will not be possible to discard this later.' The word 'with this' refers to the object given by the monk, and 'this' refers to the object given in return by the other person. Since there is a possibility of destroying a gift given out of faith among other relatives, 'even a mother or a father' is mentioned to show a place where such destruction does not occur. Regarding 'it is not possible to reject that,' some teachers say that just as a pācittiya offense is incurred when giving gold and silver to laborers to extract iron ore from ownerless land and taking the goods from those digging for wages, the same applies here in washing clothes and so on. However, that statement is not appropriate. Because iron ore obtained by digging ownerless land belongs only to the laborers. For a monk giving gold and silver for that iron ore, it is only the fault of gold and silver trading (rūpiyasaṃvohāra), just as in bartering (kayavikkaya) when having dye-bark and so on brought through unallowable trade (akappiyavohāra). Such property belonging to another does not exist here in washing clothes and so on. Therefore, one should take the pācittiya offense here only by taking the decision of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) as the standard.

'Gives thinking it will be merit' means that if a monk knows his own goods are of low value but does not say so, and says, 'Examine and take it now, do not regret it later,' and the other person, not knowing the high value of what he is giving, says, 'Whether it is less or more, let it be for you alone' and gives it and leaves, then like Venerable Upananda in the case of taking the robe of the wanderer (paribbājaka), that monk incurs no offense. To the person who returns out of regret with the perception of it being his own property, the excess taken must be returned. In exchanging one property for another, these three are the factors of this training rule: both items being allowable (kappiya), not being a co-religionist (asahadhammika), and engaging in bartering (kayavikkaya).

## The Description of the Kayavikkaya Sikkhāpada is finished.

## The second, Kosiyavagga, is finished.

## 3. Pattavagga

## 1. Description of the Pattasikkhāpada

In the first training rule of the third chapter, the phrase 'twelve and a half palas' refers to water measuring twelve and a half palas by the Magadhan measure.
348:
Similarly, some teachers say that it refers to a vessel containing twelve and a half palas of barley, beans, and so forth. However, the teacher Elder Dhammapāla said: "Four ordinary handfuls (muṭṭhi) make one kuḍuba; four kuḍubas make one nāḷi; sixteen of these nāḷis make one doṇa; and they say that this doṇa is equal to twelve Magadhan nāḷis." The term 'Tamil nāḷi' refers to the ancient nāḷi. That ancient nāḷi consists of eight kuḍubas (each being four handfuls); thus, two of these ancient nāḷis equal one Magadhan nāḷi. Ancient teachers, however, say: "The ancient Sīhaḷa nāḷi contains three (ancient) nāḷis." According to those teachers, the Magadhan nāḷi is equal to four of the Tamil nāḷis (of four kuḍubas) currently in use. A vessel half the size of that Magadhan nāḷi, known as the ancient Tamil nāḷi, is called a pattha. In this way, it also agrees with the Pali statement: "An inferior bowl (omaka patta) contains almsfood cooked from one pattha." In worldly usage also:

"Two types of pattha (measuring vessels) are mentioned: the worldly nāḷi and the Magadhan nāḷi. The worldly nāḷi is sixteen palas, and the Magadhan one is known to be double that."

Thus, it is shown that in the world, the Magadhan nāḷi is twice as large as the ordinary nāḷi. If taken this way, the point that an inferior bowl (omaka patta) contains just enough almsfood for sustenance is established and clear. It is not possible to seek and subsist on almsfood that is not heaped up in a bowl that contains less than eight kuḍubas. For this very reason, it is stated in the Verañjaka Section Commentary: "A pattha is about one nāḷi, which is sufficient for one person's sustenance. It is also said: 'Almsfood cooked from one pattha is not enough for two.'" It is also mentioned that "for each person, it is enough for two or three." Therefore, it should be understood only according to the method stated here.

Regarding the phrase "suitable for a morsel," since it is stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta Commentary that "the amount of curry is one-fourth of the rice," it should be understood that only curry amounting to one-fourth of the rice-morsel is suitable. "Having the nature of rice" means they tend to go inside the rice and do not seek a separate space for themselves. "In name only" refers to names such as "medium bowl" or "medium-inferior bowl."

607-8. "Thus, in every effort (payoga)" means in every effort of swallowing the final morsel; it means morsel by morsel. "Having made" means having brought to the completion of the firing. "I will bake and keep" refers to baking until it reaches a black color...
349:
This is said in reference to (that). "Chidda" (hole) refers to a hole located two finger-breadths below the rim of the bowl. The rest is as explained in the first Kathina section.

## The Explanation of the Bowl Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Fewer than Five Ties

609-613. In the Pali of the second training rule, the phrase "I will satisfy those monks with a bowl" is the remaining text. By the word "not a bowl" (apatto), it also shows the relinquishing of the determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Even in a bowl with five ties, if the firing is incomplete, the determination does not take effect, just as in an unfired bowl. Since it is said "or with a lead plate," it is allowable to cover a hole in an iron bowl with allowable metals such as copper. Therefore, it is said "with a metal disc" (lohamandalaka). In this training rule, it should be understood that there is an offense for a monk who requests an allowable bowl that is not black in color. The four factors here are: the bowl being fit for determination having fewer than five ties, intending it for oneself, making an improper request, and obtaining it through that request.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Fewer than Five Ties is Finished.

## 3. The Explanation of the Medicine Training Rule

618-621. In the Pali of the third training rule, Elder Pilindavaccha first refused, saying, "Great King, the Blessed One has not yet allowed a monastery attendant." Then, when the Blessed One allowed the acceptance of slaves under the name of "monastery attendants" (ārāmika) for individuals, the attendants were accepted. However, since fields and such were not allowed in that way, it should be understood that it is not allowable for individuals to accept them, even using allowable terminology like "monastery gift" (vihāradāna). In the list of things to be abstained from, such as "abstaining from accepting fields and property," only the monastery attendant slave is allowed to be accepted as personal property; thus, it is clear that other things like fields should not be accepted in that way. Elder Pilindavaccha's creation of a gold garland from a handful of grass for a donor family's child was done because it does not constitute "favoring a family" (kulasangaha), according to the statement: "Monks, there is no offense for one with psychic power in the scope of his psychic power." Some teachers say: "Because Arahants have no desire for gain..."
350:
Some teachers claim that for Arahants, because they have no desire for gain, even if there is 'favoring of families' (kula-saṅgaha), there is no 'failure in livelihood' (ājīva-vipatti). This statement is inappropriate because even Arahants must avoid things like the offering of almsfood which are causes for failure in livelihood. Indeed, the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), said: 'Even if one were to lose one's life, one should not destroy the purity of livelihood.' And the Blessed One also said: 'Food obtained by chanting verses is not to be eaten by me,' and so forth.

'Self-taken' (uggahitaka) means personally taken for the purpose of consumption. 'Self-made' means made by cooking. 'Before the meal' (purebhatta) means it is allowable only during the morning of that day because it was accepted along with the substance (savatthuka) of milk or curd. 'Self-done' (sayankata) refers to butter made by cooking cream or milk. The phrase 'only free from material food' (nirāmisa) is said with reference to the morning of that day. To the question, 'Why is there no fault of self-cooking (sāmapāka) for a monk who consumes self-made butter today that is free from material food?', the answer is given starting with 'for one heating butter' (navanītaṃ tāpentassa). The word 'accepted' (paṭiggahitehi) is said with reference to milk and curd. The construction is: butter made with milk or curd whose acceptance has lapsed should be used for foot-salve and so on. The phrase 'in this same way' is said with reference to the nissaggiya (forfeiture) offense. 'Butter from unallowable meat' refers to butter from elephants and so on.

'But herein' means there is a distinction regarding fresh butter. 'What is washed is allowable' means it is not even allowable to accept unwashed fresh butter; otherwise, the Elders' intention is that it becomes 'accepted along with the substance' if taken with curd or whey.

However, the intention of Elder Mahāsiva is that because it is separated from its source, milk, it does not become 'accepted along with the substance' merely by being associated with curd-balls and so on. Therefore, the meaning is that they consumed it after taking the fresh butter just as it was extracted from the whey, cleaning it, or cooking it to make it free from material food. They did not eat it along with curd-balls and so on at the wrong time (after noon). Therefore, it was said: 'Thus, a monk consuming that fresh butter... does not become one who has accepted it along with the substance.' In that text, the meaning is that a monk who accepts uncleaned fresh butter and consumes it should remove the curd and so on before consuming. 'It will reach exhaustion' means it becomes free from material food; therefore, the meaning is that it is allowable even at the wrong time. 'By this much' means by a small amount of curd and so on that merely clings to the fresh butter and does not receive the distinct name of 'curd'. By this statement, it is shown that butter cooked along with curd and so on that has been accepted separately is counted as 'accepted along with the substance'. 'In that also' means even in butter that is free from material food. The intention of the scrupulous monks is: regarding the acceptance, because the taste is not yet mixed with curd and so on, it does not yet become 'accepted along with the substance,' like a lump of molasses and so on that is with rice.
351:
A monk cooking that fresh butter which was accepted mixed with curd or whey should cook it only after cleaning it. Otherwise, if he cooks it (without cleaning), because the taste becomes mixed with the curd-balls and so on being cooked at the moment of cooking, it becomes 'self-cooked' (sāmaṃpakka). Even when those curd-balls and so on are exhausted, it remains 'self-cooked'; therefore, it should be cooked only after cleaning it so that it is free from material food (nirāmisa). For this very reason, the cause was stated as 'because of being cooked along with material food.'

Herein, this is the investigation: when there is no 'acceptance along with the substance,' if a monk cooks it with material food, is there a doubt whether it is the 'fault of self-cooking' (sayampāka-dosa) or whether it becomes 'limited to the time' (yāvakālika)? Between these two, the fault of self-cooking is not possible here because this fresh butter is a 'seven-day medicine' (sattāhakālika). The reason is that the material food such as curd contained therein is exhausted (by cooking). Or, if one doubts whether it becomes like 'cooked with the substance' because he cooked it himself along with the accepted curd-balls and so on, then the reason should be stated as 'because it was accepted along with material food,' not 'because it was cooked.' If so, it would mean accepting the view of the Upaḍḍha Elders.

In that view, even if cooked by novices (sāmaṇeras) and so on, it would still be 'limited to the time' (yāvakālika). This is because it would be like butter and so on made by unordained persons after cooking accepted milk and so on. However, such a 'limited to the time' status is not appropriate. The reason is that fresh butter and so on obtained during the almsround are likely to be mixed with material food like whey, which would lead to the consequence of them being inedible. In truth, there is no fixed rule that donors must clean or purify (the butter) before pouring it into the bowl. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is also said: 'Just as broken rice and so on fallen into it are not cooked... if one cooks it again and offers it, it is allowable for seven days as in the previous method.' This statement contradicts the claim (that it becomes yāvakālika).

Therefore, in cooking this fresh butter mixed with curd and whey after accepting it, no reason for the arising of remorse (kukkucca) is seen for scrupulous monks. Just as the reason is not clear here, the reason for the statement 'A shameful novice, so that broken rice and so on do not cook, removes the part mixed with material food, melts it in the fire... and it is allowable' is also not seen. If this statement were made to avoid mixing with 'limited to the time' food, then one would have to do the same oneself. Even in butter and so on offered by lay donors, the suspicion of being mixed with material food would not disappear. This is because donors do not usually melt it, remove the rice and so on, and then cook it again.

Furthermore, medicinal oils and so on cooked by others, where milk and so on are added along with medicines and cooked until the milk is exhausted, would also be 'limited to the time' (yāvakālika); but that too is not appropriate. This is because it was said 'he cooks it again and gives it' for the purpose of exhausting the curd and so on. Therefore, in the view of Elder Mahāsiva, without having remorse, it is allowable to cook fresh butter even if uncleaned, whether on that day or on subsequent days. It is also allowable to melt butter and so on mixed with rice and so on in the fire oneself, strain it, and cook it again so that the whey and so on are completely exhausted.
352:
In the case of ghee or top-oil mixed with rice and such, even if the yāvakālika (temporary food) substance with its mixed taste exists at the moment of cooking, because it is negligible (abbohārika), the decision should be made here that being 'accepted with its substance' (savatthukapaṭiggahita) or 'accepted on a previous day' (purepaṭiggahita) is also negligible. For this very reason, it is said: "By this much, it is not called accepted with its substance."

Specifically, if a monk or others cook medicinal oil by mixing ghee and such with āmisa (food) like milk that was accepted separately, it counts only as 'accepted with its substance' (savatthukapaṭiggahita). This is because the yāvakālika substance entered therein is not negligible. If one adds unaccepted milk and such to medicines accepted on a previous day and cooks medicinal oil, even if cooked by unordained persons, it becomes both 'accepted with its substance' and 'stored up' (sannidhi). This is because the milk and such added to that medicine accepted on a previous day becomes 'accepted on a previous day' due to the mixing of tastes at that moment. However, if the taste of āmisa (food) is evident in medicinal oil cooked by others or with only unaccepted medicines, it should be known as yāvakālika only. "Uggahitvā" means taking by oneself.

"Taken after straining" means taken after straining to remove rice and such, or taken after cooking again to remove whey and such. "With medicines kept after being accepted" means with medicines accepted for more than seven days. By this, it shows that even if mixed with those medicines, ghee and such do not count as being accepted for more than seven days. "Vaddalisamaya" means the rainy season, the time when there is no sun.

"Because of being produced" means because of being extracted from a yāvakālika substance (like sesame). By this, it shows that oil is not yāvakālika by nature, and it only becomes yāvakālika because of the monk's act of accepting it with its substance. "Both" refers to that made by oneself or by others.

"Pig fat" (acchavasa) is a marker for other bases of dukkaṭa (wrongdoing, such as tiger or snake fat); thus it is said, "excluding human fat." "Mixed" means strained. "Three dukkaṭas" refers to the three dukkaṭas occurring with every swallow. Although the Pali and the Commentary do not mention an offense for preliminary efforts such as accepting, cooking, or straining during the wrong time (after noon) for the purpose of consumption, an offense should indeed be recognized here. This is because of performing a forbidden act, just as there is an offense in accepting yāmakālika and such during the wrong time for the purpose of nourishment.

Since the dregs in medicinal oil cooked with milk and such are of the nature of āmisa (food), it is not proper for a monk to accept or cook the oil along with those dregs. Therefore, it is said, "He is as scrupulous as one is regarding the dregs of cooked oil." If it is not proper because it was cooked with fat, why is this [other case] proper? Asking thus, the disciples inquired, "Venerable Sir, if there are drops of curd or drops of whey in the ghee, is it proper?" Upatissa Thera, being extremely scrupulous (atikukkuccha), said, "This also is not proper."
353:
The disciples asked, "Venerable Sir... is it proper?" The Elder, due to being extremely scrupulous, said, "Friends, this (curd or whey drops) also is not proper." Later, reflecting that clear fat was allowed only for the purpose of suppressing illness, he accepted it, saying, "Very well."

"Bees called madhukarī"—some say these two terms are modifiers for both khuddakamakkhika (small bees) and bhamaramakkhika (large bees). Others say, "Bees that make hives on branches are called madhukarī-makkhikā; including them, there are three types of honey-bees." Bhamaramakkhikā are those that make large hives. "Like a sticky substance" means something that has become thick due to being dry or being cooked. The other kind is thin honey.

By the phrase "depending on sugarcane juice," it shows the seven-day limit (sattāhakālika) of sugarcane juice that has no dregs. This is because it is stated generally in the Pali as "produced from sugarcane." The statement in the Suttanta Commentary—"Sugarcane is yāvakālika; sugarcane juice is yāmakālika; treacle is sattāhakālika; the bark is yāvajīvaka"—should be understood as referring to the yāmakālika nature of sugarcane juice when mixed with mango juice and such. Or, it is said to be not authoritative because it is not a word of the Vinaya [Commentary]. For that very reason, it is said, "With unstrained sugarcane juice accepted in the morning," and so on. "Only that which is free of āmisa (food) is proper; the yāvakālika (sugarcane dregs) contained in that treacle is negligible"—this refers to the fact that when sugar-treacle is made, the sugarcane dregs present therein become yāvajīvaka (lifetime medicine) because they dry up through cooking. If those dregs remained yāvakālika, it would not be consumable even in the morning because of being cooked by oneself (sāmaṃpāka).

"Because of being accepted with its substance" refers to the sugarcane dregs that remain as fine powder in the sugarcane juice. By this, it shows that treacle made by laypeople or novices with unstrained, unaccepted sugarcane juice is proper for seven days. "Roasted sugarcane treacle" means treacle made by heating sugarcane in fire. "Pounded sugarcane treacle" means treacle made by cutting into small pieces, pounding, squeezing, and cooking.

Because the sugarcane dregs present therein give up their yāvakālika nature when cooked, it is said, "That is appropriate." "Made with cold water" means treacle made by kneading madhuka flowers with cold water, straining, and cooking. Some say it is made without kneading, but no reason is seen for saying so. "Khīrajallika" means milk froth. The passage beginning with "As for the madhuka flower..." is begun to show that although it exists in a yāvakālika form, it is a substance for the seeds of liquor (merayabīja) and is not proper.
354:
"Sabbānipi" means that although the five kinds [of medicine] such as ghee perform the function of nutriment, the commentator, wishing to show the medical indication (bhesajjodissa) to dispel the objection as to why these substances like ghee should be consumed in this way, spoke the words beginning with "Sattavidhaṃ hi" to show all seven indications together in connection with that medical indication. Because they are not ordinary medicines, they have an altered appearance; because they have great power to dispel snake venom and have a vast range, they are "great." Due to these two reasons—being altered and being great—they are called "Mahāvikaṭa." In the word "Upasampadādīni," the word "ādi" includes items such as multi-layered sandals.

"Adhiṭṭheti" means he generates the thought, "This is for external use (e.g., anointing the body)." It means that when the intention is for external use, he relinquishes the formal acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) because he no longer regards it as food to be consumed. In the same way, regarding other time-limited (kālika) items, because there is no desire to swallow and consume them, he relinquishes the formal acceptance when designating them for external use with a pure mind. It should be understood that this lack of regard for consumption is also a separate reason for relinquishing formal acceptance.

625. In the sentence "Sace dvinnaṃ... pe... na vaṭṭati," the Pali text was omitted. Here, the Pali should be understood as: "If an item belonging to two people has been formally accepted by one and not yet divided, even if seven days pass, there is no offense for either; however, it is not allowable to consume it." This is because if taken otherwise (as in the original), the use of the word "pana" would not be consistent. The Sāratthadīpanī states, "This same reading is shown in the Gaṇṭhipada as well." "No offense for either" is said because it has not been divided. "It is not allowable to consume" is said because of the statement "That which has been stored for more than seven days should [not] be consumed." By the Pali "Because it was relinquished by the one who accepted it," it is shown that "vissajjeti" (relinquishes) is said with reference to giving to a monk. In an object given to a monk without regard [for its return], although the formal acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) has not ceased, the status of being one's own property has ceased; therefore, a Nissaggiya offense does not occur. A Nissaggiya occurs only from the combination of these two factors: having accepted it oneself and it being one's own property; it does not occur from one factor alone. However, when giving to a layperson or a novice without regard, both factors (formal acceptance and ownership) are relinquished, and thus consumption is allowable. When giving while still having regard, it does not constitute a true gift (dāna), so both factors are not relinquished, and consumption is not allowable. In the Pali word "vissajjeti," it should be understood that discarding something without regard and without giving it to anyone is also included. The phrase "giving without regard" is also said only to show the manner in which formal acceptance is invalidated. This is because once formal acceptance is relinquished, if one accepts it again and consumes it, it will naturally be allowable; and that relinquishing of formal acceptance cannot happen without the renunciation of ownership of the object. Therefore, by this Pali "without regard," it is clear that if there is still regard for consuming the object, the relinquishing of formal acceptance cannot be obtained separately. Otherwise, if the relinquishing of formal acceptance could be obtained separately, it would have been said, "Having relinquished formal acceptance without regard, he accepts it again and consumes it."
355:
It should have been said, "Having relinquished formal acceptance without regard, he accepts it again and consumes it." By the phrase "due to not being formally accepted," it shows that even if one person's property is formally accepted by another, it becomes a Nissaggiya.

"Thus" refers to the reflection on relinquishing with a pure mind without the regard of "I will take it back." "To show that there is no offense for the one who consumes" means the intention is to show the absence of offenses such as Pācittiya which have Nissaggiya as their root.
