Here, "to show that there is no offense in consuming" means the intention is to show the absence of the Dukkaṭa offense mentioned regarding the physical use of an object that was relinquished and then received back. The three factors here are: the formal acceptance of ghee etc., it being one's own property, and the passing of seven days.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Medicines is Finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Rainy-Season Robe

In the fourth training rule, from the day after the full moon of Nayun... the phrase "the period for making" means the first half-month (the waning moon of Nayun) is also called the period for making. This is said by taking the meaning of the phrase "having made it, it should be worn" to mean that having made it in either the first half-month or the second half-month, it should be worn only in the second half-month (the waxing moon of Wāso). This is because the offense is taught only regarding the wearing. In the Mātikā Commentary, the statement "The last month of the hot season is the period for seeking; the last half-month is the period for making and wearing" is said by taking the meaning that it should be made and worn only when that half-month arrives. If the meaning is taken according to the method stated here, there is no contradiction.

"If the duty is neglected, a Dukkaṭa" is said with reference to donors who have never given a rainy-season robe before. Therefore, he said, "Those people..." etc. Donors who habitually give rainy-season robes are those who give every year without being invited by the Saṅgha or by oneself.

"He receives protection for six months" means that even during the Vassa, a rainy-season robe that is not yet completed receives protection until the last day of the rainy season. "One month" is said by counting together with the last Uposatha day of the cold season. In that...
356: That original robe should be made only on the Uposatha day (the last day of the winter season); otherwise (if not made on the full moon day of Phagguna), it results in a Nissaggiya offense. In the phrase "obtained and finished... one day, two days, etc.," it should be understood as: the rains-cloth obtained and finished one day before the day of entering the rains-residence (vassūpanāyikā), two days before... ten days before, or the rains-cloth obtained and finished during the rains. In this context, a rains-cloth obtained on the full moon day of the waxing fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī and finished on that very day through the completion of the dyeing process is called "obtained and finished one day before the day of entering the rains-residence." In this same manner, a cloth obtained and finished on the 6th day of the waxing fortnight of Āsāḷhī is called "obtained and finished ten days before the day of entering the rains-residence." A cloth obtained and finished up until the first full moon of Kattika is called "obtained and finished during the rains." As for a cloth obtained and finished after the first full moon of Kattika, the meaning is that one is permitted to keep it without determination (adhiṭṭhāna) as long as the robe-season (cīvarakāla) has not expired. Here, although it is stated generally that "it should be determined only within those ten days," for a rains-cloth obtained one or two days, etc., before the rains, one should only determine it upon reaching the period for determination, starting from the day of entering the rains-residence, without letting ten days pass from those initial days. However, a cloth finished more than ten days before entering the rains should not yet be determined, as it is not yet the proper time for determination. Such a cloth should be determined only on the day of entering the rains-residence; if dawn rises without it being determined, a Nissaggiya offense is incurred. If it is asked, "What is the purpose of the phrase 'ten days before' in such a case?"—it is said to show that a rains-cloth finished more than ten days before the rains should be determined only on the day of entering the rains-residence. Therefore, it was said: "A cloth finished more than ten days [before] should be determined on that very day (the day of entering the rains)." "If ten days are not enough, the robe-season should not be exceeded" means that when ten days are not sufficient within the three months of the rains, a rains-cloth obtained and finished from nine days before the full moon of Kattika (the 7th day of the waxing moon of Kattika) onwards should not exceed the robe-season. This is because it was taught, "When one month of the summer remains, the rains-cloth should be sought," thus stating the period for seeking, and "The rains-cloth should be determined for the four months of the rains."
357:
Because it is taught: "In the last month of the hot season, a rain-cloth should be sought," to show the period for seeking, and "A rain-cloth should be determined for the four months of the rainy season," it is established that neither a finished rain-cloth nor an unfinished rain-cloth should be left undetermined for a month. The reason is that an unfinished rain-cloth does not count as a "rain-cloth," and because the failure to finish it is due to some deficiency and not due to lack of respect; therefore, because it was not made for the four months, it receives protection (exemption). However, this meaning is obtained: a finished rain-cloth receives protection by the dasāhaparamasikkhāpada (ten-day rule) during the determination period, and an unfinished rain-cloth receives protection by the same rule during the robe-season.

"Why?" is a question asking for the reason based on one's own opinion. "Therefore" is because it is taught that the rain-cloth should be determined only during the rainy season. The sutta "ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ" is cited here to prove that other robes do not have such a time limit. Indeed, there is no other special purpose for that Pali here.

By the words of the Kurundī, such as "When should it be determined?", the view that "it is allowable to determine it whenever" is rejected, and it shows that a finished rain-cloth must be determined only within ten days.

In the Pali, in the words such as "acchinnacīvarဿ," the meaning should be understood as referring to a monk whose robes other than the rain-cloth were snatched by thieves, or a monk whose robes were lost. Indeed, for those monks, non-offense is stated only for the offense incurred by seeking or wearing at the wrong time. Therefore, it is said in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: "Thieves snatch the robes other than the rain-cloth, or they are lost; in such emergencies, there is no offense for the monk who wears them, nor for insane persons, etc." In this Samantapāsādikā commentary, however, this Nissaggiya non-offense is established by the Pali itself. Without showing this self-evident non-offense, the words "acchinnacīvarassa," etc., are stated to show the non-offense for the Dukkaṭa offense of a monk bathing naked, which is not self-evident. Indeed, this non-offense would not be established if it were not stated.

The state of the rain-cloth being intended for oneself, the state of seeking at the wrong time, and the obtaining of it—these three are the factors for the offense of seeking. As for the factors for the offense of wearing: the state of having other robes, the absence of emergency, the rain-cloth being one's own property, and wearing at the wrong time—these four are the factors.

## The Explanation of the Rain-cloth Training Rule is finished.
358: ## 5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Snatching Robes In the fifth training rule, regarding the Pali text "Yampi... pe... acchindi," the meaning should be applied as follows: The angry Upananda snatched it, saying, "Friend, I gave you this robe with the understanding that 'you would travel with me,' not for any other reason." "Ekā dukkaṭaṃ" means that if the monk who was commanded definitely snatches it, there is only a Pācittiya offense at the moment of the command. If he does not snatch it, then it should be understood as only a Dukkaṭa offense. "Ekavācāya sambahulā āpattiyo" means that if the commanded monk snatches it without any hindrance, many Pācittiya offenses are incurred at the moment of the command according to the number of objects, because the offense should be reached at the very moment of making the effort (payoga). The robe, however, becomes Nissaggiya only after it has been snatched. If that monk does not snatch it, it should be understood that there is only a single Dukkaṭa offense at the moment of the command. The same method should be understood in other similar training rules. By the phrase "upajjaṃ gaṇhissati," the giving of a robe to a novice (sāmaṇera) is shown. By that statement, it is shown that a Pācittiya offense is incurred even for a monk who snatches a robe that he gave while the recipient was a novice, after the recipient has become fully ordained. The statement "having personally given a robe to a monk" is said by way of the most prominent case. If the work is not yet done, it is said that "it is allowable to have it brought back" because it is similar to a wage. The five factors here are: it being a robe of at least the minimum size for assignment (vikappanā), being given personally, the perception of it being one's own, the recipient being fully ordained, and the snatching or causing to snatch out of anger. ## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Snatching Robes is finished. ## 6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Requesting Thread In the sixth training rule, the square wood on which they wind the woven thread is named "turī" (shuttle/spindle). When weaving, they insert the cross-thread and strike it with a beater to make the cloth thick; that beater is called a "vema" (loom-beater). By the words "In other cases, likewise a Dukkaṭa," it is shown that from the time the effort to weave begins, the Dukkaṭa offense occurs only when the aforementioned portion is finished, and no offense occurs during the efforts of weaving before that portion is completed.
359:
"Only the cloth still on the loom should be determined (adhiṭṭhāna)." In this statement, once it is determined, the cloth woven afterwards follows the status of the determined cloth; there is no need for further determination. However, if it is woven with fringes (dasā) in between so that there are separate sections, it should be understood that each section must be determined individually. In this training rule, if a monk takes allowable yarn and has it woven by an uninvited non-relative weaver who is unallowable, using indirect means such as "The yarn exists, but there is no one to weave it," there is no offense. For this reason, in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, the word "vāyāpeyya" is explained as "having it woven by an unallowable request, saying: 'Friends, weave a robe for me.'" A monk who speaks thus is said to have it woven by an unallowable weaver; if he speaks in any other way, he is not said to have it woven.

In the Pali passages such as "There is no offense in having a robe sewn," it means there is no offense under this specific training rule; however, they say that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to the improper request (viññatti). The three factors (aṅgas) here are: 1. The yarn is unallowable, 2. It is intended for oneself, 3. Having it woven by an unallowable weaver through an unallowable request.

## The Commentary on the Sutta-viññatti Training Rule ends.

## 7. Mahāpesakāra-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh training rule, the phrase "he gives something small" is merely to show the variety of effort (payoga); giving itself is not a factor in this rule. Therefore, in the Vibhaṅga of that rule, it is stated, "at the very least, he even preaches the Dhamma." The remaining words here are clear. The four factors (aṅgas) here are: 1. Approaching and making specifications to weavers who are not relatives and have not invited him, 2. The robe is intended for oneself, 3. Increasing the yarn because of his words, 4. Obtaining the robe.

## The Commentary on the Mahāpesakāra Training Rule ends.
360:
## 8. Accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, for a monk who has received a robe on the 6th day of the waxing moon of Assayuja, the dawn of the 11th day rises within the robe-season; thus, it is said, "saṭṭhito paṭṭhāya" and so forth. Because it is stated in that Pali text as "dasāhānāgataṃ" (ten days remaining), even if the dawn rises within the 10 days from the 5th day of the waxing moon until before the full moon day, that robe does not yet become forfeiture (nissaggiya). This training rule means that 11 days, including the full moon day, are obtained. It shows that all robes received from the 6th day of the waxing moon do not become forfeiture until the end of the robe-season, solely by the power of the first Kathina training rule.

Now, wishing to present the protection (parihāra) of various robes obtained through the first Kathina and other training rules collectively in this very training rule, it is said, "atirekacīvarassa" and so forth. The reading "1 month and 11 days if the Kathina is not spread, 5 months and 11 days if the Kathina is spread" alone accords with the Pali. Although some teachers say, "It should be 1 month and 10 days, 5 months and 10 days," that statement is not appropriate. This is because if it were so, it would have to be said as "navāhānāgataṃ" (nine days remaining). In the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, it is written: "In fact, although this meaning is already established by the training rule 'dasāhaparamāṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabbaṃ,' the training rule was established by showing the meaning as if it were new through a special occasion (aṭṭhuppatti)." This is merely a clerical error (pamādalikhita). The reason is that it is stated: "It shows the period for storing the robe received starting from the 5th day of the waxing moon of Assayuja." It should be understood that the teacher Venerable Buddhadatta also based his statement "The protection is 1 month and 10 days" etc., on this very clerical error.

"Accekacīvarasadise aññasmiṃ" means mistaking another robe—which is similar in terms of the time and manner of acquisition to an urgent robe that was previously determined (adhiṭṭhita)—for an urgent robe and letting the robe-season pass. Because of letting pass that which was already determined, the dukkaṭa offense and non-offense (anāpatti) are mentioned here. Otherwise (if it were a robe not determined), a pācittiya offense should occur in all three cases. It should be understood that for a monk who lets the robe-season pass even for a non-urgent robe, it is a pācittiya offense, just as in the urgent robe triad.

The four factors of this training rule are: (1) being one's own property, (2) being received 10 days before the full moon of Assayuja, (3) not being determined or shared (vikalpa), and (4) passing the robe-season. The Commentary on the Accekacīvara Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, a village is called "antaraghara" because there are houses at intervals. Therefore, it is said, "antogāme" (inside the village). Just as in the analysis (vibhaṅga) of the passage "paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati," the word "upasampajja" is extracted along with the niggahīta, so here too it is said, "upasampajjanti" and so forth. The word "vutthavassānaṃ" is also in the genitive case in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa). By this word, it is established that monks who have not spread the Kathina do not get the allowance to travel without taking their robes (asamādānacāra) even during the Kathina month.
361:
Being one's own property, being received before ten days have reached the full moon of Assayuja, not being determined or shared, and passing the robe-season—these four are the factors in this training rule.

The Commentary on the Accekacīvara Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

652-3. In the ninth training rule, a village is called "antaraghara" because there are houses at intervals in this place; therefore, it is said "inside the village" (antogāme). In the analysis of "paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati," the word "upasampajja" is extracted along with the niggahīta. Referring to that word, it is said "upasampajjantiādīsu viya." "Tassāpi" refers to the meaning of the word-analysis "vutthavassānaṃ." The word "vutthavassānaṃ" is also a word with the genitive case in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa). By this word "vutthavassānaṃ," it is established that monks who have not spread the Kathina do not get the allowance to travel without taking their robes (asamādānacāra) even during the Kathina month. If one were to get the allowance to travel without robes during the robe-season without spreading the Kathina, the robe training rule would be useless; thus it should be noted.

In the phrase "parikkhepārahaṭṭhānato," a stone's throw (leḍḍupāta) starting from the precinct (upacāra) of a house situated at the edge of a village is called an area suitable for an enclosure. In the Visuddhimagga also, it is said, "starting from the first stone's throw of a monastery without an enclosure." "Taṃ" refers to that first monastery and so forth. In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, however, it is stated that the precinct of the monastery should be excluded just like the precinct of a village, and the measurement should be taken between two stone's throws.

Because it is mentioned that "a certain monk in the city of Kosambī was ill," it is said "the Kosambaka-sammuti (agreement) is allowed." By this Pali "this monk has also gone to the west," it is allowable for a monk living in that monastery to remain separated from his robes for the entire robe-month, having deposited the robes inside the village. If there is business to go to a place other than that monastery, it is shown that staying separated from robes outside the monastery for six nights is allowed. Therefore, it is said "having come to the monastery, he should let the seventh dawn rise" and so forth. "Vasitvā" means having stayed (after letting the dawn rise). "Tattheva" means in that very place where he went. The factors in this training rule have already been stated in the Commentary.

## The Commentary on the Sāsaṅka Training Rule is finished.
362:
## 10. Pariṇatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, the phrase "ropitamālavacchato" refers to a flower bush planted by someone with a specific purpose. It is allowable to pick a withered flower that has not yet been picked and worship anywhere without restriction. "Ṭhitaṃ disvā" means seeing [someone] standing while holding the remaining gift-objects. In the phrase "yattha icchatha tattha detha," even if one says specifically "give to such-and-such a person," there is no fault because it was said "according to your wish." The three factors in this training rule are: (1) the state of being diverted toward the Saṅgha, (2) knowing that it is diverted and diverting it to oneself, and (3) receiving it.

## The Commentary on the Pariṇata Training Rule is finished.
